Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Winter said to the court "not one of them [Brand's accusers] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave".

Winter also asked the jury if they could be sure that out of the "many, many women" Brand had had sex with over a decade, "he raped just three of them".

Norris wrote in his letter to the BSB: "[The board] must send a strong signal to the profession on the harm arising from rape myths, and that the perpetuation of such myths within a court room is unacceptable, just as they are unacceptable in our society at large."

The charity Rape Crisis says it is "really common for people who experience rape, sexual assault, sexual abuse or other types of sexual violence to find they can't move or speak".

The judge presiding over Brand's case was praised by the Criminal Bar Association and campaign groups for comments he made during his sentencing remarks to dispel rape myths.

Mr Justice Bennathan told Southwark Crown Court: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

A spokesperson for the BSB said such cases "must be decided on the basis of the evidence and not prejudice", adding: "Any other approach may discourage others from coming forward and adversely affect public confidence in the criminal justice system more widely."

Kirsty Brimelow KC, chair of the Bar Council of England and Wales which is part of the group examining the need for further training, said it was important for the BSB to remain "independent of the government".

She told BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour that a "regulatory gap" had not been made clear to her and there were already powers to discipline barristers if breaches of the code of conduct happen.

She said training for "vulnerable witnesses" was already undertaken but it could be "problematic" if it was made mandatory.

Brimelow said there were currently a lack of barristers defending cases of rape and sexual assault and the possibility of further compulsory training could see more pushed out.

"What I wouldn't like to see is publicity around one case to take a life of its own rather than looking at what we already do," she told the BBC.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice said the justice secretary was "determined to make protections for victims as strong as possible".

"Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts, giving evidence in cases of this nature is a brave act and can be traumatic for victims: they must never feel as though they are the ones on trial," the spokesperson said.

"Independent judges are already able to, and do, give directions to counter rape myths but we always want to keep looking at ways we can improve how the entire justice system treats victims of sexual violence."

News.title: Women's criminal records wiped for abortion offences
News.content:
Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.

Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.

Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.

Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".

"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.

"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."

Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.

"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."

It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.

"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."

At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.

It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.

News.title: UK budget leaves NI underfunded, O'Dowd says
News.content:
Northern Ireland's public funding has worsened relative to rest of the UK as a result of the Westminster budget, Stormont's finance minister has claimed.

John O'Dowd said the Treasury's figures show that NI will now be funded below its objective "level of need" next year and the year after.

Needs-based funding recognises that it costs more to deliver public services in some parts of the UK compared to others.

The Secretary of State Chris Bryant has offered Â£1.5bn over the next three years and said if Stormont ministers accept this, that will take funding comfortably above the level of need.

O'Dowd said: "Treasury's own assessment shows that we are underfunded, relative to our current estimate of need, in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

"My officials' analysis also indicates that we are underfunded this year, and therefore in each year of the Spending Review."

It is understood O'Dowd believes that in cash terms this means public services will be underfunded by around Â£450m over the next three years.

It comes as executive ministers are due to hold further talks about the budget deadlock on Monday afternoon at Stormont Castle.

News.title: Police officers lied about searches connected to fatal crash, hearing told
News.content:
By the evening of Saturday, 3 March, the families of the three young women "were so worried that they decided to report them missing to Gwent Police", having been unable to contact them for hours and noting their lack of presence on social media

Ross's mother, Claire Ross, and Russon's father, Nathan Russon, went to Newport central police station to report their children missing.

The panel was told logs were created at this time which would help with subsequent enquiries.

During this time, Smith's mother, Emma Borg, had gone to the caravan the young people had travelled to and found her daughter's handbag there but no sign of the group.

Morley told the hearing that the "people in the caravan weren't particularly helpful", making Smith's mother realise that "something was very wrong".

Smith was eventually reported missing by her sister Lauren Doyle a couple of hours later, which included "sensitive information" adding overall to what was described as a "very worrying set of circumstances".

He added that the force also received "some concerning information about the men that was added to the system" which he said he would not read out in public.

The hearing was told that PC Hardwick and PC Livingstone were on a 16:00 to 03:00 shift and were given the "straightforward task of attending two home addresses to take any details from family members and to search".

Morley said this was something that "should always happen" during a missing person's enquiry and was "common sense" - allowing officers to assess whether the missing person might actually be at home, might have left something of importance behind like a note or might have taken something of importance.

The panel heard PC Livingstone had been assigned the search of Smith's house and PC Hardwick that of Russon's, but the two officers went to both addresses together and when they returned filled in the relevant paperwork.

PC Livingstone said she had first spoken to Smith's brother and then her mother.

In relation to the search, the following was written down: "Nothing missing out of the usual.

"Mum and Dad was concerned and Mum believed she went out in the same clothes and has not taken any new clothes with her."

That, the panel were told, was a "dishonest and misleading entry".

News.title: Prince and Princess of Wales arrive in India ahead of meeting with Modi
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have arrived in India for a three-day visit that will include a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The visit is the first time William and Catherine have been on an official overseas trip together in four years.

Her cancer treatment has limited the amount of international travel she has undertaken but she will be with her husband for several engagements this week.

Most are related to the Earthshot Prize, founded by Prince William, which awards five Â£1m prizes for the best solutions to the biggest climate challenges.

"The princess is enormously proud of what the prince has achieved with Earthshot and is really looking forward to being alongside him for what is one of the most important moments in his year," said a spokesperson for the royals.

"She's seen it develop into something truly remarkable and is excited to experience first-hand just how far it has come."

News.title: Miliband says he won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field
News.content:
Appearing on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Miliband was reminded that in 2023 he said the project would be a "colossal waste of taxpayer money and climate vandalism", external.

Asked if it could be assumed he would resign if his successor decided to develop Rosebank, Miliband replied: "No, definitely not because I obey collective responsibility.

"Miatta Fahnbulleh will make the decision on this. As you know, it's what they call a quasi-judicial decision so she looks at all the evidence and then reaches a conclusion."

Miliband said he would not "second guess her decision" on Rosebank.

He added he supported the energy secretary recently giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field after years of uncertainty and a court case.

Pressed further about his previous remarks on Rosebank, Miliband said: "I'm a member of the government and I will abide by collective responsibility on this."

He went on to say there are "direct and very bad impacts at home" for the cost of living linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the Iran conflict.

Miliband added: "What does that teach us? That we can't get economic and energy security from fossil fuels, we've got to keep on with this transition to wind power, solar power, nuclear power; homegrown clean energy we can control."

Catherine Fookes is among a group of Labour MPs, reported to number at least 75, who have signed a letter opposing Rosebank.

The MP for Monmouthshire told Today: "We need to really look at what we're doing and ensure we don't exacerbate our climate challenges and make climate change worse.

"And that's exactly what drilling in the North Sea would do."

Steve Yemm, Labour MP for Mansfield, offered his support to Rosebank and said it would be a "test of whether, as a country, we can support investment and skilled work in the North Sea whilst meeting our climate obligations".

One Labour MP, who is pro Rosebank, said they were increasingly confident the decision would go their way, but added the "gloves will now come off" after Fookes's intervention.

They said people on both sides of the argument had been attempting to avoid so-called "red on red" clashes but predicted Labour MPs would now start to disagree more forcefully in public about the issue.

The same MP accused Miliband of "running two departments" and said the current group of energy ministers were "all his people" and "all coming from the same place".

They said they were becoming increasingly frustrated with Labour MPs who opposed Rosebank and added "Trump is right, we do need to open the North Sea".

Some people in Parliament believe that a decision on the oil field could be made as soon as the end of this month.

News.title: David Chadwick confirmed as new leader of Welsh Lib Dems
News.content:
In his first speech as leader at St David's Hotel in Cardiff, he admitted the party had lost ground in communities where they had previously seen success.

"This year's Senedd elections showed how much work remains to be done. But we should never confuse our recent electoral results with the limits of what we can achieve," he said.

"I want us to rediscover the ambition of a party that competed for parliamentary seats across Wales, led cities like Cardiff, Wrexham and Swansea, and was a serious force in communities from north to south."

Chadwick, who was elected as an MP in 2024, told the audience in Cardiff that becoming the party's leader in Wales was not something he could have imagined 10 years ago.

It was around then he had survived a near fatal car crash and developed a rare illness that had left him completely paralysed.

"I went from being a healthy, independent young man, travelling the world and planning my future, to being entirely dependent on others. It changed my life," he said.

"It taught me how quickly any of us can find ourselves needing help, and how much our futures can depend on the care and support available to us."

News.title: 'Incredibly special' - William reveals his favourite view from first home with Catherine
News.content:
The Prince of Wales has named the view from his former home on Anglesey as his favourite view in Britain.

In a guest edition of Country Life magazine, Prince William recalled living in Bodowen Farmhouse, on the Bodorgan Estate in north Wales, soon after he and Catherine, Princess of Wales, were first married.

The prince reminisced about the view of Newborough Forest, the beach and Llanddwyn Island from the farmhouse - the first home of their elder son, Prince George - describing running along the beach and the "magical" landscape.

As guest editor, he also took the opportunity to talk about the importance of protecting women in the armed forces and shared his "fanatical" support for Aston Villa.

In the magazine's column, Prince William said the view from his former home on Anglesey was "incredibly special to me", reminding him of the early days of family life with Catherine and George, and when he worked full-time as a Search and Rescue pilot based at RAF Valley, near Holyhead.

"I loved the job and I loved flying across this kind of landscape," he wrote.

News.title: Tourette's film I Swear wins three Scottish Baftas
News.content:
I Swear's director, Kirk Jones, thanked the town of Galashiels and Tourette's groups in Scotland for supporting the film as he picked up the first of three awards.

He also paid tribute to John Davidson for sharing his story.

"I know it's been a long and difficult journey," he said. "Thank you for having the strength to continue that journey and for stressing the importance of acceptance and empathy at a time when the world desperately needs it."

He added: "My big hope was that it would help people understand those with Tourette's.

"What I didn't realise was that there's a much wider community of people with neurodiverse conditions who have connected with the film and feel for the first time there's a representation of a condition which is often hidden."

For Davidson, Sunday's wins are the celebration he was hoping for at the Baftas earlier this year.

"Tonight's not really about me, although it is my story," he said.

"It's about celebrating the actors and a beautiful film. I was blown away when I first saw it. I've never watched it since because it makes me cry.

"So I'm chuffed to bits that it's won tonight."

News.title: Tributes as wife and daughter of DUP chairman die hours apart
News.content:
Sympathies have been expressed to a senior Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) politician following the death of his wife and daughter within hours of each other.

The party said Lord Morrow, who is chairman of the DUP, lost his wife Lady Jennifer Morrow and their daughter Rachel Burrows at the weekend.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that "words cannot adequately express the heartbreak and sorrow felt across our party".

"There are no words that can ease the pain of such an unimaginable loss," he added.

Lord Morrow is a former Stormont minister and a former assembly member for the Fermanagh and South Tyrone constituency.

A funeral notice for his daughter Rachel said she was a married mother of two children. It said she died on Sunday "peacefully surrounded by her loving family".

Robinson added that Lord Morrow's wife and daughter died "within hours of each other" on Sunday.

"On behalf of the Democratic Unionist Party, I extend our deepest sympathy to Maurice, to Rachel's husband John, and to the entire Morrow and Burrows families at this most difficult of times," he said.

"Maurice Morrow has been a rock of strength and support to so many of us through difficult moments in our lives. Now, in his darkest hour, it is our turn to be a rock for him.

"Throughout Jennifer and Rachel's long battles, Maurice has demonstrated extraordinary love and strength."

Speaking at Stormont, Robinson said the last couple of weeks for Lord Morrow would "have been incredibly difficult".

"But to lose your daughter and know how gravely ill your wife is, and to lose your wife some four hours later yesterday, is a deep personal shock and tragedy for him, for his surviving daughter Victoria, for Rachel's husband John and their two children, and for the wider Morrow and Burrows family."

Robinson said that as party chairman for the last 26 years, Lord Morrow has been "steadfast and fundamental to the foundations of the DUP".

"The commitment that runs through us runs through Maurice, and so this time all of us are here as colleagues to pay tribute to Maurice, to offer him comfort and prayers," he added.

Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister also extended his sympathies to Lord Morrow and expressed "sincere Christian condolences".

First Minister Michelle O'Neill also expressed her sympathies to Lord Morrow and his family "at this horrendous time for them".

"Such a tragedy to be visited upon any family. I can't imagine what they're going through," the Sinn FÃ©in vice-president told reporters at Stormont.

News.title: The moment that galvanised England to deliver major statement against Spain
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Spain vs England was a game that had almost everything, and may yet mean more; perhaps the most significant moment might have come before it had even started.

The hosts took the opportunity of a first match back in Madrid since the World Cup to showcase the trophy, in what almost felt another homecoming.

The mood was very much of revelling in their embossed status, something that would have had a particular edge for this specific nation.

No country that has won the World Cup has waited as long for another trophy as England.

And, as the 2010 winners Iker Casillas, Fernando Torres and Fernando Llorente presented Unai Simon that with that precious piece of brilliant gold, it was almost literally in England’s faces.

Thomas Tuchel’s side had to watch the goalkeeper wave the World Cup about right in front of them.

It had been noted on the Spanish side that Jude Bellingham was the only player who clapped, this now being the city that he calls home with Real Madrid. He then played like he was demanding the same appreciation, and he was not the only one.

As one figure with knowledge of the England camp said: “They will have been thinking ‘that’s what we want’.”

Seeing the World Cup so close and yet so far, with more than three years until the next edition, only deepened a mood that had been felt in the build-up to this game.

open image in gallery England celebrate against Spain in the Nations League ( Getty )

England, in the words of both Declan Rice and Thomas Tuchel, knew they were going to win.

“I could feel the true belief in the dressing room before the match that this is exactly the moment where we want to prove ourselves and push our limits,” the manager said.

They had that conviction to show what they were really about, and to show they would be the only team in the world not cowed by Spain. It was that mentality that comes when you feel ready to beat a rival that has long had it over you; that has been a benchmark.

A pace was set just moments after seeing that trophy, as a ferocious England subjected Simon to a flurry.

Just as importantly, they displayed a new level of their own, even beyond Tuchel describing it as the best performance of his time.

This wasn’t, after all, the usual counter-attacking approach to playing Spain - at least not for when England actually got so far ahead.

It was England imposing their game, an evolving ideology, on Spain.

open image in gallery England manager Thomas Tuchel celebrates after the win over Spain ( PA Wire )

“We are well aware which steps we took after the World Cup,” Tuchel said, conspicuously repeating this more than once.

The manager was deeply stung after all the criticism following the Argentina defeat.

And yet, much as he might bristle about it in public, it does feel as if some of that criticism has been acknowledged.

England look much more technical, but still with pace.

Throughout the World Cup, after all, there was a definite sense of his team just seeking to force their way through.

This was something much more considered and coherent.

“We wanted to get better in the deep build-up, we wanted to get better at defending in a low block and on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play on every opponent,” Tuchel remarked.

This similarly feeds into another theme of the night, which was how James Trafford’s performance may start a path that sees him become England’s No 1.

It was conspicuous that, when asked about the goalkeeper’s brilliant late double-save, Tuchel immediately pointed to his pure football effect.

“But there was a lot to do in the deep build-up as well, to overcome the first line of press, which he did very well with everyone around him,” he said. “So there was a lot to do, never lose the concentration, never lose the focus, never lose the vision, to find the free man to overcome the press and put the game into the opponent’s half.”

Tuchel clearly wants to change the very focus of this team.

open image in gallery Jude Bellingham and Thomas Tuchel embrace after England's win in Spain ( Getty )

And, in doing so, he wants to change its entire outlook.

There was naturally a lot of talk about “confidence” after a victory like this, which Tuchel was only too happy to immerse himself in.

“You want confidence, not only through results but confidence through performance and the result follows,” Tuchel said. “That’s the ideal process and that’s what we got.”

That’s also what goes much deeper.

When Spain beat France in the World Cup semi-final with what was the performance of the tournament - “the statement performance” as Tuchel would have it - some close to Didier Deschamps’s squad felt the reason for the win had actually come much earlier.

Spain had beaten France in a series of high-profile games, above all the Euro 2024 and World Cup 2026 semi-finals. Lamine Yamal had been right to emphasise that, because he knew it played on French minds.

It gave Spain an edge. They knew they could beat France, but France were unsure if they could beat Spain.

That’s also why the frantic ending to this game in Madrid, so at odds with the first hour, may have been so important.

Had Spain equalised, or potentially won, England would have just been another team to fail to beat them. It could similarly have been the deepening of England’s own complex about Spain, since this would have been three high-profile set-backs in succession.

Even if this had just been a draw, after all, it would have felt like a defeat given it was a 3-0 lead.

But it wasn’t a draw.

open image in gallery Spain's Unai Simon displays the World Cup trophy at the Metropolitano ( Reuters )

It was a win, and a first defeat that Spain have endured in 44 games over two and a half years.

As such, England are not just another team the Spanish are reigning over.

They’re a team that know how to beat them, that can carry that through to a home Euros.

It might even create a bit of consideration on the Spanish side, even allowing for how assured they are in their own approach.

It might be the beginning of a proper modern rivalry.

Might, of course. England have to go and use this to do what Spain have made customary, and actually win one of those trophies.

News.title: Thomas Frank appointed Crystal Palace manager after nightmare Tottenham reign
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Thomas Frank has been appointed as Crystal Palace's new head coach to replace Pierre Sage.

Sage was dismissed last week with Palace rooted to the bottom of the Premier League table, and Frank has now been brought in with the aim of turning the club’s fortunes around.

Frank, who has signed a deal until 2029, will take charge of his first match when Palace travel to Coventry on Saturday.

His return to English management follows a bruising eight-month spell in charge of Tottenham, which came after a successful seven years at Brentford.

Frank said on the Palace website: “It’s an honour to sit here and be in charge of this fantastic football club. I’m really, really looking forward to it.”

Sage’s Palace tenure proved a short one as he oversaw just two wins in 10 league fixtures.

open image in gallery Pierre Sage was sacked last week ( Reuters )

The French coach had taken over in the summer from Oliver Glasner, who departed following a trophy-laden tenure at Selhurst Park that saw the Eagles win the FA Cup and Conference League.

But Sage immediately encountered problems after his own successful spell at Lens. He watched key Palace defenders Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Munoz depart, and the club lost three of its first four league fixtures.

Palace did progress into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals under Sage, but one win in the Europa League and seven defeats in 10 Premier League matches led chairman Steve Parish to move him on.

Frank was identified as the best fit to lead Palace away from a potential relegation battle, having masterminded multiple successful survival bids at Brentford.

The 53-year-old guided the Bees to top-flight promotion in 2021. They then impressively stabilised in the Premier League despite a minimal budget in comparison to divisional rivals.

Frank's chance to succeed in a different setting at Tottenham, though, turned into a nightmare despite a strong start in north London.

Amid growing fan discontent and a run of two wins in 17 league fixtures, he was sacked on 11 February.

He holds the worst win record of any permanent Spurs manager in the Premier League, but will aim to flourish at Palace.

News.title: This city could be Europe’s most underrated Christmas destination
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Those looking for a winter escape this festive season might flock to Christmas markets in Germany or Vienna, Finland’s snowy forests, or even head to Lapland to visit Santa Claus.

However, the Baltics are home to an underrated festive destination with a fairytale old town, delicious food, and a Christmas market packed with mulled wine and festive treats.

Tallinn, the capital of Estonia, has everything travellers could want from a festive destination. Its historic Town Hall Square is home to a charming Christmas market centred around a towering Christmas tree that has stood on the site since 1441 and, according to recent research from Rome2Rio, Tallinn is the European Christmas market city most likely to see snow this season.

From mulled wine to carousels, chalet-style stalls selling handicrafts, festive Estonian cuisine and (fingers tightly crossed) snow, Tallinn is the perfect place to get into the festive spirit without braving the crowds at larger, more popular markets elsewhere in Europe.

open image in gallery Rachael stands in front of the Christmas tree, which has stood in Tallinn’s Town Hall Square since 1441 ( Rachael Davis/PA )

After visiting the market, I found myself perfectly placed to explore the city’s Old Town – a Unesco World Heritage Site known as one of Northern Europe’s best-preserved medieval cities.

With buildings still standing from as far back as the 13th century, the Old Town has survived countless wars, Nazi and Soviet occupation, and air strikes, retaining its original city plan and towering city walls.

At just under half a square mile, the Old Town is compact and easily walkable – but make no mistake, there’s more than a day’s worth of activities here.

Attractions include Town Hall Square, dominated by the Gothic Town Hall, and the Alexander Nevsky Orthodox Cathedral, built between 1894 and 1900, when Estonia was part of the Russian Empire.

There are also several impressive viewpoints, including at Patkuli, Kohtuotsa and the city walls and cannon towers.

When it’s time for refreshments, a visit to Maiasmokk – the city’s oldest cafe, which opened in 1864 – is worth making, even if just to marvel at the incredible handmade marzipan treats.

open image in gallery Central Market in Tallinn during the festive period ( Getty Images )

A short walk from Town Hall Square is Rataskaevu 16, a cosy restaurant known for its delicious homemade malted brown bread, fresh from the oven.

Also highly rated is Pegasus, a trendy Art Deco-ish cafe-restaurant which was designed for the Estonian Writers’ Union, making it an important centre of literary and art culture since its opening in 1962.

From its Nordic-inspired menu, I enjoyed the pan-seared pike-perch fillet with chorizo-potato cream, but other highlights included roasted calf’s liver with cured beetroot and slow-cooked duck leg.

open image in gallery Tallinn is full of beautiful streets to explore ( Rachael Davis/PA )

Beyond the compact Old Town, in the trendy Telliskivi district, is the Fotografiska museum, a contemporary photography gallery with locations worldwide, including Stockholm, New York, and Shanghai.

Walking around Tallinn, it’s easy to forget the city’s tumultuous history, especially the most recent Soviet occupation of Estonia from 1944 to 1991.

Those interested in learning more about the impact of Soviet rule on the country can pay a visit to the KGB Prison Cells at Pagari 1 – an apartment building that was transformed into a brutal prison for those under interrogation by the KGB.

open image in gallery Tallinn’s trendy Telliskivi district ( Rachael Davis/PA )

There’s also the Vabamu Museum of Occupations and Freedom, which has a permanent exhibition introducing Estonia’s history during and after the Soviet and Nazi occupations.

If you’re seeking a wellness hit, Estonia has a deeply ingrained sauna culture, and one of the best places in the city to enjoy an invigorating sauna is Iglupark. Located on the coast to the north of the city, visitors can enjoy a sauna experience with sea views over Tallinn Bay.

From history to culture, food and drink to festive spirit, Tallinn has the perfect combination for a winter city escape – an ideal way to get in the Christmas spirit.

Rachael Davis was hosted by Accor for this trip.

How to get there

Several airlines fly to Tallinn from Stansted, Luton, Gatwick, Manchester, Leeds Bradford, and Edinburgh. The flight time is two hours and 45 minutes and costs from £24 one way without bags.

Where to stay

After a day of exploring the city, a perfect location for a good night’s rest is the ibis Styles Tallinn. Located just a few minutes’ walk from the city walls, and around a 15 to 20-minute walk from the Old Town proper, it’s a stone’s throw from the charming cobbled streets – ideal for city breaks where visitors want to be moments away from the action.

Those looking for a more upscale hotel could try the Mövenpick Hotel Tallinn, where some of the rooms even come with their own sauna.

This piece was first published in December 2025 and has been revised and updated.

News.title: Trump administration delayed Medicaid work requirements for six months — here’s what that means for you
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Trump administration is giving states the option to delay Medicaid changes that would have left as many as 10.1 million people uninsured.

The controversial Medicaid changes, which require applicants to provide proof of work to receive benefits, were set to kick in on January 1, but states now have the option to delay disenrollment through July 1, 2027, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

“This disenrollment delay is a small step in the right direction, but it does not avert the disaster ahead,” Democratic Senator Ron Wyden and Democratic Senator Ron Wyden and Democratic Representative Frank Pallone said in a statement about the delay.

“We are preparing to lead a relentless fight to preserve Medicaid coverage and care for every eligible person.”

For the average recipient of Medicaid, a state-run program that provides low- or no-cost medical services and treatments for low-income individuals, those in states that use the delay can have more time to find qualifying employment without losing coverage.

States now have the option to delay federal Medicaid enforcement rules, a move with the potential to impact millions of program recipients ( Getty )

The act includes new Medicaid rules that require applicants to prove they work at least 80 hours a month or earn at least $580 monthly to receive benefits, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

Between 4.9 and 10.1 million people will lose Medicaid coverage in 2028 because of the changes, according to estimates from the philanthropy Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.

“Researchers find that between 19 percent and 37 percent of people who already work will nevertheless lose Medicaid coverage, including some who are meeting the work requirement but would face challenges documenting their work activity,” the foundation said.

Another 2 to 3.1 million will lose their Medicaid coverage because of more frequent eligibility checks that the OBBA demands, the foundation said.

“Millions of people's health care is at risk because of the Republican reconciliation law’s work requirement, as states scramble to implement on a rushed timeline & respond to shifting federal requirements,” Sarah Lueck, vice president for health policy at the research and policy institute Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, posted to X Friday.

“Today’s news lets states delay the harm.”

News.title: Elon Musk delivers five-word verdict on Jeremy Culhane’s SNL impression
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Elon Musk is not impressed by Saturday Night Live’s take on him.

The world’s wealthiest person, 55, has been impersonated on the sketch show in recent episodes by comedian Jeremy Culhane. Musk was previously portrayed on the show in 2025 by Wayne’s World star Mike Myers, and in 2024 by Myers’ co-star in the hit film, Dana Carvey.

Culhane, who plays Musk as an idiotic manchild who is desperate to be found funny, appeared last week during the show’s Weekend Update segment and reappeared during this week’s cold open as part of a group of tech moguls gathering in the wake of revelations about Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

In real life, Musk has backed calls to restore Huang as boss of chip giant Nvidia.

Musk responded to a post on X, the social media platform he purchased in 2022, rating Culhane’s impression of him a 5 out of 10 and saying: “They need to try harder.”

The real Elon Musk, and as portrayed by Jeremy Culhane on 'Saturday Night Live' ( Getty/NBC )

In 2024, former SNL star Chloe Fineman claimed that Musk made her cry when he hosted the show.

The Tesla founder divided SNL viewers with his “surreal” hosting stint in May 2021, an appearance that led to criticism from some of the show’s cast due to Musk’s controversial views.

Fineman shared her alleged experience with Musk when the billionaire spoke out against the sketch show after he was mocked during a segment about Donald Trump.

In a since-deleted TikTok post, Fineman wrote: “OK, I just saw some news article about Elon Musk being like butt-hurt about SNL and his impression, but I’m, like, you’re clearly watching the show. Like, what are you talking about?”

“And I’m like, you know what? I’m gonna come out and say at long last that I’m the cast member that he made cry. And he’s the host that made someone cry. Maybe there’s others.”

She continued: “But I’m like, no, if you’re gonna go on your platform and be rude, like, guess what? You made I, Chloe Fineman, burst into tears because I stayed up all night writing the sketch.

“I was so excited, I came in, I asked if you had any questions and you stared at me like you were firing me from Tesla and were like, ‘It’s not funny.’ I waited for you to be like, ‘Ha ha, joke.’ No. Then you started pawing through my script, like flipping each page, being, like, ‘I didn’t laugh once, not one time.’”

Fineman said she ended up having a “really good time” performing the sketch, adding: “I thought you were really funny in it. But, you know, have a little manners here, sir.”

News.title: How the James Bond casting race got turned upside down at the 11th hour
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

At 3pm on Monday 16 November, after years of feverish speculation over who would don the tux to play the new James Bond, his identity was finally revealed. This time, there was no excruciating press conference featuring a speedboat and an awkward man in a life vest (Daniel Craig later called this unveiling a “train wreck”), nor was there any signed of a coiffed actor, posing with a chunky cigar on the roof of the Dorchester (ahem, Roger Moore). Instead, the grand reveal was made to the world in that most modern of ways: on, er, Instagram.

The announcement video, which had 688,000 likes and counting just two hours on, opens with a scene of black, inky nothingness. As the unmistakable Bond riff plays out, a hand begins to emerge from the darkness, gripping a shining pistol. The tip of a shirt sleeve appears as our new Bond gradually comes into view, then the dark, silky arm of a suit jacket, and at last, the steely, staring face of none other than Robert Pattinson.

When it came to the never-ending Bond rumour mill, Pattinson – the magnetic star of Twilight, The Drama, and, of course, the Batman films – was hardly a name on anybody’s lips before last week. For months, the main actors touted for the biggest role in cinema had been Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, Josh O’Connor and Nicholas Hoult. We watched like hawks as they squirmed and flip-flopped their way through recent interviews. “I genuinely know nothing. I just find it quite amusing,” Turner insisted to The Hollywood Reporter, avoiding eye contact and peering down at his feet. “It’s all very flattering...” Lowden told GQ.

But none of them seemed to quite fit. They didn’t have quite the right hair, or enough gravitas, or they’d been a bit cringe in a recent flop. It was speculated, too, that the Bond team weren’t quite impressed enough with any of the contenders they’d been testing. Perhaps it was inevitable, then, that incredibly late in the game, reports began to emerge from film insiders that Pattinson had entered the race. It was speculated that he was the favourite, as he had reportedly been offered a more attractive deal than his fellow auditionees. Sources claimed he had been asked to 

Many thought Pattinson as 007 was too good to be true, and that he was too famous, and possibly too old (early reports had said filmmakers were looking for a thirtysomething to take the role; Pattinson is 40). And besides, can one man really be both Batman and Bond?

First look at Pattinson as 007 ( Jaap Buitendijk )

On Monday morning, excitable messages were shooting back and forth between the phones of journalists across the world. There were rumours the announcement was imminent. We heard that writers at one newspaper were furiously updating their pre-prepared announcement stories, comment pieces and profiles. We sharpened our pencils, too. It’s been a bleak few weeks reporting in the world of culture – finally, we were going to get to report on something fun. Something that could unite us, but around a more wholly positive story.

At the same time, many didn’t believe that the announcement could really be coming today. Surely there would be a press conference of some kind, or a series of teasers at least, preparing us all for the big moment? But no, all of a sudden the announcement was plonked, with little to no fanfare, on Instagram and X. (Mercifully, not from Jeff Bezos’s own accounts: back when Amazon first took the reins on the franchise, he drew ire when he tweeted to the masses: “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?”)

Details are scant at the moment of the exact process behind this casting, but what we do know for sure is that Pattinson’s selection comes hot on the heels of a series of October screen tests by Dune director Denis Villeneuve, casting director Nina Gold and Amazon executives. The new film has been written by Peaky Blinders’ Steven Knight. It still remains to be seen what kind of Bond Pattinson will be. One agonising wait is over, now another begins.

News.title: Is Germany v Netherlands on TV? How to watch Nations League group decider
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Germany face Netherlands as the rivals vie for top spot in their Nations League group.

Jurgen Klopp’s side earned a 1-1 draw against the Netherlands in Amsterdam in his first game in charge of Germany last month.

But it is Xavi Hernandez’s Dutch side who are in control of Group A2, sitting on 11 points after thrashing Greece 7-0 last time out.

Germany are three points behind the Netherlands in third place, which means they need to win to overtake the Dutch into top spot.

A Greece victory over pointless Serbia combined with a Germany victory, however, would mean all three sides finish the group on 11 points.

With the Netherlands needing to avoid defeat to guarantee top, and Germany at risk of missing on the Finals altogether, here’s everything you need to know.

Is Germany v Netherlands on TV?

The Nations League clash is available to watch on Amazon Prime pay-per-view, at a cost of £2.49. Coverage begins at 7:35pm GMT, with kick-off at 7:45pm.

When is the Nations League 2026/27 knockout stage and play-off draw?

The draw will take place at 11am GMT on Friday 20 November.

When are the Nations League 2026/27 quarter-finals?

England will feature in the last eight of the Nations League 2026/27, with a two-legged tie to decide who will play in the semi-finals and final, both to be played across a ‘finals’ week.

As well as the Nations League quarter-finals, the League A/B and League B/C promotion/relegation play-offs will be drawn, set to be held in March 2027. The final tournament is scheduled to take place across 9–13 June 2027.

Who could England play next?

England's potential opponents in the last eight of the Uefa Nations League as things stand are Belgium, Greece or Denmark.

Beating Spain ensured the Three Lions will face a second-placed team in their quarter-final; Belgium have finished second in their group, while Greece could be pipped by Germany and Denmark could still be replaced by either Norway or Portugal. England topping the group also means they will play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

News.title: Trump says Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia ‘certainly isn’t a bad idea’ as he downplays Chinese spy allegation
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump said Monday that he would welcome the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia - days after the chipmaker's co-founder was forced out over an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman - and insisted that no one had proven the woman was a spy.

"There's a big group of people that would like him to return," Trump told reporters as he left the White House to travel to Asia ahead of his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin later this week.

“I think having Jensen go back, a lot of people are asking Jensen. They think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea. I recommended Tim Cook, who, as you know, built Apple, I recommended Tim Cook to go and do a job,” Trump continued.

Huang resigned last week after acknowledging an affair with Alice Huang — no relation — a businesswoman that U.S. officials have described as a suspected asset of China's Ministry of State Security.

The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined she had been recruited by the spy agency and tasked with influencing Huang to push Nvidia toward selling Beijing more of its advanced chips. The Times also reported Jensen Huang’s second affair, with a Nvidia subordinate, moved the company’s board to force him out last week.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump talks to reporters while departing the White House November 16, 2026 in Washington, D.C. Trump is traveling to the Philippines and then to China later in the week ( Getty )

In the days since, allies of the former Nvidia boss have been attempting to rally support for his return with an online petition that has thus far garnered more than 100,000 signatures, including from Nvidia shareholders and employees.

Tesla and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the founder and chief executive of the video game publisher Epic Games, were among major industry figures supporting an open letter calling for his return.

Pressed repeatedly on whether he accepted the U.S. intelligence on Alice Huang, Trump questioned it.

"I don't know that she's a spy at all. Nobody's proven that," he said. "He probably shouldn't have been doing, on a personal basis, what he did. You know, from — who knows? That's a different story. But nobody's proven that she's a spy. She may not be a spy."

Trump earlier offered a broader version of the same claim. "Usually what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Trump said. "I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."

Asked whether he trusted the U.S. intelligence that the woman was a Chinese agent, and whether Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him so, Trump said he had not heard it.

"Who told me that? ... I haven't heard that. I haven't heard that," he said. "No, I don't know that she is a spy."

open image in gallery Alice Huang (left) is thought to have ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. She is pictured with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at an event in Taipei, Taiwan in June 2024 ( Reuters )

The president’s claims do not square exactly with what is publicly known about U.S. officials’ concerns over the affair.

According to The New York Times, Rubio was so alarmed by what intelligence officials were learning about Alice Huang through electronic surveillance that he drafted a classified memorandum on her alleged recruitment and briefed Trump on it aboard Air Force One in May, en route to China.

But Trump brushed aside warnings from Rubio and nonetheless pressed ahead with a relationship that saw Huang become a frequent White House visitor after donating $25 million to the president's ballroom project.

The president defended the decision to keep selling chips to China and brushed aside the suggestion that his closeness to Huang had endangered national security. "It was not put at risk," he said Monday, before pivoting to a claim that the country "is now stronger than ever before."

Trump also dismissed statements from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC last week that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick resisted putting Megaspeed - a China-linked company run by Alice Huang and thought to be a pass-through to help Beijing evade export controls - on his department’s “Entity List” of firms not allowed to purchase American products.

Asked about that, Trump said Lutnick "might have delayed it, but he was doing that because ... you could have a blowup with China."

"One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China. Different views," Trump said, declining to say whether he would replace Lutnick, who is traveling with him to China aboard Air Force One despite the scandal surrounding him and is scheduled to testify on the Nvidia affair before Congress in the next few weeks.

Huang was barred from selling Nvidia's most advanced processors, including its Blackwell line, to China, a restriction Trump defended while playing down its stakes.

"The only thing he was able to sell to China were chips that were sort of obsolete, a little bit like our avionics," Trump said. "Selling the other chips is a good thing, not a bad thing."

The president said he might raise the alleged spying operation with Chinese President Xi Jinping when the two leaders meet on Thursday but would not commit to doing so when pressed by reporters.

"I'll ask him what I want to ask him," he said.

Sports.title: Analysing this season’s Champions League minutes for Dream Team’s most popular players
Sports.content:
Next

MOST Dream Team managers know how important it is to target the European fixtures.

Clubs active in the Champions League, Europa League or Conference League have a lot more point-scoring opportunities than those limited to domestic commitments.

The very best gaffers squeeze the schedule for all it’s worth and this requires a certain degree of analysis.



It’s all well and good stacking your XI with players who have regular double Gameweeks but if they aren’t getting enough minutes on the pitch then corrective action may be required.



With that in mind, let’s analyse the Champions League playing time for each of the five English clubs competing this season.

Arsenal

David Raya, Declan Rice and Gabriel have played every minute in the Champions League so far, a reflection of their deserved reputations as the first names on the Gunners’ team sheet.

Ezri Konsa would have joined them had he not limped off after an hour against Slavia Prague in Gameweek 9 and it will be interesting to see whether the England centre-back continues as a guaranteed starter after the break now that William Saliba has regained fitness.



Ben White and Jurrien Timber have split right-back duties evenly so far with the former getting the nod for Napoli and Slavia Prague while the Dutchman was selected against Lille and Bayern Munich.

Mikel Arteta seems to enjoy the luxury of this rotation but, unfortunately, it means both defenders are unselectable in Dream Team.

Similarly, the Spanish tactician has been hesitant to use Riccardo Calafiori in Europe — the Italian has been an unused substitute three times already this campaign.

Up top, Kai Havertz has been favoured in the league but limited to just 110 minutes in the Champions League.



Whereas Viktor Gyokeres has actually played more minutes in Europe than the Premier League.

Martin Odegaard is a lock at the weekend but has only started two of Arsenal’s four European fixtures to date — he’ll be more assured of minutes come the knockout stage.

Still to play: Borussia Dortmund (h), Real Madrid (h), Real Betis (a), Sabah (h)

Aston Villa

Zion Suzuki, Victor Lindelof and Pau Torres are the ever-presents with John McGinn only 13 minutes short.



Nicolas Jackson’s owners don’t have to worry either as he’s started every Champions League game this season.

Midfielders Joao Gomes, Boubacar Kamara and Emi Buendia have started three of the four and there’s no need to worry about Johan Manzambi, who has been a first-choice selection since he recovered from injury — although Unai Emery has managed the Swiss playmaker’s minutes to some degree.

Predicting who will occupy the full-back positions isn’t easy as Matty Cash, Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Ian Maatsen have all started half the European games available to them.

Leon Goretzka has been limited to just 55 minutes so far.

Still to play: Galatasaray (a), PSG (h), Borussia Dortmund (a), Slavia Prague (a)



Manchester City

Gigi Donnarumma is the only player in the squad to have played every Champions League minute this campaign.

Enzo Fernandez, Abdukodir Khusanov and Elliot Anderson lead the way among outfielders — the Uzbek defender has been given over 100 minutes more than Josko Gvardiol, Man City’s best-performing defender in terms of total points.

Despite valid concerns about his minutes in recent weeks, it’s important to note that Rayan Cherki has started every European game although he’s found points harder to come by compared to his domestic exploits.

10.2%-owned Jeremy Doku has been restricted to 72 minutes, partly due to injury, but Enzo Maresca will surely rely on the electric winger as the stakes ramp up in the coming weeks — City are one of nine teams level on nine points with four of those sides outside the coveted top eight places.



Iliman Ndiaye (156 minutes) and Nico O’Reilly (91 minutes) are the other notable names who have spent too much time on the bench in Europe for their owners’ liking this season.

Still to play: Napoli (a), Barcelona (a), Lens (a), Sporting CP (h)

Liverpool

Alisson is the only ever-present for the Reds while Jeremy Jacquet leads Virgil van Dijk among outfielders — the Frenchman is 22 points ahead of his senior centre-back partner after 10 Gameweeks.

It may come as a surprise to some Dream Team bosses that Rio Ngumoha has started every Champions League game this season and has played the most minutes in the competition among Liverpool’s midfielders and forwards.



Andoni Iraola has opted to rotate at left-back in Europe with Milos Kerkez (102 minutes) giving way to Kostas Tsimikas (258 minutes).

9.7%-owned Dominik Szoboszlai has only played half the available minutes.

Alexander Isak (136 minutes) and Cody Gakpo (114 minutes) are among those we would expect to play more as the tension increases — Liverpool are inside the top eight on goals scored and will be desperate to avoid a two-legged play-off after Christmas.

Still to play: Club Brugge (a), Porto (h), Inter (a), Lens (h)



Manchester United

The following all comes with the caveat that the man who selected the Red Devils’ line-ups over the first quarter of the campaign has been replaced by Mauricio Pochettino.

Senne Lammens, Bryan Mbeumo and Bruno Fernandes were Michael Carrick’s most trusted assets, having played 320+ minutes each in the Champions League.

Diogo Dalot, Leny Yoro, Youri Tielemans, Matheus Cunha have been regular enough too, although the latter will be suspended against Sporting CP in Gameweek 11.

Elsewhere, there’s been a lot of turnover with midfielders Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba, Kobbie Mainoo and Mason Mount all in the frustrating middle range between 150-165 minutes, not so little they can be completely disregarded but not enough to be wholly relied upon.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Still to play: Sporting CP (a), RB Leipzig (h), Bayern Munich (h), Villarreal (a)



Keep an eye out for our breakdown of the Europa League and Conference League sides later this week.

Sports.title: Who are England playing next? Why Men’s national team’s next game has not yet been decided – when it could be announced
Sports.content:
Next

THOMAS TUCHEL hailed a “statement victory” in Madrid on Sunday night as England beat world champions Spain 3-2 to top their UEFA Nations League group.

Goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White put the Three Lions 3-0 ahead before Elliot Anderson’s red card sparked a late Spanish fightback.



Inspired goalkeeping from James Trafford, who started ahead of Jordan Pickford, ensured England held on for a fifth straight win in Group A3, sealing top spot on goal difference ahead of Spain.

With momentum building on the road to Euro 2028 following last summer’s World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina, supporters are already looking ahead to what comes next.



When is England’s next match?

England do not return to action until the March 2027 international break, when the Nations League quarter-finals take place.

The two-legged ties are scheduled to be played between March 25 and March 30, 2027, with the first legs taking place from March 25–27 and the return fixtures from March 28–30.

Victory over two legs would send England into June’s four-team Nations League Finals.

Who is England’s next opponent?

England’s opponents in those games have not yet been decided because the Nations League group stage is still being finalised.

While England secured top spot in Group A3, other groups are still playing their final matches to determine who finishes in second place.

The final round of fixtures in two of the other three League A groups takes place on Monday and Tuesday evening.



By finishing top of Group A3, England are seeded for the last eight, but UEFA uses an open draw to determine the quarter-final pairings once all four groups are complete.

That means England’s route is not pre-set by a fixed tournament bracket, though Tuchel’s side will play the first leg away from home before welcoming their opponents to Wembley for the decisive second leg.

Who could England play?

As group winners, England will be drawn against a runner-up from one of the other three League A groups, meaning an immediate rematch with Group A3 runners-up Spain is ruled out.

Only one potential opponent is confirmed so far: Belgium, who secured second place behind France in Group A1 on Sunday night with a 4-1 victory over Italy in Brussels.

The other two possibilities will be decided over the next 48 hours.



When will the fixture be announced?

England will discover their quarter-final opponents on Friday, November 20.

The draw takes place at UEFA’s headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland, at 11am UK time, with exact match dates and kick-off times confirmed shortly afterwards.

Fans will be able to watch the draw live on UEFA TV.

Sports.title: Newcastle make Lewis Hall transfer decision as Euro giants consider entering £80m race with Man Utd
Sports.content:
Next

NEWCASTLE are adamant Lewis Hall is going NOWHERE any time soon.

Boss Matthias Jaissle is understood to want to strengthen his toothless Toon attack in the January transfer window.



But Mags insiders indicate there is no chance £80m-rated Manchester United target Hall will be sold to fund a spending spree.

The left-back, 22, penned a new long-term deal at St James’ Park last summer after Newcastle fought off interest from the Red Devils.



And despite losing star names such as Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes, there are no plans to cash in on the defensive gem in January or next year.

Hall produced a coming-of-age performance in England’s epic 3-2 Nations League victory in Spain on Sunday.



The star, a £35m signing from Chelsea in 2023, shut out the threat of Spanish golden boy Lamine Yamal in Madrid.

That was the second time in the space of eight months he has gotten the better of the 19-year-old winger having previously shone in the Champions League against Barcelona.

While United retain a strong interest in the boyhood Newcastle fan, Hall’s stunning performance for the Three Lions has also put him on the radar of some of Europe’s big guns.

But the exodus of Gordon, Tonali, Guimaraes, plus Kieran Trippier’s exit from the wage bill, solved any financial compliance issues the North East club had.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

That means they are under no pressure to sell, and with Jaissle viewing Hall as a key man in his rebuild, Newcastle will resist and bat off any potential suitors.

The Mags also had the same stance regarding Alexander Isak in 2025 before eventually caving in and selling him to Liverpool after a long-drawn out transfer saga.

They also agreed to sell skipper Guimaraes to Arsenal in August after the Brazilian outlined his desire to leave.

There are no indications Hall is looking to push for an exit and insiders indicate they believe he will be wearing Black and White at least until the summer of 2028.



However, there is also a realisation that the club have to match his ambitions and show they are capable of challenging at the top end of the table again.

In order to do that, Jaissle is believed to want reinforcements to help bolster his goal-shy attack.

Striker Yoane Wissa and Will Osula have both only managed a solitary goal each so far this term as Toon’s German coach, who replaced Eddie Howe in August, continues to struggle with getting his squad to implement his favoured 4-2-3-1 formation.

A striker and a potential new No.10 are both on Jaissle’s wishlist, and while the Mags do have a small kitty to play with, they will likely have to offload first.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

£17m-rated Joe Willock, who has been used as a ten this term, is top of Turkish club Besiktas’ shopping list with his Newcastle contract up in June.



Meanwhile, goalkeeper Nick Pope is also available having been relegated from first to third-choice since Jaissle’s arrival.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo’s mum says ‘I was happy about it’ in furious swipe at Portugal after ‘well deserved’ Denmark loss
Sports.content:
“The day has come back for me to hand back the number 7 shirt of our national team.

“I never felt it belonged to me alone. But for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it, and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.

“Today, the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision. Because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart.

“A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end.

“When I look back at everything with the national team, I don’t just see the matches, goals, records or trophies.

“I see people. I see the Portuguese people living abroad who, for 90 minutes, felt a little closer to home.

“I see millions of Portuguese people I have never met but who became part of my life.

“Because at the end of the day, football is so much bigger than a game. Football is about people.

“Throughout my entire career with the national team, I always pushed myself beyond my limits.

“I wanted to win. I wanted to be better. I wanted to make history.

“I always demanded the most of myself. I always wanted more. I always believed we could go further. And I gave everything I had for this shirt.

“There were perfect afternoons and evenings, there were victories I will never forget, there were defeats that are still difficult for me to recall.

“I also failed, I also suffered, there were also moments when I was unable to give the Portuguese people what they so desired. But I never gave up. And above all, I never stopped feeling proud to represent Portugal.

“Over these years I’ve learned some very simple things. Goals fade, trophies stay in museums, records eventually get broken. But there’s something time can never erase: the place we occupy in people’s hearts.

“If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a difficult moment, or feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it. Because being Portuguese is also about that.

“We suffer together, we rise together, we believe again. Portugal will always need young people who dream, players who never give up, new generations who believe it’s possible to reach where no one has reached before. Because a country that continues to create new heroes is a country that never stops believing in itself.

“To my team-mates, I want to say a special word. Thank you for every run, for every hug, for every discussion, for every silence before stepping onto the field.

“For every victory we celebrated together and for every defeat that made us stronger. I had the privilege of being your captain, but no captain walks alone. And you are part of my story.

“To all the coaches, managers, doctors, physiotherapists, kit men, staff, and so many people who have worked with me over these years, my thanks. Many of you never appeared in the photographs, but without you, none of these photographs would have been possible.

“To my family, thank you for sharing this dream with me. Thank you for understanding my absences, the sacrifices, and the times when the national team had to take up space that also belonged to you. If I’ve come this far, it’s because we’ve always been hand in hand.

“And to the Portuguese people, to all the Portuguese scattered around the world, I want to say one last thing.

“There’s an image I will always carry with me: the moment the national anthem begins. I look around, I see my teammates, I see the stands, I see children, mothers, fathers and grandparents, I see Portuguese people who have come from so far away just to be there.

“And during those minutes we cease to be different. There are no clubs, no colours, no classes, no professions, no opinions. There is only one passion: Portugal.

“I will carry this feeling with me for the rest of my life. Today my journey on the field with the national team ends. I leave with my head held high, proud of the path I have taken and with the awareness that I gave everything I had for Portugal.

“But I will never stop being one of you.

“I will continue to suffer, to thrill, and to celebrate every victory for Portugal with all my heart.

“I’ve spent my life working to be the best player in the world. Today I realise that the greatest victory was having earned the right to represent the best country in the world.

“Thank you for these 23 years. Thank you for believing in me. Thank you for allowing me to live a dream that began when I was just a boy in Madeira, chasing after a ball.

“The number 7 jersey will stay with me; the pride of having worn it will be mine forever. Portugal will always be a part of me.

“Farewell, Cristiano Ronaldo.”

Sports.title: Chelsea set to be raided by new Crystal Palace boss Thomas Frank for set-piece coach
Sports.content:
Next

CHELSEA chief Xabi Alonso is facing a battle to keep Bernardo Cueva on his backroom staff – with Crystal Palace circling.

The Eagles are preparing to confirm the appointment of Thomas Frank as their new boss.



And the former Tottenham boss, 53, will have the chance to bring in his own coaching staff following Pierre Sage’s sacking that SunSport exclusively broke last week.

Frank has set his sights on raiding Chelsea when he heads into the Selhurst Park dugout.



Palace will make an approach to add Cueva, who was shifted to a set-piece analyst and advisory role at Stamford Bridge during the summer, to their new-look management team.

The Mexican, 39, previously worked with Frank at Premier League rivals Brentford for four years.

And Cueva is expected to be installed as an assistant first-team coach if he seals a reunion at Palace.

The set-piece expert arrived at Chelsea when Enzo Maresca bagged the top job ahead of the 2024/25 season.

Cueva then stayed at Stamford Bridge as Liam Rosenior succeeded the Italian halfway through last term.

Xabi Alonso also chose to keep him on board in a fresh role after being appointed as Chelsea’s new supremo in the summer.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

But Frank is desperate to work with Cueva again after he played a key role in spearheading Brentford to promotion from the Championship.

Jamal Alioui, Damien Della Santa and Sandy Guichard left Palace when Sage was dismissed last week.

That has given Frank the chance to bring in his own coaches when he is officially unveiled as the South Londoners’ supremo.

The Dane has been working as a pundit for Match of the Day since the season got underway.



But, having been axed by Tottenham in February, Frank has been looking for a route back into Premier League management.

He is expected to sign on the dotted line before Palace’s trip to Coventry on Saturday.

Sports.title: Inside new James Bond star Robert Pattinson’s love affair with Arsenal, including surprise favourite player
Sports.content:
Next

NEW JAMES BOND star Robert Pattinson does not keep his love for Arsenal top secret, but his favourite player might surprise you.

It was announced on Monday that the British actor will step into the role as the world’s most iconic spy, for the newest instalment.



He will succeed Daniel Craig after his 15 years and five films in the role, including starring roles in modern classics like Casino Royale and Spectre.

Now Pattinson, known for his early works Harry Potter and Twilight to newer releases such as The Odyssey and Primetime, is ready to receive his license to kill.



But when Pattinson, 40, is not starring on the silver screen, he is keeping up with his beloved Arsenal.

The Barnes-born superstar revealed that missing the football was one of the hardest parts of his jet-setting lifestyle.

He told Metro about always being on the move: “I miss reading the sport section [of English newspapers]. I miss the football… Arsenal.”

He further opened up about his fandom last year, revealing a surprise pick for his favourite player to wear the shirt.

When asked which Gunner he would clone at the premiere of sci-fi flick Mickey 17, he said: “I’d have to go back to like 1995.”

After a moment to think the question over – and an admission that he is not as familiar with the current crop of players as he used to be – he answered: “Emmanuel Petit.”



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

The ponytailed Frenchman won the hearts of many a North Londoner during his stint with the club between 1997 and 2000.

The midfielder made 118 appearances in all competitions in that spell, scoring 11 times.

But Pattinson admitted that he did not share his hero’s prowess on the pitch in a 2022 interview with GQ.

He joked when talking about his footballing skills: “I still have the same terror when I’m walking past little kids, and the football rips into the path.



“I just have this terror of passing it back, and I go straight back to being a 10-year-old, and kicking it in the wrong direction. People being like: ‘Wow! What an idiot!’

“Eventually, I’m probably gonna have a child. So I’ve started training myself so that I can be somewhat… so that I can play soccer with a three-year-old.”

Hopefully he has since brushed up on his abilities, having welcomed his first child with model fiancee Suki Waterhouse in 2024.

He is the latest in a lineage of football fan Bonds.
