World.title: Zimbabwe cruise past Equatorial Guinea in AFCON qualifier
World.content:
Zimbabwe's Warriors celebrate during their AFCON 2027 qualifying campaign. Image: ZIFA

Zimbabwe’s Warriors have boosted their hopes of qualifying for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations after securing a convincing 3-0 victory over Equatorial Guinea at the National Sports Stadium on Monday, 16 November 2026.

The victory takes Zimbabwe to seven points from four matches in Group E, strengthening their grip on second place behind leaders DR Congo, who have nine points from three matches.

The Warriors went into the encounter knowing that maximum points would be crucial after sharing a goalless draw with Equatorial Guinea in their previous meeting in Cameroon on Thursday, 12 November.



Ngwenya gives ZIMBABWE early lead

Zimbabwe made a bright start, with Thandolwenkosi Ngwenya opening the scoring in the fourth minute to give the hosts a 1-0 advantage.

The Warriors maintained their lead until half-time, putting themselves in a strong position to secure maximum points against their Group E rivals.

Equatorial Guinea attempted to find a response after the break, but Zimbabwe continued to press for more goals.



Chirewa and Maswanhise seal victory

Tawanda Chirewa doubled Zimbabwe’s advantage in the 71st minute before turning provider seven minutes later.

The midfielder assisted Tawanda Maswanhise, who found the back of the net in the 78th minute to make it 3-0 and put the result beyond doubt.

The victory was particularly important for Zimbabwe after their earlier draw against the same opponents, which had left both teams level on four points.



Equatorial Guinea miss penalty before Coco’s dismissal

Equatorial Guinea’s Josete Miranda missed a penalty in the 88th minute, missing an opportunity to pull one back for the visitors.

Their difficult afternoon was compounded a minute later when Saúl Coco received a red card, leaving Equatorial Guinea to finish the match with 10 men.

World.title: Simon’s Town baboons ‘adjusting well’ to new Kogelfontein home
World.content:
The 44 baboons relocated from the Simon's Town area to a new wildlife enclosure are adjusting well to their surroundings. Image: Supplied

The 44 baboons relocated from the Simon’s Town area to a new wildlife enclosure are adjusting well to their surroundings, according to the Cape Peninsula Baboon Management Joint Task Team.

The Waterfall troop has settled into the Urban Wildlife Centre at Kogelfontein, where the animals have been seen playing, foraging, using water ponds and relaxing on the roofs of specially designed sleeping structures.

READ | Last-ditch protests to keep Simon’s Town baboons wild as troops face captivity



The relocation was carried out under the approved Cape Peninsula Baboon Management Action Plan, following persistent human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment.

The joint task team, which includes representatives from SANParks, CapeNature and the City of Cape Town, says the new facility provides a protected environment where the animals can live without the risks associated with people, dogs, traffic and unsuitable human food.

Inside the baboons’ new home

The Urban Wildlife Centre is situated in a natural area adjacent to Table Mountain National Park.



Its 2.31-hectare enclosure includes riverine features, indigenous and exotic vegetation, thick ground cover, bushes, small trees, rocks and sandy areas where the baboons can forage and dig.

The enclosure also provides shelters for shade and protection from the weather, as well as two platforms for sleeping and resting.

The animals have access to fresh drinking water throughout the day, along with a pond for cooling down and enrichment.



Their natural diet is supplemented with daily enrichment activities, including browse and scatter feeding around the enclosure.

Climbing and swinging fixtures, together with different levels of vertical and horizontal complexity, provide additional stimulation.

The task team says the enclosure is approximately 5.5 times larger than the minimum area required under the Global Federation of Animal Sanctuaries standards for Old World primates.



Baboons monitored around the clock

The 44 animals are being cared for and monitored 24 hours a day, with daily assessments focusing on individual and troop behaviour, social interactions and feeding.

Veterinary oversight is ongoing.

Before being released into the enclosure, every baboon underwent a screening and health check conducted by three wildlife veterinarians.



The task team confirmed that all 44 baboons were safely captured and released at Kogelfontein without injury.

One older female was euthanised after the health screening revealed that she was in very poor health.

The task team also clarified that none of the male baboons were vasectomised, while the females received contraceptive implants.



Why was the Waterfall troop relocated?

The relocation followed ongoing conflict between baboons and people in the Simon’s Town urban environment.

According to the task team, the decision was based on the severity and persistence of these conflicts, limited natural low-lying habitat and increasing risks to the baboons’ welfare.

Public safety concerns also formed part of the decision.



The new facility is intended to protect the troop from injuries and other dangers associated with moving through urban areas, while providing an environment where their health and behaviour can be closely monitored.

More than 530 baboons remain across the Cape Peninsula

The relocation does not mean that baboons are being removed from the Cape Peninsula altogether.

The task team says more than 530 free-ranging baboons remain across the peninsula.



These troops continue to fulfil an important ecological role, and their conservation and active management remain necessary to support their health, welfare and long-term sustainability.

The authorities say the relocated Waterfall troop’s adjustment will continue to be monitored as the animals settle into their new surroundings.

World.title: Identity of next James Bond revealed
World.content:
British ​actor Robert Pattinson will be ‌the next James Bond, ​making him the first actor ​to take on the role ⁠since Daniel Craig's departure from ​the long-running spy series. Image: Instagram

British ​actor Robert Pattinson will be ‌the next James Bond, the official 007 Instagram account announced on Monday, ​making him the first actor ​to take on the role ⁠since Daniel Craig’s departure from ​the long-running spy series.

The Bond franchise – ​about a secret agent known for his charm, his tailored tuxedos and ​a fondness for martinis “shaken, not ​stirred” – is among the longest-running and highest-grossing ‌in ⁠Hollywood history.

Debuting in 1962, the movies have brought in more than $7 billion in global ticket ​sales since ​Sean ⁠Connery brought the Agent 007 to the big ​screen in “Dr. No.”

Robert Pattinson, 40, whose film ​credits ⁠this year include “The Odyssey” and “Primetime”, succeeds Craig, who bowed out ⁠of ​the role after 2021 ​movie “No Time to Die.”

The actor’s casting brings to a close years of feverish speculation over who will play 007, after Daniel Craig formally announced his departure from the role in 2017.



Names including Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Henry Cavill, Theo James, Idris Elba, Paul Mescal, James Norton, Callum Turner and Jacob Elordi have all circled the role in the past near-decade.

World.title: THIRD South African Olympic swimmer to pursue career under another flag
World.content:
South African swimming has suffered another high-profile departure, with Olympic swimmer Rebecca Meder set to represent New Zealand. Image: Team SA website

South African swimming has suffered another high-profile departure, with Olympic swimmer Rebecca Meder set to represent New Zealand after spending the past three years training in the country.

The 24-year-old’s decision follows last week’s bombshell announcement by two-time Olympic champion Tatjana Smith that she intends to represent the Netherlands, while fellow Olympic swimmer Matthew Sates has also declared his intention to pursue Australian representation.

READ | Roland Schoeman blasts Swimming SA after Tatjana Smith’s shock Netherlands switch



The developments mean that three of the eight swimmers who represented South Africa at the 2024 Paris Olympic Games have now indicated plans to pursue their international careers elsewhere.

Smith highlighted that statistic in a social media comment following news of Meder’s decision, raising questions about the environment facing elite swimmers in South Africa.

Meder explains decision to represent New Zealand

Meder has been training in New Zealand since August 2023 under Graham Hill at North Shore Swimming Club.

Hill is currently New Zealand’s national team coach and previously coached the South African national team.

The 14-time African champion said that her decision was personal and had been under consideration for several months.

“I have been praying about this decision for the past eight months, as my personal circumstances have changed,” she said.



Meder explained that she wanted to close her chapter with Team South Africa after ending her 2026 Commonwealth Games campaign with a bronze medal in the 4x100m medley relay.

She said she began the process a week after the Commonwealth Games and that her international sit-out period started on 30 July 2026.

The swimmer added that she had informed the South African Sports Confederation and Olympic Committee (SASCOC) and Swimming South Africa, and that the parties had parted on good terms.

Meder is now in the process of obtaining New Zealand citizenship, although she is uncertain how long the process will take.

Tatjana Smith raises concerns about swimmer departures

Smith, South Africa’s most decorated Olympian, responded to Meder’s move by pointing out that three members of the country’s eight-swimmer Paris Olympic squad were now pursuing careers under different flags.

“As one of those three, I know these decisions are never easy,” Smith wrote.

“We should want our athletes to represent South Africa, and they should never have to choose between swimming for their country and being in an environment where they feel supported, valued and able to thrive.”

She suggested that the repeated departures should prompt reflection on the circumstances facing athletes.

“When multiple athletes independently arrive at the same decision, perhaps it’s time to look beyond the individuals making those choices and reflect on the environment that has led them there,” she added.

Meder, however, did not cite financial concerns as a reason for her decision.

Meder’s impressive record for South Africa

Meder leaves South African swimming with an impressive international record.

She is a 14-time African champion and won two relay bronze medals at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

At the Paris 2024 Olympics, she finished 11th in the women’s 200m individual medley, setting a South African national record of 2:10.67 in the semi-finals.

She improved on that placing at the 2025 World Aquatics Championships, finishing 10th in the same event.

Her move to New Zealand will not allow her to compete for her new country immediately.

Under international eligibility rules, she must complete a waiting period of at least one year after her last representation of South Africa before becoming eligible to compete internationally for New Zealand.

This means she will miss next month’s World Aquatics Swimming Championships (25m) in Beijing, China as well as next year’s World Aquatics Championships in Budapest, Hungary from 26 June to 18 July as a potential representative of her new country.

Building a new life in New Zealand

Meder’s decision also reflects the personal life she has established overseas.

Her partner, Rance Gower-Winter, joined her in New Zealand last year after the couple spent time in a long-distance relationship following her move.

“My family means everything to me, and the first two years were tough,” Meder told Rapport.

“But it built my character as I had to navigate and adapt to a whole range of new things.”

She said she and Gower-Winter had settled in well and were happy with the life they had built in New Zealand.

For South African swimming, Meder’s decision represents another significant change ahead of the next Olympic cycle, with three members of the Paris squad now looking towards international careers with other nations.

The news comes as Curro, a for-profit school network in South Africa, announced that it will contribute R500 000 to help send the 21 South African national swimmers to the World Aquatics Championships in Beijing, who otherwise were expected to fork out R55 000 to get themselves to China.

World.title: Jolting awake at night? Here is what it could mean
World.content:
Do you frequently jolt awake when falling asleep? Researchers tell us what it could mean. Image: Katrin Bolovtsova via Pexels

You are drifting off to sleep when suddenly your body jerks. Perhaps you feel as though you’ve fallen, or your arms or legs twitch so violently that you wake up with your heart racing.

These strange episodes are surprisingly common. The action of jolting awake usually happens as the body transitions to sleep. Researchers have now uncovered an interesting connection that could change how we think about these seemingly harmless sleep disturbances.

Why do you jerk awake when falling asleep?

Known as hypnic jerks, or “sleep starts”, these are sudden, involuntary muscle movements that occur as you begin to fall asleep. They can affect a single limb or involve several muscles at once, sometimes waking you abruptly. For some people, the experience is little more than a brief twitch. Others describe a sensation of falling, stumbling or suddenly losing their balance.



These sleep starts can also involve other sensations, including tingling, electric-shock-like feelings and brief flashes of light. Some people report dream-like experiences or a sudden feeling of alarm, accompanied by a racing heart or rapid breathing.

Although these experiences can be unsettling, jolting awake is generally a normal and harmless part of the transition into sleep.

What frequent sleep jolts could mean

A study published in PLOS Mental Health has explored the relationship between sleep starts, sleep quality and psychological wellbeing.

Researchers from Paris Lodron University Salzburg in Austria surveyed 194 adults about their sleeping habits, insomnia symptoms, daytime sleepiness and mental health.

The research team divided the participants into two groups. The first group included 96 people who reported abrupt awakenings at least once a week, along with at least one other sleep-start symptom. The remaining 98 participants, who experienced these episodes less frequently or not at all, formed the comparison group.

The findings revealed some interesting differences. Compared with the other participants, those who frequently experienced jolting awake reported:



· Poorer overall sleep quality.

· Severe insomnia symptoms.

· Higher levels of anxiety and depressive symptoms.

· Stronger unhelpful beliefs and concerns about sleep.

The researchers also found that the frequency of sleep starts, or jolting awake, was associated with poorer sleep quality, stronger sleep-related worries and higher anxiety symptoms.

Depressive symptoms, although higher in the frequent hypnic jerks group, were not independently associated with how often the episodes occurred.

Another interesting finding was the relationship with emotional stress. Participants recalled experiencing jolting awake more frequently during periods of psychological tension and emotional strain. Relaxation, on the other hand, meant fewer episodes.

The findings suggest that these sudden sleep interruptions may be part of a broader pattern involving emotional and mental alertness around bedtime.

Jolting awake at night: Should i be worried?

An occasional jolt just as you’re drifting off is generally nothing to worry about. However, the researchers found that frequent sleep starts were associated with greater sleep disruption and distress in some participants.

This does not mean that anxiety causes hypnic jerks, or that experiencing them will make you anxious. The study was based on an online survey and participants’ own accounts of their experiences. It could therefore identify associations but could not establish cause and effect.

There are other limitations worth considering. The researchers used a questionnaire developed specifically for the study, but it must still be validated independently. They also collected the data between June 2020 and January 2021, meaning the findings are based on participants’ experiences during that period.

Furthermore, the researchers acknowledge that their questionnaire covered a broader range of sleep-onset experiences, some of which can overlap with conditions such as hypnagogic hallucinations. It was not possible to distinguish these reliably from hypnic jerks using self-reported information alone.

The team says they need to do further research, particularly studies using objective sleep recordings, to understand these experiences and their relationship with psychological well-being better.

For now, the findings offer an interesting reminder that sleep is influenced by more than simply how tired you feel. Stress, emotional wellbeing and your thoughts about sleep may also play a role in what happens as you drift off. Even your sleeping environment can make a difference, with research exploring why people sometimes struggle to sleep in unfamiliar surroundings.

Do you ever find yourself jolting awake as you are falling asleep? Is it an occasional twitch, or does it happen often enough to interrupt your sleep?

World.title: Five things to know about Bond, James Bond
World.content:
LONDON - British box office magnet Robert Pattinson was named on Monday as the new James Bond, thrusting the "Twilight" and "The Odyssey" heartthrob into one of the world's most famous film franchises.

Here are five things to know about the man with a licence to kill.

Born on paper

James Bond started life on the page, his name taken from the cover of a Jamaican bird-watching book because his creator, British author Ian Fleming, wanted something as mundane as possible.

Fleming was able to draw from some rich real-life experiences, having served in naval intelligence during World War II.

One of Commander Fleming's key missions was Operation Goldeneye, aimed at sabotaging ties between Spain and Germany -- which later gave him the name for his Jamaican home, and inspired the 1995 movie.

His first novel, "Casino Royale", was released in 1953 and was a huge hit, chronicling the escapades of a larger-than-life secret agent and giving the British public a brief escape from the grim reality of post-war rations and hardship.

He went on to write 13 more Bond novels and penned the children's story "Chitty Chitty Bang Bang" for his son, which also came to the screen as a hit musical.

Fleming died in 1964 at the age of 56, just two years after the first Bond film appeared.

Big money

The figures vary, but Bond is one of the most successful film franchises of all time, having spawned 25 official films.

Industry data site The Numbers places Bond in third place for worldwide box office takings, behind only the Marvel Cinematic Universe and Star Wars.

While franchises such as King Kong and Godzilla have been around longer, Bond is more regular, rarely going more than two or three years between instalments.

The longest gap was between Timothy Dalton's last outing, 1989's "Licence to Kill", and Pierce Brosnan's "GoldenEye" in 1995.

Underlining the immense value of the franchise, Amazon bought the Bond rights from MGM for a cool $8.45 billion in 2021.

International agent

The various Bonds of the past 60 years have included Englishman Daniel Craig and Roger Moore, Scotsman Sean Connery, George Lazenby from Australia, Timothy Dalton from Wales and Irishman Pierce Brosnan.

In the novels, Bond is the son of a Scottish father and Swiss mother -- both of whom die in a climbing accident when he is a boy.

Codenames

The codename "007" has a specific meaning.

The "00" designation signifies the agent's licence to kill, while the "7" is his identification within the elite unit of MI6, Britain's external intelligence service.

The M designating Bond's boss comes from the "Missions Department".

Q, who furnishes Bond with all his nifty gadgets, gets his moniker from "quartermaster" -- a military term referring to the person in charge of supplies.

The bad guys have their own codenames.

"SPECTRE", the organisation that causes Bond so much trouble, is short for "Special Executive for Counter-intelligence, Terrorism, Revenge and Extortion".

A famous fan

One big name who gave Bond an early boost was President John F. Kennedy, who cited "From Russia With Love" in his top 10 books.

Reportedly, it was also the last film he ever watched before leaving for Dallas in November 1963.

World.title: 'Not competitive' Brazil can improve, insists Ancelotti
World.content:
SINGAPORE - Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti on Monday promised an improved performance in the year-ending clash against Singapore, admitting that his squad was "currently not competitive."

The Selecao lost 3-2 against Japan in a friendly in Singapore on Saturday, where Ancelotti and skipper Raphinha were red-carded after Japan scored the dramatic clincher in stoppage time.

"Given that the team is currently not competitive, I want to do more," Ancelotti told reporters in Singapore, where Brazil play on Tuesday.

The Italian, Brazil's first-ever permanent foreign coach, said: "I want to do more because I enjoy being here, so that the team can become more competitive on the global stage.

"The priority is to play well first (tomorrow) and to do well."

Ancelotti, 67, is coming under increasing pressure, following a string of underwhelming performances including two defeats, two wins and a draw in Brazil's last five international outings.

Japan avenged a 2-1 defeat by Brazil in their previous meeting at this year's World Cup, when the South Americans beat them in a round-of-32 clash.

After Saturday's loss, Ancelotti faced a barrage of criticism, including from former Brazilian national team star Romario.

Ancelotti brushed off Romario's remarks, saying "like anyone he has the right to express an opinion."

But the former Real Madrid coach, who reacted with fury after Brazil appealed for a foul in the build-up to Japan's winning goal on Saturday -- which was upheld by VAR -- said that his team "didn't deserve to lose" against Japan.

Japan face Paraguay on Tuesday in the second match of the double-header at Singapore's National Stadium.

World.title: AI cheating sparks alarm ahead of South Korea's college exam
World.content:
SEOUL - A South Korean exam cheat who confessed to using AI to post near-perfect accountancy test scores has sent teachers and officials scrambling to prevent similar misconduct ahead of this week's crucial college entrance exam.

Known as the Suneung, the intense once-a-year exam will bring much of South Korea to a standstill on Thursday, with flights temporarily halted during the English listening section and stock trading delayed by an hour.

The trickster's admission on Sunday to using a miniature camera and smartphone in two national tax tests earlier this year has "caused panic among teachers", said Kim Seung-ho, a high school educator in the central city of Cheongju.

"Each testing centre is assigned six to seven metal detectors, but not enough for every classroom," he told AFP, adding "the problem is we don't know if they can detect miniature cameras or nano-scale earphones".

More than half a million students are set to sit the gruelling nine-hour test this year in highly competitive South Korea, where getting into a top university is seen as a ticket not only to well-paid jobs but also to better marriage prospects.

Song Ji-eun, who will take the test, told AFP that she would struggle to concentrate "if supervisors keep checking my glasses" for tiny cameras.

"There's a saying that even a slight breeze can affect your focus, your score and even your entire life," the 18-year-old said.

- Possible Wi-Fi cut -

The cheating revelation prompted South Korea's presidential office to announce plans to deploy thermal cameras at exam centres, though it was unclear whether they would be installed at all 1,312 testing sites.

Education officials were also considering suspending public Wi-Fi hotspots near college entrance exam sites.

"We are reviewing all measures, including suspending public Wi-Fi networks," an education ministry official told AFP, adding that an announcement would be made before the exam takes place.

According to local media reports, the government has also been discussing cutting off 5G and LTE mobile data around exam sites and activating signal-jamming devices.

"As devices themselves have become more advanced, including those that can be attached to the body, it is not easy to detect 100 percent of cheating without completely blocking communications," Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said.

However, experts say it would be technically impossible as it would disrupt communication in surrounding residential areas and block emergency calls.

Asked whether signal-blocking measures could be introduced at examination centres, Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin said his office was consulting with the science ministry "to see whether it would be possible, even for part of the examination".

The minister rejected calls for the exam to be rescheduled, saying it "could cause even greater confusion".

- Trust at stake -

The test cheat's video confession, which was posted on his lawyer's YouTube channel, came after questions were raised about his performance.

He ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam, answering all but one of 160 questions correctly in the first round, a feat many tax accountants had deemed nearly impossible.

His confession has also fuelled suspicions that AI-assisted deception may have already taken place in other high-stakes exams, including law school admissions and university transfer tests.

Lee Jin-woo, who earned a perfect score on a law school admission test in July and has since gained celebrity-like status, has faced scrutiny over his results, prompting him to announce plans to livestream himself solving the Korean language section of the Suneung on Thursday to prove his abilities.

It comes as officials plan to review all cases involving suspected cheating in state-administered professional licensing exams.

But teacher Kim said the response had come too late.

"We had two mock college admission exams in June and September, when we could have tested our readiness to prevent AI-assisted cheating," he said.

"But we did nothing in terms of preventive training, wasting our opportunities to prepare for the real Suneung."

Experts warn that any breach of the college admission test could have serious repercussions, threatening public confidence in an exam seen as a cornerstone of meritocracy in the country.

"Suneung is a symbol of fairness in South Korea, where students compete on equal terms regardless of their background or circumstances," said Kim Seong-sheen, a professor at Hanyang University's Institute for Creative Convergence Education.

"If AI devices can compromise this exam, the issue goes far beyond a single act of cheating. It would mean undermining public trust in the entire examination system."

World.title: MTN, Telkom back at negotiating table over potential deal
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - MTN and Telkom are back at the negotiating table, confirming renewed discussions over the mobile operator’s proposed acquisition of Telkom.

The news sent Telkom’s share price soaring by as much as 17% in midday trading.

The proposed transaction would see Telkom shareholders receive a cash payout, with the option of taking MTN shares instead.

If successful, the deal would create South Africa’s largest telecommunications operator by customer numbers, overtaking Vodacom.

However, significant hurdles remain. Both companies say discussions are at an early stage and there is no guarantee that a deal will be concluded.

The two operators previously explored a takeover in 2022, but negotiations collapsed amid disagreements over exclusivity and regulatory concerns.

World.title: Next K-wave? Chinese dramas, celebrities draw foreign fans
World.content:
BEIJING - For more than 20 days, rain or shine, Thai fan Thammarawee Lin joined other overseas admirers outside a hotel in eastern China, phones trained on the entrance for actor Zhang Linghe to emerge.

Chinese heartthrob Zhang, known for his towering height and boyish features, has rocketed to international fame with his recent hit series "Pursuit of Jade", part of a growing wave of Chinese dramas, or C-dramas, capturing the hearts of overseas watchers like Lin.

The booming popularity of C-dramas is also fuelling a new kind of tourism industry in Hengdian, as businesses cash in on foreign fans travelling to "China's Hollywood", hoping for a glimpse of their favourite celebrities.

Pressed against barricades decorated with his posters, Zhang's fans reserved their spots outside the hotel a day in advance with colourful stools to ensure the best view.

The hotel sits near Hengdian's massive film set complex, a sprawl of replica historical Chinese palaces, old Hong Kong streets and temples that serve as the stage for many period dramas and movies.

Industry insiders have taken to leaking -- or selling -- filming schedules and locations on social media, sending fans thronging to places like the hotel where Zhang was getting his hair and make-up done.

World.title: Ackerman hits century as South Africa bounce back
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Marques Ackerman hit an aggressive century as South Africa bounced back on the second day of the first Test against Bangladesh at the Wanderers Stadium on Monday.

The left-handed Ackerman struck 157 off 164 balls as South Africa made 287 for four in reply to Bangladesh's first innings of 400.

Ackerman, in his third Test, and the recalled Zubayr Hamza, who made 83, put on 202 for the second wicket. They came together after the experienced Aiden Markram was caught behind off Hasan Mahmud for four in the second over of South Africa's innings.

Earlier, Bangladesh made their highest total against South Africa.

Litton Das, resuming on 92, scored 120 as the tourists added 73 runs to their overnight total of 327 for six for the loss of their remaining four wickets.

Ackerman and Hamza had to survive some hostile new ball bowling by Mahmud and Taskin Ahmed but took control on a true batting surface as the ball lost its shine.

Hamza, playing in his eighth Test but his first in more than two years, put in a strong claim to establish himself in South Africa's problematic number three batting position. He is the eighth player to be tried at three since Shukri Conrad became coach in 2023.

Hamza hit 12 boundaries in a 129-ball innings before he was caught behind in the first over bowled by part-time left-arm spinner Mominul Haque.

Ackerman, who made 95 in his second Test appearance against Australia last month, again displayed a fearless approach, using his feet and playing a variety of wristy strokes.

He showed no nerves as he cruised through the nineties, reaching his century off 125 balls. He then went on an all-out assault, scoring 57 more runs off 39 deliveries before he was caught in the deep off Mahmud. Ackerman hit 21 fours and a six.

Ackerman's dismissal brought Bangladesh back into the contest and Mahmud claimed his third wicket when Matthew Breetzke was caught behind for two.

Mahmud could have had a fourth scalp but Ryan Rickelton survived a difficult chance to wicketkeeper Das off the first ball he faced.

World.title: Etzebeth back for bruised Boks against Ireland
World.content:
DUBLIN - South Africa rugby legend Eben Etzebeth returns to the starting XV for the world champions' Nations Championship Test against Ireland this weekend with coach Rassie Erasmus saying on Monday they are "determined to fix the mistakes that cost us" in the defeat by France.

The Springboks lie second in the southern hemisphere standings, a point adrift of New Zealand who were beaten by Wales for the first time in 73 years, after they lost 21-19 in a pulsating match in Paris last Friday.

A South Africa win over Ireland and England beating the All Blacks next Saturday would be enough for Erasmus's side to feature in the top place final on November 29 at Twickenham.

"We let ourselves and the country down, and we are determined to fix the mistakes that cost us," he said in a South Africa Rugby statement.

"So we'll leave no stone unturned to ensure that we play according to our standards this weekend.

"The coaches and the entire squad took a good look at ourselves over the last few days and we know what we did wrong and what we have to improve on, so we know what we have to do this week."

- 'A quality team' -

Erasmus made five changes in all to the starting line-up that faced the French, who gained a measure of revenge for their World Cup quarter-final defeat on the same ground in 2023.

Etzebeth, who will extend his record as the most capped Springbok in history to 148, will link up with Ruan Nortje in the engine room.

The 35-year-old had been ruled out of the tour originally because of injury but recovered sufficiently to be called up earlier this month.

The other changes to the starting team are Cameron Hanekom joining forces with captain Siya Kolisi, and Pieter-Steph du Toit in the back row whilst Ox Nche, Malcolm Marx, and Wilco Louw return to the front row.

Erasmus made a further seven changes on the replacements bench, which again feature six forwards and two backs, although four of those players featured in the matchday squad against France.

Two players who do come onto the replacements bench having sat out the French game are Grant Williams as scrum-half cover in place of Cobus Reinach, while Canan Moodie comes in for Manie Libbok.

"We also think what Grant and Canan offer will suit us in terms of what we want to achieve against Ireland," said Erasmus.

South Africa are seeking their second successive win in Dublin, having won for the first time there in 13 years last November.

Ireland have had the better of the Springboks in recent years, winning four of their last six meetings, including being the only side to beat them at the 2023 World Cup -- in the pool stage.

"They are a quality team, who always give everything against us, so it's going to take an accurate 80-minute performance if we want to get the result against them," said Erasmus.

"They have classy forwards and backs, and they will give everything knowing that they are still in the running for a place in the final of the competition next weekend with England and France to finish the league stages as the top northern hemisphere team."

Erasmus' Ireland counterpart Andy Farrell will name his side on Thursday.

Team (15-1)

Damian Willemse; Kurt-Lee Arendse, Jesse Kriel, Damian de Allende, Ethan Hooker; Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Morne van den Berg; Cameron Hanekom, Pieter-Steph du Toit, Siya Kolisi (capt); Ruan Nortje, Eben Etzebeth; Wilco Louw, Malcolm Marx, Ox Nche

Replacements: Jan-Hendrik Wessels, Gerhard Steenekamp, Thomas du Toit, Lood de Jager, Paul de Villiers, Marco van Staden, Grant Williams, Canan Moodie

Coach: Rassie Erasmus (RSA)

World.title: UK actor Robert Pattinson to be new James Bond
World.content:
LONDON - British actor Robert Pattinson was Monday named as the new James Bond, stepping into the coveted role of the world's most famous fictional spy.

"Amazon MGM Studios have announced that Robert Pattinson will take on the iconic role of James Bond," the studio said on the official 007.com website.

Pattinson would succeed Daniel Craig as the super-suave MI6 agent, "ushering in a new era for one of cinema's most celebrated characters", the studios added.

It will be the first Bond film since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said.

"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added in a statement.

Amazon MGM also announced that Oscar-nominated Canadian director Denis Villeneuve, behind such box-office hits as the "Dune" films, would be directing the next Bond movie from a script by "Peaky Blinders" creator Steven Knight.

Knight said in May that Amazon has given him a licence to play with the legendary secret agent created by author Ian Fleming.

"Bond has been bulletproof. People have been able to make mistakes and variations and the character has survived," Knight told Screen magazine at the Cannes Film Festival.

"Because the core of it is like a diamond. You can't touch it," he added.

Knight also told reporters that he has done research with "the SAS and even more secret outfits" for his reinvention of the next 007 movie.

Pattinson, 40, started out in amateur dramatics before getting his break in "Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire" (2005) as Cedric Diggory, a champion for Hogwarts.

But he rocketed to global fame for his part as a brooding teen heartthrob in the romantic vampire saga "Twilight".

'Extremely inventive'

He was paid a reported $2 million for his lead in "Twilight" (2008), but by the time the saga wrapped up with the two parts of "Breaking Dawn" in 2011 and 2012, he was reportedly on $12.5 million plus 7.5 percent of the box office take.

One of his first forays into edgier cinema came with 2012 drama "Cosmopolis", in which he portrayed a self-destructive currency speculator as his life falls apart.

The film was directed by legendary US auteur David Cronenberg, who described the actor as "extremely inventive".

He received critical acclaim after later switching to more independent films and was nominated for best actor at the Cannes festival in 2017 for neo-grindhouse crime caper "Good Time" by New York-based brothers Josh and Ben Safdie.

In 2022, Amazon bought storied Hollywood studio MGM, which held distribution rights to Bond's extensive back catalogue.

But it was not until early 2025 that the company struck a deal with longtime Bond producers Wilson and Broccoli to obtain full creative control.

The franchise had been closely guarded by the Broccoli family since 1962's "Dr. No".

They famously insisted on preserving the integrity of the Bond character and brand, resisting spin-offs and licensing that many industry experts expect to see following Amazon's takeover.

World.title: KCSE candidate dies after allegedly consuming ethanol in laboratory
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

A Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) candidate has died in Homa Bay County, days after he allegedly consumed ethanol while cleaning the school laboratory, police have said.

John Otieno Okinyi, 18, who was a candidate at St Stephen Ang’iro Senior School in Rangwe Sub-county, died on Monday morning as he was receiving treatment in hospital.

Okinyi and other candidates were reportedly assigned to clean the laboratory on Saturday after a biology practical exam on Friday.

It was during the exercise that Okinyi allegedly consumed the reagent. His colleagues saw him foaming at the mouth and alerted the school management, who rushed him to Termary Hospital in Rangwe.

He was treated and discharged the same day. However, on Monday morning, he was again in pain and was rushed to the hospital, where he died.

Rangwe Sub-county Police Commander Magdalene Chebet said investigations have been launched into the matter.

He said the cause of death is yet to be established.

“The information we have is that the student consumed the ethanol. However, we are waiting for an expert to conduct the postmortem to reveal the cause of his death,” she said.

Chebet appealed for calm among the school community and the bereaved family as they await for the postmortem report.

“Let me urge the entire school community to be calm as we wait for postmortem results,” she said.

The body was removed to the Homa Bay County Teaching and Referral Hospital mortuary.

World.title: Thwake Dam project reaches 94pc completion
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Thwake Multipurpose Dam, which is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment.[File,Standard]

Thwake Dam is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment as residents seek a review of alleged construction-related damage claims.

Principal Secretary for Water and Sanitation Julius Korir told the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Blue Economy, Water and Irrigation that construction had reached 94.2 per cent.

The dam is being built at the confluence of the Athi and Thwake rivers along the Makueni-Kitui border. It is designed to provide water for domestic use, irrigation and electricity generation.

Martin Kimeu, a resident of Wote, said the project would improve access to water for farming in the region.

“Ukambani is fertile. Water has been the biggest impediment to the realization of our agricultural potential. Thwake Dam water is the clear solution to this,” he said.

Kimeu also defended the compensation process, saying he had followed the project since its inception and believed the exercise had been conducted properly.

Jacob Mwanzia, a resident of Madangi Village, said households in his area had been assessed and compensated. He argued that outstanding complaints should be addressed without delaying the project.

Mariam Mwikali, another resident, said assessments had been conducted on affected properties and residents given an opportunity to raise concerns.

However, some households have complained that construction-related blasting damaged their homes. Residents have reported cracks in walls, windows and foundations as well as dust, noise and ground vibrations.

In August 2026, residents from villages in Mavindini Ward, organised under the Thwake Dam Blasting-Affected Community Committee, sought an independent review by the African Development Bank (AfDB).

The residents alleged that some properties had been left out of assessments and compensation. They also sought access to assessment reports, photographs, measurements, valuation records and estimates for repairs or reconstruction.

A project official said the dam's safety department invited competitive bids for an independent assessment of properties potentially affected by blasting. Agile Consulting was selected to conduct the exercise.

The official said the consultant assessed 330 households within a two-kilometre radius of the construction site and submitted its report to the project implementation team. A large proportion of those assessed were satisfied with the exercise, the official added, without giving a breakdown.

Ben Mwongela, a director at Agile Consulting, said the assessment reviewed blasting records, vibration data and compliance with regulatory standards.

The exercise also involved documenting households, classifying structural defects and preparing bills of quantities and cost estimates for repairs or reconstruction, he said.

The AfDB conducted a field mission to the project between September 21 and 25, with its report published on October 21, 2026.

The bank's team, led by project task manager Nancy Ogal, met residents whose homes had been affected by blasting and identified outstanding health, safety, environmental and social issues, including homeowner grievances.

The bank called for timely compensation and continued monitoring of the project's environmental and social performance.

During a stakeholder engagement visit to Mavindini in October, Korir said the government had secured additional funding after the project experienced cash-flow constraints.

“When we ran short of cash, we engaged with our development partners, and they allocated additional funding, and this money will now go towards total completion of the project,” he said.

In June 2026, the AfDB approved additional financing of €68.39 million to support completion of the first phase, alongside funding from the Kenyan government.

The bank said the financing would support engineering refinements and safety works, including strengthening foundations, raising the dam and constructing two additional saddle dams.

The project has four phases. The first involves construction of the dam, while the subsequent phases cover hydropower generation, water supply and sanitation infrastructure, and irrigation.

The dam is approximately 80.5 metres high and has a planned storage capacity of 688 million cubic metres.

Once the water supply component is operational, the project is expected to provide 150,000 cubic metres of treated water daily to an estimated 1.3 million people in Makueni and Kitui counties and Konza Technopolis in Machakos County.

The irrigation scheme is designed to cover 40,000 hectares, equivalent to about 100,000 acres of agricultural land.

The project is also designed to generate 20 megawatts of hydropower.

The water supply, irrigation and hydropower components require infrastructure beyond the dam structure, including treatment and distribution networks and power generation facilities.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”

The report shows how widespread the abuse is. “Twenty-six percent of women age 15–49 have ever experienced technology-facilitated violence from any perpetrator,” the report says, and 21 per cent experienced it often or sometimes in the 12 months before the survey. Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced it at the hands of a current, most recent or previous partner.

The burden is not spread evenly, the report states that Nairobi City records the highest lifetime experience from any perpetrator at 33 per cent, followed by Murang’a and Baringo at 32 per cent each.

“For abuse by an intimate partner, Homa Bay 36 per cent and Baringo 35 per cent lead, while in the 12 months before the survey Trans Nzoia topped the list at 31 per cent. At the other end, Mandera and Wajir report just 3 per cent, a figure that may say as much about silence as about safety,” the report says

The picture is similar among young people. A 2024 rapid study by the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, working with the UNFPA and Women Economic Empowerment, found that nearly 90 per cent of young adults enrolled in three Nairobi tertiary institutions had witnessed TFGBV, and 39 per cent had experienced it personally.

Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced gender violence committed by a current, most recent or previous partner, and 22 per cent did so in the past year. When women were asked who was responsible, the answer was blunt. Current husbands or intimate partners accounted for 61 per cent of perpetrators, former partners for 22 per cent and strangers for just 13 per cent.

Women who have never been married or had a partner face a different threat. For them, the most common perpetrators are strangers at 45 per cent, online attackers at 23 per cent and friends or acquaintances at 20 per cent.

Warning signs

Control is the common thread. The report describes such behaviours by a male partner as “important early warning signs that may escalate into violence within a relationship.”

Sixty-one per cent of ever-partnered women say their current or most recent partner has shown at least one controlling behaviour, and 27 per cent report three or more. Half say he has been jealous or angry when they spoke to other men, and 36 per cent say he insists on knowing where they are at all times. Others describe partners who demand passwords or read messages without consent.

Age and marital status matter. Technology-based gender violence is lowest among girls aged 15–19 at 10 per cent and highest among women aged 20–24 at 37 per cent. Forty-one per cent of divorced, separated or widowed women have experienced it, compared with 27 per cent of married women and 19 per cent of the never married.

Yet the digital rights advocate Cherie Oyier, a programmes officer at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), says the low figures in some places should not be read as safety. Much of the abuse happens where nobody can see it.

“Closed applications, meaning like WhatsApp, those are the ones that most people, intimate partners will usually use,” she says. “Even as you are scrolling the internet to look for these instances, we may not be able to catch it. But it does not mean that it is not happening or that it is at a lower level.”

Culture also silences women. “Most women are told just endure, this is what marriage is about,” Oyier says. “Sometimes they don’t know, it’s so overt, like it doesn’t come out clearly that this is abuse. So most of the times, it is not reported.”

Online, abuse has been turned into entertainment. “It has become banter,” she says. “Even the people who are experiencing it have trivialised it. It’s now ingrained to you, like this is something that happens, you should expect it actually. If you post a picture, one of the things that you are thinking about is what kind of comments am I going to get.”

A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: Not so fast: Court slams brake on ARA over wealth forfeiture
World.content:
Felix Mecha Nyakundi could not provide a plausible explanation for how he amassed his wealth.

The Court of Appeal has ruled that the government cannot go after a person’s wealth without prior investigations to establish reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property constitutes proceeds of crime.

In a landmark judgment, Justices Patrick Kiage, Jamila Mohammed and Nduma Nderi said that although it does not require a person to be charged for a crime for the Asset Recovery Agency (ARA) to come knocking, it bears the responsibility to link the wealth or cash to a crime.

World.title: Back to sender: Aisha Jumwa returns to UDA
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto welcome former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa has returned to President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA), ending a three-month political fallout with the ruling party that saw her join opposition outfit Wiper Patriotic Front and declare support for the one-term movement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

President Ruto welcomed Jumwa back into UDA at State House, Mombasa, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in a political reunion that could reshape alignments in Kilifi County and the wider Coast region as parties position themselves for next year's elections.

The reunion comes barely three months after Jumwa dramatically announced her departure from UDA, accusing the party leadership of frustrating her political ambitions and failing to support her quest for the Kilifi gubernatorial seat.

On July 30, 2026, Jumwa announced her resignation during a press conference at her Kakuyuni home in Malindi, saying her attempts to have her grievances addressed by the President had repeatedly been unsuccessful.

Among her concerns was what she described as humiliation and rejection within the ruling party, including an alleged incident in which she was chased out of State House during a meeting between Ruto and Coast leaders.

She also accused sections of the ruling coalition of undermining her gubernatorial ambitions, claiming that the political arrangements being pursued in Kilifi were designed to deny her an opportunity to contest for the county's top seat.

President William Ruto recieve former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Jumwa, who was among UDA's founding members and one of Ruto's most vocal mobilisers at the Coast during the 2022 elections, said her loyalty to the people of Kilifi outweighed her allegiance to any political party.

"My loyalty to the people of Kilifi will always be greater than my loyalty to any political party. The voice of the people of Kilifi is louder than the voice of UDA," she declared during her exit announcement.

Her departure marked a significant political shift, particularly given her central role in mobilising support for Ruto in the Coast region.

In August, Jumwa turned to the opposition, where she was warmly received by Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, who visited her at her Kakuyuni residence on August 14 alongside a delegation of party leaders, including Nyali MP Mohamed Ali, Kitui Senator Enoch Wambua and Wundanyi MP Danson Mwashako.

Kalonzo subsequently proposed Jumwa for the position of Wiper Deputy Party Leader, citing her political experience and influence, while also backing her ambition to contest the Kilifi governorship on a Wiper ticket.

Jumwa embraced the new political alliance, declaring support for the one-term movement and threatening to mobilise UDA supporters in Kilifi to deregister from the ruling party and join Wiper.

"We are the ones who registered UDA members in Kilifi, and we are embarking on a grassroots campaign to deregister them from UDA and join Wiper," she said at the time.

On September 8, she attended a meeting involving Wiper leaders and Coast gubernatorial aspirants, including Mohammed Ali and Danson Mwashako, as the party intensified efforts to expand its influence in the region.

However, the political alliance has now taken another turn, with Jumwa returning to the party she had accused of frustrating her ambitions.

Announcing her return, President Ruto welcomed the former Cabinet Secretary back into UDA, signalling renewed efforts to consolidate the ruling party's support in the Coast region.

"I look forward to working with her to advance the party’s transformation agenda at the Coast and across the country. We remain committed to uniting leaders and Kenyans around our shared vision of a united, inclusive and prosperous Kenya," the President said.

Her return comes as Ruto steps up political mobilisation in the Coast region ahead of the 2027 elections, with Kilifi emerging as an important battleground for competing political formations.

Jumwa's political journey has been characterised by shifting alliances. She previously served under the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), representing Malindi in Parliament before becoming Kilifi's first Woman Representative between 2013 and 2017.

She later became one of Ruto's key political allies and served in his Cabinet.

World.title: Buxton estate tensions escalate after county officials attacked
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

A dispute over the multibillion-shilling Buxton Point housing project in Mombasa turned violent after county officials were allegedly attacked while enforcing a government order suspending construction over outstanding contractual obligations.

The confrontation came a day after County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Lands, Housing, and Urban Development Mohamed Hussein ordered GulfCap Real Estate to halt all construction activities pending the resolution of disputes involving the county government and hundreds of former Buxton Estate residents.

The officials were reportedly pelted with stones as they attempted to serve the developer with an enforcement notice, with allegations that individuals linked to businessman Suleiman Shahbal were involved in the confrontation.

Hussein condemned the incident, saying attempts to intimidate government officers would not derail efforts to enforce the law and protect public interests.

"Let them bring goons, machetes, and stones if they want. I am not intimidated. I will execute my duties, and nobody will threaten me. The law must be followed, regardless of who you are or how much money you have," he said.

"We are here for the people of Mombasa, and we will ensure their rights are protected. Nobody is above the law," he added.

The November 10 enforcement notice, issued by County Director of Physical Planning Qassim Ali, directed GulfCap Real Estate to stop further development activities and obtain valid construction permits.

The notice, issued under Section 72(1) of the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, cited construction under a varied development plan without county approval and an ongoing dispute involving the developer, former tenants, and the county government.

The notice was reportedly received by the project's manager, Billy Okendo.

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county government and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units and commercial spaces developed in the first and second phases.

An addendum to the agreement signed on January 15, 2020, outlines the county's entitlement, with the allocation expected to be transferred upon completion of the second phase.

In a letter dated April 30, 2025, the county demanded 10 per cent of the proposed 1,800 housing units, translating to 180 apartments. The demand was renewed in February 2026, with the county seeking details on how the allocation would be implemented.

However, in correspondence dated September 22, 2026, the Department of Lands, Urban Planning and Housing expressed concern over what it described as the developer's failure to provide substantive responses to previous demands.

The county also questioned whether GulfCap had provided performance security equivalent to 10 per cent of the total construction cost for each phase, as required under the agreement.

It further demanded proof of payment of the Project Development Fee, which is payable in instalments as the project progresses.

The county said it had also raised technical and planning concerns during a meeting with the developer on April 15, 2026, including the need to address outstanding issues and resubmit the masterplan application.

But the dispute goes beyond the county's financial and contractual entitlement, with more than 500 former residents accusing the developer of failing to honour promises made when they were displaced in 2019.

John Tsuma, Secretary-General of the Buxton Tenants Welfare Association, said former residents had waited for more than seven years to return to their homes despite assurances that they would be prioritised once construction was completed.

"We are very disappointed by what happened. We had a meeting with the CECM, and he made it clear that all construction activities should stop until the outstanding issues are resolved. We did not go there to fight anybody. We wanted the directive implemented," Tsuma said.

He accused the developer of benefiting from the project while former residents continued to struggle to secure the houses they were promised.

"The developer has benefited from A to Z. He was given land by the county government, and the houses were sold off-plan. Yet, when it comes to fulfilling the promises made to former residents, we are still being taken around in circles," he said.

Tsuma said residents were not demanding free houses but wanted the affordable tenant-purchase arrangement they were promised before leaving the estate.

"We are not asking for free houses. We want the tenant-purchase arrangement that was promised to us so that we can pay for the houses and return to our homes," he said.

He also questioned why the developer had allegedly failed to surrender the county government's 184 housing units under the joint venture arrangement.

Mohamed Mzee Rubea, chairman of the evicted Buxton residents, said the money paid to the families during their displacement was a relocation allowance and not compensation for their homes.

He said the former tenants were given Sh240,000, with assurances that they would rent alternative accommodation for 12 months and return once the houses were completed.

"What we received was relocation money, not compensation for our houses. We were told to take the money and rent houses for 12 months and that we would be the first people to return once construction was completed. But here we are, more than seven years later, still waiting," Rubea said.

He said the original agreement involved 522 former tenants who were promised priority access to houses under the redevelopment.

Rubea added that each household was also promised Sh60,000 as a deposit towards acquiring a house under the tenant-purchase scheme.

"We were promised Sh60,000 as a deposit for those who would take up the houses. The developer later said the money would only be given to those who actually acquired the units. We are still waiting, and many of us have not received anything," he said. At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

He further claimed that the county had written to the developer in 2023, 2024, and 2025 seeking engagement over the outstanding commitments.

Mutua Mutia, another former resident, said the prolonged dispute had left families frustrated, especially after they were promised they would return within a year.

"I have lived in Buxton since I was a young boy. My firstborn child is now more than 30 years old, and the history of Buxton is one that pains us. We were evicted with the promise that we would return after one year, but today it is seven years and we are still struggling," Mutia said.

The former residents are also demanding the reconstruction of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) centre demolished to pave the way for the project, as well as the construction of a promised community social centre.

Hussein said the county had yet to receive either facility or its share of the housing project.

"The county has not received its 10 per cent share to date. There was an agreement that the demolished ECD centre would be reconstructed and handed over to the county, alongside a community social centre, but we have not received either," he said.

The first phase of Buxton Point delivered 584 housing units in 2023, while the second phase is expected to provide between 1,400 and 1,500 additional apartments. Completion had been scheduled for August 2027.

However, GulfCap Real Estate Chief Executive Officer Chris Ochieng defended the developer's position, saying 492 housing units would be handed over to buyers by December.

While urging the county to stop politicising the project, Ochieng warned that the ongoing controversy risks disrupting the project’s completion and affecting hundreds of workers who depend on it for their livelihoods.

He said the county government's 10 per cent share would be transferred upon completion of the project.

He also maintained that the developer had supported displaced residents by providing Sh240,000 for relocation and offering them preferential rates to purchase apartments.

Ochieng said the continued involvement of county officials in the dispute was unfortunate, particularly at a time when 492 homeowners are expecting to take possession of their houses in December.

He noted that the controversy was not only creating uncertainty among prospective homeowners but also threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of people employed directly and indirectly through the project.

“It is very unfortunate that Mombasa County officials are bringing politics into a national project. We have 492 homeowners who expect to take possession of their units by December. Beyond the homeowners, hundreds of people depend on this project for employment and their daily livelihoods,” said Ochieng.

He called on the county leadership to allow the project to proceed without unnecessary political interference, arguing that Mombasa has previously witnessed housing projects that stalled despite significant public interest.

World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses opposition divisions as 'polygamous family' rivalry
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County on November 8, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims of divisions within the Opposition, describing the disagreements among its leaders as normal sibling rivalry in a polygamous family, while insisting that the coalition remains united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua said the Opposition leaders were committed to working together to challenge President William Ruto, despite their differing opinions on the timing of selecting a joint presidential flagbearer and occasional disagreements among their political camps.

Speaking during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County, the former Deputy President likened the political differences to children from the same father competing for attention but eventually uniting whenever an external threat emerges.

“The Opposition is united to a man, and we have agreed that we will have a single presidential candidate. Everybody is committed, and we talk on a daily basis. The only challenge is normal petty problems,” he said.

He added that the disagreements should not be interpreted as a breakdown of the coalition, maintaining that such differences were healthy and expected in a broad political alliance.

“Ile shida kidogo ni ya boma, watoto wengi wa baba mmoja. Watoto huko ndani, oh, baba anakupenda kuliko mimi. Mbona ulinunua kiatu kabla mimi? Si hiyo ni kawaida kwa polygamous family?” he posed.

Gachagua said the bigger threat to Opposition unity was not necessarily disagreements among its principals but the conduct of their supporters, social media influencers and political bloggers, whom he accused of fuelling unnecessary tensions through insults and online confrontations.

He cautioned Opposition leaders against allowing overzealous supporters to dictate their political relationships, warning that unchecked political attacks could eventually weaken the coalition and undermine its common objective.

“If there is anything to separate us, it is our supporters and social media bloggers. Wanawakisha moto hakuna, watu wangu na wa Matiang'i wanatukanana na sisi tunakula breakfast pamoja,” he said.

He further claimed that some political influencers associated with his DCP party had been recruited and allegedly paid by individuals opposed to him to attack his leadership and the party.

Gachagua urged coalition principals to exercise restraint and avoid reacting to every provocation from supporters, insisting that political leaders must remain focused on the bigger picture.

“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: TV host Amr Adib comments on Egyptian state selling lands to pay off debt
World.content:
Egyptian media host Amr Adib on Sunday commented on the Egyptian government’s reliance on selling land to generate liquidity and address financial crises over the past few years – citing the Ras el-Hekma deal as an example.

He questioned whether the government could replicate this approach with new tracts of land in the Red Sea Governorate, given what he viewed as a lack of liquidity among investors and the mounting burden of external debt.

During his show “al-Hekaya” (The Story) broadcast on MBC Masr, Adib said that selling land has become a frequent solution the state has turned to in recent years in order to deal with a variety of issues.

“Over the last few years, every single crisis you faced was resolved only by selling land—just like what happened with Ras el-Hekma deal. In fact, two days before the Ras el-Hekma agreement was signed, the US dollar exchange rate was approaching LE 70”, he explained.

Help from the UAE

Revisiting the details of the Ras el-Hekma deal, Adib noted that the agreement provided the state with liquidity that helped it overcome financial pressures over the past two years.

He highlighted the role played by the UAE in making these funds available.

He remarked: “The Emirati leadership, with great generosity and solidarity, provided Egypt with a substantial cash sum—this was far beyond a typical corporate transaction. It is precisely what allowed the country to catch its breath over the last two years; otherwise, things might have spiraled downward.”

While acknowledging that the deal spurred economic activity, attracted investments, and generated tax revenue for the state, Adib emphasized that he still does not support relying on the sale of land as a recurring solution to crises.

“I am not in favor of selling land, even though some see no harm in it, even if the sale of Ras el-Hekma did indeed trigger economic activity, job creation, investment, and tax revenue for the state.”

Are there any investors?

Discussing the allocation of new land in the Red Sea Governorate, Adib recounted a conversation he had with a prominent businessman, who expressed concern about the difficulty of finding investors capable of purchasing the land, given the current liquidity crunch.

Adib quoted the businessman as saying: “Go ahead and invite someone to take this new land—nobody has any money, and those who do are holding onto every penny.”

The TV host linked these concerns to what he described as a global shortage of capital, saying: “The real issue is that there is simply no money—not in Egypt, not in the region, not in Europe, and not in America.
