World.title: PUP seeks dialogue ahead of national congress
World.content:
The opposition People’s Unity Party (PUP) is seeking to redefine its political approach by placing dialogue and national development at the centre of its agenda, ahead of its November 27-29 national congress in Ruwa.

The congress, to be held at Mutangadura, is expected to shape the party’s political direction, strengthen its internal structures and explore ways of contributing to Zimbabwe’s development without compromising its independence as an opposition party.

PUP president Herbert Chamuka said the gathering would provide an opportunity for members to reflect on the party’s role beyond electoral politics and identify areas where constructive political engagement could advance national interests.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Zimbabwe mining revenue projected to hit US$14,6bn in 2027
World.content:
Zimbabwe’s mining industry is projecting mineral revenue of US14,6billionin2027,upfromanestimatedUS13,6 billion this year, on the back of increased production and favourable international commodity prices.

However, high electricity tariffs, rising production costs, taxation and foreign currency shortages threaten to undermine the sector’s growth prospects and investment plans.

Mining executives remain optimistic about the industry’s outlook for next year, anticipating improved economic conditions, higher mineral output, increased capacity utilisation and relatively firm global commodity prices.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Zimbabweans divided over proposed e-hailing regulations
World.content:
Zimbabweans are divided over proposed government regulations for e-hailing services, with some welcoming measures to improve passenger safety and accountability while others fear the requirements could shut young people out of the industry and increase the cost of ride-hailing services.

The proposed Road Motor Transportation (E-hailing Services) Regulations, 2026, released by the Ministry of Transport and Infrastructural Development last week, have sparked debate on social media, with users questioning the necessity and potential impact of some of the requirements.

Among the most contentious proposals are provisions requiring drivers to be at least 21 years old, have held a valid driver’s licence for at least five years, possess a defensive driving certificate and obtain a special e-hailing driver’s permit.

This story is for NewsDay subscribers.

World.title: Africa: Facebook Exposure Is Behavioral Intelligence - Not Vanity Metrics
World.content:
guest column

In March 2026, as Nigeria implemented its measles-rubella vaccination campaign, the World Health Organization (WHO) Africa Infodemic Response Alliance was listening to what happened online. It revealed how people were receiving, questioning and interpreting the intervention in real-time.

This demonstrates why public health must take social media seriously as a source of behavioral intelligence to inform interventions. Today, people socialize, trade, network, find love and seek information on social media. Public health must meet people where they already are. As of April 2026, there were an estimated 5.79 billion social media user identities worldwide, equivalent to about 70% of the global population.

To be sure, social media metrics cannot prove behavior change, but that does not make them "vanity metrics." When interpreted carefully, they can provide valuable behavioral intelligence about how people encounter and respond to an intervention.

Facebook is a useful case study of using social media to promote health



With over 3 billion users globally, Facebook offers a useful case study. Its metrics broadly capture exposure and engagement. Impressions and reach tell us how often content was displayed and how many people saw it, while likes, shares and comments show how people engaged with it.

Impressions: How often did people encounter the message?

Imagine a public health program places banners promoting vaccination against HPV (human papillomavirus - the leading cause of cervical cancer worldwide) at strategic locations across Abuja, Nigeria, such as at major intersections, markets, schools, bus stops, pharmacies and health facilities. A mother might pass one while taking her daughter to school, encounter another on her way to the market and see the campaign again at a health facility.

Each encounter creates another opportunity for the message to register. But we cannot assume she read every banner, understood the message or subsequently vaccinated her daughter.

Facebook impressions work similarly. An impression is counted each time content is displayed on a screen, including repeat displays to the same person.

Reach: How many different people saw the message?

Using the same banner example, imagine one mother passes the same banner 20 times while another encounters the campaign only once. Impressions capture those repeated opportunities for exposure. Reach asks how many different people had an opportunity to encounter the campaign?

Facebook reach estimates the number of unique users to whom content was displayed. If an HPV vaccination post reaches 500,000 people, it does not mean they all paid attention, agreed with the message or vaccinated their daughters. But it tells implementers something important about the breadth of the campaign.

Likes: What resonates?

A 'like' is often the easiest metric to dismiss. Someone can like a post about cervical cancer screening without ever getting screened. Someone can 'like' one of my Keep Walking With Dr. Bill videos while remaining sedentary.

But a 'like' is nevertheless a small behavioral signal. Someone encountered something and decided it was interesting, agreeable, useful or emotionally resonant enough to respond.

When certain messages consistently generate stronger reactions, program teams should investigate why. Maybe personal stories resonate more than statistics; messages about protecting one's family perform better than messages emphasizing individual risk; or hopeful messages generate stronger reactions than fear-based ones.

A 'like' does not prove behavior change. But patterns of likes can generate hypotheses that programs can test and use to improve content.

Shares: What are people willing to pass along?

Now imagine a mother who sees one of the HPV vaccination banners around Abuja, takes a photo of it and shares it with her networks on WhatsApp. Her decision to share the message tells us she considered the information relevant or important enough to pass along to others.

A Facebook share is similar. Someone deliberately passes a post within their own networks, becoming an informal messenger for the intervention.

Again, sharing does not prove behavior change. But if certain HPV vaccination messages are shared far more frequently than others, implementers should ask why. Was it the language, messenger, image, practical information or way the content addressed a common concern?

Conversely, people may also spread misinformation and disinformation.

Comments: What are people telling us?

Comments may provide the richest behavioral intelligence of all. They allow people to ask questions, express fears, share experiences, challenge claims and sometimes spread misinformation.

Comments can transform social media communication into conversation.

As Project Director of VITAL, an HPV vaccination initiative in Nigeria, I saw this firsthand. Under one Facebook post, a caregiver asked, "What is the full meaning of HPV?" Another asked, "What is HPV vaccine and can someone about 20 take it?"

These were important questions. The first revealed a basic knowledge gap that could easily be overlooked by implementers accustomed to talking about "HPV." The second showed interest but also uncertainty about eligibility, a potential barrier to taking the next step.

Neither told us whether the individuals ultimately sought vaccination. But both told us what our audience needed from us. We answered their questions immediately and used those questions to improve content.

Close 

Measuring behavior change from social media interventions

To confirm if behavior changed as a result of VITAL, we conducted an end-of-project evaluation comparing caregivers exposed to the social media campaign with a control group.

Girls in areas exposed to the campaign had 48% higher odds of being vaccinated, while exposure was associated with an 8.9 percentage-point increase in the probability of vaccination compared with the control group.

The evaluation also helped us understand how the intervention may have worked. Exposed caregivers reported greater motivation to vaccinate, better knowledge of where to obtain the vaccine and greater perceived ease of getting their daughters vaccinated. Interestingly, the campaign did not significantly improve factual knowledge about HPV vaccination. It appeared to work more through behavioral drivers such as motivation and ability to act than simply by increasing knowledge.

As WHO's listening analysis shows, when public health listens carefully to what people are telling us on social media, reactions stop being vanity metrics and become intelligence for better action.

Dr. Ifeanyi Nsofor is a public health physician, behavioral science researcher, and global health equity advocate. His work focuses on applying behavioral science and digital approaches to improve health outcomes globally. He is Co-Founder of the Africa Behavioral Science Network.

World.title: Mozambique: Regulating Smarter - How Mozambique's Tobacco Control Bill Can Protect Public Health, Farmers and the Economy
World.content:
Mozambique is right to modernize its tobacco control framework. The 2007 law was written before products that do not burn tobacco existed. The Tobacco Control Bill is a chance to align the law with today's science and with international practice. But regulation based on evidence has to do more than lower smoking rates. It also has to weigh what each measure means for the farmers, retailers and workers who depend on the sector, and for the public revenues it generates.

Starting from the science

The evidence points to one distinction in particular. Most of the harm from smoking comes from combustion, so non-combusted products are better for adult smokers who would otherwise keep smoking. The Bill would reflect this if it recognized two categories within the definition of tobacco products: combusted tobacco products and smokeless alternatives.

A clear definition does more than tidy up the legal text. It gives the whole value chain, from growers to retailers, a predictable basis for planning. It also lets adult smokers see which products carry lower risk, which supports a gradual shift away from smoking. That shift will be easier to manage for the people whose incomes depend on tobacco if it happens in an orderly way and not through sudden disruption.



Science-based regulation also needs standards. Testing methods developed for cigarettes do not necessarily suit smokeless alternatives. Japan, the Philippines, New Zealand, Switzerland, Nigeria, South Africa and more than 20 other countries have already set dedicated technical standards for these products. If Mozambique requires product standards and pre-market notification, it protects consumers, makes it easier to tell legitimate products from illicit ones, and gives compliant businesses a level playing field. Legitimate operators then do not have to compete with unregulated products that avoid scrutiny and pay no tax.

Health warnings follow the same logic. Identical warnings on combusted and smokeless products suggest that the two carry the same risk, which discourages smokers from switching. Most countries already differentiate between them. Doing so in Mozambique would improve the accuracy of the information consumers receive, and it would do so without giving up the warnings themselves.

Protecting minors and adult smokers together

None of this weakens protection for young people. The Bill should require minimum age laws for all products, combusted and smokeless. It should also use standards on packaging, flavours and nicotine limits so that products do not appeal to minors, and set advertising and sales rules that keep marketing aimed at adult smokers. A regulation that restricts access for minors and gives adult smokers accurate information about lower-risk options serves public health better than one that treats all products as the same.

Where good intentions can cost livelihoods

Some provisions in the current draft would do less for public health than for the economy they affect. As drafted, the Bill would effectively prohibit the sale of tobacco in convenience stores and at duty-free outlets, even though these are legitimate products sold in these channels worldwide. Bans on sale and display are very hard to enforce and tend to push demand toward the illicit market. There the State loses revenue and no one controls the product. Most countries regulate the sale and display of tobacco and do not ban it.

Mozambique can do the same, using the regulatory tools already in the Bill, without cutting the number of retailers so far that it deprives them of income and makes it harder for adult users to reach smoke-free products. Duty-free sales deserve the same protection. These channels are transparent and work closely with customs against illicit trade, and they sustain airport revenues and retail jobs in travel hubs.

Farmers and sustainable development

The impact on farmers is not as visible as the effect on retailers, but it matters just as much. Tobacco supports 120 000 farming households (900 000 people) in 5 provinces and contributes 5% to Mozambique's export earnings. As worded, some provisions would prohibit activities that were never meant to promote tobacco or nicotine products, including agronomy programmes and charitable contributions. Agronomy programmes give growers technical support, improve yields and help them adopt more sustainable practices.

Banning them under the label of advertising could reduce farmers' productivity and incomes, and weaken the investment in sustainability initiatives, such as sustainable farming practices, reforestation or energy efficiency, that makes the sector more sustainable over time. The same broad wording could stop normal commercial transactions and conflict with constitutional principles on access to information. Narrowing it would keep restrictions on genuine promotion while protecting farmer support.

Close 

Retailers and consumers also need information. Smokeless alternatives are newer and less well understood than cigarettes. Allowing commercial communication and online information about them, with safeguards so that it reaches only adult smokers, helps make the transition credible. Advertising of all tobacco and nicotine products should still be tightly restricted, and the rules need to be workable for businesses and enforceable by the authorities.

A balanced path forward

The recommended amendments make tobacco control more precise and more enforceable, and they do not make it weaker. They keep protection for minors in place, give adult smokers accurate information and a path to lower-risk products, and avoid measures that cost farmers and retailers their incomes while giving the State little back. A Bill built on evidence, and open about what it means for the economy and rural livelihoods, is more likely to be respected, enforced and sustained.

World.title: Ghana: Bishops Denounce Galamsey, Drug Trafficking and Social Tensions
World.content:
Accra — Environmental damage caused by illegal mining, rising drug trafficking, growing indiscipline among students, and ongoing intercommunal conflicts and tensions are among the main concerns raised by the Bishops of Ghana in a statement issued at the end of their annual Plenary Assembly.

The meeting was held at the Divine Providence Pastoral Centre in Jamasi, in the Diocese of Konongo-Mampong, Ashanti Region, from November 3 to 14, 2026. Its theme was: "Communion, Participation and Mission: Preparing the Catholic Church in Ghana for Its 150th Anniversary in 2030".

The Bishops reiterated their concern over "the damage caused by illegal and irresponsible mining (galamsey), particularly the pollution of waterways, the destruction of forest reserves, the degradation of agricultural land and threats to public health".

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Bishops call for a state of emergency to be declared in the areas most severely affected by illegal mining, in order to promote responsible and environmentally sustainable mining practices.

"Regulatory bodies, security agencies, traditional authorities, religious leaders and all citizens must pool their efforts and resources to defeat this common enemy. The fight against galamsey must address networks of complicity, provide sustainable alternative livelihoods and promote community participation in environmental protection," they stated.

The recent seizure in France of three tonnes of cocaine from a Ghanaian port (see Fides, 23/9/2026) has once again drawn attention to the worrying scale of drug trafficking involving Ghana. The Bishops denounce "alarming levels of drug trafficking and substance abuse", which pose a threat to public health, family stability, the development of young people and national security.

"We urge the relevant authorities to step up intelligence-led law enforcement, including the application of appropriate sanctions and stronger border controls, while also strengthening public education and rehabilitation services. Families, schools and religious institutions must likewise reinforce preventive education and support for those affected by substance dependence," the Bishops said.

"Of particular concern is the growing indiscipline in some educational institutions, including even some of our own faith-based schools," the statement continued. The Bishops listed several incidents, including "violence, disrespect for authority, examination malpractice and acts of vandalism".

They also described as deeply distressing reports of sexual abuse involving minors in schools, allegedly perpetrated by adults entrusted with their care. Such behaviour, they stressed, undermines the educational mission of schools and the moral foundations of society. The members of the Episcopal Conference therefore called on the authorities to conduct thorough investigations into these cases.

Close 

"We are deeply troubled by the continuing conflicts and tensions between communities in various parts of the country, particularly in Bawku and Kalba-Gbinyiri," the statement continued. These long-standing conflicts (see Fides, 4/8/2025) have claimed lives and undermined social cohesion.

"While acknowledging the recent reduction in violence in these areas, we urge all parties to exercise restraint, renounce violence and embrace dialogue, reconciliation and peaceful coexistence," the statement said.

At the ecclesial level, the Episcopal Conference has also outlined a programme of preparation for the celebrations marking 150 years of evangelization in Ghana. Entitled "A Journey of Faith, Mission and Hope", the program will dedicate each of the next three years to one Person of the Most Holy Trinity, in preparation for the 2030 anniversary:

2027: Year of Jesus Christ, the Son of God;

2028: Year of the Holy Spirit;

2029: Year of God the Father.

The year 2030 will mark the culmination of the celebrations. The date for the official launch of the initiatives will be announced at a later stage.

World.title: Mozambique: Lam Warns of Possible Flight Disruptions Due to Jet Fuel Supply Constraints
World.content:
Maputo — The publicly-owned company Air Mozambique (formerly known as Mozambique Airlines, LAM) has warned of possible flight schedule changes as a result of temporary constraints in the supply of aviation fuel (Jet A-1).

The constraint may also contribute to reduction in the number of flights and potential cancellations in the coming days.

In a statement addressed to passengers, partners and the general public, the company said it had been notified by fuel suppliers of limitations in Jet A-1 availability, a situation that could affect the normal operation of its flights.

"The supply constraints could directly affect the company's regular flight schedule, forcing the airline to adjust departure times, reduce its transport capacity and, in some cases, cancel certain flights in the coming days", reads the document.



However, the company said it is working with fuel suppliers and aviation authorities to minimise the impact of the situation, because " operational safety and passenger assistance remain its main priorities."

The Company also advised passengers to check the status of their flights before travelling to the airport and to ensure that their contact details associated with bookings are up to date so they can receive timely notifications of any changes.

The airline also said affected passengers would be entitled to free ticket rescheduling or refunds, in accordance with its current passenger assistance policy.

Air Mozambique apologised for the "inconvenience the situation may cause and thanked passengers for their understanding and cooperation."

The warning comes amid recurring fuel supply difficulties, against a backdrop of disruptions in international markets, particularly those associated with the conflict in the Middle East.

In recent months, energy sector operators and business associations have expressed concern over logistical delays, rising transportation costs and increasing pressure on petroleum product supply chains.

World.title: Africa: Can the AU's Reparations Agenda Speak for All Afro-Descendants?
World.content:
analysis

African Union leadership on reparations should build a common platform for solidarity while supporting decentralised avenues of justice.

The African Union (AU) designated 2025 as the Year of Justice for Africans and People of African Descent Through Reparations, extending it into a 2026-2035 Decade of Justice. The agenda seeks to address historical injustices, including slavery, colonialism, apartheid and genocide, and encompasses Africans and people of African descent worldwide.

However, some Afro-descendant groups question whether the AU has sufficient diaspora consent and legitimacy to negotiate reparations claims on behalf of African Americans, Afro-Latin Americans, Afro-Europeans and others. Despite shared ancestry, these communities experienced different injustices and may have distinct priorities for reparations.



Since 2022, individuals and organisations in the United States (US) and Europe have questioned whether the process affords Afro-descendant communities meaningful influence or relegates them to secondary roles within a state-centred initiative.

In April 2026, the American Descendants of Slavery Advocacy Foundation New York chapter objected to foreign representation and efforts to subsume its reparations claims under a Pan-African agenda. It emphasised the injustices of slavery in the US and generations of dispossession. African American claims often focus on unpaid labour, Jim Crow, racial violence and exclusion from wealth building. Broader concerns include colonial dispossession, genocide, cultural destruction and wealth extraction.

The debate also includes African complicity in the slave trade implemented by the West. While leaders in Benin and Uganda and traditional leaders in Ghana and Cameroon have acknowledged and apologised for Africa's role, the AU has issued no apology.

The AU and Caribbean Community (CARICOM) have developed the proposed Global Reparations Fund, which Africa would manage. The fund raises questions about how to allocate resources equitably across distinct historical harms while avoiding bureaucratic obstacles and competing agendas.

This does not mean the AU's agenda lacks support from people of African descent. African cooperation with Afro-descendants on reparatory justice dates back to the 1993 Abuja Pan-African conference, and the 2001 United Nations (UN) Durban Declaration and Programme of Action against racism.

Institutional partnership grew in 2021 following the first joint summit with CARICOM. The AU drew on CARICOM's 10-point reparatory justice plan of 2014 and the March 2026 AU-backed UN resolution describing transatlantic slavery as the 'gravest crime against humanity.'

Although the US voted against the resolution, the Congressional Black Caucus endorsed it, praising the AU's leadership and suggesting that African American advocates and lawmakers would back a common global agenda.

Cooperation and support have progressed to direct participation. Ghana, whose President John Mahama is the AU's reparations champion, facilitated the appointment of Ron Daniels, National African American Reparations Commission convener, to Ghana's Global Advisory Council on Reparatory Justice in September 2026. Several US civil society organisations have called for closer alignment with the AU and CARICOM.

But the reparations agenda's credibility depends on building lasting solidarity between the AU and people of African descent. To achieve this, the AU should recognise all historical wrongs, affected communities, responsible actors and remedies, including those associated with African participation in the transatlantic slave trade. It requires respecting affected communities' authority to define and pursue their distinct claims.

There are signs that these concerns are being incorporated into the AU process. The AU's Economic, Social and Cultural Council 2026 forum called for the process to reflect affected communities' priorities. But it did not explicitly grant them a share in decision making.

A credible AU agenda should accommodate scrutiny rather than equating diverse claims with disunity. A coordinated and decentralised approach can draw on the contributions of the AU and people of African descent, strengthening the reparations process.

Jamaica illustrates how national initiatives can reinforce a common agenda. In September 2026, it petitioned King Charles III to refer questions concerning the legality of enslavement and Britain's reparatory obligations to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The petition, backed by CARICOM, could complement the AU proposal to seek an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice.

The contribution of people of African descent and diaspora organisations could strengthen reparations advocacy in Africa through research, public education, litigation, political mobilisation and transnational campaigning. They can engage Western governments, legislatures, universities, businesses and other institutions implicated in historical injustices.

This could raise public awareness, mobilise political support, press responsible institutions to acknowledge their roles and sustain demands for reparatory justice even when commitment within the AU or CARICOM weakens.

In turn, the AU can strengthen localised reparations efforts through diplomatic advocacy, shared principles, research support and coordination among states and affected communities. It can facilitate international legal initiatives and promote common standards for acknowledgement, compensation, restitution, rehabilitation and guarantees of non-recurrence.

Argentina shows how a common platform could amplify community claims. Afro-Argentine communities have long challenged the invisibility of their history. In 2023, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination welcomed Argentina's recognition measures but raised concerns about the lack of information on reparations for historical injustices.

Argentina's vote against the 2026 UN resolution, alongside the US and Israel, complicates the challenge. The AU's agenda and diaspora networks could enhance Afro-Argentine, community-led claims internationally, connect local advocates with wider movements and bring these demands into the public debate.

Close 

For African Americans, whose initiatives have largely been pursued at local and state levels, a stronger international movement could help elevate their claims to the federal agenda and encourage bipartisan engagement.

Questions about agency and representation do not stem solely from people of African descent - they also arise within Africa. In Namibia, Herero and Nama descendants, victims of the 1904-1908 genocide under German colonial rule, challenged the 2021 joint declaration under which Germany offered Namibia €1.1 billion in development aid over 30 years. They objected to their exclusion from negotiations and the lack of direct benefits to affected communities.

To make its reparations agenda a common platform, the AU needs a strategy to strengthen minority voices. The agenda will be judged by its ability to unite distinct struggles for justice while respecting affected communities' rights, priorities and agency.

World.title: Mozambique: Supreme Court Limits Number of Media Outlets That Will Cover Mondlane's Trial
World.content:
Maputo — Mozambique's Supreme Court has chosen specific media outlets to cover the trial of Venâncio Mondlane, former presidential candidate and leader of the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola).

Mondlane is accused of five criminal charges related to post-election mass demonstrations. The mass demonstration he called to protest against the alleged fraudulent results of the general elections held in October 2024 started peacefully but then degenerated into rioting.

He is accused of having committed the following crimes: public apology for a crime, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to crime, instigation and incitement to terrorism. Recently, the Council of State, the advising body to the Mozambican President, decided to lift Mondlane's immunity in order to allow him to stand trial.



According to Pedro Nhatitima, Supreme Court spokesperson, the trial, which was scheduled to start on November 17, has only 45 seats for media companies, namely: the publicly-owned Televisão de Moçambique (TVM) and Rádio Moçambique (RM) and the daily newspapers "Jornal Notícias and "Diário de Moçambique." It includes the private TV channels STV, TV Sucesso, TV Miramar, as well as the Portuguese News Agency (LUSA), and the Portuguese Radio and Television (RTP).

"Other national media outlets will have to compete for four rotating spots by registering via an electronic platform. For correspondents from foreign media outlets, only one spot has been made available, which is also subject to registration", the spokesperson said. He did not reveal the criteria for the appointment of companies in question.

He explained that the general public will have access to 10 spots, while other institutions and civil society organizations will also benefit from reserved places, including the country's Bar Association, the Support and Monitoring Group for the Implementation of the Phases (GAMIF), the Centre for Public Integrity (CIP), and the Centre for Democracy and Human Rights (CDD).

The limited spots for journalistic coverage of the trial are deemed as a measure to restrict press freedom in Mozambique.

According to Borges Nhuamirre, a senior journalist and member of the Mozambican chapter of the regional press freedom body MISA (Media Institute of Southern Africa), for the first time, the Mozambican justice system is set to try a high-ranking politician, while journalists face limitations in their coverage of the proceedings.

"This can only be described as a regression for press freedom and, by extension, freedom of expression. Excluding the press from covering an event of significant public interest, on the grounds of a lack of space, can only be defined as a restriction on freedom of the press and, consequently, on the freedom of expression of the Mozambican people, who constitute the audience for the media outlets that have been excluded", Nhamirre wrote in his Facebook account.

Close 

The Supreme Court spokesperson also revealed that the trial will be presided over by five judges and will involve two deputy attorneys general, a legal assistant, two defense attorneys, and a total of 29 witnesses.

World.title: Uganda: Why Uganda Faces 1,000mw Power Shortfall By 2030
World.content:
News Analysis — Uganda may face an electricity shortage of nearly one gigawatt by 2030 if the government does not speed up investments in power generation and transmission, according to the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development.

Uganda Radio Network has come across documents on projections that expose a growing challenge in the country's electricity sector.

According to the documents and testimonies, the country has installed generation capacity of approximately 2,100 megawatts; some licensed power projects cannot supply electricity to the national grid because of inadequate transmission infrastructure, while operational challenges are limiting the availability of existing plants.

The Ministry of Energy has openly stated that electricity demand is growing rapidly, threatening to outstrip available generation capacity within the next four years.



Local and international experts say the government must embark on developing generation and grid infrastructure at a competitive cost to beat the challenge.

According to Eng. Julius Wamala , the Assistant Commissioner for Generation at the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development, the country's peak electricity demand reached 1,400 megawatts in June 2026, against firm generation capacity of approximately 1,650 megawatts.

He said demand was projected to grow by 15 percent annually, creating an increasingly difficult balance between electricity supply and consumption.

"When you look at the scenario, the forecast, when you look at 2027, once 2012 go into red, if we don't do anything, we're going to negatives of maybe 130 megawatts. When you look at 2028, we may go into deficits of 270 megawatts. When you go to 2029, we're looking at almost 500 megawatts," Wamala said.

"And then when you look at 2030, we're looking at almost one gigawatt of a deficit. So I call upon everyone here; we need to work as a sector to see that we don't go into such a state.

"The projections raise questions about whether planned investments in generation and transmission can be delivered quickly enough to prevent a supply crisis, at a time when existing generation and transmission infrastructure are already facing constraints.

It is evident that the country is not fully utilising generation capacity already developed or licensed.

Dr Frank Ssebowa, former Chief Executive Officer of the Electricity Regulatory Authority, has indicated that expanding generation without corresponding investments in transmission infrastructure could leave the country with electricity it cannot deliver to consumers.

"There is no point generating a lot of electricity unless you get into that word. Ugandans don't want to hear about it. You know, deemed energy, have you ever heard of it? Many people don't like it," Ssebowa said.

He explained the problem with deemed energy, which arises when a power plant is ready to generate electricity but cannot supply it because the transmission infrastructure is unavailable.

" It means you have a plant sitting there; there is demand on the other side, but in between there is no transmission line," he said.

Ssebowa said the country had approximately 5,300 kilometres of transmission lines by the end of 2025 but needed considerably more to meet its electricity ambitions.

He questioned the sequencing of generation and transmission investments, arguing that infrastructure bottlenecks must be addressed before additional generation projects are developed.

"Sometimes we have good ambitions. Someone was telling me that we have these very good ambitions, but we don't look at the bottlenecks that are required to unlock these things," he said.

The Ministry of Energy has indicated that approximately 325 megawatts of licensed renewable energy projects are yet to become operational.

Wamala said some of the existing generation capacity was not being efficiently evacuated because of inadequate network infrastructure.

"Even the capacity we do have on the ground is not efficiently evacuated. So we are looking at doing grid reinforcements and upgrades," he said.

It has been noted that almost 80 megawatts of generation capacity in the Elgon region in eastern Uganda remains stranded.

The Ministry says the proposed 132-kilovolt Mbale-Bulambuli transmission line, being developed under the Independent Power Transmission model, is expected to help evacuate the electricity.

"That evacuation line, the Mbale-Bulambuli point line, the 132 kV line, has been promoted under the IPT model. I call upon our IPT partner; please, when we need your first tracking of that line," he said.

"As government, as ministry, we are there to help you in all ways to see that that line comes on board in whatever circumstances so that we can tap into that capacity in that region.

"The Ministry is also considering reinforcing substations in the Rwenzori region, where network limitations are preventing the evacuation of approximately 14 megawatts.

Other proposed interventions include optimising small hydropower plants, some of which spill water that could potentially be used to generate electricity. The ministry estimates that these improvements could unlock approximately 30 megawatts.

Wamala said incentives for cogeneration companies could also encourage them to supply up to 100 megawatts of additional electricity to the national grid.

Transmission constraints are not the only problem affecting electricity supply. Operational challenges at Karuma Hydropower Plant, which has an installed capacity of 600 megawatts, could also affect the country's ability to meet rising demand.

The government targets an increase in Karuma's utilisation from approximately 21 percent to more than 50 percent by 2027.

According to Eng. Isaac Arinaitwe, Chief Projects Officer at the Uganda Electricity Generation Company Limited (UEGCL), the plant's average generation had increased from approximately 65 megawatts in its first year of operation to nearly 300 megawatts in its third year.

He attributed the increase to rising electricity demand, which has seen Karuma absorb a substantial share of additional consumption.

However, he identified floating vegetation and debris from Lake Kyoga as a major challenge affecting the plant's operations.

"Those have particularly challenged our plant operations. The floating islands coming out of Lake Kyoga are a challenge with excess debris. And in effect, that may be a problem that we need to address if we have to make those 600 megawatts available," he said.

The problem resulted in significant generation losses last year.

"Last year, when we looked at our numbers, we lost about 4,800 hours of generation. Now, that is equivalent to losing a unit throughout the whole year. Or you could say, putting out the plant for a whole month," Arinaitwe said.

He warned that operational difficulties could become more serious as electricity demand increases.

"Because when you need the 600, we may not have the 600," he said.

UEGCL is considering capital investments to address the problem, alongside short-term removal of floating vegetation.

The company is also partnering with Ghana's Volta River Authority to learn from its experience managing similar challenges at the Akosombo hydropower installation.

He explained that the problem needed to be addressed beyond the electricity generation subsector because it was connected to broader water resource management challenges.

The experience raises questions about the resilience of Uganda's generation system, particularly its dependence on hydropower and the vulnerability of installations to environmental and operational disruptions.

Uganda's National Energy Compact targets an increase in operational generation capacity from approximately 2,099 megawatts in 2025 to 2,500 megawatts by the end of 2030.It also seeks to bring approximately 5,800 megawatts of additional generation projects to financial close within the same period.

However, the two targets represent different stages of project development. Financial close means that a project has secured the financing required to proceed. It does not mean that the plant has been constructed or commissioned.

The additional 5,800 megawatts are expected to become operational after 2030, meaning they may not help address the supply deficit projected for the end of the decade.

The Ministry is considering several interventions, including refurbishment of the Nalubaale and Kiira hydropower stations and development of additional generation projects.

Wamala said the government was undertaking feasibility studies for the proposed 400-megawatt Kiba Hydroelectric Power Station.

He also identified thermal and gas-fired generation as possible additions to the electricity mix and said the government was working to accelerate regional electricity interconnections to strengthen energy security.

Uganda last month launched its National Energy Compact, setting ambitious targets to expand electricity access, strengthen clean cooking adoption and attract investments in the energy sector by 2030.

The compact was launched by the African Development Bank Group and the Government of Uganda, through the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development.

The country plans to mobilise $17.7 billion in investments to achieve these objectives, including $9.4 billion in private-sector capital.

Attracting the investment will be important as the government seeks to involve private companies in developing transmission infrastructure.

However, the investment environment must be supported by infrastructure capable of accommodating additional electricity.

Wale Shonibare, Director of Energy Financial Solutions at the African Development Bank, said generation projects should be planned together with the needed transmission infrastructure and electricity demand to ensure they are viable.

Close 

"The new generation cannot deliver the intended benefits if the associated lines, substations, and customers are not ready," Shonibare said.

He said the government needed to coordinate electricity generation with industrial investments and the infrastructure required to serve new consumers."We have to align the demand and industrial investment with bringing on new generation capacity," he said.

Shonibare said the discussion should identify immediate decisions needed to translate Uganda's generation and transmission commitments into reliable electricity at competitive costs.

The Compact proposes competitive procurement, guarantees and blended financing to reduce investment risks. It also provides for private-sector participation in transmission infrastructure.

The government has introduced standardised power purchase agreements and implementation agreements and revised renewable energy feed-in tariffs in an effort to improve the investment environment.

The National Energy Compact provides a framework for addressing the electricity sector's challenges. It targets expansion of the distribution network, reduction of distribution losses from 16 percent in 2025 to below 12 percent by 2030, and increased access to electricity and modern cooking solutions.

The country's compact targets 85% electricity access and 50% access to clean cooking by 2030. It also aims to achieve approximately 2,500 MW of operational power generation capacity, with an additional 5,800 MW reaching financial close for commissioning after 2030.

Other targets include developing 2,712 mini-grids and increasing regional electricity exports to between 500 MW and 650 MW.

It also seeks to mobilise private investment and strengthen regional electricity trade.

The Compact provides for a Delivery and Monitoring Unit within the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development, which is expected to publish quarterly progress reports, annual delivery reviews and a digital results dashboard.

Dr. Frank Ssebowa said the sector needed to move beyond ambitious targets and identify investments and decisions that could be implemented immediately."I don't know how many, but I agree some steps must be done in the next six months," he said.

"I say this because 2030 is hardly two or three years away, and there are things that must be done if the government compact, if our Ugandan energy compact, is going to be met."

World.title: Cape Verde: Neves Wins Second Term As Cape Verde's President
World.content:
José Maria Neves has won a second five-year term as Cape Verde's president, according to provisional results from Sunday's election.

The African Party for the â Independence of Cape Verde candidate won 63.8 percent of the vote after ballots were counted at most of the 1,300 polling stations at home and abroad.

The same results showed that his main challenger, Joana Rosa, received 31.6 percent of the vote. The four other candidates claimed less than 1 percent each.

Rosa concedes defeat

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Rosa, 61, from the centre-right Movement for Democracy party, conceded defeat and said she had congratulated Neves.

"When I embarked on this journey, I knew I had to be prepared for any outcome. I also said throughout the campaign that, as the first woman in Cape Verde's history to run for president, my candidacy would help pave the way for greater equality in our society," she said.

As part of his victory celebrations, Neves pledged to work for Cape Verdeans on the island as well as abroad.

"You can count on me to promote freedom, democracy and the rule of law, and to inspire the Cape Verdean nation towards inclusive and sustainable growth," he said.

The national electoral commission is expected to announce official results this week.

'High abstention rate'

Turnout appeared to be low on Sunday, with less than one-third of the 419,000 eligible voters participating, according to the results announced on state-owned television.

Neves said the high abstention may have been caused by the movement of Cape Verdeans between the islands.

"We therefore need to update the electoral registers," he added. "At the same time, we should modernise the electoral system through the introduction of electronic voting."

At least 63 migrants feared dead after boat found off Cape Verde

Cape Verde, a former Portuguese colony situated more than 600km west of mainland Africa, is home to around 500,000 people, with a larger number of Cape Verdeans living overseas, mainly in the United Staes and Portugal.

Hybrid presidential-parliamentary model

Cape Verde operates under a hybrid presidential-parliamentary model. The prime minister heads the government while the president retains significant powers including veto authority over legislation.

During the election campaign, the main candidates promised to implement measures to improve air and sea travel between the 10 islands in the archipelago and also to build accommodation for tourists.

They also vowed to address other concerns such as the increased cost of living, fuel prices and youth unemployment.

Close 

Since the end of the Covid-19 pandemic many young Cape Verdeans, including graduates and those with professional training, have emigrated and continue to move abroad, causing a labour shortage.

World.title: WWE's Charlotte Flair reflects on Royal Rumble wins ahead of 2027 event, feels 'pressure' after making history
World.content:
Charlotte Flair has accrued an impressive list of accolades during her time in WWE. She’s a 14-time world champion, a Triple Crown champion and a Grand Slam champion.

What is arguably more impressive than those feats is that she is the one and only two-time women’s Royal Rumble winner. She won the match in 2020 and defeated Rhea Ripley at WrestleMania 36 for the NXT Women’s Championship. In 2025, she won after coming all the way back from a devastating injury but fell short of capturing the title against Tiffany Stratton at WrestleMania 41.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"The first Royal Rumble that I won in Houston, it definitely was a ‘this is my division’ (moment)," Flair told OutKick Dropkick in a recent interview. "I actually could not believe I won. It was such a surreal moment. I felt it in all my being.

"But when I came back the second time in 2025, after my knee injury, I very much was a shell of myself. Hadn't been in the ring in a year, year and a half. Were people gonna remember ‘The Queen?’ Even with my accolades, ‘cause I always think, you know, you're just as good as your last match. So, I was very nervous. Wasn't sure what the reception was gonna be, but knowing that I had crossed the finish lines in terms of when I was away, being back in that ring was all that I thought about. So, all that preparation to get back and how hard it was to get back to me on a professional and personal level meant the world to me."

The Royal Rumble will take place on Feb. 6, 2027, at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona. It’s the 40th annual event and it will be the 10th edition for the women of the WWE roster. Tickets for the premium live event will go on sale Wednesday.

Flair said she is feeling the pressure since she’s won the match twice already.

"For me, I feel like because I have won two, there's even more pressure. First woman to win two, are the odds forever in my favor? Could I win three? But also in the Rumble, it's always past, present, future. I'm looking forward to seeing which NXT stars come up and make their debut in the Rumble. I think that's always so exciting, and who's gonna show up, show out, make a name for themselves, it's an opportunity.

"But also, Royal Rumble is so important because it gives two people the opportunity to punch their ticket to WrestleMania, which is our biggest show of the year, guaranteeing title match opportunities, and to me it doesn't get any bigger in our business than holding the WWE championship."

Flair, who’s the daughter of pro wrestling legend Ric Flair, recalled some of her favorite moments she’s seen outside of her own victories.

Ric Flair won the 1992 Royal Rumble from the No. 3 spot. Charlotte conceded it was one of her top moments.

"I know this is a lame answer, but when my dad won the Rumble from the three spot, with the ‘a tear in my eye’ promo, will forever be such an iconic Rumble win, in my opinion, and it's not just 'cause he's my dad."

World.title: Seattle mayor orders park named for American president renamed
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson has ordered a city park named after President Andrew Jackson to be renamed to better fit "the values of our city."

The city argues that Jackson's legacy includes policies that forcibly displaced Native American peoples from their ancestral lands. Wilson directed the Seattle Parks and Recreation to begin a community renaming process on Monday. The 160-acre Jackson Park plays host to the Jackson Park Golf Course.

"We’ve heard from community members who want to change the name of Jackson Park, and now is the right time to move this conversation forward. With new light rail connections and opportunities to make the park more accessible and welcoming, we should have a park that reflects the values of our city," Wilson said in a statement.

WASHINGTON AG'S OFFICE INDICATES IT WILL DEFEND GIRLS' SPORTS BALLOT MEASURE AFTER ACLU SUES TO BLOCK IT

"I’m directing Seattle Parks and Recreation to begin a community naming process to find a name that better reflects this place, its history, and the people who enjoy it," she added.

The renaming effort comes just days after Wilson also backed an effort to block a girls sports initiative that overwhelmingly passed a statewide vote.

SEATTLE MAYOR BACKS EFFORT TO BLOCK GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE THAT PASSED IN 36 OF WASHINGTON'S 39 COUNTIES

Wilson said last week that she supports the Seattle School Board's unanimous vote to pursue legal action against Initiative 638 — which would enforce separation of boys and girls in K-12 sports in Washington state.

Voters passed the measure by a 13-point margin last week, and it won in 36 of the Evergreen State's 39 counties. But after deliberating behind closed doors Monday, the Seattle School Board voted publicly to authorize potential legal action against the measure without hearing public testimony.

"Last night, the Seattle Public Schools Board of Directors voted to authorize legal action regarding Initiative 638. The Board's decision reflects concerns shared by educators, families, community leaders, and the City of Seattle about the measure's impact on student privacy, safety, dignity, and equitable access to educational opportunities," Wilson said in a statement last week.

Fox News' Matt Calkins contributed to this report.

World.title: After the blue wave, what happens to education policy and parental rights protections in flipped states?
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Democrats' sweeping midterm victories in several key governor's races could usher in a new era for education policy, raising urgent questions about the future of the parental rights laws Republicans spent years cementing after the COVID-19 pandemic.

While incoming Democratic governors in states like Ohio, Iowa, Georgia and Texas are unlikely to dismantle every parental notification or curriculum transparency law overnight, education battles in those states are poised to shift sharply — particularly around school choice, state takeovers, and public school funding.

Since the pandemic, contentious school board meetings have fueled a nationwide movement of parents demanding greater oversight of classroom instruction and challenging sexually explicit or LGBTQ-related books in school libraries.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

Conservative groups capitalized on that momentum. Beginning in 2022, the Virginia-based American Principles Project (APP) entered local school board races in Florida, airing attack ads criticizing critical race theory and gender ideology. Alongside groups like the 1776 Project PAC, APP helped conservatives flip school board seats across Florida after Gov. Ron DeSantis broke precedent by actively endorsing local school board candidates who backed his pro-parent agenda.

Republican governors soon followed up with statewide legislation establishing "Parents' Bills of Rights" and curriculum transparency mandates:

FLORIDA'S DESANTIS DESCRIBES GOP MIDTERMS WIPEOUT AS 'CLOSE TO AN EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' FOR REPUBLICANS

Ohio: In January 2025, outgoing GOP Gov. Mike DeWine signed House Bill 8 into law, prioritizing parental involvement over school districts regarding students' mental, emotional, and physical health. The law requires districts to notify parents of any changes to a student's health services or monitoring — including requests to identify with different pronouns or a gender not aligned with their biological sex — and prohibits staff from discouraging parental involvement in critical health decisions.

Iowa: In 2023, outgoing GOP Gov. Kim Reynolds signed sweeping legislation banning classroom instruction on gender identity and sexual orientation through sixth grade, removing books depicting sex acts from school libraries (with an exemption for religious texts), and requiring schools to notify parents if a student asks to use different pronouns or names. (The 8th U. S. Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld enforcement of the law in April 2026 following a legal challenge.)

Georgia and Texas: Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp signed a Parents' Bill of Rights in 2022, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott signed a package of four "parent empowerment" bills in 2023, including strict bans on sexually explicit materials in school libraries.

DEPT OF ED PUSHES AHEAD WITH EFFORTS TO DISMANTLE FEDERAL BUREAUCRACY AFTER BLUE WAVE

Now, voters in those four states have elected Democratic governors: Amy Acton in Ohio, Rob Sand in Iowa, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Gina Hinojosa in Texas.

Even if those incoming governors want to roll back existing parental rights laws, several will face steep legislative hurdles. Acton, Sand and Bottoms will still contend with Republican-controlled legislatures capable of blocking repeals, though Democrats made legislative gains in Texas and Georgia during the midterms.

Notably, none of the four governors-elect campaigned explicitly on repealing their states' Parents' Bills of Rights. Instead, they largely sidestepped cultural flashpoints in favor of attacking GOP-backed private school voucher programs and calling for increased public school funding.

In Ohio, Acton has vowed to overhaul the state's universal voucher expansion, which her campaign argued "funnels billions of Ohio taxpayer dollars to private schools and wealthy Ohioans with no accountability."

In Iowa, Sand has similarly targeted Reynolds' universal school choice law. "Iowa’s public schools have been consistently underfunded while hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars are increasingly funneled into the state’s unaccountable private school voucher program," his campaign stated.

In Texas, Hinojosa, a former school board president and state representative, used her victory speech to pledge a reversal of Abbott's school choice expansion and state district takeovers.

In Georgia, Bottoms' view on vouchers wasn't clearly expressed during the campaign, but the state's Democratic Party has been hostile to school choice measures in favor of greater public school funding. Her education policy during the campaign focused on measures like expanded universal pre-K and teacher pay raises.

DEMOCRATS COULD CREATE 'ANGRY' 'SINGLE-ISSUE' VOTERS IN 2028 IF THEY REMOVE SCHOOL CHOICE, CEO WARNS

"This is a victory for the parents of Texas. We are taking our children’s education back from a government that has failed them," Hinojosa told supporters. "Schools will not be taken out of our control. They will not be shuttered or suffocated... On day one, I will fire [Texas Education Agency Commissioner] Mike Morath, and we will work tirelessly to repair the damage of the Texas voucher scam, and end an era in which our schools are sold for parts."

Their pushback comes as major urban districts navigate shifting enrollment dynamics. In February, for example, the Houston Independent School District's state-appointed board voted unanimously to close or consolidate 12 campuses ahead of the 2026–2027 school year, citing enrollment declines alongside the state's expanding school choice framework.

Still, conservatives warn that Hinojosa's legislative record signals a threat to parental protections in Texas.

During the campaign, Abbott's team ran ads featuring Moms for Liberty activist Denise Bell arguing that Hinojosa's policies would undermine parents and jeopardize fairness in girls' sports.

"Gina Hinojosa voted in favor of schools transitioning students behind parents’ backs, for sex change surgeries for kids, and for boys competing in girls’ sports—all radical policies that Governor Abbott has fought against time and again," Abbott’s campaign said in a statement accompanying the ad. "Parents should be the primary decision makers in their children’s lives."

Meanwhile, the Trump administration is signaling it will use federal leverage to keep parental rights policies intact regardless of statehouse flips. Last year, President Donald Trump signed executive orders tying federal education funding to strict anti-discrimination compliance and prohibiting diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs in schools.

Following the midterm results, the U.S. Department of Education told Fox News Digital it plans to escalate enforcement — including investigating school districts accused of concealing a student's gender transition from parents.

"The Department will double down on its efforts to restore parental rights, return education to the states, and open more higher education pathways for students," an Education Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

TEXAS DEMOCRATS PUT DEI BACK ON AGENDA AFTER SWEEPING TO POWER

Defending Education, which has been the tip of the spear of the parental rights movement, investigating civil rights violations and exposing far-left elements of curriculum across the country, told Fox News Digital that the federal government already has strong laws, like FERPA and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA), to protect parental rights.

"These give the administration solid footing to make sure parents aren’t being kept in the dark about what’s happening at school, can review curriculum, and can opt out of invasive surveys on topics like gender ideology," said Paul Runko, senior director of strategic initiatives at Defending Education.

He added: "The Justice Department has also stepped up, using investigations and lawsuits to push back against state and local school boards that cross the line."

Runko explained further that civil rights protections would allow parents to continue to speak out in public forums.

"On top of that, the First and 14th Amendments protect a parent’s right to speak up and decide how to raise their children. Recent federal court wins by parents in Ohio, Maryland and California send a clear message that school districts should think twice about ignoring parental rights," he said.

None of the newly elected governors responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

World.title: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson faces audit calls after CFO quits over 'financial integrity' concerns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Chicago’s chief financial officer, who formerly worked for a top credit ratings bureau, resigned Friday citing financial integrity concerns, casting a shadow over the fiscal management of progressive Mayor Brandon Johnson amid a fight over the FY-2027 budget.

Chicago CFO Ashlee Gabrysch served only three months before the onetime Fitch Ratings executive stepped down, saying she could no longer meet her professional obligations under the conditions of her employment, according to a resignation letter obtained by the Chicago Tribune.

"The chief financial officer’s statements about the city’s finances are relied upon by investors, rating agencies, City Council, and taxpayers, and they must be complete and accurate," Gabrysch wrote, according to the Tribune.

"I am not able to fulfill those obligations under the conditions in which I have been asked to serve."

Johnson did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment, but his press secretary accused Gabrysch of being "largely absent" during key parts of the next budget’s creation process.

CHICAGO MAYOR CALLS ICE RAIDS ‘TERRORISM,’ SAYS TRUMP'S AMERICA APPEARS AS ‘IF THE CONFEDERACY WON’

The mayor's office also accused Gabrysch of improperly directing a $75 million payment to city pension funds before the required legal procedures had been completed, saying it would refer the matter to Chicago's Office of Inspector General for review.

The Tribune recounted recent events in the budget process involving Gabrysch, including that she disagreed with Johnson over assertions about the size of the city’s deficit.

In September, Johnson announced that the Windy City faces a projected $882 million budget shortfall in 2027, which local media described as smaller than a typical election year and lighter than the $1.15 billion deficit projected in 2025. The city holds its elections in odd years.

"We have difficult and consequential decisions ahead of us as we work to address the structural financial challenges that have confronted Chicago for decades," Johnson said at the time, according to Chicago’s PBS affiliate.

However, according to the Tribune, Johnson claimed the true figure is now $662 million, "adjusted" in concert with planned borrowing to help fund settlement amounts involving police officers.

CHICAGO MAYOR CALLS DOGE AN ‘ACT OF WAR’

Gabrysch challenged that accounting during budget hearings, arguing that the settlement expenses should remain part of the deficit and that borrowing to pay them amounted to a temporary fix rather than a lasting solution.

While the administration maintained that 76% of its budget measures addressed underlying financial problems, Gabrysch calculated the figure at just 56%, according to the Tribune.

Alderman Marty Quinn, D-Midway, questioned Johnson’s handling at the time, according to the paper, saying he was "not surprised that the mayor may be a little disingenuous here, that seems to be his normal course."

Gabrysch also stopped short of calling Johnson's proposed $17.6 billion budget balanced during an October City Council hearing, arguing that the city needed to demonstrate progress toward reducing future deficits, according to Crain's Chicago Business.

City Comptroller Michael Belsky maintained that proposed revenues matched expenditures, while acting Budget Director Jonathan Ernst defended the administration's calculations and its plan to borrow roughly $480 million to cover legal settlements.

Gabrysch warned that the city anticipated issuing $350 million in settlement-related bonds in 2027, with an estimated $190 million in interest costs over seven years, according to Crain's.

CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Her resignation prompted Council Finance Committee chairman Pat Dowell, D-South Loop, to call for an independent audit.

The departure adds to a wave of turnover in Johnson's financial leadership, including two previous CFO departures this year and the resignation of the city's budget director in August. The upheaval comes as Chicago grapples with mounting financial obligations and credit-rating downgrades.

World.title: New Orleans cruise ship disaster timeline reveals tanker's troubled past and frantic final minutes
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A timeline of Friday's horrific crash between a cruise ship and tanker in New Orleans reveals how the massive vessel lost steering control just minutes before slamming into a docked cruise ship, raising questions about the tanker's troubled safety history.

The collision between a cruise ship and tanker caused the passenger vessel to take on water before capsizing around 22 minutes later, which sent passengers and crew scrambling to get off the ship. While 32 people were hospitalized, no deaths were reported. Federal investigators are working to find out what caused the tanker's steering failure.

Here's a timeline of the New Orleans boat crash on Friday (All in Central Time):

NEW ORLEANS BOAT CRASH CALLED ‘MIRACLE ON THE MISSISSIPPI’ AS EVERYONE IS ACCOUNTED FOR, OFFICIALS SAY

10:30 a.m.: American Heritage docks in New Orleans

The American Cruise Lines vessel arrived near the Port of New Orleans after completing a Mississippi River cruise that lasted several days. The boat was docked for two hours before the collision and was in the process of beginning to let passengers disembark, according to officials. Around 200 people were on the ship.

11 a.m.: Tanker begins voyage upriver

The Atlantic Asphalt, which carried 19 crew members and a local river pilot, departed from Lower 9 Mile Anchorage, located near Mississippi River mile marker 83.

Its destination was an oil facility in Reserve, Louisiana.

12:26 p.m.: Tanker suffers major steering malfunction

According to the NTSB, the tanker suffered a steering casualty which left its rudder fixed in the starboard position, causing the vessel to make a turn toward the Mississippi River's east bank.

It's not yet clear what caused the steering malfunction.

Between 12:26 and 12:28 p.m.: Tanker crew issues emergency commands

According to the NTSB, crew on the tanker issued various emergency commands such as a whistle, requests for assistance, commands to deploy anchors, emergency orders and radio warnings before colliding with the American Heritage.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

12:28 p.m.: Tanker crashes into American Heritage cruise ship

The Atlantic Asphalt collided with the American Heritage cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans.

Just after 12:28 p.m.: American Heritage begins taking on water

Shortly after the tanker crashed into the American Heritage, it began taking on water as passengers and crew tried to evacuate. The ship also began to tilt toward the river's middle course.

TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED

A massive rescue operation consisting of Coast Guardsmen, police, firefighters and other first responders also began, with other tugboats and commercial vessels also coming to assist.

12:50 p.m.: American Heritage capsizes

The American Heritage cruise ship capsized as it rolled onto its side and became partially submerged. According to the NTSB, the vessel capsized 22 minutes after the tanker first hit it.

Friday afternoon: All passengers and crew accounted for

All passengers and crew on the cruise were accounted for, with 32 people taken to local hospitals for non-critical injuries.

Friday's collision wasn't the first time the tanker came under scrutiny for safety issues.

The Atlantic Asphalt tanker was cited in June for faulty electrical wiring in the ship's pump room, according to records obtained by NOLA.com. In 2024, inspectors who boarded the ship found its rescue boats weren't prepared to launch effectively in an emergency.

In 2024, inspectors logged two breakdowns in the ship's navigation systems. In September 2024, the vessel "experienced loss of communication between the bridge and main engine," according to Coast Guard officials in Wilmington, Delaware.
