World.title: Radical activist with decades-old socialist ties emerges behind Dems' under-the-radar midterm operation
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A coordinated social media operation aimed at influencing voters ahead of the midterm elections was led in part by an 80-year-old socialist organizer who spent decades helping build the modern left's activist infrastructure, according to tax records reviewed by Fox News Digital.

"The Republicans never figured out what we were doing," political commentator Van Jones said earlier this month on CNN's "The Source" with Kaitlan Collins. "There’s something called the American Accountability Network: tens of thousands of online humans, not bots, coordinated to make the affordability message a winning message online … Don’t get mad at me. I was given permission to reveal this."

The American Accountability Network (AAN), which incorporation documents show was founded in early 2025, is an online activist organization that recruited both large content creators, as well as everyday Americans, and tasked them with posting, sharing and otherwise amplifying rhetoric that framed Democrats as the party of affordability — a message that exit polls suggest resonated with the electorate.

Tax documents identify the woman behind the effort as Heather Booth, AAN’s president and an 80-year-old self-described "socialist feminist" who has been deeply involved in far-left activism since the anti-war movement of the Vietnam era.

DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE

Podcaster and former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino didn't buy into Jones' claims that AAN played a large part in determining the midterm elections earlier this month.

"Are influencers really influencing you? Or are the influencer days numbered as people wake up to the grift. Folks, I'm leaning more towards the latter," Bongino said on the Nov. 9 episode of his show. "I don't buy any of this. ... Maybe they had some effect in certain places. My humble opinion, I don't believe it ... I'm not sure the social media ecosystem had the effect Van Jones is saying it does. I heard the same thing, the exact same argument was used to say Donald Trump stole the election through Russian Facebook ads. And that was crap, too."

"Van is selling himself for the next campaign, I'm not buying it," Bongino told Fox News Digital.

Booth's decades of socialist activism are documented extensively in the historical record, including in her own correspondence. In the mid-1970s, Booth and her husband were key allies of the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee, a precursor to the Democratic Socialists of America, helping the fledgling organization build ties with community groups and draft a high-profile manifesto aimed at pushing the Democratic Party economically leftward, according to letters Booth wrote in 1975.

Booth also disclosed in an interview that she was a founding member of the Chicago chapter of the Women’s International Terrorist Conspiracy from Hell (WITCH), what she described as a "guerilla theater" group that staged provocative protests ranging from releasing mice at a bridal fair, staging mock curses against financial institutions and using hair and nail clippings in a mock hex protesting the dismissal of a women’s liberation activist who advocated overthrowing capitalism from the University of Chicago.

In a 1972 socialist feminist manifesto, Booth and her co-authors advocated for disarming police, publicly funded abortions and significant redistribution of wealth, while describing capitalism as an "institutionalized form of oppression."

Booth’s late husband, whom she worked closely with throughout her career, was no less prolific or radical than she was.

RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY

Paul Booth is credited with authoring portions of the Port Huron statement, which framed American anti-communism as corrosive to democracy, proposed transferring certain national powers to international institutions as part of disarmament and called for greater democratic control of economic life.

Booth’s husband also served as national secretary of Students for a Democratic Society, a leading New Left organization that fractured in 1969 amid ideological infighting, with one faction giving rise to the militant Weather Underground. While Heather was also an SDS member who left before the Weathermen seized control, not all of her activism was legally above board.

In interviews, Booth has admitted to founding Jane, or the Abortion Counseling Service of Women’s Liberation, an organization that helped women obtain over 11,000 underground abortions before the Supreme Court mandated that the practice be legal nationwide in 1973. Law enforcement arrested seven women working for the organization in 1972 for abortion and conspiracy to commit abortion, though the charges were dropped following the court’s decision.

As Jane’s operations shuttered, Booth turned to a new aim: training the next generation of activists. Booth helped establish Midwest Academy, which incorporated in 1972 and began offering general organizing training in 1973, building an institution that says it has trained more than 50,000 organizers.

AAN, Jones and Booth did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital.

While the individuals who lead AAN through their midterm messaging campaign are clearly disclosed in tax forms, the funding behind the effort is more opaque. Nonprofit tax disclosures operate on a roughly one-year delay, meaning that financial information is only available for its 2025 tax year when most of its election-related activities occurred in 2026.

MEMBER OF LARGEST TEACHERS UNION IN US CLAIMS ORG IS 'NO LONGER FOCUSED ON CHILDREN,' ONLY 'POLITICAL POWER'

What tax documents do exist, however, begin to paint a picture of the financial forces behind AAN’s social media push.

Of the roughly $280,000 AAN reported raising in 2025, $200,000 came from the American Federation of Teachers, the second-largest teachers labor union in America, according to its LM-2 disclosure. Receiving approximately 70% of its funding from a labor union during its inaugural year of operation was not AAN’s sole link to organized labor, however.

Midwest Academy, where Booth still serves as chairwoman, has done considerable work training union officials over the course of its history. Union financial disclosures show that labor unions such as the National Education Association, AFL-CIO, American Federation of Teachers (AFT) and the Service Employees International Union (SEIU) have collectively pumped roughly $2 million into the organization Booth founded since 2020.

Booth also directed the AFL-CIO’s healthcare campaign in 2008, helped run SEIU unionization efforts and her late husband was a longtime American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) organizer and leader, according to her website and oral histories about her life.

'DARK MONEY’ GROUP ACCUSED OF 'SCHEME' TO TIP ELECTION IN FAVOR OF DEMOCRATS, MANIPULATE GOP VOTERS

The 70s-era radical was not the only AAN leader to have ties to the labor movement.

Rio Tazewell, the director of the organization, has served on working groups alongside union leadership and Reggie Hubbard, identified as a leader on incorporation documents, works with major unions on education efforts and has a board seat at a union-backed nonprofit. AAN’s public-facing website, in fact, identifies the AFL-CIO, AFT, SEIU and AFSCME as organizations it has worked with.

AAN partnered with an organization called DemCastUSA, which has received $613,500 from the SEIU since 2022, to promote at least some of its social media amplification efforts. Former Democratic Sen. Doug Jones, who received significant support from organized labor during his political career, sits on DemCastUSA’s board.

As AAN worked to amplify Democratic messaging across social media ahead of Election Day, Americans viewed Republicans as more politically extreme than Democrats, according to Gallup polling. The survey found that 59% of Americans considered the Republican Party too extreme, compared with 43% who said the same of Democrats. AAN’s social media boosting strategy sought to reinforce favorable perceptions of Democrats and pin Americans’ economic anxiety on GOP policies, though the polling does not establish whether the campaign influenced those views.

Alongside DemCastUSA, AAN ran a program called "Amplifier Army" that aimed to give left-of-center voices a privileged slot in social media algorithms by coordinating interactions that would give such posts a larger reach.

"Together, we're building a network of organizers, creators, and everyday people who use their social media to flood the feed with the content and calls to action that move this fight forward — at the inflection points where public pressure actually shifts the outcome," a sign-up page for the program reads. Participants are invited to "share coordinated priority content at the moments that matter most" and "amplify calls to action from movement partners across all major platforms."

FAR-LEFT GROUPS PIVOT FROM MAY DAY PROTESTS TO MOBILIZE VOTERS FOR 2026 MIDTERMS, PUSHING DEMS LEFTWARD

Fox News Digital attended an Amplifier Army training session earlier in November, obtaining an audio recording, screenshots of the pitch deck shown to participants, a link to the program’s group chat and an invitation online platform used to coordinate social media engagement.

The WhatsApp group chat only has around 80 members; however, during the training session, the organizer in charge mentioned that they had recently created a new chat because their original forum on Signal had reached maximum capacity. The maximum number of participants in a Signal chat is 1,000.

At the end of the presentation, participants were instructed to create an account on an online app called ProSocial. The platform feeds an array of posts to users, all from mid-to-large Democratic-aligned social media accounts, and instructs users to like, comment, share, save and repost the content in question. Points are assigned for each action and the individual who gets the most points at the end of every month receives a prize from the organization.

A slide included in the training session’s slide show indicated that posts with partnered accounts selected for amplification saw a double-digit increase in shares and likes relative to posts from partners held back from amplification at random. Fox News Digital was not able to independently verify this data.

The organizer running the training session claimed that those behind the Amplifier Army coordinated with socialist activists in Brazil to help build their system, seeking to emulate the online push that helped Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva win an upset victory in Brazil’s recent presidential election.

Despite the considerable reach AAN claims for its social media operation, questions remain about how much influence the effort actually had on the midterm elections. Increased energy costs, rising grocery bills and stubbornly high housing prices, for instance, gave Americans reasons to be dissatisfied with the administration, regardless of what they did or didn’t see on social media.

Additionally, even with a thousand active members dutifully boosting posts curated by AAN, it is unclear how much of a difference that could have made on social media platforms trafficked by billions of users.

That said, AAN claims to include massive left-leaning media outlets in its network, including ​​MeidasTouch, which consistently generates hundreds of millions of monthly views and downloads.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy to be retried for murder in killing of three children
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Massachusetts judge set March 29 as the start date for Lindsay Clancy's retrial on murder charges in the strangling deaths of her three young children.

The former nurse's first trial ended on Sept. 4 with a jury deadlocked 11-1, with only a single juror voting to find her guilty of murder. The others sided with her defense, which argued that she should not be found criminally responsible due to mental illness.

Judge William Sullivan repeatedly told the parties to pick a date in March or April. Prosecutors had wanted May at the start and later pushed for the end of April. Sullivan ultimately chose the late March date.

LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS FACE DILEMMA: RETRIAL OR PLEA DEAL IN CASE INVOLVING 3 STRANGLED CHILDREN

"You've all done retrials, and generally, the sooner it is the case is retried, the better it is for all parties," he said.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Although prosecutors did not specifically address whether they intend to seek the same charges, Clancy's defense lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said he anticipated that they plan to move forward on the same counts of first-degree murder.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Lesser charges could open the door for a plea deal or even a bench trial, according to legal experts.

Reddington told Fox News' Bryan Llenas in September that if prosecutors reduced the top charge to second-degree murder, he would opt for a bench trial — one without jurors — in the hope that she receives probation as punishment.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

GOT A TIP?

"I would like to see [Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz] reduce it to a second-degree so we could possibly waive a jury and try the case before a judge," he said. "I would see Tim determine that the case should not go forward and dismiss it, or in the alternative fashion, something where Lindsay gets the mental, physical help that she needs rather than criminal prosecution — because I would not ever, ever in a million years have that woman go to Framingham State Prison."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Jack Lu, a retired Massachusetts judge and law professor, said a bench trial would use significantly fewer resources than a second jury trial. Prosecutors could seek second-degree murder charges if they decide her mental illness prevented her from forming the intent required for first-degree murder, he said.

Because of Sullivan's looming retirement, any delays could force the second trial to be held in front of a new judge.

"Perhaps this will be the unusual murder trial that goes off without a hitch," he told Fox News Digital. "For example, have the attorneys double-checked and locked in the availability of experts? This could delay the trial."

He also questioned whether Clancy's retrial should take priority over other cases in the same court.

"My answer: It should not," he said Monday.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"It appears to be pushing aside older murder trials," Lu said. "I agree with the prosecutor on this point: ‘It is unfair to them.’ Them is victims and defendants in other murder cases."

Assistant Plymouth County District Attorney Jennifer Sprague had raised other cases slated for trial in her argument for a May trial date, but Sullivan set it for March over her objection.

On Jan. 24, 2023, Clancy's ex-husband Patrick Clancy came home to find her critically injured in their backyard and their three young children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — strangled to death inside.

LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE FILES MOTION TO DISMISS UNDER DOUBLE JEOPARDY GROUNDS, WITH FOCUS ON HOLDOUT JUROR

Prosecutors said Clancy attempted to take her own life after killing the children while her husband was out doing errands. Her injuries left her paralyzed. She's been held at a Massachusetts hospital as her case plays out.

Clancy's defense had unsuccessfully raised double jeopardy concerns, which Sullivan dismissed last week.

Her final pretrial conference will be held on Feb. 18.

Fox News' Maria Paronich contributed to this report.

World.title: Robert Pattinson named as newest James Bond
World.content:
Agent 007 has a new face.

Actor Robert Pattinson has been tapped to take on the role of James Bond as Amazon MGM Studios seeks to continue the blockbuster film franchise.

The studio announced the “Twilight” and “The Batman” alum as its choice to pick up the secret agent mantle, making the 40-year-old the latest in a list of leading men who have had the honor of playing the spy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement, adding, “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

The news comes after years of speculation over who would take over the role after Daniel Craig announced in 2019 that he was leaving the franchise.

In the last week, rumors over Craig’s successor centered on Pattinson after a report from Puck suggested he was the front-runner.

Denis Villeneuve is directing the new Bond film, which further fueled the speculation given that Pattinson collaborated with Villeneuve on the “Dune” franchise. The third installment that franchise hits theaters in December.

From starring in A24’s indie film “The Drama” to blockbuster epic “The Odyssey,” Pattison has had a massive year, making him among the handful of Hollywood stars who have dominated the big screen. Most recently, he starred as “Dateline NBC” alum Chris Hansen in “Primetime,” the A24 film that follows the TV personality’s “To Catch a Predator” era.

Pattinson at the Venice Film Festival in September. Tiziana Fabi / AFP via Getty

The script for the new Bond film is being written by Steven Knight, who created the TV series “Peaky Blinders.”

Amazon MGM Studios, the tech giant’s film unit, took over “creative control” of the James Bond series under a new deal with the franchise’s longtime producers, Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli, that was announced in February 2025.

Now, “Spider-Man” producer Amy Pascal and “Harry Potter” David Heyman will take on the latest installment, producing through Pascal Pictures and Heyday Films.

In a statement, Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios emphasized that Pattinson’s casting is helping to “usher in a new era of Bond.”

“This iconic character has captivated audiences around the world for more than six decades, and there’s no doubt that Robert’s remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice to carry that legacy forward,” he said, praising the “world-class creative team in place” that will be carrying on the franchise’s legacy.

Bond fans have had many thoughts as to who would take on the mantle, with many hoping that Idris Elba would be tapped as the next British super spy. But Elba told People magazine in August that he was never truly in the race to become the next Bond.

In recent months, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner reportedly also tested for the role.

Bond has evolved into one of the most coveted roles for male actors in the United Kingdom. The book-to-screen character written by Ian Fleming has had a unique staying power across generations, beginning with Sean Connery in the 1962 film “Dr. No.” The Scottish actor played Bond across seven films and two decades.

Sean Connery as James Bond in "Goldfinger." Michael Ochs Archives / Getty

George Lazenby, the only Australian to play Bond, starred in the 1969’s “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.” He only played Bond for that film, which some have called one of the most underrated. Among the film’s fans is director Christopher Nolan, who called it his favorite of the franchise.

But it was Roger Moore who was considered to be the one who replaced Connery in the iconic spy franchise. Moore was often criticized in comparison to Connery, but he was chosen to star in seven of the franchise’s movies.

Roger Moore and Jane Seymour in the James Bond film "Live And Let Die." Express / Getty

After Moore’s final Bond film in 1985, actor Timothy Dalton was given a smaller stint as the British agent. Dalton starred in two films, including “Licence to Kill,” in which he chose to portray Bond with a darker, more serious tone than previously seen by fans.

The character took another turn when Pierce Brosnan was given the role. Brosnan said he grew up adoring both Connery and Moore in the role, telling GQ in 2014 that it never felt “real” to him that he held the job.

Pierce Brosnan as James Bond. Getty

Brosnan was told following his final Bond film, “Die Another Day,” that the character was being rethought and negotiations with his agent to continue his role had stopped.

“And that certainly dug into the solar plexus of life, just because it was pretty gut-wrenching and because it had been somewhat heralded that I was coming back,” the Irishman told GQ. “So, it’s just business. And you’re the one caught in the crosshairs.”

Brosnan was replaced by Craig, who was lauded by critics and fans alike after he made his 007 debut in the franchise’s “Casino Royale” installment.

Daniel Craig and Ana de Armas in "No Time to Die." Nicola Dove / MGM

The actor chose to leave the fictional spy life behind after five films, saying on “The Graham Norton Show” in 2021 that he was glad to be leaving on his own terms even though it was an emotional decision.

“I’m grateful to the producers for allowing me to do that,” Craig said. “But I shall miss it. I’ll probably be incredibly bitter when the new person takes over.”

In a statement posted to X, Ian Fleming Publications, which owns and manages the literary rights to James Bond, praised the casting news.

“As Bond himself reflects at the end of Moonraker when facing the fact that the object of his affections is engaged to another man, ‘He must play the role which she expected of him. The tough man of the world. The Secret Agent. The man who was only a silhouette.’ We look forward to Pattinson stepping into that silhouette and making it his own,” the account wrote. “We have no doubt that Ian Fleming would be amazed at the longevity of his creation and the fact that the world is still hungry for tales of the world’s greatest spy.​”

Online, many diehard Pattinson fans — particularly millennials who identified as “Twihards” — were thrilled by the star’s newest role.

“A great day for us Team Edward girlies” wrote one X user, referring to Pattinson’s role as brooding, telepathic vampire Edward Cullen.

Several users even posted a scene from the first “Twilight” film, released in 2008, in which Pattinson’s Edward is seen opening the car door for his romantic interest Bella Swan (Kristen Stewart) after one of their peers announces the school dance theme is Monte Carlo.

“Gambling, tuxedos and Bond, James Bond,” one of the characters says, before it cuts to Pattinson and Stewart.

“Twilight literally predicted Robert Pattinson being James Bond btw,” wrote one X user who shared the clip.

Within minutes after the news dropped, many had also already cut thirsty fan edits compiling clips of the actor in his various roles and appearances.

But there were many who blasted the choice. “robert pattinson as bond is such a boring choice man, please for the love of god choose an unknown,” one x user noted.

And others who worried that Pattinson will be too busy with Bond for other roles.

“we’re never getting that second Batman movie…” wrote one X user.

“He’ll do great, I’m sure of it,” wrote another user. “But man am I still disappointed.”

World.title: U.S. attorney warns Sen. Elizabeth Warren against investigating Trump associates
World.content:
A Justice Department official on Sunday accused Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., of intending to target private individuals close to President Donald Trump with investigations. The allegation came in a letter similar to others sent to congressional Democrats.

U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz sent a letter to Warren — who is likely the incoming chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee — calling on her to preserve documents related to investigations of Trump allies. Reitz noted that Warren appears “eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates.”

Reitz referenced a Nov. 11 letter in which Warren, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., asked Meredith O’Rourke, a National Park Foundation board member and top fundraiser for Trump, to retain documents related to funding for the White House ballroom and other projects.

Reitz accused the three lawmakers of “demanding sweeping information about her and other private citizens and entities who associate with President Trump.”

The letter to Warren signals an expansion of Reitz’s inquiry into congressional Democrats tasked with government oversight. When Democrats take control of Congress next year, Garcia is likely to take the gavel of the House Oversight Committee, while Blumenthal is expected to lead the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs’ Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

Last week, the White House issued a threat to congressional Democrats against probes into the administration. Since their midterm victories, Democrats have said Trump family businesses and immigration enforcement are some of their top targets for investigation.

Reitz’s letter referenced an op-ed from Warren earlier this month in Time magazine, in which the senator wrote, “With astonishing brazenness, Trump has attempted to reengineer the federal government into a corruption machine designed to rake in profits for himself, his family, and his cronies.”

Reitz also accused Warren of planning to target businesses that associate with Trump, referencing an appearance on CBS’ “Face the Nation” in which Warren said tech CEOs, Wall Street executives and giant corporations who have broken the law “better get ready for some investigations — serious ones.”

“The context sends a strong smoke signal: you intend to target private individuals close to President Trump,” Reitz said.

A spokesperson for Warren did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday night.

Reitz, a former chief of staff to Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has sent similar letters to Blumenthal and Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., warning them against investigating Trump associates and calling on them to preserve documents.

Reitz posted his letter to Warren on X, and Trump reposted it to Truth Social later Sunday.

The letter to Warren also contained numerous references to Native Americans, such as “scalps,” “war cries” and “tomahawk,” a dig at Warren over her past claims of Native American descent.

World.title: Why Mary Peltola is on track to win in Alaska, even if ranked choice ballots come into play
World.content:
As Alaska continues to count and report votes weeks after Election Day, it is increasingly unlikely that Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan will hang on to his job.

His Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, is on track to win the still-unresolved Senate race under either possible scenario — with an outright majority, or if the race goes to ranked choice ballots, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis of outstanding and tabulated votes.

Peltola currently leads Sullivan by 3.7 percentage points, or just over 10,000 votes. With 96% of the expected vote in, NBC News’ Decision Desk now believes Peltola is likely to win this race, though we may need to wait until Wednesday, Nov. 18, to know the final result.

If no candidate receives over 50% of the vote, Alaska determines a winner using ranked choice voting, in which the lowest-ranked candidates are eliminated one by one and their votes are redistributed according to each voter’s ranked preferences. If a voter did not rank the remaining candidates, their ballots are considered “exhausted” and are excluded from the final vote count.

Mary Peltola at an election night watch party. Justin Sullivan / Getty

Wednesday is Alaska’s deadline for final mail absentee ballots to be received by election officials, one reason why this close race has lingered for so long. Alaska reports its votes unevenly, and NBC News expects to see the remainder of these votes early next week.

Nov. 18 is also the day the state Division of Elections would run the ranked choice tabulation, if needed.

If Peltola receives over 50% of the vote, she will win the election without needing to go through the ranked choice tabulation process. She needs to win just 53.8% of the remaining ballots to clear this mark — a real possibility given her strength in recent vote reports. On Friday night, she received 58% of the newly reported votes.

Sullivan, the incumbent, has two separate paths to gain ground and win the election: making up the gap with first-choice rankings, or making up the gap via the ranked choice process. An NBC News Decision Desk analysis of the ballots already tabulated shows that the first route is highly improbable and that the second route is likely impossible.

The first route that Sullivan could use to come back would be passing Peltola in first-choice rankings. With approximately 12,000 votes outstanding, Sullivan would need to win around 92% of those in order to tie with Peltola. That would amount to about 46 points better than he has performed in the vote counted so far, and far above the percentage either candidate has achieved in any batch of ballots received up to this point. On Friday night, he received just 38% of newly reported votes.

Sen. Dan S. Sullivan casts his ballot on election day. Justin Sullivan / Getty

The second route for Sullivan to retake the lead is through the ranked choice process, but an analysis of the ballots shows why this route is effectively closed to him.

There are currently 11,300 tallied ballots with first-choice votes for candidates other than Peltola and Sullivan. Those ballots may be redistributed in the ranked choice process. With 4% of the total vote outstanding, the number of ballots with first-choice votes for candidates other than Peltola and Sullivan could rise to around 12,000. For Sullivan to net 10,400 ballots out of a pool of 12,000 and close the gap with Peltola, he would need to win around 93% of redistributed votes.

However, even that steep figure is misleadingly optimistic for Sullivan because of what we already know about how people are ranking the candidates.

The Alaska Division of Elections posts a “Cast Vote Record” for the over-270,000 ballots currently tabulated. These records show exactly how each candidate is ranked on each ballot.

Our analysis of those ballots shows that Sullivan does gain some votes from the ranked choice process, receiving a large transfer of votes from voters who backed Republican Gerald Heikes, who is in third place. But the most important thing about these votes is that a large percentage of ballots from those who backed other candidates are “exhausted” in the ranked choice tabulation process.

Over 45% of voters who ranked Heikes, Dan J. Sullivan Jr. or a write-in candidate did not rank Peltola or Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a later choice, which means that these ballots will play no role in the ranked choice tabulation.

This ballot exhaustion means that there are far fewer than 12,000 ballots available for Sullivan to make up the gap of about 10,000 votes between him and Peltola in the ranked choice process.

If current rates are maintained, only about 6,600 ballots will actually be redistributed to the top two finishers in the ranked choice tabulation. If Sullivan is more than 6,600 votes behind Peltola’s first-choice margin after all ballots have been counted, it is mathematically impossible for the Republican incumbent to catch up to Peltola in the ranked choice tabulation.

The NBC News Decision Desk will need to assess the remaining ballots as they are received to determine if our standards are met to officially project the race, or whether the outcome will be determined by the ranked choice process carried out by the Alaska Division of Elections.

World.title: Grammys 2027 nominees: Raye, Rosalía and women artists dominate major categories
World.content:
Baby, where the hell is her Grammy?

Female artists led the 2027 Grammy nominee list, which was unveiled during an early morning livestream Monday. The nominees were announced by a star-studded lineup of past Grammy winners and nominees, including Alan Menken, David Guetta and Pharrell Williams.

Nominees across 100 categories were selected by 16,000 voting members of the Recording Academy. Eligible artists released their music during the period encompassing Aug. 31, 2025 — Aug. 28, 2026.

The 69th Grammy Awards will take place at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles on Feb. 7. The show will air on ABC and stream on Disney+ and Hulu.

Here are some of the key takeaways from this year’s announcement.

Raye and Rosalía lead nominees

British singer-songwriter Raye came out on top with a whopping 11 nominations, including for song, record and album of the year. The 28-year-old rose to the top of the charts this year with her hit, “Where Is My Husband!” She now joins Beyoncé in tying the record for the most nods earned by a female artist in a single year.

Rosalía performs Thursday at the Latin Grammy Awards. Gilbert Flores / Billboard via Getty

Rosalía, who recently made history at the Latin Grammys by becoming the first female artist to win album of the year three times, snagged nine nominations. “LUX,” her fourth full-length album, features 13 different languages.

Olivia Rodrigo snagged seven nods for her latest album “you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love.” Phoebe Bridges, Ella Langley and collaborator Miranda Lambert all also earned seven nominations apiece.

Leaving space for ‘Wicked’

It may feel like an eternity ago that “Wicked: For Good” was released in theaters.

But Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande notched a best traditional pop vocal performance nomination for their song “For Good,” from the sequel to the 2024 Broadway adaptation about an unlikely friendship between two witches.

Erivo starred as the Wicked Witch of the West and Grande as the Good Witch, Glinda in the Universal Pictures film. (NBC News and Universal Pictures share Comcast as a parent company.)

Erivo and Grande are no strangers to the Grammys, having won two Grammys and three Grammys, respectively.

The film was also nominated in the best score soundtrack for visual media and best song written for visual media categories

Dolly Parton receives posthumous nods

The “Queen of Country” music, who died at age 80 in August, was among the nominees in the best country duo and group performance categories.

Parton will also likely be heavily featured in the annual emotional in memoriam segment.

Beyoncé earns her 100th Grammy nomination

Queen Bey made history Monday with her 100th Grammy nomination for best R&B solo performance for her song, “MORNING DEW (DONK).”

Beyoncé has won 35 Grammys in her storied career — the most of any female artist.

Taylor Swift’s recognized for ‘Showgirl’ and ‘Toy Story’

Yes, Swift’s 12th album, “The Life of a Showgirl” came out over a year ago, and yes it still earned several nominations Monday morning.

“Showgirl” took a spot in two of the three top categories, with lead single “The Fate of Ophelia,” earning a place for record of the year, and the album making the list of potential album of the year winners — an award Swift has won more than any other artist in her 20-year career.

Taylor Swift performs in 2024. Pedro Gomes / Getty for TAS Rights Management

“Showgirl” also nabbed nominations for best remixed recording of “Opalite,” and for best pop duo/group performance for song “The Life of a Showgirl,” which features Sabrina Carpenter.

The album, however, did not rise to a nomination for best pop vocal album.

Swift also got two nominations for her single “I Knew It I Knew You,” which she wrote for “Toy Story 5” and released in June — including song of the year.

Swift on Monday tied for the most song of the year nominations, with nine total throughout her career, including hits like “You Belong With Me,” “Blank Space” and “Anti-Hero.”

Madonna makes a comeback

Madonna received her first nominations in 16 years, since 2010, with “Bring Your Love.”

The pop icon, 68, has won 7 Grammy Awards in her decades-long career.

This year marked a comeback for the artist, who also performed at the MTV Video Music Awards for the first time in 23 years. There, she also took home three awards, including artist of the year.

Oscar buzz starts now

The best score soundtrack for visual media (includes film and TV) is typically stacked with Oscar contenders. This year was no different.

Six-time Grammy-winning composer Ludwig Göransson scored two more nods Monday, for his work on two films: “The Odyssey” and “Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu.”

Göransson has won three Oscars and is expected to be nominated again at Hollywood’s biggest night.

Ludwig Göransson accepts the award for original score for "Sinners" at the 2026 Oscars. Kevin Winter / Getty

Universal’s “The Odyssey,” which kicked off its Oscar campaign last week, is an expected front-runner in several categories for the Academy Awards.

Daniel Pemberton’s “Project Hail Mary” score was also recognized. The Amazon MGM Studios film, which stars Ryan Gosling, is also among the buzzy Oscar contenders. The Grammy nomination marks a first for Pemberton.

The score for “One Battle After Another,” from composer Jonny Greenwood, was also in the mix of this year’s nominees. The film won six Oscars at the 2026 Oscars.

Swift’s “Toy Story” single, which received Recording Academy recognition, is also expected to be nominated at the Oscars next year. The pop star has already been busy campaigning for the song, with the Grammy nominations now helping fuel her to the top of the contender list.

World.title: How Trump administration responded to FAA ground stop
World.content:
President Trump was informed within 30 minutes after the Federal Aviation Administration imposed a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, according to U.S. officials.

The ground stop resulted in thousands of canceled flights and stranded travelers across the U.S. The FAA announced that all planes would be grounded at 3:36 p.m. ET — while 3,500 flights were in the air.

Within minutes, the FBI, director of national intelligence, Department of Homeland Security, Transportation Department, Justice Department, Defense Department, Joint Chiefs of Staff, U.S. Cyber Command, FAA and Federal Emergency Management Agency began looping each other in.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement at 4:16 p.m. ET that the ground stop was necessary due to "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," and that FAA technicians were investigating. Within minutes, the White House led a call with the agencies to determine what had happened. A game plan was put in motion.

The intelligence community soon preliminarily ruled out the likelihood of nefarious activity after searching through its various channels for chatter or pings. Nothing came up.

Senior staff briefed Mr. Trump, who was in an economic policy meeting, one U.S. official said. The staff relayed his directives to others on the multi-team call, led by White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Later Mr. Trump met with Duffy and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, left, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin during a news conference at the White House on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. Shawn Thew / EPA / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Mr. Trump started calling congressional leaders on Friday to work on getting the FAA more funding. The White House congressional team called key congressional members to work with them on air traffic controller modernization.

The Homeland Security Council invited key members of the government and some outside stakeholders to a meeting Monday to discuss the next steps and what should be done to prevent a recurrence as modernization efforts continue.

The council is an interagency government body responsible for coordinating national homeland security policy. Established by President George W. Bush in 2001, under the current White House structure, the Council operates through the National Security Council framework and can draw on senior officials from agencies like the Transportation Department, FAA, DHS and Defense Department.

But not all planes were grounded during the four-hour stop: medical services flights were green-lighted to proceed to their intended destinations.

By the fourth hour, the problem in the system had been identified, and the grounding was lifted. Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware.

At a news conference on Saturday, Duffy said the trouble apparently began as FAA telecommunications contractor L3Harris Technologies performed maintenance updates at a remote facility, replacing aging copper communications lines with fiber optic connections. During that work, a router began generating more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, overwhelming routers across the entire FAA network.

Mullin and Duffy were more than 30 minutes late for a 7:45 p.m. ET press conference on the ground stop Friday because they were close to getting the grounding lifted and didn't want to interrupt the effort to hold the presser, U.S. officials said.

While federal officials have identified a likely sequence of events behind Friday's disruption, key questions still remain about the underlying cause of the systemwide failure.

On Monday morning, speaking to reporters at the White House before leaving for Asia, Mr. Trump said the ground stop wasn't his fault, or Duffy's. The president said he was at the White House having meetings at the time of the ground stop.

"I don't take any responsibility," he said. "They did a great job. Secretary Duffy — they acted incredibly. Everybody was safe, nobody was hurt, no crashes, no nothing."

The president placed all the blame on what he described as an outdated system.

"Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," Mr. Trump said.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy to be retried on first-degree murder charges in March
World.content:
Prosecutors plan to retry Lindsay Clancy on first-degree murder charges, after her first Massachusetts murder trial ended in a mistrial. The judge set a jury trial date for March 29, 2027.

Clancy was back in Plymouth Superior Court Monday morning as prosecutors addressed how they plan to proceed with her case. The commonwealth argued for a later trial date in May, citing other cases on the docket, but Judge William Sullivan, who is retiring in June 2027, was firm in seeking a March date.

Clancy was charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children in their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. In her first trial, Clancy's attorney admitted she killed 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, but argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis.

Prosecutors said Clancy knew right from wrong and planned to strangle her children. The jury ended up deadlocked and a mistrial was declared on Sept. 4.

A new trial date of March 29, 2027 has been set for the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy in the strangulation death of her three children. Pool photo Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger

Judge Sullivan has already made a number of rulings since the last hearing in the case on Nov. 9, when he denied Clancy's motion to dismiss the murder charges.

Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz has the power to decide to retry Clancy on first-degree murder charges again, which would require another jury trial. Cruz, who was not in court Monday, could also have tried Clancy on a lesser charge, such as second-degree murder or manslaughter.

Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington has said in the past that he would never accept a plea deal that puts her in jail at all. If Clancy was re-tried on lesser charges she would have the choice to have either a judge or a jury decide the outcome of this case.

WBZ-TV legal analyst Jennifer Roman said the prosecution's choice to pursue first-degree murder charges again does not come as a surprise.

"They came out pretty strongly after the first trial that they wanted justice for these three children, and the prosecution has made it clear that justice for them is a conviction on first-degree murder," she said.

Roman said the prosecution "needs to do a better job of telling their narrative this time around."

"I think that's where they fell short the first time and it hurt them ultimately when we had this hung jury," she said. "I think they really need to be clear as to what the theory of their case is, right from the outset."

Finding another jury for Clancy's second trial will not be easy, Roman said.

"This has gotten national, worldwide coverage. Everybody has heard of this case, even if they didn't follow the trial, they've certainly heard about it now," she said. "I think we are going to see an extended jury empanelment period of time for them to get the 14 or 15 members of that jury pool."

World.title: Woman buys Ford Bronco, drives 27 hours home after flights grounded
World.content:
From a sea of lost luggage to endless delays, patience has been tested for tens of thousands of travelers impacted by Friday's historic nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop.

The ground stop doubled or tripled travel times for some, while others said they slept on airport floors as nearby hotels charged premiums for a shrinking list of rooms. But one woman, Tara Harding, got creative.

After their flights were rescheduled four times before eventually being canceled, Harding bought a Ford Bronco and drove herself and two employees from Charlotte, North Carolina, back home to North Dakota. The trip took 27 hours, Harding told "CBS Mornings." It covered about 1,500 miles.

"It wasn't about just me. It was about my employees, too, and getting them home safely, and getting them home to their families," said Harding.

Harding said she decided to buy the Bronco in North Carolina after first looking into rental car and rideshare options, as well as the availability of Amtrak trains and Greyhound buses. But none of those options panned out.

She told "CBS Mornings" that she's planning to keep the SUV after their cross-country excursion.

"I feel very connected to it, with the story, and I think we might end up keeping it," Harding said, laughing. "We're going to end up keeping it now."

Tara Harding bought a Ford Bronco and drove 27 hours home with two colleagues after their flight was canceled. Tara Harding

Harding wasn't the only traveler who acquired a vehicle at the last minute after becoming stranded during the ground stop. Kevin McGrew was on his way to watch his first home Notre Dame football game when his flight was diverted — twice.

"U-Haul popped in my mind," McGrew told "CBS Mornings." "They had a 10-footer. So then I drove through the night, five hours."

The ground stop has caused about 18,000 flight cancellations as of Monday, according to data from the tracking site FlightAware. The FAA announced the ground stop on Friday afternoon, while 3,500 flights were in the air, as a result of what Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." It lasted for more than four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since Sept. 11, 2001.

Duffy said at a news conference Saturday that the telecommunications outage was linked to maintenance updates being performed at a remote facility in Arkansas by the FAA contractor L3Harris Technologies. The updates involved replacing aging copper communications lines with fiber-optic connections, and those replacements, apparently, managed to overwhelm the FAA's router network and knock out communications.

"This is part of our maintenance that we do on this really old architecture of a telecom network," Duffy said Sunday on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," adding that the network "has to be updated, upgraded, and, I think, built brand-new."

At the time, Duffy said the FAA and the FBI were investigating in hopes of determining the root cause of the outage.

"Was it the install from L3Harris? Was it the router?" he said. "I'm going to tell you and the American people what we find."

World.title: Diesel prices dip below $6 a gallon for first time since September
World.content:
The national price of diesel in the U.S. fell below $6 a gallon on Monday, the first time it has been below that level in over two months.

Diesel now averages $5.99 a gallon, according to AAA, down from a record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22.

Diesel prices surged past $6 a gallon in September as the wars in Iran and Ukraine squeezed global refining capacity and disrupted oil flow. The run-up in prices rippled across the economy, increasing costs for the diesel-dependent transportation, construction and agriculture industries and keeping inflation elevated.

Prices ease as oil supplies stabilize

Diesel and gasoline prices have fallen in recent weeks after President Trump signaled he wouldn't escalate the war in Iran, according to Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy.

At the same time, the global oil market is also showing signs of stabilization.

"Oil prices slipped to start the week as expectations of a coming supply surplus outweighed fresh security incidents around the Strait of Hormuz," De Haan said in a report on Monday.

Brent crude, the international standard, traded on Monday at $93.56 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $86.72.

Last week, the International Energy Agency raised its oil production forecast, predicting a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year.

"The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the organization said in its November report.

While tanker attacks continue in the Strait of Hormuz, traffic through the strategically vital waterway has picked up. Shipments have largely returned to levels before the war erupted in late February, according to De Haan. Gasoline prices have also dropped, falling below $4 a gallon last week for the first time in nearly four months.

A brief reprieve?

Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, said November is typically a good time to rebuild diesel inventory, given that demand in the agriculture sector fades after the summer. At the same time, demand for heating oil, also derived from crude oil, hasn't fully ramped up.

"It's too early for severe winter demand to remove diesel molecules for the heating oil business," he told CBS News in an email.

Kloza expects diesel and heating oil prices to ebb over the next six weeks, but warned that they could tick up around the new year as colder winter temperatures drive demand for heating oil.

"There is plenty to worry about between Christmas week and February 15 or so," he said.

World.title: Warren Buffett donates $5.5 billion to charity, urging kindness
World.content:
Warren Buffett on Monday said he is donating about $5.5 billion in Berkshire Hathaway shares to four foundations, writing in a letter to the company's shareholders that kindness "compounds, and at a better rate" than financial investments.

The gift from the famed investor, who regularly donates Berkshire Hathaway shares to charitable organizations around Thanksgiving, is about four times as large as his donation a year earlier.

Buffett said he is donating the shares to the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, the Sherwood Foundation, the Howard G. Buffett Foundation and the NoVo Foundation, with the last three foundations run by his three children. The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation is named after Buffett's late first wife.

In his letter, Buffett said that all of his stock holdings — worth $162 billion after the latest donation — will eventually be distributed to the four foundations. He also used the letter to encourage others to engage in kindness.

He added, "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else."

Shares of Berkshire Hathaway, which owns insurance company GEICO and holds investments in major companies such as Apple, rose $2.09, or 0.4%, to $595.32 in early trading. The stock has gained almost 20% in 2026 and has soared 110% over the last five years.

Buffett, 96, stepped down as Berkshire Hathaway's chairman in September, but remains on the company's board of directors.

World.title: Trump says he "would not mind" if Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang
World.content:
Washington — President Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, after he resigned last week amid allegations of two affairs. The president said he doesn't know if Alice Huang, one of the women allegedly involved with Jensen Huang, was a Chinese spy.

"I would not mind. I would not mind that," the president told reporters Monday as he departed for a trip to the Philippines and China, and he said "that certainly isn't a bad idea."

He also floated the name of the former Apple CEO as a possible Huang replacement at Nvidia, saying, "I like, you know, I do have the name of Tim Cook." Mr. Trump added, "But I would say that Jensen's reinstatement — I think he learned a big lesson, I guess."

He also said that the U.S. has banned Nvidia from selling the "important chips, the modern-day chips," in particular, the most powerful AI chip in the world, the company's Blackwell chip. And just before the president left, the Trump administration announced a new rule that's intended to curb efforts by China to bypass the restrictions by remotely accessing the chips through data centers in third countries.

The president also dismissed concerns that Alice Huang may be spying for China. She's a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a former gaming company that is now an AI infrastructure and cloud computing company and is one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers.

"Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Mr. Trump said. "I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."

The president said he may speak with Xi about Alice Huang and whether she was a spy. Mr. Trump and Xi will be meeting in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit.

Last week, Attorney General Todd Blanche said he "certainly" hasn't said Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.

Elon Musk, tech executives and Nvidia employees have signed a petition calling for Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia. The former CEO resigned last week amid reports of two extramarital affairs — one with Alice Huang and one with an Nvidia employee.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy to face a new trial in spring of 2027 over children's killing
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy to face a new trial in spring of 2027 over children's killing

toggle caption i Greg Derr/POOL/AFP via Getty Images

Prosecutors are seeking a new trial for Lindsay Clancy in the deaths of her three children. The trial is scheduled to begin on March 29, 2027.

There had been speculation that the mistrial of her first trial might spur prosecutors to consider lesser charges that wouldn't require a jury, such as manslaughter or second-degree murder. But no changes to the charges were made in Monday's court hearing.

"Given what the charges are, it requires a jury trial," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Mass.

In response, Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington stated, "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments."

Sponsor Message

Judge Sullivan is expected to preside over the new trial. He oversaw Clancy's murder trial that ended in a mistrial two months ago.

The decision to retry Clancy emerges after the judge denied a request from Clancy's defense team to dismiss the criminal charges against her on double jeopardy grounds.

Clancy's defense has argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her young children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.

Clancy was initially tried on three charges of first-degree murder, one for each of her children. Her case has drawn intense media interest, due to the shocking killings of her young children. And as WBUR has reported, the trial has also sparked conspiracy theories online.

Read WBUR's coverage of this case here.

Mistrial sparked defense motion to dismiss

Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4, after five weeks of testimony and seven days of jury deliberations. The jurors, nine women and three men, repeatedly told Sullivan they were deadlocked, unable to reach a unanimous decision. Jurors said a lone juror refused to join 11 others in finding Clancy not guilty of murder.

Clancy's defense filed several motions after the mistrial. The first asked the court to issue a "required finding of not guilty," a Massachusetts state law term for instances where judges determine there's insufficient evidence to sustain a conviction. Another focused on the holdout juror, asking the court for an inquiry and to examine their responses to a juror questionnaire and other records. Sullivan denied both of those motions.

When deliberations were dragging out at the end of the trial, Reddington had asked the judge to remove the holdout juror, saying the jury foreperson reported one juror refused to follow the law in regards to reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to dismiss the juror, saying he reaffirmed his instructions with all the jurors about the law.

Sponsor Message

Tragic case highlights postpartum mental health

Clancy, 36, did not testify during the trial. But her attorneys didn't deny that she killed her three children in January of 2023. Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, were found strangled in the basement of the home Clancy shared with her then-husband Patrick in Duxbury, Mass., south of Boston.

In court, Clancy's defense argued that she can't be held criminally liable because of her mental state at the time of the killings. Her attorney said Clancy was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis, and didn't get adequate mental health help when she sought it out.

"I'm appalled and disgusted," Reddington said of Clancy's medical care, as NPR and WBUR reported. "It's repulsive what happened here."

But prosecutors argued Clancy was mentally capable of committing a premeditated crime, accusing her of sending her husband out on errands so she would be alone with their children. And they raised doubts about Clancy's claims that a voice told her to kill them.

"This case is not about our mental health system or how it treats women," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said in her closing statement. "That's a distraction to get you angry and passionate about an important issue, but an issue that's not on trial here."

During the trial, the jury visited the house where the Clancy children died. Their bus route also took them past two places Patrick Clancy visited that evening — a CVS and a takeout restaurant -- before returning home to a horrific scene. Sullivan told the jurors that the visit, called a "view" under Massachusetts state law, was meant to "help you better understand the evidence" by seeing the locations and the house's layout.

Clancy remains in the custody of a state psychiatric hospital where she's been held for more than three years. She was severely injured by attempts to end her own life, and she used a wheelchair during the trial.

Sponsor Message

Massachusetts' highest court recently reversed a conviction in a separate case involving a mother killing her children – a case that both Cruz, the prosecutor, and Sullivan, the judge, also worked on.

In August, the state Supreme Judicial Court ordered a new trial for Latarsha Sanders, saying Sullivan committed an error in not allowing the jury to see medical records documenting Sanders' mental illness after she was arrested. Sanders was convicted of murder in 2022; she had argued that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible because she suffered a psychotic episode.

If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or be in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

World.title: FAA ground stop still affecting thousands of flights. And, Trump meets Xi, Putin in Asia
World.content:
FAA ground stop still affecting thousands of flights. And, Trump meets Xi, Putin in Asia

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Travelers are expected to face continued disruptions at airports as airlines recover from Friday's nationwide ground stop. As of Sunday evening, more than 2,300 flights have been canceled, and more than 8,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. have been delayed, according to FlightAware.com. Dallas-Fort Worth and Atlanta airports saw the most disruptions, with over 250 delayed flights each. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said L3Harris Technologies Inc., a federal contractor, was doing routine maintenance in at least one remote location, changing copper wire to fiber optics.

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

🎧 The U.S. air traffic system remains safe, and this recent incident is considered an unusual meltdown, NPR's Joel Rose tells Up First. The Federal Aviation Administration believes it has identified the issue, and airlines will be ready for the holiday travel rush. Rose says the nation's air traffic system has suffered from decades of underinvestment by Congress and administrations from both parties. Before the ground stop, Duffy had requested $30 billion to upgrade the air traffic control system. Now he seems to be asking for $50 billion by the end of the year, on top of the $12.5 billion for air traffic equipment that the Trump administration secured from Congress last year. Democrats, who will control Congress in January, are not responding positively to Duffy's latest request. Rose expects Democrats to seek more clarity on the administration's spending and the causes of the ground stop.

Sponsor Message

As Democrats gear up for substantial majorities in Congress, one question looms: who will take the helm? So far, no one has challenged Rep. Hakeem Jeffries for the House speaker role. Meanwhile, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is setting his sights on unseating longtime leader Chuck Schumer in the Senate.



🎧 A wave of incoming senators has spent months hearing voters demand change in Washington. NPR's Eric McDaniel says this presents a real opportunity for Van Hollen and a potential risk for Schumer, especially after the recent election results. Van Hollen needs 30 Democrats to secure a simple majority. He has support he needs from popular progressives like Bernie Sanders, and incoming members like Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, McDaniel says. Since votes are cast by secret ballot, it's uncertain how many will back each leader when they convene in a few weeks, and McDaniel says anything could happen.

President Trump is traveling to the Philippines and China this morning for a high-profile trip, which includes a trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This marks Trump's second visit to China this year. The trip to Asia comes as the administration faces scrutiny following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman linked to China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. He traveled to China with Trump earlier this year; this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is accompanying Trump to Shenzhen.



Sponsor Message

🎧 It's not unusual for presidents who face midterm election defeats to shift their focus to foreign policy, NPR's Mara Liasson says. But Trump's recent foreign policy efforts, including tariffs and the war in Iran, have been widely unpopular and seen as reasons why his party lost in the midterms, Liasson says. The White House said that Trump isn't expected to address pressing issues like the war in Ukraine or tensions with China during this trip. Instead, he plans to discuss the war in Iran and nuclear weapons. Trump will also skip mentioning Huang's affair. Bringing up the Nvidia situation could serve as a reminder that many in Congress believe the U.S. should restrict access to advanced chips in China. Trump disagrees with Congress on the matter, likely due to his ties with Huang, who committed millions of dollars for Trump's ballroom, Liasson says.

Living better

toggle caption i Mono/Getty Images

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

Sleep plays a crucial role in weight management. Studies have found that poor sleep can increase appetite and lead to overeating, making it harder to shed pounds. On the flip side, quality sleep might actually enhance your weight-loss efforts. One study found that participants in a year-long weight-loss program who enjoyed better sleep lost more weight and fat. So, prioritizing sleep could be your secret weapon in the journey to a healthy weight. Here's what researchers say:

😴 While evidence linking more sleep to weight loss is limited, there is consistent science connecting insufficient sleep to weight gain.

😴 Lack of sleep increases activity in brain regions associated with pleasure and reward, making it harder to make good food choices.

😴 Not having enough sleep can disrupt circadian rhythms and reduce insulin sensitivity, encouraging fat storage and weight gain.

😴 The relationship between sleep and food goes both ways. Eating added sugars and saturated fats disrupts sleep and reduces deep sleep, while consuming fruits, vegetables and fiber improves sleep quality and decreases nighttime awakenings.

Sponsor Message

Picture show

toggle caption i Eric Baradat/

AFP via Getty Images





Route 66 is celebrating an incredible century as America's most iconic highway. Stretching across eight states — from the vibrant streets of Chicago to the sun-soaked shores of Santa Monica, Calif. — this legendary route invites you to embrace the spirit of adventure on the open road. Imagine cruising through vast plains, rolling prairies, stunning canyons and shimmering deserts. Along the way, you'll discover a mix of big cities, charming cow towns and ghost towns. Over the decades, Route 66 has inspired countless songs, been captured in books, been seen in artwork and been celebrated in Pixar's 2006 animated movie Cars. So hop in, buckle up and experience the magic of Route 66 through these photos.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i AP/NASA

NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than any human-launched object and is about to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that's one light-day away from Earth. New Orleans port officials have filed a lawsuit against the owner and operator of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship in the Mississippi River. They are seeking at least $1 million in damages. Mauricio Pochettino, who guided the U.S. men's national soccer team to a Round of 16 finish in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, is leaving to become the head coach of Manchester United in the English Premier League.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Chris Van Hollen says he can beat Chuck Schumer. Here's his case
World.content:
Chris Van Hollen says he can beat Chuck Schumer. Here's his case

toggle caption i Mark Makela/Getty Images

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Monday that he is gaining momentum in his bid to unseat longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, taking a traditionally private Senate leadership contest into public view.

"Well, I'm the underdog, but we are really moving in the right direction here," Van Hollen told NPR's Steve Inskeep on Morning Edition.

Over the weekend, he appeared on CNN, ABC and Fox News to make his case for new Democratic leadership after his party's sweeping midterm victories. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, says he has enough votes to remain leader.

Sponsor Message

Van Hollen is hardly a Washington outsider. The progressive Democrat has spent nearly 25 years on Capitol Hill, served as a deputy to then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and led Democratic campaign efforts in both chambers. He has been a vocal opponent of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development, and he has called for investigations into the administration's foreign aid cuts.

Schumer has continued to support U.S. military assistance to Israel despite his criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Van Hollen, by contrast, has pushed to restrict weapons sales and military aid to the Israeli government over its war in Gaza, while pressing for more humanitarian aid to Palestinians.

"I certainly oppose the idea of an American taxpayer blank check to the government of Israel, regardless of its actions," Van Hollen said.

Van Hollen also wants Democratic leaders to stay out of contested primaries. He pointed to the victories of incoming Sens. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.

"We have two senators-elect who would not be there if the current majority leader had his way," he said.

He described the midterm victories as a populist rejection of President Trump, rather than an election orchestrated by Washington Democrats.

Sponsor Message

Van Hollen also cited legislation to strengthen labor unions, which never received a vote on the Senate floor. On the war in Iran, he called for an end to further funding.

"We should not be voting for one penny in mid-December to continue this war," he said.

Van Hollen will need close to 30 votes, a simple majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, to win. The election will be decided by secret ballot behind closed doors, making it difficult to know how many votes either candidate secured.

Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.

The digital version of this live interview was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: These birds fly 17,000 miles every year. Climate change could make it harder
World.content:
These birds fly 17,000 miles every year. Climate change could make it harder

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Pectoral sandpipers are ultra-marathoners. They fly more than 17,000 miles a year, crossing entire continents on their migration from Alaska to Argentina and back again. They don't soar or coast on the wind – they flap the entire way. And these elite athletes are only the size of a robin, weighing around three ounces.

The sandpipers are among more than 12 million shorebirds that migrate to Alaska every year to breed, spending the short summer season in open lands near water. For years, scientists have been trying to understand how these unassuming birds accomplish such monumental journeys from places like New Zealand, Asia, South America.

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

"Shorebirds are not these little brown birds on the beach, but they're miraculous migrants that travel these huge distances by these crazy adaptations," says Rick Lanctot, a wildlife biologist with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

Sponsor Message

For 24 years, Lanctot and other researchers have tracked the return of shorebirds to northern Alaska. The data shows a concerning trend. Overall, almost half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are declining . Some have lost more than half of their population over the last 30 years.

Ryan Kellman/NPR

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Migration, like any kind of travel, requires careful timing. Birds orchestrate their journeys to take advantage of the seasons, arriving when food is ample and the weather is ideal. But for many species, their itineraries are going increasingly awry. Habitats they count on, such as wetlands and grasslands, are disappearing. In a hotter climate, spring is arriving earlier, which affects when their food is available. It's like making a pit stop on a road trip and finding all the restaurants are closed.

The question is whether long-distance migrators, which already push the limits of survival, can adapt to a rapidly warming world.

"Shorebirds truly are sentinels about what is happening to the planet, because they're touching down in so many of the places across that planet," says Nathan Senner, who studies shorebirds at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. "If we can't listen to what they're telling us about the unpredictability of what we're currently doing to the planet, then we're not going to be able to respond to a lot of changes."

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Tiny trackers

Lanctot gently holds a brown and white pectoral sandpiper in his hands as field technician Braden Meyer attaches what looks like a tiny backpack. This tracking tag will log the bird's locations as it flies thousands of miles.

Sponsor Message

Nearby, male pectoral sandpipers call out, searching for females and attempting to ward off other males. Some have already found places to nest, spread out among the low-lying plants of the Arctic tundra. The sun is still well above the horizon at midnight, since summer days last for 24 hours in Utqiaġvik, the northernmost city in the U.S., formerly known as Barrow .

The female Lanctot holds recently arrived from Argentina, after a pit stop in the Central U.S. to eat. Flying here used all her energy reserves.

Loading...

"When we catch birds when they first show up, they're really skinny," Lanctot says. "You can feel the keel or the breastbone really prominently. They have hardly any fat on them."

His team secures the backpack tracking tag with stretchy loops around the bird's legs. It will collect her GPS position every 15 minutes, storing the data until the bird flies by any cell tower on her journey, where it's uploaded. Lanctot's team also uses tiny tags that attach to a bird's leg like an anklet, which weigh about as much as a grain of rice and were originally designed for butterflies .

Ryan Kellman/NPR

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Tracking technology has revealed that shorebirds undertake far more arduous journeys than once thought. While scientists have studied the migrations of larger animals for decades, tracking tags have only become light and compact enough for small birds in the last 15 years. Since then, new migratory records have been broken.

One bird, a bar-tailed godwit, flew more than 8,000 miles for 11 days straight without stopping from Alaska to Australia. Researchers are still figuring out how these birds navigate an entire ocean. They also seem to take advantage of weather patterns , waiting for the optimal winds.

"That's why I still haven't retired, frankly," Lanctot says. "Because there's always a new tag or something coming out that lets you learn things you couldn't learn otherwise."

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Disappearing shorebirds

To fly thousands of miles, shorebirds must drastically reshape their body. Some double their body weight to store enough fat to fuel them on the journey. Some internal organs, like the digestive system, even shrink before takeoff, since they're not needed during a nonstop flight.

Sponsor Message

It's why the roughly six weeks pectoral sandpipers spend in the Arctic are crucial. The birds must eat enough to build their fat reserves for the next migration, while laying eggs and raising chicks. Those chicks only have about a month after hatching to eat and grow large enough to join that migration.

The numbers of shorebirds, like pectoral sandpipers, migrating to the Arctic have been declining over the last few decades. It's noticeable around Utqiaġvik, including within the community that's lived with them for centuries.

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

"Birds have always been very special to the Inupiat people," Robin Mongoyak says, walking on the coastline where the Chukchi Sea meets the Beaufort Sea. "They give us something to always look forward to after a long, cold winter. The Inupiat people have always thought of it as a quvianaq time – a very wonderful time when the birds start flocking in."

Mongoyak is a wildlife guide who grew up in Utqiaġvik. He says each bird species has a different cultural meaning, telling a story of the world around them. That environment is shifting rapidly. Mongoyak remembers when sea ice lasted multiple years. Now, he says that's becoming rare and the ice is breaking up earlier in the spring. Temperatures in the Arctic have risen four times faster than the rest of the globe.

"The climate is getting warmer," Mongoyak says. "I don't see as many birds as I used to like seeing. It's really changed a lot in the last 35 years, at least."

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Birds out of sync

To understand the decline in Arctic birds, researchers are studying how warmer temperatures affect their food – insects.

"Whenever there's a sunny day, there's going to be clouds of non-biting midges," says Julia Berliner, a graduate student at the University of Texas at Austin, looking across the tundra. She holds up a bug vacuum, a modified leaf vacuum from the hardware store, that sucks insects into a net to collect a sample.

Sponsor Message

These small flying insects only emerge briefly during the short Arctic summer. Normally, the ground is frozen solid, but as the weather warms up, the top few inches of permafrost thaws, and flies and spiders emerge for their short life cycles.

Loading...

"Insects and spiders are really tied to the weather," says Amanda Koltz, an assistant professor of integrative biology at the University of Texas at Austin. "So it could be that one week, there aren't any prey flying around, and then next week, there might be tons of flies flying around. And so that really changes the menu from week to week."

Shorebirds time their trip to this buffet of bugs, ideally hatching their chicks when the insect population peaks. But when spring arrives earlier with warming temperatures, the insects also emerge earlier. That puts the shorebirds out of sync with insects, which means the birds could miss their peak food supply, what's known as mismatch.

toggle caption i Amanda Koltz; Ryan Kellman/NPR

Missing the peak food supply seems to have the biggest impact on shorebird chicks. Research shows that when chicks hatch late, fewer of them survive . Koltz says because different insects emerge at different times, what the birds can eat also matters.

"We need to know how much food they have available, but also what's the quality of that food?" she says. "If they eat a spider and beetle, the spider and the beetle have different nutrients in them, just the same as if you ate a pepper or a banana versus a potato chip."

Koltz and Berliner are sampling insects to measure crucial nutrients like calcium, which birds need to produce eggs. If insect populations shift their timing, it could also shift the nutritional menu, another way climate change could impact Arctic bird populations.

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Shifting migrations
