Researchers are trying to figure out whether migratory birds have the ability to adapt to a warming Arctic. When spring arrives early, some shorebirds can speed up their nesting and lay eggs slightly earlier than normal, but not enough to keep up with the changes.

Sponsor Message

Birds that migrate long distances can also shift the timing of their migrations by a few days, but scientists are still studying how birds make those decisions, whether they use environmental cues or learned behaviors. Some cues may not help them adapt. They may be relying on signs in environments thousands of miles away from the Arctic, or in some cases, on signals that don't change, like when days get longer in the spring.

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Habitat loss, largely from development, is also driving the decline of many shorebirds, particularly the wetlands and grasslands they use as rest stops along their journey. Drought is also affecting these places and is only intensifying with climate change.

Many migratory birds in the U.S. use agricultural fields and ponds instead, which may be useful habitat for only short periods of time. In a handful of places, conservation efforts are underway to boost that habitat, such as paying farmers in California to keep their rice fields flooded for longer periods so birds can use them while migrating.

"Shorebirds are actually frequently quite well-adapted to finding where patches of habitat are, but our current environmental state is that we've really messed with the predictability of a lot of landscapes," Senner says. "That's what starts to make it really difficult for some of these species."

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Senner says if shorebirds keep declining, extinction is a possibility for many species. Now, the race is on to understand how much these birds can adapt to a changing world.

"We need to figure out: what are those tactics and then can we manage environments to maximize the likelihood that those tactics will be successful?" Senner says. "Because no one species can be ready for all of the types of changes that could possibly come their way."

Reporting for this story was supported by a Braided River Overlooked and Untold Alaska Journalism Grant.

World.title: NPR's Student Podcast Challenge is back for 2027
World.content:
NPR's Student Podcast Challenge is back for 2027

LA Johnson/NPR

Students and teachers, it's time to turn on your microphones and start recording – in January, the NPR Student Podcast Challenge returns for its ninth year.

Since its launch in 2018, our annual audio storytelling competition for students in grades four through 12 has introduced more than 90,000 students to the world of podcasting.

During that time we've heard from students, teachers, parents and educators around the country about how they've enjoyed participating – and how much they've learned along the way.

"I can't tell you how many of my students come back to tell me this project was the most meaningful thing they did while in middle school," says Laura Frisbie, an advanced learning teacher at Minnetonka Middle School West, in Excelsior, Minn. "What a powerful way for students to use their voices in an authentic way and share a message that is important to them."

Sponsor Message

For teachers coming to the competition for the first time, maybe looking to shake things up in your classroom and try something new, we've got tons of resources available to help you get started. And for our returning educators, there's plenty there to draw on to help your students get better.

How it will work

The 2027 competition will open Jan. 4, to students in grades four through 12. You'll have until May 30 to submit. Grand prize winners will be announced after summer break in September.

Our NPR education team will listen to every single one (more than 22,000 podcasts so far!) and narrow them down to a list of finalists and honorable mentions.

From those entries, our judges will select the grand-prize winners: one for grades five through eight, and another in grades nine through 12. Since 2024, we've also opened our contest to fourth-graders, and we choose winners and honorable mentions from that category as well.

"The Student Podcast Challenge gives kids an opportunity to shine and tell their own stories," says Ameya Desai, a middle school student in San Jose, Calif., who was our first-ever two-time winner. "Every kid should podcast about something they feel strongly about, something that's personal to them, something they have ties to."

Sponsor Message

Over the years, we've found that the best podcasts are the ones where students bring a particular passion for the story they want to tell.

For example, here are some of our favorite entries from last year:

These fifth graders in Hewlett, N.Y., for the celebration of the USA's 250th birthday, asked each other: "What do you really know about our country?"

An Iowa middle schooler told the story of her grandfather's dementia, and her struggle to understand how the disease took him from her.

A group of high school students explored a scientific mystery linked to a gas leak in their town of Glasford, Ill. And a student in Los Altos, Calif., told the story of how a football coach's courage and dedication defied the odds and changed the lives of students.

Resources

To learn more about making a podcast, you can start by reading the rest of this announcement post, and check out our student podcasting resources page. And subscribe to our newsletter for updates from the contest team.

It's worth noting that several of our finalists and past winners (including this year's middle school and high school grand prize winners) were first-time podcasters, so you can do it too!

And here are two important rules to keep in mind:



Podcasts must be between three and eight minutes. We're pretty strict about this so make sure your story falls within that range.

Because of legal considerations, we have specific rules about what music you can, and can't, use in your podcast.

A special note here: Parents and educators, step away from the microphone! Please, no podcasts produced or edited by adults. The entries should be original work by students (see FAQ section below). Each year, we've had to disqualify some entries for clearly breaking this rule.

And, students, please keep it clean! No offensive language will be allowed.

As noted above, students do need to work with a teacher, educator or family member — who is 18 years or older — to fill out the submission form to enter the contest.

Sponsor Message

Other important stuff

Our judges will select a middle school and high school grand prize winner. The grand prize includes a certificate, a trophy and a visit from the NPR education team. The team will interview the winner and their teacher for a story to appear on an NPR program, such as Morning Edition or All Things Considered.

In previous years, many podcasts created by our other finalists and honorable mention recipients, including some of our fourth graders, have aired on various NPR programs and podcasts. They've also received additional recognition from their schools or school districts, and many winners have been interviewed by local media.

In other words, it's a great opportunity to share your story and get a lot of people to listen to it.

Some "Sound Advice" from the contest team

Before you hit the record button, check out our podcasting resources. We have a starting out guide for student podcasters and a curriculum guide for educators.

In them, we cover everything from how to tell a good story, how to sound like yourself on mic to how to use music in your podcast, among other topics. Even, and we're serious about this: how making a pillow fort can make you sound better!

There are other good resources out there too: Check out this audio storytelling toolkit and recording tutorial from PBS News Student Reporting Labs. Or The Student Podcast Playbook, a four-week podcasting curriculum created by our friends at The Bell.

You can find more tips and tricks on The Students' Podcast, which our team created to help you make a good podcast. We also encourage you to get a feel for what we're looking for by listening to last year's high school winner and middle school winner, and previous years' winning entries.

Quick FAQ

Here are a few questions we get over and over again each year. For any other questions, don't hesitate to reach out to us at studentpodcastchallenge@npr.org.

Sponsor Message

What's an appropriate way teachers and adults can be involved?

All eligible contest entries must be written, recorded and produced by students. We welcome teachers and educators to incorporate podcasting into their class curriculum and walk students through the basics of audio recording and editing. And as a part of this process, we understand that students may be getting feedback from the adults involved. Bottom line, we ask the adults to provide coaching and guidance, but to make sure that the podcasts submitted are original work by the students.

And, of course, that goes for the use of AI in your podcasts as well! Here's NPR's policy on the use of artificial intelligence for our journalists. While students these days may be using AI tools in gathering information or conducting research, we've added a box on our application asking you to acknowledge that you didn't use AI in the writing or performance of your podcast.

Am I allowed to use this song or sound effect in my podcast?

Here's an excerpt from our rules page that discusses music and copyrighted audio:

"Pre-recorded music may not be used. Entrants may include live performances of public domain songs or non-copyrightable rhythm elements if it is relevant to the story. For avoidance of doubt, for the purposes of these Official Rules, "public domain" does not mean "publicly available"; it means that copyright has expired and the material is no longer under copyright protection. We encourage Entrants to err on the side of excluding music if the Entrant is not sure whether the music is copyrighted or not."

You can use your own audio, interviews, field recordings or natural sound, music or sound effects you recorded for the podcast. We advise not using audio if the student isn't sure about copyright.

On our entry form, we ask you to confirm that any music in your podcast is either copyright free, or self-produced.

Sponsor Message

Can I submit more than one podcast?

Yes! You can submit as many entries as you'd like. Just make sure that each of your podcast entries are (1) between three and eight minutes in length and (2) don't use copyrighted audio. We wouldn't want any of your work to be disqualified.

And we really do listen to every single entry. So whether it's you and your friend's podcast, a class assignment or a passion project you're finally putting together, we're excited to hear from you and listen to whatever you got for us.

And, as we said above, for more tips, advice and the latest updates on this year's contest, make sure to

World.title: Why sleep matters when it comes to weight gain and loss
World.content:
Why sleep matters when it comes to weight gain and loss

Mono/Getty Images

If you want to maintain a healthy weight, you probably know you should watch what you eat and get some exercise, maybe hit the gym. But what about hitting the hay?

There is a lot of evidence linking lack of sleep to overeating and an increased body weight. But does that mean that getting more sleep could also boost efforts to lose weight?

"That's a good question," says Seth Creasy, an associate professor of medicine at the University of Colorado Anschutz who studies the interplay between weight management and lifestyle behaviors like sleep, diet and physical activity. "It's actually still an active area of research."

Creasy says the best evidence so far comes from a randomized clinical trial involving 80 overweight adults who were chronically short on sleep. Researchers randomly assigned half of them to get counseling on how to extend their snooze time.

Sponsor Message

"They got them to sleep a little over an hour more per night," Creasy says. "And they saw that, without intervening on food, these people started to eat less by about 270 calories per day. So once they were getting adequate sleep, they ate less."

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Other research has found associations between better sleep and weight loss. For example, one study found that people enrolled in a year-long weight loss intervention program who had good sleep health lost more weight and more fat mass compared to poor sleepers.

The poor sleepers in that study were also much more likely to report having trouble sticking to their diet and exercise goals, says Christopher Kline, the study's lead author and an associate professor of health and human development at the University of Pittsburgh.

And good sleep health doesn't just mean how long you sleep, Kline says. He says that factors like sleep timing, regularity and satisfaction also play a role.

"A good analogy I like to make is if you get your eight hours of sleep, but those eight hours are between 4 a.m. and noon, that might not be as healthy as someone who regularly obtains their sleep between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.," says Kline, whose research focuses on how physical activity, sleep and cardiometabolic risks are related.

Sponsor Message

The links between sleep loss and weight gain

Researchers say right now, the evidence that more sleep can boost weight loss efforts is still scant, but the science is much more consistent when it comes to linking insufficient sleep to weight gain.

When researchers restrict people's sleep, they eat more — by an average of around 300 calories a day if you look across studies, says Creasy, who recently published a review of the research on sleep and weight management.

Most of those studies required participants to severely curtail their sleep, usually to around four or five hours a night. That's much less than the seven to nine hours of sleep that adults are supposed to get.

But Creasy worked on a recent study that found even milder sleep loss can result in weight gain. In that study, people who were assigned to sleep just 90 minutes less than usual gained an average of one pound over six weeks. While that may not sound like much, "over time, it adds up," says Marie-Pierre St-Onge, the study's senior author and a sleep and nutrition scientist at Columbia University.

Imaging studies from St-Onge and other researchers have found that, when we're short on sleep, activity ramps up in areas of the brain involved in pleasure and reward. In other words, it becomes harder to make good food choices.

"Our brain is less able to inhibit our desires for those sweet and salty foods" — especially later in the day, Kline says. The result is we end up overeating when short on sleep.

Kline says he experienced this phenomenon first-hand when he was still a doctoral student working the overnight shift in a sleep study lab. Once a week, every week, one of his fellow lab workers would bring in glazed donuts from Krispy Kreme.

"I can tell you there was no chance I was going to end a shift without having at least one or two of those donuts. And I don't even really like glazed donuts," Kline says ruefully.

Sponsor Message

Skimping on sleep can also disrupt our circadian rhythms and impair our sensitivity to insulin, which may promote fat storage and make it easier to gain weight.

Creasy says early studies suggested poor sleep also affects hormones that regulate appetite, but newer research hasn't always borne that out. "Some studies have shown an effect on them and some have not. So it's just been inconsistent," he says.

Better sleep through food?

St-Onge says the relationship between sleep and food goes both ways. "As we find that how we sleep influences our food intake, we also find that what we eat during the day also influences our sleep at night," she says.

Research from her team and others has linked eating added sugars and saturated fat to more sleep disturbances and less deep slumber. Meanwhile, fruits, vegetables and fiber were associated with better sleep and fewer awakenings at night, she says.

If you want to eat better to sleep better, St-Onge says you can start with small, easy changes. "As a first step, cut out foods that are higher in added sugars and sweetened beverages," she says.

Switching to whole grains instead of refined carbohydrates is also a good idea. Her research has linked added sugars and refined carbs to a greater risk of insomnia.

And she says look for opportunities to eat more fruits and vegetables throughout the day.

"I always put a ton of leafy vegetables in my dishes, like stews and soups and stir fries," St-Onge says.

And of course, don't forget good sleep hygiene, says Philip Cheng, a sleep and circadian rhythms researcher and professor of medicine at Henry Ford Health in Michigan. That means things like keeping your bedroom cool and dark, and sticking to a regular schedule for going to bed and waking up as best as you can.

Sponsor Message

"That's going to stabilize your sleep in the long run," Cheng says.

But if your poor sleep lasts months or even years, he says it's time to see a medical provider for help.

World.title: They saw people losing food benefits. So they started handing out free groceries
World.content:
They saw people losing food benefits. So they started handing out free groceries

toggle caption i Kori Suzuki for NPR

SAN DIEGO, CALIF. — It should have been her day off. Instead, early Saturday morning, Rosa Rodarte was back at the social service office where she works, pushing carts of food and loading them into people's cars.

Rodarte's official job is to help people apply for programs like food assistance. But lately, she's been simply helping people get food.

"We have the same goal," she says. "We want to make sure everybody is being helped and not judged."

toggle caption i Kori Suzuki for NPR

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, better known as SNAP, has seen participation plummet over the past year. Some five million people nationwide have lost federal food benefits ever since the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill, a piece of sweeping tax and spending legislation that slashed SNAP funding, tightened eligibility, and prohibited food aid for most asylum seekers and refugees. It's considered the fastest decline in decades and far exceeding the federal government's own estimates of the impacts.

Sponsor Message

Not only has it been difficult for families facing food insecurity, but it's also taken a toll on the government workers who help administer SNAP. Over the past year, offices across the country have had to contend with new rules, heavier workloads and immense financial pressure to avoid errors. All the while, they've watched people lose food assistance en masse.

"The emotionally draining part is where you see someone that's telling you on the phone that they need your help and they need it today, and when you can't do something," says Nina Olivas, who oversees San Diego's Access Customer Service Call Center, where people inquire about assistance programs, such as SNAP or Medicaid.

There are 36,000 fewer people on San Diego County's SNAP program this September compared to July 2025, when Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill was signed into law. In response, the county has been partnering with local food banks to hand out free groceries at their social service offices. It's not a long-term fix, but county officials say they couldn't sit back while their neighbors went hungry.

"We are not ending the call with nothing," Olivas says.

toggle caption i Kori Suzuki for NPR/Kori Suzuki for NPR

Inundated with paperwork

Olivas says she routinely reminds her staff of their impact: "There's not a lot of jobs that you can do where everyday you can come in and put food on someone's table."

Sponsor Message

Her office helps San Diego residents access government assistance. In a way, she says, they're frontline workers — sometimes meeting people at the lowest point of their life, such as losing a job or getting sick.

"You're helping someone put food on the table. You're helping someone pay rent. You're helping someone buy diapers," Olivas says. "Those are things that are just so rewarding when you're able to do it. But when you're not, or when you can't do it right now, that can be really difficult."

Among the challenges has been grappling with new work requirements imposed on homeless people, former foster youth, veterans, parents with a child older than 14 and able-bodied adults aged 55 to 64. Supporters of the policy change argue it's bringing back the dignity of work.

"For many, welfare is no longer a lifeline to self-sufficiency but a lifelong trap of dependency," U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and other Trump officials wrote in a New York Times op-ed piece last year.

But for social service employees on the ground, these requirements have mostly meant more paperwork to process, on top of the wide swath of documents already required to receive food aid.

"Many of them already work," Olivas says of SNAP recipients. "So really what it is, is just that extra burden of having to really quantify how many hours they're working."

San Diego processed over 830,000 more documents between January and October, compared to the same time last year, according to the county. That accounts for mailed documents alone, which make up only about a third of all incoming paperwork.

toggle caption i Kori Suzuki for NPR/Kori Suzuki for NPR

What's happening in other states

Over the summer, the San Diego County Board of Supervisors chose to get ahead of the federal changes by securing $15.8 million to offset the loss in federal funding. They also approved the hiring of 122 new social service workers. These efforts helped keep call wait times relatively low and a majority of paperwork processed on time.

Sponsor Message

Other local and state governments are stepping up to fill the gaps. Illinois sent out a one-time $400 benefit for individuals who were kicked off SNAP. Similarly, Phoenix, Ariz. offered a similar $600 payment toward utility bills for those who lost federal food aid. Maine created a state-funded food assistance program for certain noncitizens.

Meanwhile, some states are showing just how severe the fallout from the federal policy changes can be. Texas' SNAP application backlog ballooned from 3,700 pending in January to 175,000 in September, according to a recent letter of concern penned by several members of Congress from Texas. Over 700,000 Texans have lost food aid since July 2025, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.

During the same time frame, Arizona's SNAP rolls shrunk by nearly half — the steepest decline in the nation. State officials attributed the decline to a staffing shortage that left them ill-equipped to handle a surge in paperwork, member station KJZZ reported. They also pointed to the state's efforts to more closely scrutinize SNAP applications in order to reduce the its payment error rate and avoid federal penalties.

And in Louisiana, SNAP enrollment fell by 154,000 between July 2025 and this September, according to state data. Three-quarters of removals stemmed from procedural issues such as missing forms or missed interviews, according to an analysis by the think tank Invest in Louisiana.

"We have to do something"

The idea to hold food distribution events outside San Diego's social service offices came from a restless night.

Monica Montgomery Steppe, vice chair of the County Board of Supervisors, was shaken by how many people in the area were projected to lose food benefits. Having relied on the assistance when she was younger, this felt personal, she says.

"So one night, ideas just started coming to me, so I took my phone and just started writing them in a Google Doc," she says. "And I gave them to my staff and said, 'We have to do something.'"

Sponsor Message

The food distribution events began in August. Between then and September, nearly 70,000 pounds of food have been distributed to over 5,200 people in partnership with Feeding San Diego and the San Diego Food Bank, according to the county.

Earlier this month, the line started to form about 90 minutes before the event officially began. Among those waiting were young families, seniors and some wearing hats that read "veteran."

As social service workers guided people to the food line, they also fielded questions about the federal changes and addressed any issues that SNAP recipients may be experiencing with their food aid. Their goal: making sure no one is falling through the cracks.

Ambar Santiago was one of those people. She came needing help with groceries after her benefits didn't arrive that month. There was a hiccup in her case regarding her paperwork. After loading free vegetables, canned goods and diapers into her car, Santiago sat with a worker and explained her situation. The employee listened carefully, then offered Santiago a sense of relief.

"Let's look," the worker said. "We can do that."

toggle caption i Kori Suzuki for NPR/Kori Suzuki for NPR

Back home, Santiago prepared dinner with the very ingredients she received that day: tomato sauce, potatoes, onions. She whipped up her mother's carne guisada, a Puerto Rican beef stew that can stretch for days.

As she stirred, she told her husband that she felt grateful. Santiago had lived in different parts of the country and, not long ago, experienced homelessness. She knew getting help the way she did on Saturday wasn't the norm.

" I feel like the assistance that I would've gotten in the hood or in the Southeast or anywhere else is completely different from my ZIP code that I give them now," she says. "It's just a blessing."

World.title: Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout
World.content:
Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout

toggle caption i Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

President Trump heads to Asia this week where he's set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a high-stakes trilateral summit.

The trip to China marks Trump's second visit this year, and comes as the president and his party face widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections, potentially weakening his bargaining position across the Pacific.

The president and administration officials – including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – are also under scrutiny after the recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was recruited by China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.

Sponsor Message

Huang traveled to China with Trump earlier this year – this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is joining Trump in Shenzhen.

The expectation for major deals or pronouncements coming out of the meetings this week are low – but the meeting is still expected to make waves over the imagery of the trilateral summit. Trump said as he left the White House Monday that he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Before China, Trump will first travel to the Philippines where he'll meet with allies at the ASEAN summit in Manila.

The president is expected to be in the region for just about three days.

Trilateral meeting

For weeks the president has said he's keen to discuss the Iran war and denuclearization with Putin and Xi. But Edgard Kagan, the former ambassador to Malaysia and a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said it's a topic that Xi likely won't want to get into. The White House confirmed Friday that Trump is expected to meet with Xi and Putin together.

"The Chinese strongly disagree with the idea that they should be involved in any kind of trilateral discussions with the United States and Russia on nuclear weapons," Kagan said.

Sponsor Message

"China wants to avoid this because they don't want to be locked into a subservient position. And they also don't want to create a precedent. I think the main thing for the Chinese is they know if they do a meeting and nuclear issues are discussed, it becomes much harder for them to refuse to do it in the future," he said.

A White House official said they do not expect any agreement to come out of the meeting on denuclearization.

"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said, calling the trilateral an "entry point" for the three countries to talk about reducing nuclear weapons stock.

Another U.S. official not authorized to speak on the record acknowledged that denuclearization is a "difficult" topic for China.

"But we do think it's time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things," the official said.

Putin, for his part, stands to benefit from a meeting with Trump and Xi, as Russia's war with Ukraine nears its five-year mark. Trump has made friendlier moves toward Russia in recent months, siding with Putin and striking a deal to release more Russian oil into the market ahead of the midterm elections.

Trump said last month that he was fine with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy not being present at a potential meeting with Putin about the war.

"Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not," Trump said.

A White House official said Ukraine is not intended to come up in the meeting with Xi and Putin. And there is no plan for Putin and Trump to have a separate meeting.

But Trump said Monday he would be talking about his "favorite subject Ukraine."

Sponsor Message

Kagan said the meeting with Xi, Trump and Putin could end up being on the shorter side if there isn't much all parties are willing to discuss. But at the same time, "I could see this going longer because President Trump likes dealing with Putin and Xi. He sees them as his peers. He sees them as important world leaders," Kagan said.

Either way, a photo of the three leaders meeting together is enough to make headlines.

"That picture alone is going to be worth well over a thousand words," Kagan said.

Busan Agreement

This is the second time Trump and Xi are meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit – but this year's meeting is notably different from last year's in Busan, South Korea, when tensions between the US and China were fraught amid the escalating trade war.

The meeting in Busan established a sort-of truce between the two countries. The U.S. immediately lowered some tariffs on Chinese goods and China agreed to loosen exports on rare earths. But the execution of the agreement has been spotty.

"There's friction in this truce. It's not smooth, but it's basically functional," Kurt Tong, Managing Partner at The Asia Group, said.

A White House official said the U.S. isn't getting rare earths from China at the pace or level they'd like.

"We really want to focus minds among our counterparts in China on compliance with this," they said.

Still, Tong expects the agreement to be renewed past its January expiration. The two sides will likely agree to the renewal either in Shenzhen or later this year at the G20 summit Trump is hosting in Miami, according to Tong.

Meetings in Manila

Before the president arrives in China, he's holding meetings with several allies in Manila, including a meeting with the other leaders of the Quad nations: India, Japan and Australia.

Sponsor Message

"I think it's quite significant symbolically and politically that the U.S., Australia, Japan and India, the major democracies of Asia and the Pacific, get together… it's especially significant that they're doing it just before the meetings in China," Tong said.

The White House said Trump will also sign a trade deal with Thailand while in the Philippines.

The opportunity in Manila for Trump is to repair and reinforce relationships with countries like Japan and India, and the host country the Philippines. The ASEAN summit is also the region's first look at the president since his party lost control of Congress and on a global stage, a chance to see what the last two years of Trump's presidency may look like.

"I think the real thing that people will be looking at first is, how does he present himself?" Kagan said. "How does his behaviour towards Modi and towards India change? Those are things people will be looking at very, very closely for clues for what the next two years are likely to be like."

Nvidia fallout

A White House official said they don't expect Trump to raise the issue of Huang's affair and resignation with Xi. The focus of the meeting is about trade, the official said.

Huang resigned last week after admitting the extramarital affair with Alice Huang. Trump administration officials are now facing scrutiny and questions about how much they knew about Huang's affair and how much Huang had access to Trump and his orbit.

Trump reiterated Monday he wasn't sure if Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and that he wouldn't mind seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia's CEO.

"I think the main impact is here in the United States, where there are calls for accountability with respect to Mr. Huang's activities with the U.S. government and questions about what happened… the net result of that is to provide a tailwind to persons who are interested in tightening up the technology denial regime toward China," Tong said.

Sponsor Message

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed last week to appear in front of the Senate Banking Committee to answer further questions. Trump stood by Lutnik on Monday, saying there were differing views on how to treat China in his administration.

World.title: CBSA demoting border officers who permanently lost ability to use sidearm
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) has informed 63 employees that they will have to take on new, lower-paid positions because of medical conditions that prevent them from carrying a sidearm.

The agency told CBC News in a statement that it is willing to offer temporary accommodations to employees who are unable to carry a firearm because of medical or psychological conditions.

However, when employees require permanent accommodation, it said they must be transferred "to a position for which carrying a firearm is not a condition of employment."

Several employees and their union are denouncing the planned demotions, saying that the affected border officers carry out duties that do not require the use of a firearm on a daily basis.

They also say the agency is penalizing experienced employees because of medical or psychological conditions, such as workplace injuries or mental and physical health issues that prevent them from requalifying for firearm use every two years.

The 63 officers affected by the measure represent 0.7 per cent of the 8,500 CBSA positions that require the ability to wear a sidearm.

Union calls process discriminatory, unfair

In a recent message to the employees, the CBSA warned that they would have to go through a "downward deployment without salary protection" as part of the "reasonable accommodation process."

"We think it's discriminatory, it's arbitrary and it's unfair," said Mark Weber, president of the Customs and Immigration Union.

One of the affected officers criticized the message as bureaucratic and impersonal.

Mark Weber is the president of the Customs and Immigration Union. He says the CBSA's decision is discriminatory. (Simon Lasalle/Radio-Canada)

"I felt like a file being closed, not a human being," the employee said.

The officer said they cried when they received the message telling them they would be getting a pay cut after years of service.

"The firearm never helped me do that job. My experience did. That experience didn’t disappear when I stopped being able to carry my gun," they said.

"I want to keep doing work that is important. I’m asking to be able to do that without being punished financially for having a medical disability."

The employee spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss their personal situation without their employer's permission.

In addition to the 63 officers being demoted, 14 employees on sick leave remain under review.

Another 36 officers have retired since January rather than lose the accommodations that allowed them to work in their current roles.

In all, 190 employees had been receiving workplace accommodations related to firearms. Aside from those facing demotion or who have already left, 27 were transferred to positions at the same level and 50 returned to their regular duties after receiving medical clearance.

The CBSA has 18,000 employees, including roughly 8,500 in front-line positions that require carrying a firearm, notably at border crossings and other ports of entry.

Dangerous work at CBSA includes intercepting illegal drugs, firearms and other prohibited goods at the border, as well as deporting individuals who are not authorized to be in Canada.

The use of force remains rare, with CBSA officers across the country drawing their sidearms an average total of 28 times a year.

Several employees who have been granted accommodations related to the carrying of firearms perform office work. (Radio-Canada)

In certain workplaces such as airports and postal centres, border services officers do not always carry their sidearm. Officers can also perform duties without carrying a gun, including working on the Nexus program, analyzing flight manifests and training new officers, according to the union.

A CBSA spokesperson said that "carrying protective and defensive equipment is intrinsically linked to the performance of duties" of border officers, including enforcing the law "when necessary."

"When an individual can no longer be fully armed or meet the requirements of their duties, the CBSA has a duty to accommodate them," said spokesperson Kelly Cameron.

However, she added the agency must spend public funds judiciously and ensure its employees meet the "essential requirements" of positions, including those that require being staffed by an armed officer.

"The CBSA is not required to permanently exempt an employee from performing the essential duties of their position or to create work that is not necessary," she said.

In its letter to the 63 employees who are still unable to carry a firearm, the CBSA stated that there are "no longer any suitable placement opportunities" at their current level.

At least one letter said that available placements would be shared "in the coming weeks."

Weber said the agency is needlessly depriving itself of long-serving employees with decades of experience.

"Essentially, they are being told by their employer that they no longer have value simply because they can no longer carry a firearm," he said.

World.title: WestJet denied family's cancelled flight was actually cancelled, claiming passenger rights didn't apply
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Dustin and Shania Klause's family vacation to Hawaii was thrown into jeopardy after WestJet scrapped their return flight a few months before departure and refused to rebook them on another flight for the same day.

The airline justified its refusal by claiming the flight hadn't been cancelled but, rather, rescheduled — even though it was completely removed from the family's itinerary.

"It's purely a flight cancellation," said a frustrated Dustin, who lives with Shania in Stony Plain, Alta., near Edmonton. "I feel like we were just kind of left in the dust."

The couple had planned the November trip to Kona, Hawaii, with six family members to spend time together following the death of Shania's mother from ovarian cancer.

"It's just really important to our family to do this together," said Shania. "We had finally had it all worked out."

The family, five adults and three children, planned the November trip to Kona, Hawaii, to spend time together following the death of Shania's mother. From left to right: Shania's sister-in-law and brother, Tenise and Chad Verbeek; Shania's late mom, Robin Verbeek; Shania's dad, Dale Verbeek; Shania and Dustin Klause. (Submitted by Dustin Klause)

However, in August, WestJet sent an updated itinerary omitting the Kona-to-Vancouver segment of their Nov. 24 return flight to Edmonton — leaving the family without a way home. When Dustin called to complain, the airline offered a replacement return flight departing two days later, which conflicted with several family members' work schedules.

So Dustin, who had researched his rights, insisted WestJet rebook them on another airline for their original travel date — a requirement under Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations (APPR) for cancellations within an airline's control.

WestJet refused. Multiple customer service agents told Dustin — in calls he recorded — that the regulations didn't apply because the flight disruption was a schedule change.

"If it was a cancellation then, yes, we would be obligated to put you on any carrier we could get you on, but in this case, this is a schedule change," said an agent.

Got a story you want investigated? Contact Sophia and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

After Dustin argued repeatedly that his flight had, in fact, been cancelled, the agent replied, "It is considered a schedule-change cancellation. There's a difference."

Not so, according to the Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA). Its online guidance states that passenger protection rules apply regardless of how an airline labels a flight disruption.

"A schedule change is effectively a cancellation," said Zohair Khan, co-founder of Airfairness, which, for a fee, helps passengers claim flight disruption compensation.

"The flight that you were booked on is gone, and now you're on a different flight."

WATCH | WestJet says cancelled flight was a 'schedule change': WestJet denies family’s flight was cancelled, says passenger rights don’t apply | Go Public | Duration closed caption 1:51 A family thought they’d have to cancel their long-awaited Hawaii vacation after WestJet refused to follow passenger protection rules, claiming their flight was merely 'rescheduled' rather than cancelled. After Go Public stepped in, the airline reversed course.

WestJet reverses course

Airlines have repeatedly flouted Canada's rebooking rules for flight cancellations, resulting in forfeited trips or passengers paying out-of-pocket to salvage their vacations.

WestJet suggested as an option that Dustin accept a refund for the return flight. However, because airfares had increased, Go Public confirmed it would cost the family thousands extra to buy tickets for the same date on another airline.

"We should not have to pay any more money," said Dustin. "At this point, our hands are so tied that we probably have to cancel."

After hearing from Go Public, WestJet reversed course and rebooked the family on their original departure date with partner airline Delta.

"They should have done that from the beginning," said Shania.

WestJet didn't comment directly on Dustin's case except to say that it would offer the family an apology.

The airline also didn't explain why its email notifying the family of the scrapped return flight included refund options under U.S. regulations, but omitted rebooking rights under Canadian regulations.

"Those APPR regulations should be front and centre," said Khan.

$755,000 in fines for rebooking violations

Under the APPR for flight cancellations , major airlines must offer passengers a choice between a refund or rebooking on the next available flight operated by them or a partner airline. But if the replacement flight delays travel by more than nine hours — or 48 hours for cancellations outside the airline's control — the carrier must rebook the passenger on any available airline.

Since 2025, the CTA has fined major airlines WestJet , Air Canada , Air Transat , and JetBlue Airways a combined $755,000 for 199 violations of rebooking rules.

Air Canada is challenging its $426,000 penalty for 71 violations last year, arguing the airline was affected by a labour dispute.

Zohair Khan, co-founder of Airfairness, says a schedule change is the same as a flight cancellation. (Prasanjeet Choudhury/CBC)

Khan suggests airlines often violate the requirement to rebook on other airlines to cut costs.

"That is the cheapest option, for you to stay on one of their flights," he said. "Unfortunately, most people will accept that."

Under the APPR, passengers are also entitled to up to $1,000 in compensation if an airline cancels a flight for reasons within its control 14 days or less before departure. According to the CTA, airlines have frequently violated this rule as well.

Bigger fines?

To improve compliance with Canada's rebooking rules, Khan supports the federal government's proposal to increase maximum penalties for repeat APPR violations from $25,000 to $1 million.

"I hope no airline has to pay it, but the fact that it exists itself should be a deterrent," said Khan.

However, it's still up in the air whether the new fine limit will be approved, let alone when it would take effect.

Shania and Dustin Klause, far right, are currently enjoying their vacation in Hawaii with family. (Submitted by Dustin Klause)

Meanwhile, Dustin and his family are in Hawaii, relieved that WestJet finally secured them a flight home on their original departure date.

"I'm happy that they actually followed their passenger protection regulations," he said.

World.title: Robert Pattinson announced as new James Bond
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Robert Pattinson will take on the iconic role of James Bond, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday morning.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a press release from the studio.

The upcoming film will be directed by Canadian Denis Villeneuve — known for directing the recent Dune movies, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049 — with a script by Steven Knight.

"Few films carry the kind of anticipation that comes with James Bond, and we have strived to honour the passionate fans, the legacy and the future of this iconic character," said Courtenay Valenti, head of film at Amazon MGM Studios.

"We are thrilled to officially welcome Robert Pattinson as our 007 and are confident he will bring something truly special to this role."

Pattison will take the reins from Daniel Craig, who played the iconic British spy in five films, ending with No Time to Die in 2021.

Robert Pattinson is coming off a big year, staring in Primetime as Chris Hanson and Antinous in The Odyssey. (Yves Herman/Reuters)

The year of Robert Pattinson

Pattinson is coming off the roles of Antinous in The Odyssey and Chris Hanson in Primetime, with more blockbusters to come.

In December, Pattinson will play Scytale in Dune: Part Three, also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson will star in the next Batman film scheduled for 2028, where he will continue as Gotham's Caped Crusader.

Amazon, which acquired Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM) in 2022, gained creative control over the James Bond franchise after making a deal with film producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli in 2025.

Amazon MGM first confirmed in May that they were searching for the next Bond. Pascal previously said in an interview with Deadline in August that the new James Bond would probably be revealed by "the end of the year."

More to come

World.title: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem to step down in 2027
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem will step down from the top job at Canada's central bank when his term expires on June 2, 2027.

In an announcement on Monday, the Bank of Canada said Macklem will not seek a second term as governor when his current seven-year term expires in June. The central bank says it has begun its search for his successor, and hopes to complete this process by spring 2027.

"My time as governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world," Macklem, 65, stated on Monday.

"The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate."

Macklem's retirement was widely expected, as the last time a ​Bank of Canada governor served a second term was ​in 1980.

On Monday, the Bank of Canada said the 12 independent directors on its board have formed a search committee to select the next governor. Zurich-based recruiting firm Egon Zehnder will provide assistance, according to the announcement.

While the new governor will be technically selected by this board, the final decision will rest with Prime Minister Mark Carney, himself a former governor of the bank, and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne.

A 14-page document about the job says candidates must hold Canadian citizenship, have a PhD or other graduate-level degree in economics, speak both official languages at a high level and have experience "at the highest levels of central banking, public policy, financial regulation, financial markets, academia, and/or international institutions."

During his tenure, Macklem faced unprecedented challenges, including the inflation shock resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, and the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war.

After Canadian inflation peaked at 8.1 per cent in mid-2022, Macklem executed one of the most aggressive rate tightening cycles in the central bank's history, raising its policy rate from 0.25 per cent to five per cent.

This involved 10 consecutive rate hikes over 16 months.

World.title: Quebecor makes $31B offer to acquire Telus
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebecor has made a proposal worth $31 billion to take over Telus.

The Montreal-based telecom company said Monday in a news release it submitted a non-binding proposal to Telus in June to serve as a basis for negotiations. Telus is currently reviewing an enhanced proposal submitted by Quebecor earlier this month, according to the release.

Quebecor says the proposed deal would combine complementary networks, spectrum and operating capabilities to strengthen investment capacity and competitive positioning.

The proposed deal would give Telus shareholders $6.35 in cash and 0.17 Quebecor shares for each Telus share they have — roughly a 60 per cent premium, according to the company.

Quebecor, Canada's fourth-largest telecom company, has boomed in value in recent years since acquiring Freedom Mobile in 2023, and using its competitors' networks to provide mobile service to customers.

The company argues that acquiring Telus would create a stronger company that could better serve consumers with a faster deployment of 5G, better rural connectivity and more affordability.

"This proposal will create a strong pan-Canadian competitor, able to compete on equal terms with the other national providers and to stand up to foreign companies, for the benefit of Canadians," Quebecor said in the statement.

Any deal would require approval from the Competition Bureau, as well as authorities like the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, Quebecor acknowledged.

The federal government has taken steps to try and enhance competition in the telecom sector, like regulations requiring large internet providers to open their networks to competitors and spotlighting affordable cellular plans, which it outlined in its recent telecom competition roadmap.

TELUS corporation's headquarters at TELUS Garden in downtown Vancouver, British Columbia, on Wednesday, May 6, 2026. Telus' board is considering the proposal from Quebecor, but says it has concerns that remain unanswered by the Montreal-based telecom company. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Telus says it has formed a committee to review the offer to determine the value of the potential deal. So far, the committee has surfaced a number of "significant risks" according to chair of Telus's board of directors, John Manley.

Quebecor "has yet to explain how what it is proposing could be approved under the current telecom regulatory framework in Canada and that a regulatory review of such a transaction would be a long and costly process for our shareholders," Manley said in a statement.

He added that Telus would continue to engage with Quebecor, the government and regulatory authorities about those concerns, while exploring alternatives.

Quebecor said it has retained experts to assess the proposed deal and issues that might be raised by authorities. It's also ready to discuss "measurable commitments" about pricing, employment and regional connectivity with those authorities, the company said in its release.

World.title: Silicon Valley leaders call for reinstatement of Nvidia CEO with 'Stand With Jensen' petition
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO is drawing support from prominent Silicon Valley personalities, four days after his resignation stemming from revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy.

More than 179,000 people had signed the petition, according to the website hosting it. Those listed as signatories included Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.

Nvidia shares suffered early losses, but remained more than one per cent lower after U.S. President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang return as CEO.

"I think he learned a big lesson," Trump said.

The Stand With Jensen website coincided with an open letter from two prominent investors, Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, who urged Nvidia's board to avoid rushing to replace Huang before all the facts were known.

"We are current and former NVIDIA employees, partners, shareholders, and supporters. We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests," according to an open letter published on the website.

The website showed that more than 8,400 signatories identified themselves as current Nvidia employees, claiming this represents approximately 21 per cent of all Nvidia employees. A further 94,000 signatories identified themselves as shareholders, although the website cautioned that professional affiliations were self-reported and had not been independently verified.

WATCH | Nvidia CEO steps down: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO | Duration closed caption 3:19 Chip-maker Nvidia has announced that Jensen Huang has resigned as president and CEO of the tech giant he co-founded. In a statement, Nvidia said Colette Kress, the current executive vice-president and chief financial officer, has agreed to lead the company.

The campaign comes as some prominent investors also urge Nvidia's board not to rush to replace Huang. Atreides Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner said in an open letter that the board should wait until all the facts were known.

Shockwaves through industry

Huang stepped down on Thursday after reports of alleged affairs with employees, including one who reported directly to him, plunging the AI chip heavyweight into crisis and sending shockwaves through an industry he helped bankroll.

Corporate boards have previously removed chief executives over relationships with employees. McDonald's fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019 over a consensual relationship with an employee that violated company policy, while Intel CEO Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 after a similar policy breach.

But the episode also highlights the challenges boards can face when ousting high-profile executives who retain strong employee and investor backing. OpenAI reinstated Sam Altman as CEO in November 2023, just days after his removal triggered an employee revolt and opposition from investors.

The turmoil at Nvidia comes as the company is taking on growing strategic importance in Washington.

WATCH | Scandal causing ripples in Washington: Is the Nvidia scandal fracturing Trump's administration? | Duration closed caption 9:32 Katherine Tai, former U.S. trade representative under president Joe Biden, weighs in on the blame game between Trump's cabinet secretaries as the fallout over Nvidia continues. Tai tells CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that the timing of the scandal post-midterms is not a coincidence.

Trump's reported trades this year suggest he held between $13 million US and $62 million US in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures.

The Trump administration also plans to designate Nvidia and more than two dozen other AI companies as "national champions," the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for Nvidia to appoint an outsider as its next CEO, saying the company needs a "dramatic shakeup" following Huang's departure.

Colette Kress was named interim CEO in the wake of Huang’s resignation. She previously served as executive vice-president and chief financial officer.

The website hosting the petition included a call to institutional investors to dial into an earnings call slated for Tuesday and raise the issue of Huang’s ousting.

World.title: What will it take for the world's superpowers to agree on AI regulations in war?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the UN prepares to discuss autonomous weapons this week, insiders say hopes of meaningful, binding regulations around AI in warfare are slim — and time may be running out.

Diplomats will discuss lethal autonomous weapons systems, including a possible framework for regulations, at a Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons meeting running Monday to Friday in Geneva, Switzerland. More than 100 countries that are party to the convention will be represented, including Canada, the U.S., Russia and China.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned in August that the world was nearing a " moral red line " where autonomous weapons like AI-powered drones could kill without human involvement. He's said he wants a legally binding treaty on autonomous weapons by the end of 2026 as AI increasingly becomes a factor in deadly strikes.

Meanwhile, some experts say the use of AI to determine where and when to strike in the first place is an even more pressing concern than the weapons themselves.

But so far, the world's biggest military superpowers — including the U.S., Russia and China — have shot down any serious attempts at binding rules.

Leaders are afraid of losing their competitive advantage because of the idea that "whoever wins the AI race will dominate the world," said Paul Lushenko, a senior fellow at Cornell University Tech Policy Institute and a retiring U.S. military officer.

He says everyone he speaks to in the military recognizes the moral implications of AI. At the same time, the prevailing consensus among the most powerful militaries is that even if they follow a set of rules, they can't trust their competitors to do the same, creating a Cold War-esque stalemate.

"That's a really challenging position to be in," he said.

Paul Lushenko, senior fellow at Cornell University Tech Policy Institute, says the world's military superpowers worry that if they follow regulations around AI, their competitors won't do the same. (Lisa Maco/Cornell University)

Lushenko said he does not expect any kind of "bona fide international policy" or regulation to come out of this week's meetings.

About one-third of the countries that attended a February military AI summit in Spain, including Canada, agreed to a declaration on how to govern use of the technology in warfare, but the U.S. and China were among those that opted out.

UN diplomats were negotiating a treaty in September to regulate the use of lethal autonomous weapons when U.S. and Russian diplomats cut out key safety provisions on the final day.

According to reporting by the Washington Post, those provisions included language that would have required systems to operate in a predictable and reliable manner, mandated ethical considerations and required that humans review military targets picked by AI before striking.

AI in action

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, addressing the UN in September, warned there is a "real possibility" that AI will soon begin to decide what happens on the battlefield.

"We need peace before we reach that point," he said.

Ukraine and Russia are both increasingly using AI to gain advantages in battle as the war between the two countries approaches its fifth year. In August, the New York Times reported that a Russian drone operated entirely by AI killed three Ukrainian civilians.

In one of the most prominent examples of AI-assisted targeting, Israeli intelligence officers described to Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine and the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call how the military's Lavender AI system allegedly identified 37,000 targets in Gaza, with one saying soldiers had about 20 seconds to review each target before they carried out a strike.

The U.S. has since made a major push to ramp up AI use, with the Pentagon declaring the country's military an "AI-first fighting force."

The U.S. used Anthropic's Claude chatbot to help identify nearly 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours of its war with Iran in February. After a U.S. missile strike on a girls' school in Minab, American senators raised concerns over the use of AI tools, including Palantir's Maven Smart System, in target selection.

Those concerns did not deter the military. In June, Cameron Stanley, chief digital and artificial intelligence officer for the department of defence, said Elon Musk's Grok chatbot had been used to launch thousands of missiles at Iran.

WATCH | Concerns around Canada's deal with Palantir: Why Canada’s military deal with Palantir sparks sovereignty fears | Duration closed caption 9:59 There is growing scrutiny over Canadian defence contracts with American tech giant Palantir. For The National, CBC’s Ashley Fraser breaks down how its software is being used and why politicians and privacy experts are warning about national security and data sovereignty risks.

The frequency of AI-assisted targeting in Gaza and Iran has raised concerns from experts who worry that even though a human technically may have the final say before strikes are made, that human could effectively serve as a rubber stamp.

'Dystopian future'

Craig Martin, a former Canadian navy officer and an expert in armed conflict laws who teaches at Washburn University in Topeka, Kan, also worries about automation bias, whereby humans tend to become overly confident in AI's accuracy and validity.

"This may have been the case in the ... use of Lavender in Gaza, similarly the incident of the strike on the school in Minab by the United States," he told CBC News.

Craig Martin, a former Canadian navy officer and an expert in armed conflict laws, would like to see a ban on fully autonomous weapons. (Andrew Lee/CBC)

Martin is calling for changes to international law that would ban fully autonomous weapons and restrict semi-autonomous weapons.

He says he has hope for some form of agreement on AI, but it "would be a mistake to say that one is extremely optimistic," given that international law is in "a bit of a crisis right now."

"My greatest fear would be that we miss this window of opportunity and we increasingly develop weapons that are governed by AI over which we have little control and often little understanding and no legal regime that's governing those weapon systems," he said.

"It could lead to some kind of dystopian future."

Lushenko says his concerns extend to nuclear weapons.

While noting that AI offers the possibility of built-in deterrents and has potential to reduce human error and civilian casualties, he says war games conducted in research programs have found AI chatbots tend to rapidly escalate to suggesting the use of nukes in evolving crises between powerful countries.

Fears of escalation

The fear among major powers of being left behind is driving a "race to the bottom," said Branka Marijan, senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and senior researcher with anti-war organization Project Ploughshares.

"Without those guardrails we really, I think, are in a very dangerous moment," she said.

Branka Marijan, senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and senior researcher with Project Ploughshares, says the world is in a 'dangerous moment' without guardrails around AI in war. (Submitted by Branka Marijan)

Marijan says what keeps her up at night is not necessarily the sheer destruction that could be caused by autonomous weapons or by AI selecting targets in the midst of an ongoing war, but mistakes that could cause an international incident to escalate into a full-blown crisis.

CNN reported in September that the U.S. military almost boarded a Chinese vessel in the Middle East because an AI chatbot mistakenly said the ship was carrying nuclear materials.

WATCH | An exclusive look at drones being built for Ukraine: The Canadian company arming Ukraine with drones | Duration closed caption 4:19 Warning: This story contains graphic footage taken by drones used in warfare, including the targeting of soldiers. | Ukraine needs more war drones than it can manufacture and a Canadian company has stepped in to help. CBC’s Jennifer Yoon gets an exclusive look at what’s being built for the battlefield and how it could help Canada modernize its own defence capabilities. | NOTE (July 8, 2026): This video has been edited to remove identifying details of a location.

Marijan says incidents like that "are likely to keep occurring" and next time, the military might not put the brakes on soon enough.

"You could have a system that completely influences a state actor to act in a way that might be based on faulty information ... that results in some catastrophic mistake."

World.title: Lindsay Clancy will be retried in March for the killing of her 3 children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.

Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother whose highly divisive murder trial shone a global spotlight on postpartum mental health, will be tried again on murder charges for the killings of her three children.

Clancy, whose previous trial ended in a mistrial in September after the 12-member jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict, did not appear to show emotion in Plymouth Su perior Court in Plymouth, Mass., on Monday during the pivotal hearing in her case.

Last week, Judge William Sullivan rejected a bid by Clancy's attorneys to have the case against her dismissed.

A date for the new trial was set for March 29, 2027, despite arguments from assistant district attorney Jennifer Sprague that it wouldn't leave them enough time to prepare.

"The sooner this case is retried, the better it is for all parties," Sullivan said.

Plymouth County district attorney Timothy Cruz's office had ​ not yet announced plans for how it would prosecute the case moving forward, which had raised questions as to whether Clancy would be retried for first-degree murder or on lesser charges instead.

But in court on Monday, after Sprague said they would need to set a date for a jury trial, Clancy's defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said it appeared "the die has been cast."

"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is gonna require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments," Reddington said.

WATCH | Breaking down Lindsay Clancy's 'impossible case': ‘Impossible case’: Breaking down the Lindsay Clancy mistrial | Duration closed caption 5:33 The National’s Erica Johnson asks attorney and professor Margo Lindauer to break down why a mistrial was declared in the Lindsay Clancy case and what could happen next.

Murder charges in deaths of her 3 children

Clancy, 36, faced first-degree murder charges over the deaths of her daughter Cora, 5; son Dawson, 3; and eight-month-old son Callan. If convicted of those charges, she would be sentenced to life in prison without parole.

No one at Clancy's initial trial disputed that she strangled the children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end ​her own life, leaving her paralyzed.

But her defence argued she isn't criminally responsible because she had bipolar disorder and was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and little-understood mental health condition that can affect a new mom's sense of reality.

Prosecutors had argued Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder because she plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the killings.

The case has gripped the public, sparking debates about maternal mental health, launching online conspiracy theories and creating dramatic moments both inside and outside the court throughout the livestreamed trial.
