World.title: Flying Between Costa Rica and the US Today? Cancellations Have Dropped Sharply
World.content:
If you’re flying between Costa Rica and the United States today, the worst of the disruption from Friday’s nationwide US ground stop looks to be over. FlightAware reported 144 Monday cancellations and 641 delays as of Sunday afternoon. That’s a fraction of what travelers faced over the weekend. Of the 41,000 flights scheduled Saturday, more than 6,600 were canceled, according to FlightAware. On Sunday, FlightAware reported 2,291 cancellations as of 3 p.m. ET.

US officials say schedules should be close to normal today. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy expects air travel to be “back to normal” by Monday, and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had said airlines expected to recover by the end of Sunday. Check your flight before you leave for the airport anyway. When a ground stop strands planes and crews in the wrong cities, later flights can be delayed or canceled because crew members can’t get to them, and that knock-on effect can last a day or more.

Two airlines with major Costa Rica routes were among the hardest hit. American had the most cancellations on Sunday with 611, followed by JetBlue with 253. For JetBlue, that was about 27% of its schedule. At Juan Santamaría International Airport, the impact on Friday night was limited. Airport operator Aeris reported 12 departures and 11 arrivals affected, with six departures and four arrivals canceled, while the rest operated overnight and into the early morning. Aeris advised passengers to check flight status directly with their airlines, since schedules may change.

If your trip was affected, you may be able to change it without paying a fee. JetBlue’s fee waiver covers travel from Nov. 13 to 15, American extended its waiver through Nov. 18, and Delta is urging travelers with flexible plans to move their trips to Monday or later. Read your airline’s terms before rebooking, because waivers usually cover only certain dates and fare types.

The FAA has ruled out foul play. Bedford said the ground stop was caused by faulty equipment and that there was “zero evidence of anything nefarious.” Departures nationwide were halted for more than four hours on Friday after an equipment outage cut radar feeds and communication with aircraft, and the agency lifted the stop at 8:15 p.m. ET.

Duffy has given a more detailed account. He said the outage began during work to switch lines from copper to fiber at an FAA site in El Dorado, Arkansas, when turning on a new router there caused a router in Amarillo, Texas, to start flooding the system. The FAA has since disabled the broadcast feature on 69 routers of that type.

It could happen again as Duffy warned that further disruptions are possible until the copper lines are fully replaced at the end of 2028. With the busy holiday travel season about to start, turn on your airline’s app notifications and give yourself extra time on connections through US hubs.

World.title: Costa Rica Hemp Permits Are Free for Six Years, but Now You Must Apply Online
World.content:
If you want to grow hemp or medical cannabis legally in Costa Rica, there is now only one way to apply. Since November 12, every new grow application under the cannabis law must be filed online through the Single Investment Window according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MAG).

The ministry will no longer take new requests through any other channel. Applications that were already in progress, or that reached MAG before November 12, will still be processed outside the VUI until a decision is reached, the ministry said.

The change covers the two permits MAG handles under Law 10113, the 2022 law that legalized medical cannabis and hemp. The first is an authorization to import seeds and other propagation material, grow hemp and carry out primary production for food and industrial use. The second is a license to import propagation material and to grow and produce psychoactive cannabis for medical and therapeutic use.

According to MAG, the hemp authorization carries no fee and is valid for six years, renewable. The psychoactive cannabis license is also valid for six years but carries an annual fee, with differentiated rates for small businesses and small agricultural producers. The fee amounts were not included in the ministry’s announcement.

MAG made the switch through a administrative resolution and was published in the official gazette La Gaceta which orders the ministry and its attached agencies to move their procedures gradually onto the VUI. The ministry said it had also recently added agrochemical registration procedures to the same platform.

The VUI is run by PROCOMER, Costa Rica’s foreign trade promotion agency, and handles more than 40 procedures that companies need to set up and operate in the country. In February, the Health Ministry, MAG and the Costa Rican Drug Institute (ICD) opened a shared VUI channel for hemp and cannabis procedures, from production and processing to import, export and sales. The November measure makes the online route the only route for MAG’s grow permits.

Filing online does not mean automatic approval. Applicants still have to meet every requirement set out in the law and its regulations and then wait for a decision from MAG. PROCOMER warns on the platform that the VUI does not and will not ask for confidential information by phone, messaging apps or other channels. Applicants with questions can reach VUI support toll-free at 800-7762-6637 or at (506) 2505-4700.

The Law, approved in March 2022, allows cannabis only for medical and therapeutic purposes and allows hemp for food and industrial products. Recreational cannabis is outside its scope. Since then the industry has moved slowly but steadily. Authorities have issued new hemp licenses and approved medical cannabis sales, and in August the first medical cannabis manufacturing laboratory opened its doors.

For anyone following Costa Rica’s young cannabis sector, the change means the first step toward a legal crop now starts on a computer screen rather than at a ministry counter.

World.title: Costa Rica Bill Would Let Towns Cap Airbnb Rentals
World.content:
Costa Rica’s municipalities could limit how many short-term rentals operate in a neighborhood, a residential building or even on certain floors of a condominium tower under a bill filed in the Legislative Assembly by the opposition Frente Amplio party. The same bill would create a 10% tax on the commissions and service fees that platforms such as Airbnb earn from stays in Costa Rica.T

The bill, brought forward by Frente Amplio caucus leader José María Villalta, would overhaul Law 9742, the 2019 framework law that governs vacation rentals booked through digital platforms. It would also rename the law to emphasize coexistence between short-term rentals and the residents around them. The bill does not ban vacation rentals or set a national cap.

Under the proposal, local governments could limit the number, density, concentration and type of tourist lodging by district, neighborhood, zone or property. Any limits would have to rest on technical studies of housing, infrastructure, public services, the environment and mobility, with public participation and periodic review.

In mostly residential buildings, municipalities could restrict rentals to certain floors or sections if studies show they harm access to housing. The bill would also amend the Condominium Property Law so that building rules could not override those municipal limits, and it would recognize a right of residents not to be displaced by a disproportionate expansion of short-term rentals.

The 10% tax would apply to platform commissions, service fees and other income from stays in properties located in Costa Rica, regardless of where the platform is based. The bill as described in its filing does not say whether platforms could pass the cost on to hosts or guests.

Half the revenue would go to municipalities, in proportion to what each canton generates, for affordable housing and community infrastructure. Another 30% would go to the Banco Hipotecario de la Vivienda (Banhvi) for housing and affordable rental programs in cantons under housing pressure, and the remaining 20% would go to the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) for registry and oversight work.

Registration rules would also tighten. No property could be advertised without ICT registration, and each would receive a unique number that must appear in every listing. Hosts would have to prove ownership or authorization, comply with zoning and municipal licensing, be current on tax and social security payments, meet safety and sanitary standards, declare maximum capacity and provide an emergency contact. Platforms would have to register with the ICT, share information with state institutions and withhold and pay applicable taxes, with joint liability if they fail to do so.

Fines would be set in base salaries, the unit Costa Rica uses to calculate legal penalties. Hosts would face 1 to 3 base salaries for minor infractions, 4 to 10 for serious ones and 11 to 20 for very serious ones, along with possible suspension or cancellation of their registration. Platforms would face 20 to 100 base salaries for serious infractions and 50 to 200 for very serious ones. Publishing a listing without verifying its registration, leaving out the registration number or ignoring an order to remove a listing would all count as serious infractions.

The bill’s explanatory text argues that short-term rentals, especially those booked through platforms, have affected the housing market and the makeup of neighborhoods, and it cites a 2025 OECD study on housing pressure in coastal areas. It says the current law treats vacation rentals mainly as a tourism, commercial and tax matter without accounting for their effect on housing, and it states that the reform does not aim to restrict tourism.

Villalta has said the proposal seeks to balance tourism development with communities’ right to remain where they live and to find affordable housing. Law 9742 already requires owners of vacation rentals to register with the ICT and with the Finance Ministry’s tax administration, and stays booked through platforms are already subject to the 13% value-added tax. The ICT and the Finance Ministry would have nine months after the reform took effect to set up information-sharing protocols with municipalities.

The bill faces a long path. The Legislative Assembly is in extraordinary sessions through Jan. 31, a period in which lawmakers may only debate bills placed on the agenda by the executive branch, and the government’s latest agenda includes no bills from opposition parties, including the Frente Amplio.

To become law, the proposal would need to clear committee and pass two votes in the full Assembly.

World.title: Nearly Half of Costa Rica Driving Tests Failed in 2026, the Most Since 2015
World.content:
Nearly half of all practical driving tests for a standard car license in Costa Rica have ended in failure this year, the highest rate in more than a decade. Of 104,497 practical tests for the B1 license with a recorded result through Nov. 12, 51,050 ended in failure, a rate of 48.9%, according to the Road Safety Council (Cosevi).

That is the highest failure rate for the category since 2015, when it reached 52.5%. The rate fell to 28.4% in 2023 and 29% in 2024 before climbing to 37% in 2025. The figures count tests, not people, and leave out no-shows. A driver who failed twice is counted twice. Motorcycle tests were the next hardest to pass. The A1 category had a failure rate of 35.2% and A2 had 30.2%, while categories such as B2 and C2 came in near 18%.

Across all license categories, 74,946 of 202,714 practical tests ended in failure this year, or 37%. Cosevi’s records show one person has failed the practical exam 40 times, the most it has recorded, while the individual record on the regular written exam is 55 failures. The data released did not include reasons for the failures. If you are working through the licensing process, the numbers suggest planning for the possibility of a second attempt.

The figures come as Costa Rica marks the World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims on Sunday. The National Insurance Institute (INS) counted 535 road deaths through its October cutoff, up 13.6% from 471 at the same point in 2025. Motorcyclists accounted for 268 of those deaths, roughly half. They also made up about two-thirds of the injured, 27,182 of the 41,388 people hurt in traffic crashes from January to September, according to the INS.

The INS recorded 37,392 crashes in those nine months, and the number of people injured rose 9% from 37,974 in the same period of 2025. The Costa Rican Red Cross says it responds to a traffic crash about every eight minutes. The cost is borne in part by mandatory vehicle insurance. The INS said the compulsory policy, known as the SOA, has spent 50,576 million colones (about $112 million) this year on medical care and compensation for crash victims, or more than 185 million colones (about $411,000) a day.

With two months left in the year, the road death toll on Costa Rica’s highways and streets is already 64 higher than it was at the same point in 2025.

World.title: Gasoline Could Drop in December as Cooking Gas Jumps
World.content:
Filling your tank in Costa Rica should get cheaper in December but cooking with gas will cost more. The Costa Rican Oil Refinery (Recope) has asked regulators to cut the price of regular gasoline by ₡103 a liter, while the standard 11.3-kilogram (25-pound) cylinder of cooking gas would rise by ₡912, according to preliminary figures Recope presented on Friday to the Public Services Regulatory Authority (Aresep).

Under the proposal, regular gasoline would fall from ₡807 to ₡704 a liter, a drop of about 13%. Super would fall ₡28, from ₡805 to ₡777, and diesel would ease by ₡9, from ₡807 to ₡798. The 25-pound gas cylinder, the best-selling size in the country, would climb from ₡7,721 to ₡8,633, an increase of about 12%. None of the new prices is final. Aresep must review Recope’s figures and approve them before they take effect.

For anyone driving, the cut on regular is by far the largest of the three. At the proposed price, a liter of regular would cost about $1.58, or roughly $5.97 per US gallon, at the current exchange rate. On a 45-liter (11.9-gallon) tank, the change would save about ₡4,635, or roughly $10, each time you fill up. It would also undo an unusual situation that began in October, when regular became more expensive than premium. In December, regular would again cost ₡73 less per liter than super.

Recope attributed the lower gasoline and diesel prices to falling international oil prices, easing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and greater availability of crude on world markets, according to Teletica. The gas increase has a different cause. Recope said cooking gas it bought on international markets at higher prices during October kept later price declines from showing up in this adjustment, Monumental reported.

The cylinder increase will be felt in a lot of kitchens. About half of Costa Rican households use liquefied petroleum gas, mostly for cooking, according to Aresep. At the proposed price, a 25-pound cylinder would cost about $19.35, up from about $17.31. If you are due to swap a tank, buying before the new price takes effect would save you the difference, and it is worth taking 30 seconds to check that the cylinder is safe before you carry it home.

The December adjustment follows a stretch of rising energy costs. Fuel and transport fares drove consumer prices higher for a second straight month in October, when diesel alone rose more than 17%, and Costa Rica has paid $701 million more for imported fuel this year. Aresep has not said when the new prices would take effect. Adjustments normally apply from the day after the regulator’s resolution is published in the official gazette, La Gaceta.

World.title: El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo Opens ATP Finals With a Win
World.content:
El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo and Croatian partner Mate Pavić began their ATP Finals campaign with a 7–6 (7), 6–4 victory over France’s Theo Arribagé and Albano Olivetti on Sunday. The fourth-seeded pair recovered from a 2–0 deficit in the second set to win their opening match in the Todd Woodbridge Group at Turin’s Inalpi Arena. The match lasted one hour and 27 minutes.

Arévalo and Pavić had to work through a tense first set before taking control. They missed five chances to win the set, including four in the tiebreaker, but eventually claimed it 9–7. The French pair responded by breaking early in the second set. Arévalo and Pavić fought back, winning six of the next eight games to finish the match in straight sets.

The final numbers showed how close it was. Arévalo and Pavić won just five more points than their opponents but converted two of their four break-point chances. The win gives the Salvadoran-Croatian team a strong start in a tournament where one loss does not mean elimination. The eight doubles teams are divided into two groups of four, and each pair plays the other three teams in its group.

The top two teams from each group advance to the semifinals. Also in their group are defending champions Harri Heliövaara of Finland and Henry Patten of Britain, and Brazil’s Orlando Luz and Rafael Matos. Heliövaara and Patten won their opening match Sunday, beating the Brazilians 6–3, 5–7, 10–4.

Arévalo and Pavić are seeking their first ATP Finals title together. They reached the final in 2024 and return to Turin as one of the more experienced teams in the field. This is Arévalo’s fifth appearance at the year-end event and Pavić’s ninth. Their opponents on Sunday were making their ATP Finals debut after winning six doubles titles during the season.

Arévalo and Pavić still have two group matches to play. The semifinals are scheduled for Nov. 21, with the doubles final on Nov. 22.

World.title: Costa Rica Free Zones Barely Grew and Jobs Disappeared
World.content:
Production in Costa Rica’s free zones, the export parks that host most of the country’s multinational employers, grew just 0.6% year-on-year in September, according to the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR). That is 13.6 percentage points slower than in September 2025, when the sector was riding a surge in medical-device exports.

Employment in the regime is also slipping. The Central Bank’s three-month moving average put free-zone jobs at 195,410 in August 2026, down from 197,101 a year earlier, a loss of 1,691 positions.

The Central Bank now projects free-zone output will expand about 3% in 2026, compared with a preliminary 12.7% in 2025. The rest of the economy, known as the definitive regime, grew 3.3% in September and accounted for 96% of national growth, according to the bank’s monthly economic activity index (IMAE).

The slowdown has revived a long-running dispute over the strong colón. The weighted average dollar price on the Monex exchange market fell from 503.02 colones on Nov. 6, 2025, to 449.58 colones on the same date this year, a drop of 10.6%. Exporters and multinationals earn in dollars but pay salaries and local costs in colones, so each dollar they bring in now covers less of their payroll. The dollar hit a record low of 446 colones this week.

According to minutes of the Central Bank board’s Oct. 23 session, Henry Vargas, the bank’s division manager for data and statistical analysis, told directors that the 2025 export spike had to normalize and that international uncertainty is the main drag on the sector. He cited a U.S. Commerce Department study of possible new tariffs. Vargas said the exchange rate did not rank among the leading factors that companies named in a regional business survey the bank conducted with other central banks in October and November 2025, in which about 70% of firms said international uncertainty affected them deeply, though he acknowledged that business chambers do raise it.

Board member Jorge Guardia questioned why the exchange rate did not appear among the factors, noting that outside reports frequently point to it, according to the minutes. Central Bank President Róger Madrigal said job reductions in the sector are tied mainly to decisions by parent companies rather than directly to the exchange rate, while allowing that profit margins may have narrowed even where output has not.

Vargas also told the board that the closures of operations by Intel and Qorvo had been fully completed by September. The bank has attributed part of the year-on-year slowdown to that base effect, along with the exceptional medical-implement exports of 2025. September did bring the first month-to-month acceleration in free-zone output after 12 consecutive months of deceleration.

Business groups dispute the bank’s reading and the free-zone association Azofras has said the colón’s appreciation pressures operations and could weigh on company decisions to stay, expand or keep staff. Sergio Capón, president of the Costa Rican Chamber of Industries, has said it is unreasonable to separate multinationals’ decisions from the exchange-rate trend.

The debate comes after free zones lost jobs for the first time in seven years, and as several companies have scaled back hiring plans, including a call center that cut its Costa Rica job pledge over competition from Asia. Analysts have also warned that office vacancy could climb as multinationals cut jobs.

The Central Bank has bought more than $1.2 billion on the exchange market this year to slow the colón’s rise, and Madrigal has said the market has an excess supply of dollars.vFree zones employ close to 200,000 people and are one of Costa Rica’s largest sources of dollars, so a sustained slowdown would reach well beyond the export parks themselves. Whether the sector’s first monthly uptick in a year marks a turning point or a pause will become clearer as the Central Bank releases its October and November figures.

World.title: Should You Buy Travel Insurance for Costa Rica After the US Ground Stop?
World.content:
The nationwide ground stop that froze US air travel on Friday lasted a little more than four hours, but it left a question that will outlast the backlog. If a failure inside the air traffic control system can strand thousands of people bound for Costa Rica, should you buy travel insurance for your trip?

The quick answer to this is that insurance would not change what you get back for your flight, but it could cover almost everything else. Ten flights were canceled at Juan Santamaría International Airport on Friday and 23 were affected in all, according to airport operator Aeris, as the US ground stop spilled over into Costa Rica.

In the United States, airlines canceled more than 5,000 flights on Saturday as planes and crews worked their way back into position, according to the flight-tracking service FlightAware. For visitors, that meant missed first nights at hotels, lost tours and unplanned nights at a gateway airport or in San José.

Airfare is the one part of your trip you do not need insurance for. Under US Department of Transportation rules, if your flight is canceled and you choose not to travel, you are owed a full refund, even on a nonrefundable ticket, and that holds no matter what caused the cancellation. Airlines also waived change fees after the ground stop.

What airlines do not owe you is the cost of being stranded. Their promises of meals and hotels cover only disruptions they cause, and federal rules treat air traffic control failures as outside their control. After an outage like Friday’s, you pay for your own hotel, meals and ground transport unless the airline chooses to help.

That gap is where a comprehensive policy comes in. This kind of plan insures the full prepaid cost of your airfare, hotels and tours and bundles several benefits together. Trip delay coverage pays for a hotel room, meals and transport when you are stuck, usually after a wait of 3 to 12 hours and up to a daily limit. Trip interruption coverage reimburses prepaid nights and tours you lose when you arrive late. Missed connection coverage helps with the cost of catching up, which matters if you are booked on a domestic flight to the coast or a boat transfer to a remote lodge.

The wording matters more than the brand. The strongest policies cover a delay by a common carrier for any reason. Others list specific causes, so check that air traffic control failures or government action are on that list. Coverage that comes with a credit card tends to be narrower. During last year’s US government shutdown, American Express said its card benefits, including trip delay and trip cancellation coverage, would not pay for cancellations or delays caused by the FAA’s emergency order.

There are other limits. Insurance pays only what you cannot recover from the airline, hotel or tour operator. Canceling your entire trip over a one-day delay is rarely covered. Cancel for any reason upgrades cost more, usually return only part of your trip cost, often up to 75% or 80%, and generally require you to cancel at least two days before departure. You also have to buy a policy before trouble starts, because once a disruption is in the news, new policies will not cover it.

Comprehensive policies are commonly priced at about 4% to 10% of the insured trip cost, depending mostly on your age and coverage limits. For a couple spending $6,000 (about ₡2.68 million) on a Costa Rica vacation, that works out to roughly $240 to $600 (about ₡107,000 to ₡268,000). The same policy usually includes medical and evacuation coverage, which many US health plans, including original Medicare, generally do not provide outside the United States.

Whether that is money well spent depends on how you book. If your hotels are refundable and you have a spare day at each end, you have little to lose beyond a night or two. If you have a prepaid week at a jungle lodge, a sportfishing charter and a tight connection home, you have far more at stake. With the high season only weeks away and no way to rule out a repeat, it is worth doing that math before you book.

If you decide to buy, you can compare quotes from multiple travel insurers side by side and filter by the coverage that matters most for your trip, such as trip delay and missed connections.

World.title: International News: UN reports more than 1,100 killed in Haiti between July and September amid gang violence
World.content:
International News: UN reports more than 1,100 killed in Haiti between July and September amid gang violence

By Zoila Palma: More than 1,100 people were killed and hundreds injured in Haiti between July and September as armed gangs continued to terrorize communities, according to a new report from the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH).

The report documented at least 1,167 deaths and 459 injuries during the third quarter of the year, with gang violence spreading across Port-au-Prince and other departments.

According to the report, armed gangs were responsible for more than 45 percent of the killings and injuries, while more than half occurred during ground and aerial security operations targeting criminal groups

. The violence included territorial battles, retaliatory killings, kidnappings and attacks on civilians. In August, at least 19 people, including 12 elderly women, were beheaded in Cité Soleil, while two attacks in Kenscoff left at least 105 people dead, including 19 children. More than 36 victims were reportedly shot dead in the courtyard of a Protestant church.

The UN also documented at least 137 kidnappings for ransom and 344 victims of sexual violence committed by gang members, with 77 percent of the reported sexual violence cases involving gang rape.

Children continued to be recruited and exploited by armed groups, with at least 32 boys between the ages of 14 and 16 killed during clashes with security forces in Gressier. The report also recorded 44 cases of extrajudicial executions and attempted executions involving members of the Haitian National Police.

UN officials are calling on Haitian authorities to strengthen protection and assistance for affected communities while urging the international community to maintain its support for Haiti.

World.title: Dean Welcome crowned Mr. Garifuna 2026-2027!
World.content:
Dean Welcome crowned Mr. Garifuna 2026-2027!

By Zoila Palma: Dean Welcome of Dangriga Town has been crowned Mr. Garifuna 2026-2027 as part of activities leading up to this year’s Garifuna Settlement Day celebrations on November 19.

The celebrations have featured cultural showcases, entertainment and community activities, with Welcome receiving congratulations following his crowning.

Other activities included the Mr. Garifuna after-party, featuring a performance by Nino Arzu, as well as activities in Hopkins. The Miss Garifuna Belize 2026 Cultural Pageant was also among the events organized to celebrate and showcase Garifuna heritage, traditions and talent.

The celebrations also featured a mass and a tribute to ancestors in recognition of the history and contributions of the Garifuna people.

This year’s theme is “Úaraguni, Anichigu, Awanseruni – Wani Amuñegü!” which means “Unity, Culture, Progress: The Future Is Ours!”

The activities will culminate on November 19 with the observance of Garifuna Settlement Day across Belize.

World.title: Is Sargassum eroding Placencia’s beaches?
World.content:
Is Sargassum eroding Placencia’s beaches?

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Lennox Lamb: My good friend Joe owns a resort in Placencia, and his wife was from the village. A couple of weeks ago, he attended a meeting there with government officials and community members about sargassum. We’ve had several long conversations since. He told me what it’s doing to his business and to daily life in Placencia. He also told me he believes it’s causing the beach to erode. That’s what sent me back to the research and why I’m writing this piece.

After I’d started reading, I ran into Ms. Haylock at the airport. She manages a resort in Hopkins. I mentioned what Joe had been telling me, and she said Hopkins was facing the same problem. I’d been so focused on Placencia that I’d overlooked Hopkins. That brief exchange brought Hopkins into the discussion.

The research I’ve reviewed does not establish that sargassum caused the extensive beach erosion residents describe in Placencia or Hopkins. I also haven’t found enough consistent measurements to say how much beach has been lost along the stretches they’re talking about. If we want to know what’s taking the sand, we have to measure where it’s going.

My first degree was in marine science and biology. I spend more time on political analysis these days, and it’s been a while since I put that marine science hat on. I plan to speak with people who study shorelines and nearshore ecosystems today. The answer for Placencia and Hopkins has to come from what’s happening on their own coast.

The clearest evidence I found concerns what happens during cleanup. A study of 12 beaches in Mexico and the Dominican Republic estimated that about 9,872 cubic metres of sand were taken away with the sargassum. That was roughly half the total volume of material the researchers examined. If we want to know whether cleanup is contributing to erosion here, we can start by measuring how much sand goes out with each load.

In Galveston, Texas, crews raked sargassum toward the dunes, keeping it within the beach system. One Texas A&M study found no statistically significant difference in elevation change between raked and unraked beaches over a year. A separate study on Galveston’s west end found that sand built up during peak sargassum season, then beach elevations returned to earlier levels within months. Closer to home, a 2025 University of South Florida survey of the Placencia Peninsula, conducted with Belizean collaborators, examined how structures built out from the beach can interrupt the movement of sand along the shore.

We also know that decomposing sargassum can do real damage in shallow water. Researchers off Ambergris Caye measured very low oxygen and lower pH in water affected by decaying sargassum. In the Mexican Caribbean, researchers documented severe losses of seagrass roots and rhizomes after a major influx. Those roots help hold sediment in place, so losing them can make a shoreline more vulnerable. That’s a reason to monitor seagrass and water quality, and to measure the same stretches of beach over time in both Placencia and Hopkins.

About a year ago, I worked with marine engineers and specialists in removing oil and debris from the sea to put together a sargassum removal proposal for the Government of Belize. It didn’t move forward at the time, so I put it on the shelf. If the government is still looking for a workable way to remove sargassum at this scale, our group is ready to sit down and discuss what we put together.

Mek we be clear. Joe raised this because he sees what sargassum is doing to his business and to life in Placencia. Ms. Haylock told me what people in Hopkins are dealing with too. The government has enough reason to help both communities now. While we deal with the sargassum, we can start measuring where the beaches are losing sand, how much leaves during cleanup and what’s changing in the shallows. That’s how we give Joe and the people asking the same question an answer they can use.

World.title: Dangriga woman lends neighbour bank card to withdraw $100 his sister sent from States but he drained her account from $500 to $193 and never came back with her card
World.content:
Dangriga woman lends neighbour bank card to withdraw $100 his sister sent from States but he drained her account from $500 to $193 and never came back with her card

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A favour for someone overseas ended in a police report after a 19-year-old Dangriga woman said she lent her neighbour a bank card for one $100 withdrawal and later found it had been used at several stores without her permission.

The woman told police that a woman living in the United States contacted her on November 13 and asked to deposit $100 into her Belize Bank account for the U.S. woman’s brother. The woman said the man had been her neighbour for 11 years, and she agreed to help.

She said the neighbour came to her house around 7 a.m. the following morning to collect her pink Belize Bank card and withdraw the money. By 5 p.m., she said, he had not returned it. The woman checked her account on her phone and said her balance had dropped from $500 to $193. She also saw several store transactions she said she had not authorized.

The woman said she could not reach or locate the neighbour. She reported the matter to Dangriga police that evening and requested court action. Police detained a man in connection with the report but did not list a charge.

World.title: 18-year-old girl charged with aggravated assault on police officer after catching 41-year-old common-law husband with another 18-year-old woman
World.content:
18-year-old girl charged with aggravated assault on police officer after catching 41-year-old common-law husband with another 18-year-old woman

By Breaking Belize News Staff: An 18-year-old Belize City woman has been charged with aggravated assault on a police officer after a confrontation at an Oleander Street home. The homeowner, a 41-year-old man, told police that the teenager, Alisha Alford, was his common-law partner.

The man told officers that Alford arrived at his house around 3 a.m. on Thursday, November 12, accused him of having another woman in his room and forced her way inside. According to the police report, Alford found her partner there with another 18-year-old woman, and a confrontation followed.

Police arrived around 3:30 a.m. Two officers escorted Alford out of the house, but police say she refused to leave and shouted that she would beat and kill the other woman. When Alford tried to go back inside, she allegedly shoved a constable in the left shoulder and slapped her left hand.

A struggle followed before another officer helped detain Alford. Police took her to the Queen Street Police Station and formally charged her the following day, Friday, November 13, with aggravated assault on Smith.

World.title: International News: Guatemala declares 30-day State of Emergency in Zacapa and Izabal following deadly attacks
World.content:
International News: Guatemala declares 30-day State of Emergency in Zacapa and Izabal following deadly attacks

By Zoila Palma: Guatemala has declared a 30-day state of emergency in the eastern departments of Zacapa and Izabal following a series of armed attacks that left a lawmaker and three police officers dead.

The decree, announced Saturday, takes immediate effect and imposes restrictions on public gatherings while granting security forces expanded powers, Reuters report.

Under the emergency measures, authorities can disperse gatherings by force, make arrests and enter residences without warrants.

The restrictions are intended to strengthen security operations and address growing concerns over organized crime in the two neighboring departments, which cover an area roughly the size of Qatar.

The declaration follows the November 6 shooting of lawmaker Julio Cesar Portillo in Rio Hondo, Zacapa. Portillo later died from his injuries, while three police officers were also killed in the attack.

Although authorities have not identified those responsible, the United States recently designated several criminal groups operating in Zacapa as terrorist organizations and accused them of having links to Mexican drug trafficking cartels.

World.title: Nearly $900,000 to build Belize a human rights watchdog
World.content:
Nearly $900,000 to build Belize a human rights watchdog

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize is officially on the road to having its own National Human Rights Institution, and the European Union is footing the bill.

Government and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) launched the project in Belmopan, backed by EUR 400,000 from the EU. That is BZ$882,640.

The goal: an independent body where Belizeans can turn when their rights are violated, built to meet the international standard known as the Paris Principles.

Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca signed the project document with the UNDP.

“We aim to develop an institution that reflects Belize’s realities, strengthens accountability and ensures that every person has access to effective human rights protection,” Fonseca said.

The new institution will build on what already exists, including the Office of the Ombudsman. The project will pay for technical assessments, legal expertise and national consultations to design it. The exact laws and structure will be decided through Belize’s own processes.

The EU’s Valerio Diaz Martin said the aim is to make human rights protections “accessible to all, particularly the most vulnerable.”

UNDP Deputy Resident Representative Michael Lund said strong, independent institutions are essential to public trust.

Next up: national consultations from November 24 to 26, bringing together government, the National Assembly, civil society, academia, the private sector and young people.

World.title: Buju, Shaggy, Chronixx, Protoje, Runkus and Ziggy vie for Grammy Best Reggae Album
World.content:
Buju Banton’s Too Too Bad, Shaggy’s Lottery, Chronixx’s Exile, Protoje’s Art of Acceptance, Supernova by Runkus and Brightside by Ziggy Marley are the nominees for Best Reggae Album for the 69th annual Grammy Awards.

The nominations were announced Monday morning.

Too Too Bad is Buju Banton’s eight nomination. He was previously nominated in 1999 for Inna Heights, 2004 for Friends for Life, Too Bad in 2007, Upside Down in 2020, Rasta Got Soul in 2010, Born for Greatness in 2024 and Before the Dawn (which won in 2011).

Exile has given Chronixx his second nomination. He got a nod in 2018 for Chronology.

Brightside gives Marley his seventh solo nomination in the reggae category. He won in 2014 for In Concert, the self-titled Ziggy Marley in 2017, Love is My Religion in 2007 and Fly Rasta in 2015. His other nominations were for Rebellion Rises (2019), and Wild and Free in 2012.

As the lead singer for Ziggy Marley and the Melody Makers outfit, the group was nominated seven times but only won three times: Conscious Party (1989), One Bright Day (1990) and Fallen is Babylon (1998).

The Art of Acceptance, the latest effort by Protoje, gives the St Elizabeth-born artiste his third nomination. He earned nods for 2019’s A Matter of Time and 2023’s Third Time’s The Charm.

Supernova is the first nomination for Runkus, while Lottery is the eighth nomination for Shaggy. Shaggy won in 1996 for the platinum-selling Boombastic and again in 2019 for 44/876, a collaborative effort with Sting.

The 69th Grammy Awards ceremony is scheduled for February 7 at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.

World.title: More beach access
World.content:
Jamaica Labour Party Leader Dr Andrew Holness arrives at Montego Bay Convention Centre on Sunday for the party’s 83rd annual conference. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Responding to growing local and international concern about the level of access Jamaicans have to local beaches, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness on Sunday announced that he has mandated Minister of Tourism Edmund Bartlett to tackle the issue head on. Holness’s comments came as he addressed the 83rd annual conference of the governing Jamaica Labour Party (JLP).

“I know that in the public order and public spaces session the issue of beach access would have been raised, a sore topic for many Jamaicans, and a growing cause for international concern and indeed bad publicity for Jamaica,” the JLP leader said from the stage at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James.

In August, the tourism minister blasted people who he said are creating a false impression internationally that Jamaicans are being denied access to the country’s beaches, and the Government listed 60 beaches across the island that it says provides free access to the public. Now the prime minister has indicated a new course of action.

“The Government has been paying close attention to this, and while it is not my proposal to discuss the full issue here, your minister of tourism has been charged — they have assessed all the beaches in Jamaica — I am giving him a task to ensure that in the next budget at least 10 public beaches are improved,” Holness said during Sunday’s address.

“So that the average Jamaican can get not just access, not just walk on the beach, but can have a facility that is clean and a facility that is also safe; and thereafter, to execute a programme through the Tourism Enhancement Fund to ensure that every parish has at least two public beaches with free access,” the prime minister added.

At the podium for about two hours, Holness also announced plans to revitalise the country’s tourism sector.

“Our tourism product generally needs a refresh. Tourism has been growing and expanding — without question. Now we have to look at the quality of the product we offer and how that impacts the brand of Jamaica. That means we need some investment in the tourism infrastructure, but more importantly, in the tourism human resources,” he said.

“The first large-scale effort in this will be the establishment of tourism improvement districts. The first will be the Hip Strip in Montego Bay, then this wonderful elegant corridor [in Rose Hall],” Holness added. (See related story: Holness signals progress on MoBay master plan.)

He said similar initiatives are also planned for Negril, Ocho Rios, Portland, St Mary, Westmoreland, and St Elizabeth.

“These will have special municipal legislation for the areas declared, and they will come with some amount of fiscal incentives to incentivise investments in those areas. We must improve the quality of the product we offer,” the prime minister urged.

He also spoke of plans to clean up the country’s cities and towns, an initiative he said that took shape during the conference.

“One of the greatest complaints that we have here in St James, and indeed in all our town and our cities, is that the public space is not clean. The public space is not orderly…We will, in the next budget, launch an island-wide campaign to clean up all our cities and towns and public spaces, and to maintain them and keep them at that standard,” the prime minister said.

He then instructed Minister of Finance Fayval Williams to double, to 60, a request before her for new garbage trucks to ensure “more effective garbage collection throughout the country”.

“I will be calling in all the mayors of the municipalities because this is not just a central government problem; it is also a local government problem. Local government, the mayors and the councillors, need to play their part in ensuring not just the collection, but we have to now start talking to the homeowners about how you dispose of your garbage…This Government will mobilise and treat with the transformation of our country to make it more beautiful, more appealing,” Holness promised.

World.title: Holness signals progress on MoBay master plan
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (right) being given a tour, Saturday, of an under-construction town house at Richmond Hill Club by developer John Surdeen. Joining them is state minister in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Ministry, Delano Seiveright.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — After decades of Montegonians clamouring for a master plan to be implemented in an effort to breathe new life into the city’s major business districts and revitalise some of its most iconic spots, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has signalled that their lobbying has paid off.

“People want to be able to move around in the city and in the town seamlessly, and so that’s the next phase of the Government’s public thrust towards developing the area,” said Holness as he apologised for challenges faced in now moving around while a number of major infrastructural projects are being done.

He was speaking during Saturday’s ground-breaking ceremony for the US$125-million Richmond Hill Club mixed-use development on the hills above the resort city. The work being done on the water supply and the road network, Holness said, will pay off in the long run and is linked to the Government’s wider plans for the parish.

“All of that [is] to help with the seamlessness of coming to Jamaica. A major part of that will be the establishment of two tourism development corridors in St James. One will be the Hip Strip and the other will be the elegant corridor [in Rose Hall]. We have already started work on developing the legal and administrative framework of those business improvement areas,” the prime minister disclosed.

“It will involve some fiscal incentives, but it will also involve direct investments in the roadway, in the streetscapes, and it will also involve the creation of a new way of managing the municipal arrangements for those areas. The idea is to truly create an iconic public space for tourism in the tourism capital of the country,” Holness added.

Several hotels are among the major projects now under construction. These include the 165-room AC Marriott Montego Bay on the Hip Strip. The lifestyle hotel is on the site of the former Sandals Carlyle, or “Baby Sandals”, and marks a transformational shift from all-inclusive to a modern, European plan (EP) model.

Meanwhile, on the elegant corridor, Moon Palace’s 1,200-room US$700-million luxury resort is set to be the tallest hotel in Jamaica at 33 storeys. It will also include staff quarters that are reportedly being built on an area of land adjacent to the property. In the same area is the Unico 18°77° hotel, a 451-room, adult-only luxury resort. Then there is the under-construction US$850-million Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Jamaica. It will be a luxury, all-inclusive resort.

The Richmond Hill Club, located in the heart of the city, has now added another layer to its growth and development. Overlooking Montego Bay, it sits on land whose heritage dates back to the early 1800s. The property, which once housed a hotel with the same name, hosted diplomats, celebrities, and locals celebrating major milestones before it was destroyed by fire in December 2019.

Now, John Surdeen, through his JARRAN Developments, is looking to preserve that rich history while he repurposes the space as a lifestyle destination. There is a resort component, there’s an apartment component, and then there’s a low-density housing component. The plan includes 120 condos and 526 residences.

Amenities within its twin residential towers include a pool, gazebos, terraces, a health and wellness centre, rooftop terraces with impressive views of the city, and large living and apartment spaces with unprecedented access to the views via a bridge that connects both structures. There will be 202 one-, two-, or three-bedroom units. There will be about 700 parking spots available for the condos and towers, which will sit on nine acres of land.

Expectations are that the roll-out of properties will begin sometime in 2027.

World.title: Frugality and resilience
World.content:
A section of the crowd gathered at Montego Bay Convention Centre, Sunday, for the 83rd annual conference of the Jamaica Labour Party. Garfield Robinson

ROSE HALL, St James — Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness on Sunday unveiled “frugality and resilience” as the governing theme for the next four years, alongside major announcements regarding the sourcing of $9.65 billion in additional roof repair grants and plans to position Jamaica to seize opportunities made available through artificial intelligence (AI).

“Labourites, today I want to introduce to you the theme for the Government for the next four years. I told you about frugality. The next pillar of our theme is resilience,” Holness told party faithful gathered at Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James for the Jamaica Labour Party’s (JLP) 83rd Annual Conference.

He addressed the frustration of citizens still awaiting housing recovery assistance.

“It does break my heart every time I see someone saying, ‘My roof, I can’t put it on yet because I haven’t received my grant. I’m still waiting on my grant.’ And it becomes even more difficult when your neighbour has got the grant and you don’t get the grant yet. You wonder if the State abandoned you or forgot about you. Well, no,” assured Holness.

He said funds have been identified for a previously announced additional expenditure for the Restoration of Owner or Occupant Family Shelters (ROOFS) programme.

“I am pleased to announce that your minister of finance sharpened her scalpel and, like a surgeon, she went in and she cut out all the fat, and we were able now to find the $9.65 billion so that the remaining 50,000 Jamaicans who are patiently waiting on their grants, they will get their grants,” Holness stated.

The prime minister noted that 11,000 beneficiaries have already been verified and are waiting for funds to hit their accounts before receiving a text, call, or cheque. He said he has given Minister of Labour Pearnel Charles Jr a December 20 deadline to have 90 per cent of the grants distributed by Christmas.

The minister has also been given a mid-January deadline to ensure “that all persons who have been assessed and verified as being in need would have received their grants”.

Turning his attention to the issue of AI, Holness urged Jamaica to capitalise on emerging global technology, rather than trailing behind. He said the Government has taken concrete steps to attract AI investment locally.

“We have put in place an AI task force that’s advising the Government on what we need to do in this regard. But the announcement that I would like to make here today is that the Government has just approved an MOU with a group of investors to explore the establishment of artificial intelligence infrastructure right here in Jamaica so that Jamaica can have a footprint and not only be a consumer of the technology, but we can be a part of the creation of the technology,” stated Holness.

He said the initiative is aimed at ensuring future generations are equipped to secure jobs in the rapidly evolving AI-driven global economy.

World.title: Grammy predictions
World.content:
The nominations for the 69th annual Grammy Awards are to be announced today, Monday, November 16.

The Best Reggae Album category (formerly known as Best Reggae Recording) was first introduced in the 1985 ceremony, with Black Uhuru’s Anthem winning the first award.

Some 119 projects, including various artiste compilations, gospel, reggae, and dancehall albums, were submitted this year, compared to 73 the previous year.

Work that qualify for the submission period should have been released between August 31, 2025 to August 28, 2026.

It’s a very tough year to really nail down who may be the possible nominees in the Best Reggae Album category as so many notable releases created an impact both locally and overseas.

There were notable releases by Capleton, Buju Banton, Beenie Man, Burning Spear, Alkaline, Queen Ifrica, and Kabaka Pyramid.

Below are predictions as to which albums could make the cut in the Best Reggae Album category, when the 2027 nominees are announced:

Brightside: Multi-Grammy-winner Ziggy Marley was probably the only act who did any meaningful campaigns around his project. He could snag a nomination for

Brightside, which was released last May via Tuff Gong Worldwide.

Exile: Released last October to rave reviews, Exile by Chronixx is poised to possibly end up among the nominees. He previously secured a nod for Chronology in 2018.

Art of Acceptance: This work may give Protoje his third nomination. He was previously nominated in 2019 for A Matter of Time and Third Time’s The Charm in 2023.

Supernova: Critically acclaimed Supernova by Runkus was ranked among the 50 Best Albums released so far in 2026 a few months ago by respected music and trade publication Billboard. One of the better reggae projects released this year, it has the elements that could help steer it among this year’s nominees.

There is a toss-up among Masicka’s Forever Reign, Lottery by Shaggy, and God and Time by Vybz Kartel.

The truth is, Masicka has put in a lot of work and Forever Reign is a decent project that deserves a fair listen. It doesn’t hurt that the project was released by major label Def Jam Recordings that may utilise its connections to secure a deserving nod for the deejay.

Shaggy knows the system and is a favourite among voters in the Recording Academy. Lottery didn’t quite hit the spot sales-wise on the Billboard charts. But, truth is, voters don’t care if you were big on the charts or you’re the most popular. Lottery did spawn a few crossover hits on Billboard’s Rhythmic chart, and being a familiar name will probably help Shaggy in his bid for an eighth nomination in this category. Mind you, he has already won twice.

God and Time: Vybz Kartel has had a great year with several chart hits, songs that made an impact within the dancehall space and a Billboard-charting album with God and Time. A two-time nominee, it wouldn’t come as a surprise if the King of the Dancehall nabs his third nomination.

World.title: Gov’t to regularise squatter settlements via Jamaica Build
World.content:
Minister with responsibility for land, Robert Montague speaking during Sunday’s conference. Garfield Robinson

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) Chairman Robert Montague has announced plans for a new land regularisation initiative, Jamaica Build, which is aimed at addressing the country’s 527 informal settlements, home to almost 700,000 Jamaicans.

Montague, who is minister without portfolio in the Ministry of Economic Growth and Infrastructure Development, with responsibility for land titling and settlements, said consultations have already begun ahead of the programme’s launch.

Addressing the JLP’s 83rd Annual Conference at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James on Sunday, he said the initiative was being developed on the instructions of Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness to find a lasting solution to the widespread problem of informal settlements.

“The prime minister has given strict instructions that we must find a way, and we have found a way. We have begun the consultations,” Montague said.

He said Jamaica Build would seek to regularise the settlements over time, allowing residents to secure legal titles to the land they occupy and pass the property on to future generations.

The programme’s name, he explained, reflects its broader objective of promoting unity and independence through land development.

“We call it Jamaica Build because it is building unity and independence through land development. We’re building Jamaica not for today only, but for the future,” Montague explained.

He said the initiative would provide a pathway for thousands of families living in informal communities to obtain greater security of tenure and establish a lasting legacy for their children and grandchildren.

Montague did not outline a launch date or provide details of the programme’s implementation framework.

World.title: BACK IN THE MIX!
World.content:
SPEID... I need players that I can trust, and I think we’re getting there with the players that we have (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

FOLLOWING Jamaica’s stunning victory over Mexico on Saturday, Reggae Boyz interim head coach Rudolph Speid believes the country has re-earned its place among the relevant nations in international football and expects further progress in the years ahead.

The national men’s team are one step closer to the Concacaf Nations League semi-finals after a 3-2 win over the Mexicans at the National Stadium in their first leg quarter-final.

The region’s best and world number 10-ranked Mexicans started the game as heavy favourites with nine of the 11 players who pushed England to the limit in the round of 16 at the 2026 FIFA World Cup in July.

However, they were stunned in the 27th minute when Jesus Gallardo headed the ball into his own net from a Ronaldo Webster corner to give Jamaica the lead.

New Head Coach Rafa Marquez, seeking his first win since his appointment in July, saw his half-time team unravel within seconds as Renaldo Cephas doubled the lead just less than a minute into the second half.

The celebrations among the just over 5,000 Jamaican fans inside the stadium intensified in the 63rd minute when Richard King converted from the penalty spot after the video-assistant referee (VAR) intervened to award a penalty for Gallardo’s challenge on Kaheim Dixon.

However, the Mexicans were given a lifeline heading back to Monterrey thanks to goals from starlet Gilberto Mora in the 70th and Julian Quinones in the 81st minute.

Despite giving up a three-goal lead, Speid was pleased with his team’s performance.

“We always thought that the game would be played over 180 minutes. We’re grateful that we have a one-goal lead,” he said. “It could have been more, but we were sloppy in the second half and gave up two. It would have been nice to keep them off the score sheet, but they are such a quality team that it would have been very difficult for 90 minutes.”

The win marked Jamaica’s first victory over Mexico in almost a decade and only the sixth in 33 meetings between the two sides.

Speid believes the team needed a significant improvement in standards following the Nations League group stage in September and October, with the early results already suggesting progress.

“From the last [international] window, we got a difficult draw and we decided that there was going to be a culture change in the team,” he said. “I think this is a continuation of that and I’m sure you’ll see much more disciplined performance like this going forward.”

“You have to give the players credit because they are the ones that execute out there. They are the ones that kept the discipline going. I know we did change a lot of players [and] a lot of people were naming a [starting] 11 [with players] that weren’t here, and said they are the better players. But we always know that I need players that I can trust, and I think we’re getting there with the players that we have.”

Last November, Jamaicans were left heartbroken as the Reggae Boyz missed out on automatic World Cup qualification following a goalless draw with Curacao at the National Stadium. Their hopes of reaching the tournament were subsequently dashed after losing to DR Congo in the InterContinental Playoffs last March.

However, Speid believes the victory over Mexico has reignited hope among Jamaicans.

“It wasn’t for us really, it was always for the country,” he said. “I know that Jamaica was almost disappearing in football and from being relevant, so I think this brought us back.”

It was also a big win for Speid who has faced heavy criticism since taking charge last November. However, he was quick to downplay any personal significance.

“It’s my job to get victories, I just don’t take anything personally,” he said. “I’m always trying my best. [It’s] to win games, that’s what it’s all about and you just have to find a way. So I don’t take anything from it, it’s just a part of the job.”

Mexico Head Coach Rafa Marquex credited the Boyz, but expects a strong response from his team at home.

“There were moments where we weren’t alert and you give the opponent life. “They got confident and started to develop their game more, with their fans,” he said.

“We’ll try to turn it around there. It’s a series, we’re a goal away from going through. The bitter pills, try to swallow them as quickly as possible and work to try in just a few days to fix the doubts and problems we had today to improve.”

The Reggae Boyz landed in Mexico on Sunday after departing the Norman Manley International Airport just hours after the victory.

They are expected to train on Monday ahead of Tuesday’s second leg at the Estadio BBVA in Monterrey.

World.title: Hunt for toll dodgers
World.content:
The Portmore toll road.

Police have issued a stern warning to motorists hell-bent on dodging toll payments across the country, declaring that cops “are on a mission” to hunt down, arrest, and charge offenders.

According to Senior Superintendent Lloyd Darby, who heads the Public Safety and Traffic Enforcement Branch, dozens of these rogue motorists have been detained over the past two years.

“The Highway and Safety Patrol Division, which is a part of the Public Safety and Traffic Enforcement Branch, have the responsibility of policing both toll roads. We are effecting arrests on both for the offences of toll evasion. Since the start of the year we have arrested over 30 persons for the offence, last year we arrested over 40 persons. We will be doing it more frequently and we won’t stop until there is a drastic decrease in the amount of offences that are taking place,” Darby told the Jamaica Observer on Friday.

The east-to-west leg or T1 leg of Highway 2000, officially known as the PJ Patterson Highway, runs along the southern corridor of the island, connecting the Mandela Highway area near Kingston and Spanish Town through Old Harbour, May Pen, Toll Gate, and out to Williamsfield in Manchester, with planned future extensions towards Montego Bay. The north-south leg (T3), named the Edward Seaga Highway, Connects Caymanas (St Catherine) in the south to Mammee Bay/Ocho Rios (St Ann) in the north.

Darby’s comments came on the heels of last Thursday’s disclosure by Jamaica North South Highway Company Limited (JNSHCL), who are the developers and operators of Edward Seaga Highway, that unruly motorists have forced it to develop a blacklist system that flags vehicles linked to toll road violations to restrict them from accessing the motorway. To deal with the issue of toll evasion, operators have installed cameras capable of recording the offences, flagging the vehicles by licence-plate-readable devices which identify them each time they use the toll plaza and tabulates the amount of times they commit the offences.

Said Darby, “The toll operators can’t arrest, but we are in collaboration. The blatant disregard for the law cannot continue, and the manner in which toll evasion takes place is dangerous. I understand that a worker from one of the booths was injured in one of those instances and there has been damage to the property by persons, so we are concentrating on it and we will not relent until there is a dramatic decrease in the incidents.”

He said while the operators “are [only] able to list the offenders that have multiple offences…they pass on the information to the police” who then take action.

“Recently, an individual taken to court in Spanish Town had 35 violations, he pleaded guilty and he was fined $10,000 on each so he was $350,000 poorer on that day. I am sure that the [toll charges] would not have amounted to $350,000 had he paid for his passage as he should,” the senior cop pointed out.

He said some Jamaicans erroneously view toll evasion as a trivial matter.

“We would prefer if you obey the law, pay the toll; but if not, we are there to arrest you. It is not a ticketable offence, it is an offence where you are arrested and you have to get somebody to bail you, and the fines at court are substantial. We just want motorists to understand that it is an offence, there is a Toll Road Act, a piece of legislation that has penalties,” Darby pointed out.

During the interview, he also addressed concerns by members of the public about the process by which individuals who are blacklisted are removed from the roadway without creating problems for other motorists.

“We don’t intend to turn back anybody…What the offenders must realise is that on the toll roads, when you go through the booths, the exits are far, so we know where to set up to await to catch you. We go out sometimes and look for specific vehicles based on the method in which they operate, the times of day the vehicle in the violations will pass a particular point and we will set up operations to intercept them…We have had instances where we go to persons’ addresses with warrants to answer for the offences they have committed,” he explained.

Darby said there is little room for individuals to escape these operations and pointed out that offenders include road users from various categories.

“We have seen almost all the occupations that you can think of doing these violations. The toll operators provide video evidence of the vehicles going through the toll and a lot of times even the drivers are captured. We see a lot of times where they evade the toll and speed away as if they are trying to run from the camera, but it already picked them up,” the lawman said.

“We see company vehicles, large trucks, motorcycles, every description of vehicle you can think of committing these offences. So we are on a mission now, we have been policing this issue for years, but the safety hazards it creates when persons violate the toll and the disregard for the legislation is making us really ramp up our efforts now to do some more work,” he added.

Darby urged individuals not to collude in order to evade the toll, and reminded motor vehicle owners to be discerning when loaning their automobiles as the Toll Road Act holds the owner of a vehicle responsible if it is used in committing a violation.

“The owner can’t say, ‘I wasn’t driving.’ He has an obligation under the Act to furnish the person who was driving or he has to take the responsibility; so it means that owners of vehicles have to be very careful who they allow to drive their vehicles,” Darby stated.

“It is very important that the public understands what toll evasion is. Toll evasion happens in basically two ways: where persons tailgate other motorists, especially the motorist who has an e-Pass — meaning that they don’t have to stop and pay so when the bar lifts up, they [evaders] just travel at a fast speed behind. They also do it at the paying booth where, as persons pay and the bar is lifted to allow them through, they speed through. The other way that they do it is simply just hit the bar, damaging the property in a lot of instances, and going through. We have many repeat offenders and from time to time police officers travelling in marked or unmarked vehicles will detect these offences and take action,” he added.

JCF toll evasion operation data seen by the

Observer revealed that eight vehicles account for a total of 101 offences. Of that number one vehicle was recorded in as much as 25 violations, while another was pegged for 23. On Friday, the senior superintendent of police said two operations conducted on two days last week saw six people arrested and charged.

Toll evasion is a criminal offence under the Toll Roads Act, resulting in fines up to $10,000 or 30 days’ imprisonment per count for non-payment.

World.title: 5 countries announce plan to deport failed asylum-seekers to Rwanda
World.content:
There are still some “technical things” that have to be “sorted out,” Frederiksen said. “But the framework, the idea and the partnership is now in place.”

A reform of EU legislation adopted earlier this year made it possible for countries to negotiate deals to set up such deportation centers — as long as they comply with fundamental rights obligations.

But human rights groups have slammed plans to set up deportation hubs, warning that their use risks removing vulnerable people far from EU oversight.

The five countries plan to transfer people to Rwanda who have already gone through full asylum proceedings and were ordered to leave the EU.

The countries said they intend to target adults without children, and specifically people who don’t cooperate — or whose home countries don’t collaborate — in the deportation process.

“For me, today marks a crucial step towards a new migration system; a system that safeguards the cohesion of our societies and answers the concerns of our citizens. To put it very short, it needs to be a democratic decision who can enter and who can stay in our societies,” Frederiksen said.

World.title: Google says Russian speakers pulled off first-ever fully automated AI cyberattack
World.content:
The development could mark an inflection point in the use of AI for cyberattacks.

Russian-speaking hackers built an AI agent that carried out what may be the first-ever fully-automated cyberattack, Google reported Monday.

The tech giant’s cyber threat intelligence division said it had spotted hackers using artificial intelligence to “fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.”

The development could mark an inflection point in the use of AI for cyberattacks, which has dominated headlines and worried policymakers since AI firm Anthropic released its specialized model Mythos in April.

World.title: Entwurf des COP-Abkommens sieht „sofortigen“ Ausstieg aus fossilen Brennstoffen vor
World.content:
Eine Verdreifachung der Finanzmittel für Entwicklungsländer zur Vorbereitung auf Klimakatastrophen auf 120 Milliarden Dollar pro Jahr wird auch für die Industrieländer, die mit Haushaltsengpässen im eigenen Land zu kämpfen haben, schwer zu verkraften sein.

Die Ölstaaten werden unterdessen aufgefordert, sich der Forderung nach einem schnelleren Ausstieg aus fossilen Brennstoffen anzuschließen, unter anderem „durch den sofortigen Umstieg weg von fossilen Brennstoffen in den Energiesystemen“.

„Zweifellos werden die Menschen ein wenig Zeit brauchen, um das zu verarbeiten … Es ist sehr umfassend“, sagte Chris Bowen, Australiens Klimaminister, gegenüber Reportern. „Und die heftigen Reaktionen, die es gegeben hat, sind genau so beabsichtigt. Damit wird eine Diskussion darüber angestoßen, wie der endgültige Entwurf aussehen wird, den wir den Vertragsparteien im Laufe der Woche vorlegen werden.“

Der Vorschlag der türkischen Mitveranstalter, ein freiwilliges globales Elektrifizierungsziel festzulegen – das laut Ankara am Samstag von rund 30 Ländern unterstützt wird –, wurde ebenfalls in den Beschlussentwurf aufgenommen. Mehrere Länder haben Einwände gegen die Idee neuer Ziele erhoben.

Jeder endgültige Beschluss der COP erfordert den Konsens aller Regierungen.

„Dieser erste Entwurf wird sich vom endgültigen Entwurf unterscheiden – genau dafür ist der Prozess ja gedacht“, sagte Bowen. „Ich gehe also davon aus, dass es bis Ende der Woche noch mindestens einen weiteren Entwurf geben wird, aber wir werden so lange weiterarbeiten, bis wir ein Dokument haben, auf das sich alle einigen können.“

Dieser Text ist zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO erschienen.

World.title: SPONSORED EPISODE: Europe’s ambition to stop cancer
World.content:
Europe is a leader in cancer research. But turning that science into treatments that reach patients is another matter. Every minute, five people in Europe are diagnosed with cancer, and the disease costs the European economy more than €100 billion a year.

Five years after its launch, Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan has been scrutinized by the European Court of Auditors and the European Parliament. Both back its ambitions but find delivery falling short, with national cancer plans often lacking the resources to succeed and access to care varying widely among member countries. Meanwhile, Europe’s share of global commercial clinical trials has almost halved in a decade.

With the EU’s proposed Biotech Act under negotiation and talks on the bloc’s next long-term budget under way, Europe has a chance to close the gap between innovation and access.

In the second of two special podcast episodes produced by POLITICO Studio, experts in cancer policy explore what Europe must do to ensure every patient benefits from innovations in cancer care, from speeding up clinical trials to giving patients a real voice in policymaking.

Hear from Elisabetta Zanon, chief executive of the European Cancer Organisation, which brings together cancer professionals and patients from across Europe; and Jennifer Young, VP and head of International Commercial Policy and Communications for Pfizer.

POLITICAL 

The sponsor is Pfizer Inc.

The  is linked to calls for stronger cancer policy in Europe.

More information here.

World.title: Un brouillon de la COP31 préconise une sortie “immédiate” des énergies fossiles
World.content:
Tripler le financement destiné aux pays en développement pour les aider à se préparer aux catastrophes climatiques, pour le porter à 120 milliards de dollars par an, sera également une pilule difficile à avaler pour les pays développés, qui sont eux-mêmes confrontés à des contraintes budgétaires au niveau national.

Les pays producteurs de pétrole, quant à eux, sont invités à se rallier à l’appel en faveur d’une élimination plus rapide des combustibles fossiles, notamment “par le biais d’une transition immédiate vers des systèmes énergétiques sans combustibles fossiles”.

“Il ne fait aucun doute que les gens auront besoin d’un peu de temps pour assimiler tout cela […] C’est un document très complet”, a déclaré Chris Bowen, ministre australien du Climat, lors d’un échange avec des journalistes. “Et les opinions tranchées qui ont été exprimées, c'est exactement ce que nous recherchions. Cela lance le débat sur ce à quoi ressemblera le projet final que nous soumettrons aux parties dans le courant de la semaine.”

La proposition des co-organisateurs turcs visant à fixer un objectif mondial volontaire en matière d'électrification, qui, selon Ankara samedi, bénéficie du soutien d'une trentaine de pays, a également été intégrée au projet de décision. Plusieurs pays se sont opposés à cet objectif.

Toute décision finale de la COP nécessite le consensus de tous les gouvernements.

“Cette première version sera différente de la version finale ; c’est justement le but de ce processus”, a expliqué Chris Bowen. “Je m’attends donc à ce qu’il y ait au moins une autre version avant la fin de la semaine, mais nous continuerons à travailler jusqu’à ce que nous disposions d’un document faisant l’objet d’un consensus.”

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été traduit en français par Alexandre Léchenet.

World.title: European Parliament would back UK rejoining the EU, says senior lawmaker
World.content:
Gozi, who is visiting London to attend an annual summit of British and EU lawmakers, welcomed Burnham’s decision to reopen the debate over Brexit, describing the U.K.’s departure from the bloc as a “disaster.”

He said that if the U.K. were to rejoin the EU, it would be “a victory of the progressive forces against nationalism,” finding expression in National Rally in France and the AfD in Germany.

It would show that “the future is not going back to nationalistic borders, but building up a future together,” he added.

Marsha de Cordova, chair of the U.K. delegation to the European Parliament, hailed Friday’s EU-U.K. summit as “the first step” towards finding a way forward in Britain’s relationship with the EU.

She shrugged off criticism that Burnham has opened up new splits in the Labour Party and the Cabinet, saying that while some Labour MPs have “sensitivities” about moving closer to the EU, “the prime minister and the foreign secretary are right to want to seek to have that conversation and that dialogue and debate.”

“I welcome it because the evidence is there,” she added. “We didn’t have the evidence six years ago, or even 10 years ago. But now we do have the evidence. We’ve seen what happens.”

World.title: Draft COP31 text suggests ‘immediate’ fossil fuel transition
World.content:
Tripling funding for developing countries to prepare for climate disasters to $120 billion a year will also be a difficult pill to swallow for developed countries, which are struggling with budgetary pressures at home.

Petrostates, meanwhile, are being asked to get on board with a call for a faster fossil fuel phase-out, including “through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.”

“No doubt people will need a little bit of time to digest ... It's very comprehensive,” Chris Bowen, Australia's climate minister, told reporters. “And the strong views that have been raised, that's as intended. It begins a conversation about what the final draft that we put [to] the parties will look like later in the week.”

The proposal by the Turkish co-hosts to set a voluntary global electrification target, which Ankara said on Saturday has the backing of around 30 countries, has also been added to the draft decision. Several countries have objected to the idea of new goals.

Any final COP decision requires consensus from all governments.

“This first draft will look different to the final draft, that is what the process is designed to do,” said Bowen. “So I expect there will be at least one more draft before the end of the week, but we will keep working until we have a document which receives a consensus.”

World.title: EU verhängt Sanktionen gegen russische Hacker und Trolle
World.content:
Die Gruppe wurde in der Vergangenheit mit einem riesigen Online-Desinformationsnetzwerk namens „Doppelganger“ in Verbindung gebracht. Sie hatte die Europawahlen 2024 im Visier und führte „gezielte Operationen gegen EU-Mitgliedstaaten wie Deutschland und Frankreich“ durch, wie die Länder mitteilten.
