Zudem einigten sich die EU-Staaten auf Sanktionen gegen die berüchtigte russische Hackergruppe NoName057(16). Sie hat in der Vergangenheit Behörden, kritische Infrastruktur und Privatunternehmen in der EU, der Ukraine und den USA angegriffen.

Die Gruppe ist vor allem für sogenannte Distributed-Denial-of-Service-Angriffe (DDoS) bekannt, mit denen Webseiten durch massenhafte Anfragen lahmgelegt werden. Bereits im vergangenen Jahr war sie Ziel einer europäischen Strafverfolgungsoperation.

Weitere Sanktionen verhängte die EU gegen russische Propagandisten. Dazu gehören Einreiseverbote und das Einfrieren von Vermögenswerten.

Seit Beginn der russischen Vollinvasion in die Ukraine im Jahr 2022 hat die EU bereits mehrere Sanktionspakete gegen russische Desinformationsaktivitäten verabschiedet.



Dieser Artikel ist zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO erschienen.

World.title: French football chief Diallo set to run against Infantino for FIFA presidency
World.content:
French football chief Philippe Diallo is set to run for the FIFA presidency as a surprise late candidate in next year's elections.

 

European governing body UEFA proposed Diallo on Monday following a meeting of its executive committee.

"Diallo has accepted the invitation to stand. His candidacy is due to be formally ratified by the FFF Executive Committee at its meeting tomorrow," UEFA said in a statement, adding that that Diallo had "extensive experience across all levels of the game."

Diallo is lined up to run against Japanese official Kozo Tashima and incumbent President Gianni Infantino, who is seeking to shake off a major crisis that has dominated sporting headlines in recent months.

Infantino, who was first elected as president in 2016, came under huge pressure in the summer after FIFA announced a highly controversial private investment plan that would have seen third-party investors invited to take stakes in a commercial subsidiary dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE).

The proposal, which was later scrapped, drew fierce pushback from across the football community, with some accusing the world governing body of looking to "sell" the sport.

"Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of FIFA, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community," UEFA said on Monday.

"They expressed their full confidence in Philippe Diallo to provide the leadership needed to achieve this ambition," it added.

Trump, left, and FIFA President Gianni Infantino watch confetti fall at the conclusion of the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

FIFA confirmed in September that Infantino, who has also faced questions over his relationship with US President Donald Trump, would stand for re-election.

"The FIFA President announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027. Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election," a spokesperson said.

The presidential election is due to take place at the 77th FIFA Congress on Thursday, 18 March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco.

World.title: Serbia to accelerate work on EU accession, Student List representative says
World.content:
The Student List will speed up work on meeting the EU’s interim accession benchmarks on the rule of law, professor and newly elected MP Aleksandar Baucal said in the much-awaited first international public appearance of Serbia's new main political force.

 

“The next question is whether Serbia will remain on the European path. For us, the European path is one of reforms: strengthening European values, building functional institutions and a genuine rule-of-law system, developing a sustainable economy integrated in the European market,” Baucal said on Monday.

Baucal spoke at the EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels, the first time a Student List representative has addressed an international audience. Most of the room gave him a standing ovation after the speech.

For the professor, the EU accession path is not only key for good neighbourly relations, but, more broadly, for building a more democratic society.

“One of Serbia’s strategic objectives will be to accelerate the fulfilment of the interim benchmarks under chapters 23 and 24, as well. We want Serbia to be a reliable partner to the European Union and to its members,” he continued.

The party’s historic electoral victory last month raised hopes of a reset in Serbia’s troubled relations with the EU. The movement, born of nearly two years of mass protests, ousted Aleksandar Vučić’s party after 14 years in power.

Two weeks ago, Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos met a Student List delegation in Brussels, their first formal exchange with a senior EU official. The delegates said the incoming government would focus on restoring the rule of law, judicial independence and media freedom, not only for the sake of accession but above all for the Serbian people.

Baucal returned to those themes, pledging to advance on the “fundamentals” of EU accession. The professor-turned-MP said the new government would stay open to dialogue and seek to solve concrete problems rather than create new ones.

“This is not only about the European Union helping Serbia protect democracy. It is also about a democratic Serbia contributing to a stronger and more resilient Europe,” he said.

Yet prominent figures in the Student List remain cautious about aligning with EU foreign policy, notably on sanctions against Russia. These are deeply unpopular in Serbia, where memories of the Western sanctions that hit the population under the Milošević regime still run deep.

Recognition of Kosovo could also prove a sticking point with EU countries. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama warned that the new government is unlikely to change Serbia’s stance.

The Student List grew as a heterogeneous movement without a clearly defined leadership. Belgrade’s position on accession and foreign policy may become clearer once its MPs settle on the make-up of the new government.

For now, Baucal sees the party’s next challenge as turning the solidarity forged in the struggle into lasting trust in institutions.

“Citizens were able to set many differences aside. But in a democratic society, these interests and opinions will once again come to the fore. We believe that thanks to our differences, we will build a better system for our citizens,” he said.

World.title: All the ladies in the house: RAYE and Rosalía lead the way for 2027 Grammy nominations
World.content:
British jazz and soul sensation RAYE has written herself into the record books with a whopping 11 nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards.

 

The singer-songwriter is a contender in all the major categories, including record, song and album of the year for her 2026 Mercury's Prize winning work 'This Music May Contain Hope.'

Her haul of 11 nominations equals that of Beyoncé who notched up the single year nods record in 2025 with her groundbreaking album Cowboy Carter. And she's still very much in the race to extend her reign as the most-nominated artist in Grammy history after notching up her 100th nod for 'Morning Dew (Donk)' in the R&B solo performance category.

Sisters doing it themselves

Rosalía joins RAYE and Beyoncé in bringing up an impressive line-up of female artists receiving recognition.

The Spanish singer has nine nods for her sumptuous album 'LUX' and is a first-time nominee in all the categories she's competiting for, including pop solo performance, song, record and album of the year.

Her nomination also comes days after she swept the board at the Latin Grammys taking home five out of seven awards she was up for.

FILE: Rosalia, Ella Langley and Olivia Rodrigo AP Photo

Following her are Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers and first-time nominee Ella Langley, who are tied with seven nods each.

The album of the year category is rounded out by Bridgers' 'Lost Weekend,' Dean's 'The Art of Loving,' Langley's “Dandelion,' Bruno Mars' 'The Romantic,' Rodrigo's 'You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love' and Taylor Swift's 'The Life of a Showgirl.”

Swift's nomination is her fifth consecutive studio album to be nominated for album of the year, something only one other artist has ever done: Kendrick Lamar.

Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026's best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each.

The 2027 Grammy Awards will take place on Sunday 7 February, live on ABC for the first time since 1972, from the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. It will also stream on Disney+ and Hulu.

World.title: Prince William and Princess Catherine play street cricket with locals in Mumbai
World.content:
Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine joined local players for a game of street cricket in Mumbai, India, on Monday, 16 November 2026.

 

The couple took turns playing "gully cricket", a popular informal version of the sport played in streets and open spaces across the country. William was seen batting before Catherine took her turn. The princess then greeted young cricketers, and the couple posed for photographs with the players.

The game was part of a three-day visit to India, where William is hosting the Earthshot Prize, his environmental initiative.

The trip also includes a planned meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi. Cricket, one of India's most popular sports, gave the royal couple a chance to join local players during their visit to Mumbai, the country's financial capital.

World.title: Trump says he could meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in China
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he may meet with North Korean Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un in China this week.

 

Trump made the comments while speaking to reporters as he departed the White House to begin his trip to Asia, which will see him arrive in the Philippines early on Tuesday.

The president is then set to travel on to China, where he is scheduled to take part in trilateral talks with his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.

"We may meet with Kim Jong-un also," Trump told the media. "So that would be good. We have the chance to accomplish a lot."

Trump is planning to discuss nuclear disarmament when he meets with Putin and Xi in Shenzhen in southeastern China this week, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

"We're going to talk about denuclearisation. Tough subject because it's very hard for any of us say we'll get rid of our nukes," Trump said on Monday. "Especially since you do have other countries."

He added that the wars in Iran and Ukraine would also come up, as well as "economics and trade."

In August, Trump talked up his relationship with Kim and said the pair would meet at some point in the year, although he gave no further details.

"The fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing. He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons. Should have never allowed it to happen," the president said at the time, adding: "If I were president, I wouldn't have allowed it. But he's got them."

The director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, said in September that the reported expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material was a "cause for serious concern."

World.title: Five EU countries unveil Rwanda deportation plan in migration crackdown
World.content:
Five EU countries announced a partnership with Rwanda on Monday to establish the first EU return hub outside the bloc, marking a radical hardening of European migration policy.

 

Although the details of the agreement are still being negotiated, Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece say they are confident of reaching a deal and beginning deportations of irregular migrants in 2027.

The first facility is expected to accommodate around 100 people at a time. Those sent there will be free to move around Rwanda and are expected to integrate into local society and the labour market, according to officials.

“I think this [agreement] is a game changer. We will take back control and remove the incentive for illegal migration,” said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, during the announcement in Vienna, along with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and the interior ministers of other countries involved, including Rwanda’s Vincent Biruta.

The initial hub will be a small-scale pilot project, with plans to expand the scheme once it is operational and the risk of deportations being blocked by legal challenges has diminished.

Who will be sent to the return hubs?

The five countries will deport only rejected asylum seekers who are subject to enforceable return decisions.

Minors will be excluded, while each country will apply its own criteria for selecting those to be deported.

The Netherlands will focus on adult men from countries in Rwanda’s region, while Germany will target migrants who refuse to cooperate with efforts to establish their identity and come from countries reluctant to readmit their own nationals, according to people familiar with the negotiations.

After a period at the facility, the length of which has yet to be determined, migrants will be expected to rebuild their lives in Rwanda or voluntarily return to their countries of origin or another country where they have the right to reside.

The EU border agency Frontex will not have a role in deportations in the initial stages, despite a reform of its mandate recently proposed by the European Commission, which would allow it to do so.

Costs remain unclear

The five EU countries will bear the full cost of deporting migrants and accommodating them in Rwanda. However, no estimate for the initial facility was provided at the press conference, as negotiations are still ongoing.

According to people familiar with the negotiations, services in Rwanda will be considerably cheaper than equivalent services in Europe.

What Rwanda will get in return is also unclear at this stage. Kigali is, however, set to sign a partnership agreement with Denmark next week, related to cooperation on migration.

“The agreement is a shame”

Return hubs have raised concerns over their compatibility with EU law and the protection of human rights.

Critics warn they could lead to human rights violations, particularly when established in countries with limited democratic standards.

“The agreement is a shame,” said French lawmaker Mélissa Camara, of the Greens/EFA group, considering the countries involved are “crossing another disgraceful moral line by reaching an agreement with an authoritarian regime.”

The group of five countries said that all procedures will be carried out in line with international human rights standards.

However, legal complications may arise when deportations to Rwanda begin next year, as the European Court of Human Rights prohibits countries from transferring individuals to states or situations where they may be subjected to violations of fundamental rights.

The United Nations has raised concerns about Rwanda's human rights record.

A similar agreement between Rwanda and the United Kingdom, under which Britain planned to send asylum seekers to the African country, was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court in 2023 because of the risk that those transferred could subsequently be sent to countries where they faced persecution.

According to the law enabling EU states to set up return hubs outside the bloc, only non-EU countries — “where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law are respected” — are eligible.

World.title: Countries to decide future of 'killer robots' at UN conference
World.content:
Killer robots and drones are coming up for a reckoning this week as government envoys on Monday revved up a discussion and could decide this week whether to launch negotiations toward setting rules for use of the deadly machines — or not.

 

Pope Leo XIV, the UN chief and advocacy groups have framed the issue as an existential debate: Whether robots can be allowed to kill and whether humans must maintain some control of and accountability for use of lethal autonomous weapon systems.

Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones like Ukraine and the Middle East, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.

Scary would-be scenarios, like armed drones flying amok and gunning down civilians with pinpoint precision, have peppered years of discussions about killer robots. But those talks haven't produced any international restrictions.

The United States and Russia, longtime rivals, want to limit any curbs on their ability to develop and deploy powerful new tools in the high-tech arms race — just as AI is gaining steam and changing battle plans.

Proponents of an AI weaponry rulebook say time is of the essence.

"We’re at a pivotal point now, where it’s an experimentation phase. We’re seeing some cases here, some cases there, but not full operationalisation," said Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, an advocacy group.

"It will be a lot harder to regulate and create rules when these systems have already been in use for many years."

UN meeting comes after seven countries seek negotiations

The issue comes to a head at UN offices in Geneva, where the seventh review conference, about the awkwardly named Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, will consider whether to start talks on regulation of killer robots.

Supporters of an accord acknowledge powerful forces are in the way, but point to precedent: governments have already struck a deal to regulate blinding lasers.

Most countries support reining them in. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ deadline this year for the launch of talks toward regulation has given the issue urgency, but some top military powers are hesitant.

Last month, seven countries — Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama — submitted a proposal to launch negotiations of a new legally binding agreement on autonomous weapons at the conference.

The various sides have been gearing up for the diplomatic standoff.

On Friday, International Committee of the Red Cross President Mirjana Spoljaric said in a statement: "States must act to ensure the future of warfare is not handed over to machines."

Stop Killer Robots, an advocacy group, says 130 countries support new international rules on the weapons systems.

Activists began running s on the streets and in the subways of Berlin, London and Paris touting public support for reining in killer robots.

Russia: talks on restrictions are 'premature'

In his first encyclical in May, the pope denounced a "culture of power" driving the AI race, especially in developing ever more sophisticated methods of remote warfare, and said it's not permissible to entrust decisions about life and death to remote AI systems.

Under the convention’s rules, decisions must be made by consensus. That means that any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any such deal is likely to be based on a low common denominator. Another sticking point is how long negotiators might be given to try to agree on language.

In the run-up to the conference, humanitarians and activist groups said Russia looked ready to deploy tactics to slow or even stall progress toward launching formal negotiations.

"Russia attaches great importance to the successful outcome of the conference and to reaching mutually acceptable agreements that will help strengthen the Inhumane Weapons Convention and further its universalization," Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters on Wednesday.

Moscow wants "organisational matters” to be ironed out first and see a process “free from politicization," she said.

Most tellingly, Zakharova said: "We consider it premature to argue that the time has supposedly come to develop restrictive or prohibitive measures concerning such systems."

World.title: Meet the new James Bond: It's Pattinson, Robert Pattinson
World.content:
After years of rumours and speculation, arguably the most coveted role in cinema has been cast for the seventh time.

 

The (00)7th actor to portray legendary cinematic spy James Bond will be Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old actor will replace Daniel Craig as 007 and has beaten other frontrunners Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor and Nicholas Hoult to the coveted role.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," said Pattinson in an official statement. "I'm deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

He becomes the most established actor to be cast as Bond.

Indeed, the actor needs little introduction. Following his star-making turn in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire and the Twilight franchise, he has gone from strength to strength with roles in The Lost City of Z, High Life, The Lighthouse and Tenet. He is also the current Batman, having debuted as the Caped Crusader in Matt Reeves' The Batman in 2022. He is currently filming the sequel.

This year has been a particularly busy (and productive) year for Pattinson, as he starred alongside Zendaya in The Drama, played Antinous in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, and portrayed American TV presenter Chris Hansen inPrimetime. He will next star in Dune: Part Three, which is directed by none other than Canadian filmmaker and four-time Oscar nominee Denis Villeneuve – the director of the upcoming James Bond film.

Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond Instagram

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond as we proudly introduce Robert Pattinson as the next 007,” said Mike Hopkins, Head of Prime Video & Amazon MGM Studios. “This iconic character has captivated audiences around the world for more than six decades, and there’s no doubt that Robert’s remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice to carry that legacy forward. With Denis Villeneuve at the helm, Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing, Tanya Lapointe executive producing, and a brilliant script from Steven Knight, we have a world-class creative team in place to usher in a new era of Bond, and we couldn’t be more excited about the journey ahead.”

“Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin,” said director Denis Villeneuve.

“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic, and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies. The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times,” said producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman.

Pattinson was rumoured to be Amazon's favourite following a secret audition and reports from Puck News that he had been given favourable contract terms: playing Bond in three films, one less than other contenders.

“O'Connor and Lowden, for instance, were required to 

As of writing, no official statement has been made regarding his contractual obligations.

Bond 26 will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. It will be the first Bond film since Amazon took full creative control over the franchise from longtime 007 custodians Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson.

Only six actors have ever played Ian Fleming's British Secret Service agent 007 in the official film series: Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.

Production on the next Bond film is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028 at the earliest.

World.title: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades
World.content:
In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history.

How it all started

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

Bond girls were typically portrayed as ditzy blondes with little to say Image: IFTN/United Archives/IMAGO

A machismo problem

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

The first bond girl was named Honey Ryder, a name which would likely be considered sexist by today's standards Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

Questionable lifestyle choices

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

Even such artwork associated with the original Bond film would never be deemed appropriate in this day and age Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

Why are all secretaries women?

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

It wasn't until the 2012 film that we finally learn something about Bond's boss's secretary, Moneypenny Image: CAP/MFS Image/Capital Pictures/picture alliance

Inappropriate casting

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

White actor Joseph Wiseman was made to look Asian with makeup Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

Pattinson as a modern 007?

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

World.title: Nvidia scandal: China's chips dilemma, US rivalry shape AI race
World.content:
The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China.

China has ambitious plans to become the leader in the global race for artificial intelligence (AI). Beijing is aware that the country needs cutting-edge chips to achieve this goal.

Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, who chairs the Communist Party's Commission on Science and Technology, has been tasked with strengthening China's capacity for technological innovation, which would enhance its strategic competitiveness against the United States.

The party is currently using AI to monitor citizens, develop advanced unmanned weapons systems, and transform economic sectors through robotics and industrial automation, among other things.

But the US has so far been leading the way in manufacturing technology and chip design. And Washington has taken a slew of measures to retain its dominance in this strategic sector.

US moves to restrict China's access to chips

As early as 2023, the then Biden administration decided to restrict the export of advanced semiconductors and chip manufacturing equipment to China, citing national security reasons.

Beijing slammed the US restrictions, calling them "unilateral and arbitrary."

US chipmakers, however, have been drawn to China's vast and rapidly growing market.

Jensen Huang has emerged as a key adviser on AI to US President Donald Trump during his second term Image: Jung Yeon-je/AFP

Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO of the American AI chip manufacturer Nvidia last week, enjoyed something of a rock star status in China. The 63-year-old, who was born in Taiwan, is viewed in China as a successful entrepreneur.

Huang, who has emerged as a key adviser on AI to US President Donald Trumpduring his second term, has pushed for looser regulations and fewer restrictions on selling AI chips to China.

In December, the Trump administration granted Nvidia permission to ship its H200 chips to China, provided the US got a 25% cut of sales.

Although the H200 is not part of Nvidia's highest-performance series, it is significantly more efficient than competing Chinese products.

Each of these chips carries a hefty $27,000 (€24,000) price tag, and Nvidia estimates demand in China at 2 million units, which corresponds to sales of approximately $5.4 billion from this product alone.

Nvidia affair and espionage allegations

But Huang resigned last week following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for Beijing.

How AI is changing the working world To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The scandal not only sent shockwaves through the global AI and semiconductor industries, but also fueled highly contentious political debates in China and the US.

Washington, which sees its national security threatened, is said to be planning further restrictions against China to close loopholes that allow Chinese firms to acquire advanced American semiconductors.

China, on the other hand, denied it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.

Beijing also stepped up its rhetoric ahead of the meeting between President Xi Jinping and Trump at this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.

"China has consistently opposed the misuse of export control measures that jeopardize the stability of global industrial and supply chains, as this is not in the interest of either party," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on November 13.

Some Chinese media outlets have also criticized the reporting on the issue.

"Jensen Huang cheated on his wife. What does that have to do with China?" asked China's state-run Global Times newspaper in an editorial.

It accused the US media of turning the affair into a "Hollywood thriller" but without providing the "hard evidence to back up the central allegations."

Many Chinese have also taken to the microblogging and social media platform Weibo to comment on the controversy.

A user wrote that Huang's downfall was, in essence, "the result of political maneuvering within the United States," while another user asked: "Could a love affair really cause Mr. Huang to resign? Isn't this plot a little too melodramatic?"

Behind the verbal sparring lies an economic calculation.

Anthropic's market debut: Who'll win the race for AI? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Is China buying more US chips?

Ding, the Chinese vice premier, has to decide whether China should continue to rely on US chips or back its domestic industry in the hope that it can achieve the breakthrough needed to surpass American competitors.

Around 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips, for instance, are currently sitting in Hong Kong, awaiting Chinese import approval.

The White House has already given the green light, but Beijing has yet to approve the imports.

For Karson Elmgren, research manager at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy in Washington, that is puzzling. "To me, this suggests that China does not view short-term advantages as decisive and is confident in its ability to replace US chips over the medium term."

Chinese AI products are also increasingly using "Made in China" chips.

"This effectively mitigates the risks of cyberattacks by foreign actors," wrote Tiantian Wang of the Harbin Institute of Technology in a recent study on China's semiconductor strategy.

This is the case not only to civilian sectors. "Against the backdrop of the current complex geopolitical situation, strengthening autonomy and control over national defense and critical infrastructure has become a core element of the national security strategy," Wang explained.

According to her, for example, the radar systems in China's fifth-generation Chengdu J-20 fighter jet and in the Dongfeng-41 intercontinental ballistic missile are equipped exclusively with Chinese chips.

China is increasingly focused on autonomous AI chip platforms developed domestically, Wang underscored.

"This has created a closed ecosystem that encompasses data, algorithms, computing power, and chips, thereby reducing systemic dependence on foreign chips such as Nvidia," she added.

Will AI-powered autonomous weapons obey the laws of war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China lacks advanced chip-making equipment

However, China still lacks production equipment for state-of-the-art chips.

Chip manufacturing requires lithography systems that expose raw silicon materials to ultraviolet light.

Bowing to pressure from Washington, the Dutch maker of lithography machines, ASML, has stopped exporting its most advanced machines to China.

The ban helps secure the US's technological lead in AI chips, said the Center for Technology & Statecraft, a Washington-based think tank. If China were to import additional ASML systems like it did in 2024 and 2025, "its annual production could be sufficient to wipe out much of the US lead and, under certain scenarios, even surpass it."

According to the international consulting firm Deloitte, China is planning further extensive investments. "The focus is on supporting companies through long-term capital provision and research-oriented incentives to build sustainable innovation in key technologies."

Policymakers aim to stabilize the entire supply chain, expand self-sufficiency, and actively manage risks, the study noted. "The focus is shifting from supporting individual companies to fostering synergies within the supply chain, establishing quality systems, and ensuring the secure management of critical resources in order to promote the development of a more resilient industrial organizational structure."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Tesla planning €3BN investment in German factory to produce Cybercabs
World.content:
The Elon Musk-owned company is looking to further expand its only European production line. Brandenburg's state leader has welcomed the decision.

The electric car manufacturer Tesla said on Monday it was planning to invest €3 billion ($3.3 billion) in its German factory near Berlin so that it can start producing Cybercabs.

The plan to start production on the driverless taxis in Tesla's only European factory comes after billionaire owner Elon Musk announced last week that the company was shutting down Cybertruck production.

What do we know about Tesla's German factory expansion plan?

Construction work at the Grünheide complex is set to begin in 2027, with the first vehicles coming off the production line in 2029, according to company plans.

Capacity is set to reach 1 million units, according to the company, although the timeframe for the goal was unclear.

Employment at the so-called "gigafactory" in the state of Brandenburg had dipped to around 11,000 before rising to 12,600 in October. The new expansion was expected to lead to the hiring of several hundred additional staff.

"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.

The company said it would submit an application for the new building by the end of the year.

German residents near Berlin fight for their drinking water To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Brandenburg state premier says Tesla plans are a 'strong message'

Brandenburg's State Premier Dietmar Woidke welcomed the decision to expand the factory in his state.

"The €3 billion investment, and the prospect of producing up to a million Cybercabs in Grünheide in the future, is an enormously important economic decision," Woidke said in a statement.

"Especially in economically challenging times, this sends a strong message: Germany, even today, remains an attractive location for major industrial investments, and Brandenburg is showing how it's done," he added.

After a slump in sales put the expansion plans on hold, an uptick in demand he seen Tesla's fortunes back on the up.

It recently said it aims to increase weekly vehicle production to 7,500 units, equivalent to 375,000 a year. It also wants to expand its battery cell production on site.

World.title: The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: how close are the connections?
World.content:
The Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has become a focal point for the far right. Many of its members and staff have ties to ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations.

The electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, she has set herself an ambitious goal: together with her co-chair Alice Weidel, she aims to see Germany's next chancellor come from their party.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?

Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.

How much of a neo-Nazi party is the German AfD? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The normalization of right-wing extremism?

Virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas."

Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

Particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it."

The debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:

In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.

What's behind the rising polarization in German politics? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

The question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

Young, far-right and radical? Meet the AfD's future leaders To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Controversial distancing efforts within the AfD

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts ," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she said in an interview with DW.

Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?"

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization."

Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.

* Editor's note: To protect the privacy of the staff member of Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts, we have changed her name to Laura Neumann. Her real name is known to the editors.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Iran's growing exodus of young talent
World.content:
Conflict and uncertainty are driving more and more educated young Iranians to consider leaving the country.

"I had actually decided to leave Iran back in 2023," a physician in her mid-30s, who wished to remain anonymous, told DW.

Her decision followed the 2022 death in police custody of 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested by Iran's so-called morality police for allegedly violating the country's strict dress code.

Amini's death sparked widespread protests and inspired the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which challenged authorities' enforcement of Iran's hijab mandate.

The physician said that the US-Israel war with Iran ultimately accelerated her plans to leave her homeland. She has been living with her family in a rented apartment in Turkey since early summer. From there, they hope to continue on to Germany.

"It took two years for my professional qualifications to be recognized in Germany. After that, I applied for an appointment at the German Embassy in Tehran," the physician said.

"Then the 12-day war broke out in the summer of 2025. The embassy closed and suddenly we were all left in limbo, not knowing what would happen next."

Is Iran set to become an economic outcast? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

She became concerned after the US and Israel launched fresh airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 — not just about the escalating conflict, but also about the prospect of internal unrest and political instability.

Turkey as a stopover

"Like many others we encountered during the emigration process, we decided to first move to a neighboring country," she said. "The plan was to stay in a third country for six months and then apply for a visa through the German embassy there. That's why my family and I came to Turkey."

Turkey is one of the few countries that allows Iranian citizens to enter without a visa for up to 90 days.

Since the latest conflict began, thousands of Iranians have crossed the border into Turkey. Many are trying to secure their stay through residence permits rather than seeking asylum.

According to official Turkish statistics, nearly 100,000 Iranian citizens were residing there in 2025. Among them are many academics and skilled professionals hoping to settle permanently in Europe or North America, seeing little future for themselves in Iran's war-hit economy.

A US naval blockade of Iranian ports ⁠in ⁠the Gulf over the past few months has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.

The situation has put most businesses under pressure by restricting access to foreign currency and raw materials, among other problems, threatening revenues and jobs.

The worsening conditions have left many people struggling to afford food, housing, health care and education.

The physician said the situation at the German embassy in Tehran, however, has improved in recent months. Some of her unmarried friends, who also initially moved to Turkey and spent substantial sums maintaining their stay there, have already returned to Iran to submit new visa applications from home.

The hopes and fears of Iranians in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

She and her husband, however, have decided to stick to their original plan and wait out the six-month residency period in Turkey despite the difficulties.

"I can't and don't want to go to Germany without my family. I don't know how long it would take for them to receive family reunification visas," she explained. "And I don't know what might happen in the meantime. A new war could break out at any moment."

Young Iranians lose faith in the future

The departure of highly qualified professionals and students has become one of the most pressing challenges facing Iranian society. Today, there are few families in which someone has not already emigrated or is not at least considering doing so.

A 2025 study by the University of Guilan in Iran examined the relationship between opportunities for social participation and students' willingness to emigrate.

The researchers found a statistically significant correlation: Students who felt they had fewer opportunities to shape their future in Iran were more likely to consider emigrating.

Economic concerns are only part of the picture. Limited political participation, social restrictions and a sense of powerlessness are also driving many young Iranians to leave.

Mahsa, who is in her mid-20s, told DW that she has already secured admission to a German university.

Ali, meanwhile, dreams of a life outside Iran. The 23-year-old holds a bachelor's degree in engineering and is currently preparing for the entrance exam for a master's program at a public university. His long-term goal is to obtain a stronger qualification and then leave Iran — ideally with a scholarship.

"That's my dream of a better future," he said.

Fleeing Iran for freedom To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
