New sanctions target banks and business actors

She said EU foreign ministers would also decide on a new sanctions list. Under one of the sanctions packages concerning hybrid attacks, a number of natural and legal persons would be added to the EU list of restrictive measures.

In addition, the EU would impose sanctions on banks and business actors, she said.

Hungary wants Syria to help curb illegal migration

Meanwhile, Orbán said the ministers would also discuss the planned association agreement between the EU and Syria.

“Hungary’s goal is to address illegal migration in the countries of origin,” she said, adding that Syria could play a stabilising role in the entire region.

World.title: Several Hungarian banks plan service disruptions before Christmas: What customers need to know
World.content:
Customers of several Hungarian banks could face temporary disruptions to mobile and online banking, card payments, cash withdrawals and transfers in the coming weeks. Planned maintenance work in November and December will affect different services at different times, so customers are advised to check the schedules before making important payments or relying on their bank cards.

According to Pénzcentrum, Erste, K&H, MagNet Bank, MBH Bank and UniCredit have announced upcoming maintenance periods. Some disruptions will last only a few minutes, while others will affect services for several hours or over an entire weekend.

Erste: George and other services to be unavailable

Erste will carry out a system upgrade between 10 pm on 26 November and 3 am on 27 November 2026. During this period, customers will not be able to use George App and George Web, online purchases, Erste TeleBank, Corporate NetBank, Electra, Erste Business Mobile Banking, SMS services, the API channel or online product applications. The online declaration platform for housing savings deposits will also be unavailable.

A further upgrade is scheduled from 6 pm on 4 December until 11.59 pm on 6 December. During this period, customers will not be able to modify their personal data through George Web, George App, Corporate NetBank or TeleBank. Some website services will also be affected, although Erste says all other services will remain available.

K&H: Several maintenance periods, including a major weekend outage

K&H has announced a series of interruptions:

17–18 November, 10 pm–2 am: Temporary interruptions or slower operation may affect K&H e-bank, mobile banking, e-portfolio, e-mail and Electra services, as well as the bank’s website.

Temporary interruptions or slower operation may affect K&H e-bank, mobile banking, e-portfolio, e-mail and Electra services, as well as the bank’s website. 21 November, midnight–1 am: The same digital services and the ATM cash-deposit service may be temporarily unavailable or slower.

The same digital services and the ATM cash-deposit service may be temporarily unavailable or slower. 21 November, 7 am–3 pm: The investment modules in K&H e-bank and mobile banking, as well as K&H e-portfolio and related investment services, will be unavailable.

The investment modules in K&H e-bank and mobile banking, as well as K&H e-portfolio and related investment services, will be unavailable. 22–23 November, 10 pm–midnight: Temporary disruptions may affect the bank’s digital services and website.

Temporary disruptions may affect the bank’s digital services and website. 23–24 November, 10 pm–7 am: The PIN-change service for K&H debit and credit cards will be unavailable.

The PIN-change service for K&H debit and credit cards will be unavailable. 28–29 November, 11 pm–1 pm: K&H’s electronic channels, including internet and mobile banking, and its ATM cash-deposit service will be suspended. Customers will also be unable to initiate instant transfers or receive payment requests.

During the major outage on 28–29 November, ATM cash withdrawals and card payments in shops and online are expected to remain available. However, card use will be limited to the account balance available at 11 pm on 28 November. K&H also warns that online bank card and SZÉP Card payments may be disrupted, and SMS messages confirming transactions or online purchases may be delayed or fail to arrive.

The bank advises customers to ensure they have sufficient funds and suitable card limits in place before the outage. Scheduled and recurring payments due during the downtime will be processed on the first working day afterwards.

Further maintenance is planned for 12–13 December, 10 pm–6 am, affecting K&H’s digital banking services and website. Another outage, from 11 pm on 18 December until 8 am on 19 December, may also affect SZÉP Card services and 3D Secure authentication, as well as the bank’s digital channels.

MagNet Bank: Card services may be interrupted overnight

MagNet Bank has announced maintenance for 13 December, from midnight to 4 am. The work may temporarily affect domestic and international ATM withdrawals, cash withdrawals at point-of-sale terminals, card payments in shops and online, and SMS services linked to card use.

During the maintenance, customers will only be able to block their bank cards by calling MagNet’s 24-hour telephone customer service on +36 1 766 4544 or +36 1 428 8888.

MBH Bank: ATM, card payment and terminal disruptions

MBH Bank has announced several shorter interruptions:

17 November, 10 pm–11.30 pm: Card acceptance may be interrupted for up to 30 minutes at some of the bank’s point-of-sale terminals.

Card acceptance may be interrupted for up to 30 minutes at some of the bank’s point-of-sale terminals. 18 and 25 November, 4 pm–6 pm: The ATM at Eurocenter (GoBuda), 154 Bécsi Road in Budapest, may be unavailable for around 30 minutes on each date.

The ATM at Eurocenter (GoBuda), 154 Bécsi Road in Budapest, may be unavailable for around 30 minutes on each date. 18 and 26 November, and 3 December, 10 pm–11 pm: Customers with bank account numbers beginning with the identifier 101 may experience problems with online and in-store card payments, card authentication and ATM withdrawals. Card-related functions in the MBH Netbank (formerly Budapest Bank) and MBH Bank App 101 profiles will also be temporarily unavailable.

The bank recommends using another ATM if necessary. Its 24-hour customer service can be reached on 06 80 350 350 from within Hungary.

UniCredit: Digital banking and instant transfers affected

UniCredit has scheduled two maintenance periods. On 22 November, from 8 pm to 10 pm, and again from 11 pm on 27 November until 7 am on 28 November, several services will be unavailable.

These include the UniCredit mBanking and mToken apps, business mobile banking, eBanking, SpectraNet and Spectra services, Open Banking API functions, customer-identification services through the call centre, MultiCash, instant payments, ATM cash deposits, SMS services and securities-related administration.

What should bank customers do?

The announced maintenance periods do not mean that every service will stop at every bank. The impact varies considerably, even between different dates at the same institution. Customers should check their bank’s official announcements, arrange time-sensitive transfers and bill payments in advance, and consider keeping enough cash available if they expect to need it during a scheduled outage.

World.title: K-Arts in Hungary: Traditional Korean performance modernised in Budapest
World.content:
On Wednesday, November 4, the 2026 Touring K-Arts production Pungjang Korea was presented at the Eiffel Art Studios in Budapest, Hungary.

Korean art performance in Budapest

The performance was supported by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism of the Republic of Korea and the Korean Foundation for International Cultural Exchange (KOFICE), in cooperation with the National Intangible Heritage Center and Korean Cultural Center in Hungary.

Photo: Pungjang Korea

At the heart of Pungjang Korea is Nongak, a traditional Korean community performance art inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2014. Drawing on the communal spirit and vibrant energy of Nongak, the production brings together a wide range of artistic genres, including traditional Korean music and dance, contemporary dance, Pansori (traditional Korean narrative singing), and singer-songwriter performances, creating a dynamic and multidisciplinary stage experience.

The event was attended by Katalin Bogyay, President of the Hungarian National Commission for UNESCO, and H.E. Park Chul-min, Ambassador of the Republic of Korea to Hungary, both of whom delivered congratulatory remarks highlighting the cultural significance of the performance.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Korean culture dressed in modernity

The production offered a fresh, contemporary interpretation of traditional Korean music and successfully connected with local audiences beyond language barriers. By blending the distinctive rhythms of Korean traditional music with modern musical elements, including rock, the performance made traditional Korean sounds accessible and enjoyable to a broad audience.

One of the highlights was the performers’ greeting in Hungarian, followed by a rendition of Gyöngyhajú lány (Pearls in Her Hair in English), a well-loved classic by Omega, the legendary Hungarian rock band. The gesture struck a chord with the local audience and created a special connection between the performers and Hungarian spectators.

Photo: Pungjang Korea

The performance concluded to enthusiastic applause, with the entire audience rising to their feet in a standing ovation. Audience members also expressed overwhelmingly positive reactions, saying that they had thoroughly enjoyed the show and found it both exciting and entertaining.

Following its successful presentation in Hungary, Pungjang Korea will continue its European tour with upcoming performances in Podgorica, Montenegro, and Ankara, Türkiye.

World.title: Hungarian priest was removed by Pope Francis himself for abusing minors, still works around children
World.content:
A former Hungarian Catholic priest who was removed from the priesthood by Pope Francis in 2016 following allegations of sexually abusing minors is reportedly still working around children and young people in Transylvania, according to an investigative report by Hungarian news outlet 444.hu.

Former priest reportedly lives alongside teenagers in Székely Land

Balázs Szűcs, whose ecclesiastical career ended following an investigation into alleged abuse involving several young people, is said to be living in the Székely Land region of Romania, sometimes alongside more than ten teenage boys and young adults. He was also reportedly involved in organising camps for young people until recently.

The investigation by 444.hu traced Szűcs to a property in the Harghita Mountains and identified a company linked to him in a village near Miercurea Ciuc. Journalists also found TikTok videos showing young men renovating a roadside guesthouse. Local accounts reportedly indicated that Szűcs had been living with groups of teenage boys and young adults.

Abuse allegations led to removal from priesthood

Szűcs became widely known after Attila Pető publicly revealed that he had been sexually abused by a Catholic priest when he was 13. Pető was among the first victims in Hungary to speak openly about abuse by a member of the clergy, using both his name and face.

The Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest launched an internal investigation into Szűcs in 2015 over suspected sexual offences involving minors. He was subsequently prohibited from carrying out priestly duties and from working with young people. In 2016, the case was referred to the Vatican, which first imposed a ten-year ban on priestly ministry before making the exclusion permanent.

The investigation also highlighted the scale of the impact on the community in Piliscsaba, where at least 20 victims were reportedly identified. Hundreds of other people, including families and members of the wider school and camp communities, were said to have been indirectly affected.

Questions remain about safeguarding after laicisation

The latest report raises questions about what happens after the Church removes an individual from the priesthood, particularly when safeguarding concerns remain. One young person who contacted 444.hu reportedly described learning that Szűcs was working around children as a devastating experience, adding that his laicisation did not provide a reassuring conclusion to the case.

According to the investigation, Szűcs had also previously worked at Budapest’s Szőlő Street juvenile correctional facility. There, he reportedly introduced a programme known as the “quiet room”, intended to help young people develop a more positive view of themselves and the world.

World.title: Budapest Airport profits soar, but tensions grow between Hungary and French owner Vinci: what could this mean for travellers?
World.content:
Budapest Airport is enjoying record passenger numbers and strong financial results, but disagreements between the Hungarian state and French operator Vinci Airports are reportedly putting major development plans under strain.

Budapest Airport had an exceptionally profitable 2025, generating HUF 183 billion (approximately EUR 458 million) in revenue and HUF 71 billion (EUR 178 million) in net profit. Passenger traffic is also expected to set another record in 2026, with more than two million travellers passing through the airport in both July and August.

However, an investigation by Telex suggests that relations between the airport’s two owners have deteriorated. The Hungarian state holds an 80% stake, while French company Vinci Airports owns 20% but also has management rights. Although neither side reportedly wants to terminate the partnership, disagreements have emerged over the airport’s future.

Disputes over the new terminal and airport railway

One major point of contention is the EUR 1 billion Terminal+ development programme. Hungarian government representatives reportedly consider the plans too modest, arguing that the proposed facilities and passenger services are inadequate for Hungary’s climate and ambitions. Budapest Airport, however, says preparations are progressing according to schedule and that it is maintaining close professional discussions with the government.

The proposed railway connection to the airport is another source of tension. A Vinci–Strabag–Aberdeen consortium was the only bidder for the concession project, but the Hungarian government has yet to finalise an agreement. According to Telex’s sources, the transport ministry wants favourable terms before signing.

One reported disagreement concerns airport parking spaces. The airport management has allegedly raised concerns that railway construction could reduce parking capacity and revenue, a position that has reportedly caused frustration on the government side.

Who should control the airport’s future?

The new government is also reportedly unhappy with the influence granted to Vinci under the ownership agreement negotiated by the previous administration. Some Hungarian officials believe the French company prioritises short-term profits over Hungary’s long-term interests. They have also questioned the involvement of companies close to the former governing establishment in airport cleaning and security services.

Commercial operations are another area of disagreement. Hungarian representatives would reportedly like to see more domestic businesses involved in airport retail and catering, rather than relying heavily on large international operators.

There are also differing views on the type of tourism Hungary should attract. Some Hungarian stakeholders would prefer more visitors interested in cultural programmes and higher-spending tourism, rather than relying heavily on low-cost flights bringing party tourists.

Vinci, however, does not appear to share the government’s assessment of the relationship. In its response to Telex, the company emphasised its strategic commitment to Hungary, saying its goals include sustainable passenger growth, stronger international connections and improving the airport’s regional competitiveness.

Budapest Airport also stressed that differences of opinion are natural in any partnership and should be addressed through constructive dialogue.

What could this mean for travellers?

For now, passengers are unlikely to notice any immediate changes to airport operations. However, the disagreements over terminal expansion, railway access and the airport’s long-term development could affect how quickly Budapest Airport improves its facilities and connections in the coming years. The planned airport railway, in particular, could make a significant difference to how easily visitors reach the city centre.

World.title: PM Magyar announces busy week ahead as Parliament prepares to debate 2027 budget
World.content:
Hungary’s parliament will begin its session earlier than usual on Monday, while the governing Tisza Party’s parliamentary group is preparing for its first off-site meeting since the elections. Several major decisions and legislative debates are also on the agenda.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar has warned that a busy week lies ahead, with parliament set to discuss the 2027 state budget and the government expected to make important decisions on Wednesday.

In a Facebook post on Sunday evening, towards the end of his visit to Ireland, Magyar announced that Monday’s parliamentary session would exceptionally begin at 9am. “There will be plenty to talk about. Join us and let’s look the collapsing mafia in the eye together,” he wrote.

According to the Hungarian news agency MTI, the prime minister described the proposed budget as one focused on “justice and development”. He also said the Tisza parliamentary group would hold an off-site meeting on Thursday and Friday – its first since the elections.

If you missed it: PM Magyar: Meeting with Ukrainian President Zelensky could take place in Transcarpathia as early as November

Extraordinary parliamentary session to cover four issues

As Index reported, Deputy Prime Minister Bálint Ruff had previously requested an extraordinary three-day parliamentary session between 16 and 18 November on behalf of the government.

The original proposal included two main items: the 2027 central budget and legislation establishing the foundations for its implementation. Two additional agenda items were subsequently added.

One concerns the publication of an agreement between the Hungarian and US governments aimed at facilitating cooperation on Hungary’s civilian nuclear energy programme.

The other involves a report on amendments to the government decision regulating Hungarian troops’ participation in the EU-led ALTHEA peacekeeping operation in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The additional items were included to allow the proposals to be discussed as soon as possible, according to the justification cited by Index.

First off-site Tisza meeting since the elections

The Tisza parliamentary group’s two-day meeting on Thursday and Friday will be its first off-site session since the elections. Magyar said the government would also make important decisions on Wednesday.

Describing the previous week as demanding, the prime minister said a similarly busy period was coming, adding that the country was moving towards a more functional and humane Hungary.

World.title: Bosnia’s New Presidency Takes Office for 2026-2030 Term
World.content:
Darijana Filipovic, Zeljka Cvijanovic and Denis Becirovic pose for a photo after their inaugural session. Photo: N1.

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s newly elected tripartite presidency took office on Monday at a session in Sarajevo, with Denis Becirovic, Zeljka Cvijanovic and Darijana Filipovic beginning their four-year mandates.

Speaking after his inauguration, Bosniak representative Becirovic, who is beginning his second consecutive term, said his priorities would include defending Bosnia’s sovereignty, protecting human rights and advancing the country’s European Union and NATO integration.

He also pledged to promote equality and fight discrimination. His vision, he said, was of an economically strong, technologically developed and socially just Bosnia and Herzegovina, fully integrated into both organisations.

He called for an end to divisive political rhetoric, saying political energy should be directed towards building a safer future. “People draw no benefit from populism and arguments. They want peace, security, social justice and good prospects for their children,” he said.

Serb representative Cvijanovic, also beginning her second consecutive term, called on domestic politicians to take full responsibility for the country’s future rather than expect solutions from abroad.

She criticised international intervention in Bosnia’s politics, arguing that decisions imposed over the previous four years had deepened political crises. She also said the domination by one constituent people over the other two was unacceptable.

Croat representative Darijana Filipovic called for the presidency to show more responsibility towards voters. “From today, the question is no longer who was given trust, but what we can do with that trust,” Filipovic said.

She said she would work to ensure that Croats in Bosnia felt politically represented and equal.

“We are not asking for Croats to have more, and we do not accept that they have less. I believe the same rule must apply to everyone else in this country, because Bosnia and Herzegovina … must be a country in which people have equal worth,” she said.

Filipovic succeeds Zeljko Komsic, who served four terms as the Croat member of the Presidency but who was widely seen as owing his place to Bosniak votes.

The new Presidency is the first since the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement established the institution to include two women, Cvijanovic became the first woman to serve on the body in 2022.

The three members were elected in the October 4 general elections, with the Central Election Commission confirming the results on November 3.

Under the Presidency’s rules, the chairmanship rotates every eight months.

Bosnia’s state presidency is responsible for foreign policy, appointing ambassadors and other representatives to international organisations and proposing the annual state budget to parliament, based on a recommendation from the Council of Ministers.

World.title: EU Commissioner ‘Regrets’ Serb Song About Kosovo at Brussels Event
World.content:
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos speaking in Brussels, 16 November 2026. Photo: EPA/Olivier Hoslet.

The European Commissioner for Enlargement, Marta Kos, on Monday said she regretted that a controversial song about Kosovo was performed before the opening of the European Enlargement Forum in Brussels.

“I regret the choice of the song by the musicians. It touches sensitive feelings, particularly given the history and different experiences of the communities in Kosovo,” Kos, a Slovenian diplomat, said in Brussels.

“I want to stress that this song in no way reflects the position of the European Commission or myself with respect to Kosovo and history,” she added.

The song,“Oj Kosovo, Kosovo”, celebrates Serbia’s claims to its former province. Its lyrics say that Kosovo “has always been ours” and vow never to give up the territory.

It was performed as an instrumental version, by a Slovenian band, at a concert on Sunday, preceding Monday’s European Enlargement Forum. The choice of song was made by the performers rather than the organisers, according to Kos.

The performance drew an angry reaction from Kosovo officials.

Jeton Zulfaj, Kosovo’s chief negotiator with the EU, asked Kos “to explain how this happened and what measures she will take, and why Kosovo, the biggest democratic climber in the Western Balkans this decade and fully aligned with EU foreign policy and EU values, was not invited”.

On X, Zulfaj called the incident “scandalous and unacceptable. An EU event on enlargement cannot give a stage to Serbian nationalism.”

The Albanian Prime Minister, Edi Rama, also condemned the incident.

“I don’t know if it was deliberate or ignorance but a tasteless nationalistic song was performed on the eve of this event in the contrary of everything it represents,” Rama said.

Riho Terras, a European Parliament member and Kosovo rapporteur, also demanded an explanation from the European Commission and Kos. “Performing a Serbian nationalist song asserting claims over Kosovo at an EU enlargement event is an extraordinarily tactless and tasteless blunder,” he said.

The author Ljubomir Manasijevic recounted in 2019 that the song was created in 1989, inspired by the celebration of the Battle of Kosovo’s 600th anniversary near Pristina, at which Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic gave a fiery speech which has been identified by some historians as marking the beginning of Yugoslavia’s collapse.

“What it is clear is that we cannot change our shared past but we can choose our shared future and the future must be European. European in the sense that we will respect differences, but this would be the future without divisions, where everybody feels at home,” Kos said.

“It is very clear to me that we are not asking to forget differences. We are building, and this is my important task, a Europe where actually differences will no longer be a reason to live apart,” she added.

World.title: Second Trial of Kosovo’s Thaci, for Obstructing Justice, Nears End
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

The second trial of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci at The Hague is coming to an end, with the verdict to be announced on Tuesday.

Thaci, who was also a wartime guerrilla leader, is being tried alongside four co-defendants for obstruction of justice. He is accused of interfering with witnesses in his war-crimes trial.

The Kosovo Specialist Prosecutor’s Office in The Hague, in its closing statements on September 10, demanded six years’ prison for Thaci, claiming he told his co-defendants to instruct witnesses what to say while testifying in his war-crimes case.

It sought “nine months of imprisonment for [Hajredin] Kuci; three years for [Fadil] Fazliu; three years for [Isni] Kilaj; three years for [Bashkim] Smakaj; and six years for Thaci,” prosecutor Joshua Hafetz said during the closing statements.

Thaci and his four-co-accused have denied wrongdoing.

The prosecution claimed that Thaci tried to exert influence over two former Kosovo Liberation Army fighters, Bislim Zyrapi and Rrustem Mustafa, who were testifying in his war-crimes case. The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence.

In his testimony in 2023, former KLA area commander Mustafa claimed that the KLA zone commanders made the key operational decisions, not the General Staff. He said the KLA leaders, who included Thaci, did not have control over lower-ranking fighters – testimony that bolstered the defence’s case.

Zyrapi, former chief of the KLA’s General Staff, gave his testimony in 2024. He also said the General Staff often was not informed of the actions of fighters in the operational zones and that, despite attempts, it had not been possible for the KLA to fully exercise control over its lower-level units, partly because of Serbian offensives.

On September 16 this year, the Specialist Chambers sentenced Thaci to 25 years in prison for the war crimes of murder, arbitrary detention, torture and cruel treatment as a leader of the KLA during the Kosovo war from April 1998 to June 20, 1999.

His co-defendants, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli, and Rexhep Selimi, were sentenced to 25, 18 and 13 years respectively.

The defence is preparing to appeal the first-instance verdict. The September 16 verdict triggered protests in Kosovo and in Europe by Albanian diaspora members and supporters of the KLA.

Kosovo’s parliament on October 6 voted to amend the law on the Specialist Chambers to curb its powers. The law has been returned to parliament for review by the President, however. The EU and the UK have warned Kosovo MPs not to vote for the law change without consultations with the international community, as the court was established via an international agreement.

The Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

World.title: Hundreds of Thousands Protest Czech Government Reforms to Public Media
World.content:
There has been growing discontent in the country over the plans of the coalition – a mix of populist, far-right and Eurosceptic parties – to scrap licence fees and fund the broadcasters directly from the state budget. According to the proposal, CT would receive an annual 5.7 billion crowns (234 million euros) from the state budget in 2027 (a billion crowns less than its 2026 license fee revenues), while CRo would see its funding cut by 400 million crowns to a little over 2 billion crowns.

The police told Czech News Agency that they would not publish an estimated count of the protest, though if the organiser’s estimate is correct, it likely would make this the largest demonstration since the Velvet Revolutionary protests of 1989 in then Czechoslovakia.

World.title: The Lives of a Photograph, as Seen in a Bosnian Museum
World.content:
Artist Vladimir Miladinovic, for example, worked with the museum’s wartime archive as part of Art & Reconciliation: Conflict, Culture and Community in 2018. Rather than extracting a single image, he carefully redraws entire pages, retaining headlines, text and layout. The photograph is thus reintroduced into the media environment through which it originally reached the public. His work invites viewers to look again at material that might otherwise be read quickly or treated as familiar historical evidence.

As part of the follow-up to the Art & Reconciliation project, Jason File and Zoran Lesic developed two works for Reconciliations II, following two very different paths toward the documentation of war.

File came to the subject from law and his work with evidence at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, ICTY, while Lesic came from the world of theatre and photography and moved toward documenting the war and, later, working with the Tribunal.

Their works in the museum brought these two different paths into contact: one moved from legal evidence toward artistic practice, while the other moved from artistic practice toward documentary and institutional forms of evidence.

In the museum, both were given another context, allowing materials connected to the war to acquire new meanings through their encounter with contemporary art.

File’s work moved material from the courtroom into the museum, where evidence became a subject of artistic interpretation; Lesic, in turn, placed images from wartime Sarajevo alongside images made in the Netherlands after the war, allowing meaning to emerge through their juxtaposition. In both cases, the museum became a place where documents could move beyond their original function and acquire another life.

One of the most sensitive stories in the Besieged Sarajevo collection is that of a boy named Nermin Divovic. When British artist Paul Coldwell came to the museum, this is the story he could see in the exhibition: Nermin was seven years old when he was killed by sniper fire in Sarajevo in November 1994. The museum’s story is presented through both an object and a series of photographs: his sweater is displayed alongside images taken by Gervasio Sanchez, showing Nermin playing in the snow with a photographer Enric Marti.

Just one year after the photos were taken, Marti photographed the aftermath of the shooting that killed Nermin. Coldwell returned to this material in A Life Measured – Seven Sweaters for Nermin Divovic.

His work began with the existing relationship between the photograph and the object in the museum, but gave that relationship another form. The sweater, preserved as a trace of a child’s life, became the starting point for an artistic work that asked how a life can be remembered through the things and images that remain after it.

Coldwell used the sweater and photographs as the starting point for an artwork consisting of seven knitted replicas, each representing a year of Nermin’s life. Arranged in increasing sizes, they trace the years he lived and make visible the years he never had. Here, the photograph does not simply illustrate a story. In combination with the surviving garment, it prompted the creation of a new work that explores what a museum can preserve – and what no collection can restore.

The History Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina has changed with the society around it.

Its name, institutional framework, exhibitions and ways of working have shifted over time, responding to different political and social circumstances. Photography, however, has remained an important part of the museum’s practice and exhibition history.

Even when resources were limited, the museum found ways to bring its collections back into view, placing historical materials in new contexts and allowing them to speak to new audiences.

This is, perhaps, one of the most important resources a museum has: not only its collections themselves, but the ability to make them visible, to return to them, and to allow them to acquire new meanings. There are many more stories in the museum’s depot waiting for that to happen.

Elma Fisic is an art historian and curator from Sarajevo who has worked at the History Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina since 2013, focusing on exhibitions, museum collections, heritage interpretation and the role of museums in shaping collective memory and engaging with society.

World.title: Serbia’s Post-Election Wave of Arrests Raises Hopes, But Also Questions
World.content:
After two days of celebrations in the wake of the momentous elections that ended the 14-year rule of the Serbian Progressive Party last month, police arrested Radivoje Stojkovic, the director of the Jovan Jovanovic Zmaj High School in the northern city of Novi Sad.

During the course of nearly two years of student-led anti-government protests, which began in Novi Sad in 2024, school director Stojkovic had become one of the symbols of the pressures exerted on teachers who went on strike to express their support for their students and their own dissatisfaction.

Stojkovic was detained on October 28 because he refused to enforce four court rulings and reinstate four teachers who had been ousted after they supported the student protests.

The high school headed by Stojkovic is well-known in Serbia as the source of a key piece of protest lore. It was here that anti-protest graffiti reading "Caci u skolu" ("Pupils, go back to school") appeared. Because it was written with a spelling mistake, the term "caci" became a nickname for all supporters of the Serbian Progressive Party and its long-dominant figurehead, Aleksandar Vucic.

Because of this, Stojkovic's arrest served as a symbolic beginning to what has followed since October 28: almost daily arrests of people close to the outgoing Progressive Party-led government, who are now being accused of abusing their positions, engaging in corruption or committing other illegal acts.

World.title: Albania Free Media Advocates Fear Anti-SLAPP Bill Isn’t Tough Enough
World.content:
The government of Albania, an EU candidate state, last week put out a long-awaited draft law for publication introducing a new legal mechanism to protect journalists and media outlets from unfounded lawsuits or abusive court proceedings, known as SLAPPs.

The draft legislation, part of Albania’s efforts to align domestic legislation with European law, aims to curb lawsuits that are often launched by wealthy and powerful people to put pressure on journalists and campaigners who speak out on matters of public interest.

If it is adopted, the law will create procedural safeguards for people sued as a result of their engagement in matters of public interest.

The key provisions will ensure that the legal costs of SLAPPs are borne by the claimants, the possible early dismissal of lawsuits deemed “manifestly unfounded”, priority handling of cases to prevent lengthy proceedings and give defendants the right to receive support from civil society organisations, unions or other entities.

World.title: Bulgaria annual inflation rises to 6.0% in October
World.content:
Bulgaria’s annual consumer price index (CPI) recorded six per cent inflation in October, rising from 5.7 per cent a month earlier, the National Statistical Institute (NSI) said on November 16.

The monthly CPI figure showed 1.2 per cent inflation in October, which was the second largest increase in the previous 12 months.

Food prices were 0.7 per cent higher in October compared to September, while non-food prices rose by 1.1 per cent and services prices were 1.9 per cent higher.

Compared to October 2025, food prices were up two per cent, while non-food prices rose by 8.1 per cent and services prices were 7.3 per cent higher.

The harmonised CPI figure, calculated by NSI for comparison with European Union data, was 0.7 per cent higher compared to September, and the annual harmonised CPI inflation rose to 5.9 per cent, up from 5.6 per cent a month earlier.

Food and beverage prices were 1.8 per cent higher in October, on an annual basis, while the price of utilities and housing rose by 5.4 per cent and transportation costs were 16.5 per cent higher compared to the same month of last year.

World.title: Cargo ship sinks off Bulgaria’s coast after being hit by two drones
World.content:
A rescue operation was mounted on November 16 as cargo ship Betul 8, which was 40 nautical miles south-east of Bulgaria’s Cape Kaliakra, issued a distress call that it was sinking, the Transport Ministry said.

Two drones hit the Betul 8, which capsized east of the mouth of the Kamchia River, Maritime.bg reports. Sailors from the crew provided the website with photos of the drones, which, it said, look like the drones used against the Contship Jet. According to the website, the 12-member crew left the ship and boarded life rafts.

The distress call was received by the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Varna at 9.15am, the ministry said.

Four ships from the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Naval Group (MCM Black Sea) – two Bulgarian, one Romanian and one Turkish – have been dispatched to the scene of the incident, the Transport Ministry said.

The operations are coordinated by the General Directorate of Emergency and Rescue Activities at the Executive Agency of the Maritime Administration.

The operation also includes two Cougar helicopters and a Su-25 aircraft of the Air Force, which will conduct surveillance and reconnaissance of the area.

The Betul 8, sailing under the Somali flag and with a crew of 12, was travelling from Tulcea, Romania, to Egypt and was carrying nearly three tons of bulk wheat, the statement said.

Bulgarian National Television reported on November 16 that according to its information, the ship already had sunk.

There have been several drone strikes against merchant ships off Bulgaria’s and Romania’s coasts recently, attacks widely blamed on Russia.

(Photo: Transport Ministry)

World.title: EU ministers approve new sanctions to further restrict Russia’s ability to finance its war
World.content:
In response to Russia’s indiscriminate attacks against Ukraine, particularly against civilian infrastructure, the European Union foreign ministers on November 16 imposed additional restrictive measures on 12 individuals and 101 entities, a statement by the Council of the EU said.

Those listed are being sanctioned for their role in those economic sectors which provide a substantial source of revenue to Russia’s war of aggression and support its shadow fleet, the statement said.

Today’s listings include nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions. By progressively tightening and expanding sanctions on Russia’s banking sector, the EU is cutting off the financial channels that process state revenues and fund Russia’s war effort, the Council of the EU said.

Moreover, the Council is cracking down on Russia’s e-commerce. Today’s package includes the sole shareholder of Russian retail giant Wildberries, and an individual controlling the majority stake in another major Russian e-commerce company, Ozon.

The Council is also listing additional entities and businesspersons in the Russian oil and energy sector. The energy companies listed today manage Russian refineries and the St. Petersburg oil terminal and are active in the exploration and production segment.

The Council is targeting Russia’s shadow fleet, by listing various companies from the United Arab Emirates, China, Seychelles and Oman that are buyers of crude oil products of Russian origin, as well as certain businesspersons who own or manage vessels that are subject to EU restrictive measures, and illegally transport Russian oil, while engaging in high-risk shipping activities.

Today’s listings were adopted under the EU’s restrictive measures framework targeting actions undermining or threatening Ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. Those listed under this sanctions regime are subject to an asset freeze and it is prohibited to provide them with funds or economic resources either directly or indirectly or for their benefit. Additionally, a travel ban to the EU applies to the natural persons named in today’s listing.

The relevant legal acts have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union.

(Photo: EC Audiovisual Service)

World.title: Electricity Coordination Group: EU electricity market prepared for the winter
World.content:
The EU electricity market is suitably prepared for the winter, but it is necessary to continue monitoring the market closely, according to discussions between the European Commission (EC), national experts and key stakeholders in the Electricity Coordination Group (ECG) meeting that took place on November 12, the EC said in a statement posted on November 16.

The meeting also had a detailed presentation of the Winter Outlook by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) , which was published on November 13.

In addition, the Group took stock of the electricity system’s winter preparedness.

Even though hydro storage levels are lower than before and planned nuclear maintenance will slightly reduce plant availability, the overall situation throughout the winter is expected to remain stable.

The Commission underlined the importance of continuing to monitor the situation and remaining closely coordinated.

The situation in Ukraine and Moldova remains difficult, in particular in Ukraine, given the continuous targeted attacks on critical energy infrastructure– and the Group expressed its solidarity with the situation of electricity in both countries, confirming the importance of continued technical assistance and regional coordination, the statement said.

“For the coming winter, security of electricity supply in the two countries will depend on weather conditions, the state of critical energy infrastructure, and the availability of interconnections with the EU,” it said.

EU solidarity, technical assistance and regional coordination remain essential to supporting electricity security in Ukraine and Moldova, the statement said.

(Photo: John Mason/ freeimages.com)

World.title: Bulgaria gets two Russian banks removed from proposed EU sanctions list
World.content:
Two Russian banks with majority Bulgarian ownership have been removed from the EU sanctions list and no restrictive measures will be imposed against them when EU foreign ministers meet on November 16, it emerged from a statement to reporters in Brussels by Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova.

One of the banks is First Investment Bank (FIB) , which, however, has nothing to do with the eponymous Bulgarian FIB. The other is Investment Corporate Bank (ICB) . Both are small banks with majority Bulgarian ownership that operate on the Russian market.

Both banks are majority Bulgarian-owned. Bulgaria’s motives for removing them from the list are that if they are sanctioned, instead of causing damage to the Russian state, it will benefit from it.

“We requested their removal for a similar reason to the one with which France requested the removal of a certain entity from the sanctions package,” Petrova said.

“The two banks do not operate with financial funds of people who fall into sanctions lists. And to a large extent, the way in which they are structured in the Russian Federation does not allow them to take their investment out of there,” she said.

“If they are sanctioned, the only thing that will happen is that they will have to come into the possession of the Russian state and accordingly they will lose their asset. This will be counterproductive, because in fact, instead of there being some kind of damage and restrictions for the Russian side, it will actually be income,” Petrova said.

This is not the first time that Bulgaria’s Roumen Radev government, which took office in May, has acted to remove individuals from proposed sanctions lists. Previously, it got Russian Patriarch Kirill and a Russian oligarch removed from a proposed list.

World.title: EU ministers approve largest-ever payment of eight billion euro to Ukraine
World.content:
European Union ministers adopted on November 16 a decision that will allow Kyiv to soon receive just under eight billion euro under the Ukraine Facility, of which about five billion euro comes from resources made available from the Ukraine Support Loan in 2026, a statement by the Council of the EU said.

This is the largest-ever single payout to Ukraine made by the EU under the facility, the statement said.

This payment follows Ukraine’s fulfilment of over 20 target steps that relate to various reforms in key areas such as: the judicial system; the fight against corruption and money laundering; financial markets; the management of public assets; human capital; the business environment; decentralisation and regional policy; energy; the agri-food sector; digital transformation; and environmental protection, it said.

Funding under the Ukraine Facility is designed to bolster Ukraine’s macro-financial stability, recovery and modernisation, keep its public administration running, and support its reform efforts.

Payments are linked to the Ukraine Plan, which outlines Ukraine’s strategy for recovery, reconstruction and modernisation, along with a timetable for the implementation of reforms broadly aligned with the country’s EU accession goals.

The Ukraine Facility was established on March 1 2024 and has more than 50 billion euro available in grants and loans to support Ukraine’s recovery, reconstruction, and modernisation through 2027.

Of this total, more than 40 billion euro is earmarked for reforms and investments set out in the Ukraine Plan – Ukraine’s roadmap for recovery and EU accession – with regular disbursements tied to Ukraine meeting the Plan’s targets.

Once this ninth disbursement is made, Ukraine will have received more than 40 billion euro under the Ukraine Plan since mid-2024.

(Photo: G Schouten de Jel)

World.title: Bulgarian PM Radev tells his Cabinet: Stop blaming previous governments
World.content:
Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev, addressing his Cabinet on November 16, told them to stop blaming previous governments.

Radev, whose government was elected by Parliament on May 8, has himself had the habit of shifting blame to previous administrations, and his ministers habitually have followed suit.

A statement by the government information service said that Radev – who was speaking at a Cabinet meeting held to adopt the draft Budget 2027 and proceed to table it in Parliament – appealed to the ministers to focus on the work and not to justify possible difficulties with the legacy of the previous administrations.

“Today we put an end to the justifications with the legacy of the previous ones,” Radev said.

“A former prime minister spent two terms in office making excuses with the previous ones. Therefore, today we are paying the bill for the unfinished business. So from now on – no excuses, but work,” he said.

Radev said that Bugaria needs a strong opposition to act as a corrective, and assured that the government will listen to reasoned criticism and valuable proposals.

At the same time, he called on the ministers not to allow themselves to be drawn into “manipulations and staged scandals”.

“Unlike them, we have a lot of work and responsibility ahead of us, but not to them, but to the Bulgarian citizens,” he said.

Regarding what the statement called the speculations that have appeared in the media, Radev said that Bulgaria’s credit rating has not been downgraded and remains BBB+ and there is no forecast for recession.

He said that Standard & Poor’s predicts economic growth of 2.8 per cent for the current year and 2.6 per cent over the next three years for Bulgaria, with only the assessment of the country’s outlook being downgraded by one notch, but the possibility of its improvement remains open.

Radev emphasised that the Bulgarian economy continues to demonstrate sustainable growth and attract increased investment interest.

Bulgaria also ranks fifth in the European Union in terms of economic growth in the third quarter, and foreign direct investments have increased by 100 per cent since the beginning of the year compared to the same period last year, he said.

“This clearly shows that confidence in us is growing, that we are on the right path and we will confidently follow it,” Radev said.

(Photo: government.bg)

World.title: Opposition parties slam Bulgaria’s Radev government over S&P Global Ratings downgrade
World.content:
In statements on November 14, opposition party GERB and the Democratic Bulgaria coalition slammed Bulgaria’s Roumen Radev government over the decision by S&P Global Ratings to revise downward its outlook on Bulgaria’s BBB+ credit rating to stable, citing “growing twin deficits” as one of the reasons for its decision.

Vladislav Goranov of GERB, a former finance minister, said that the ratings decision was a sign that the government is failing to find a solution to the country’s economic problems.



“The assessment by S&P Global Ratings will serve as an excellent foundation for next week’s debate on the first reading of the budget,” Goranov said.

“Unfortunately, the conclusions are already clear. The administration is failing to address any of the problems facing our society, and, regrettably, it is just wasting our time,” he said.

GERB MP and former finance minister Temenuzhka Petkova described the proposed draft budget as “a budgetary illusion” and criticized the government’s performance.



“There is no real reduction in spending, and no reforms have been carried out,” Petkova said.

“The only area where spending has been cut is capital expenditure. One of the most serious shortcomings of this government is precisely its inability to communicate, as well as its arrogance and haughtiness,” she said.

“I hope that Roumen Radev’s government will not show its traditional arrogance, will familiarise itself with the Standard & Poor’s assessment and will not drag our country into crises and problems,” Petkova said.

Democratic Bulgaria said that because of the expectation of reforms, six months ago S&P had raised the outlook on Bulgaria’s credit rating.

Today it has changed it back – from positive to stable, Democratic Bulgaria said.

The government submitted two of the worst draft Budgets – for 2026 and 2027, and the reform plan turned out to be an unfulfilled promise, it said.

S&P forecasts a record budget deficit of 5.1 per cent of GDP in 2026. The current account deficit is expected to reach 8.7 per cent of GDP – the highest level in 18 years, the statement said.

“The economy is overheating, spending is growing, debt is increasing and we are losing competitiveness,” Democratic Bulgaria said.

When the 2026 Budget was being discussed, Democratic Bulgaria proposed a deficit of 3.9 billion euro instead of 7.3 billion euro (below three per cent of GDP), “but the majority rejected all 18 of our proposals”.

The statement said that S&P describes the measures to control the Budget deficit for 2027 as ineffective and explicitly points out the one-time tax on excess profits, from which the government expects 800 million euro.

“One-time revenues do not finance permanent expenses,” Democratic Bulgaria said.

“This is the problem that we at Democratic Bulgaria have been warning about for months. Radev’s fiscal policy is already weighing on the country’s creditworthiness and increasing the risk of recession and debt spiral in 2028,” it said.

The coalition said that Radev’s government has an independent parliamentary majority.

“No one is stopping it from carrying out the necessary reforms. Instead of explaining that everything is the opposition’s fault, the government should show which inefficient expenditures it will stop, how it will reform the administration and the Interior Ministry, and how it will create conditions for more investment, production, and exports.”

If budget problems are not brought under control, the agency warns that the next step could be a credit rating downgrade – something that has not happened since the bankruptcy of Corpbank in 2014, Democratic Bulgaria said.

The opposition coalition said that it is demanding a rewrite of the 2027 Budget with a deficit below three per cent of GDP in order to reduce the risk of losing growth and falling into recession.

World.title: Minors in Croatia Will Soon be Unable to Order Energy Drinks in Cafes
World.content:
November the 16th, 2026 – Minors in Croatia will soon be unable to order energy drinks in cafes after shops banned their sale to under 18s back in June.

Energy drinks have not been allowed to be sold to minors in shops since June this year, and a ban on serving them in hospitality establishments is provided for in the Hospitality Activity Act. Poslovni reports that the Ministry of Health has launched the procedure for adopting the Act on Restricting the Use of Energy Drinks and Products Similar to Energy Drinks by persons under the age of 18.

The aforementioned Hospitality Activity Act will go before Parliament for a second reading. The new law will thus form a joint package of measures for the protection of children’s health together with those rules.

“Energy drinks are not harmless, and their effects can be more pronounced in children and young people whose bodies are still developing. That is why with the law we are not stopping at warnings on the packaging, but are also taking into account the composition of the products and their effect on the child’s body. We protect children best through prevention, timely information and clear rules, and with this proposal we are turning those principles into concrete measures, from expert risk assessment to clearly established responsibility of everyone who places these products on the market. In this way the Government continues to strengthen the system of child protection, providing support to parents and creating a safer environment for growing up,” said Minister of Health Dr Irena Hrstić.

Caffeine, other stimulants and sugar, with which energy drinks abound, can negatively affect the heart and blood vessels, the nervous system and mental health, and children are exposed to a greater risk of such consequences than adults. Although drinks with a high caffeine content already carry a mandatory warning that they are not recommended for children, pregnant women or breastfeeding women, research by the Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ) shows widespread consumption among schoolchildren, and some of them drink 750 millilitres or more on a single occasion.

That is why the Ministry of Health is going a step further and giving a health foundation to the bans from the areas of trade and hospitality. According to the draft, an energy drink will be considered a drink with more than 150 milligrams of caffeine per litre, from any source, with products based on coffee, tea and cocoa being excluded. The law will ensure the implementation of these bans, and minors will not be able to buy products that by composition or physiological effect correspond to an energy drink or are comparable to it, regardless of the form in which they come on the market or are used.

Protection does not stop at the point of sale. Advertising of all these products will not be allowed to be aimed at a minor audience, and in schools and other institutions where children stay it will be completely banned, as will their display. Educational institutions will also receive an obligation to promote knowledge about the harmfulness of energy drinks and similar products as part of preventive programmes, and monitoring of the impact on health is also envisaged.

The key expert role will be played by the HZJZ. It will keep a register of products to which the law applies, and entry into it will be mandatory for everyone who places them on the market. The Institute will also assess how much these products endanger the health of persons under the age of 18 and determine which product is considered similar to an energy drink. On the basis of that assessment a temporary ban order may also be issued, which will enable a rapid response to new risks.

The Ministry has submitted the Form of Legislative Activities to the Government’s Office for Legislation with a view to including the new law in the List of Laws outside the Plan of Legislative Activities for 2026. Public consultation on the Form will be conducted on the e-Consultations portal, the text of the Draft Proposal of the Act will be published in the next phase, and submission to the Government procedure is planned by the end of this year

World.title: Will Croatia Finally Get a Break From Price Increases in 2027?
World.content:
November the 16th, 2026 – Will Croatia finally get a break from price increases and constant pressure on the public’s bank accounts and wallets in 2027? A slowdown is on the cards…

The finance minister also spoke about whether citizens can expect a better standard of living and what the Government’s offer is for increasing salaries in public and state services. Poslovni reports that price growth could weaken already in the first months of next year, but the realisation of the Government’s forecasts will largely depend on the movement of energy prices and the geopolitical situation.

Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Tomislav Ćorić expects that inflation in Croatia will begin to slow significantly already in the first quarter of 2027. Appearing on the central HTV News, he assessed that the economic projections for next year are optimistic, especially in comparison with expectations for the European Union and the Eurozone. According to the Government’s projections, inflation in 2027 should fall to 2.7 percent on an annual basis, while economic growth of 2.1 percent is expected.

when can we expect a price slowdown?

Ćorić believes that the beginning of the year should bring a weakening of inflationary pressures thanks to the gradual disappearance of base effects from previous price increases and the expected calming of oil prices. These are factors that should contribute to slower price growth, although this does not mean that products and services will necessarily become cheaper. The minister considers the greatest risk to the realisation of these expectations to be a possible deterioration of geopolitical circumstances, primarily the continued escalation of the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.

If there are no new disruptions on international markets, he believes that the planned economic indicators could be achieved.

will quality of life actually improve in 2027?

Asked whether he expects that the general public will live better in 2027 than currently, Ćorić replied that he hopes so and believes in it. He bases such expectations on the reduction of inflationary pressures, an increase in the standard of living and the continuation of economic growth. He also believes that the investments envisaged in the new state budget should further strengthen the resilience of the Croatian economy.

The minister also commented on the negotiations on salaries for employees in state and public services. For 2027, the Croatian Government has offered an increase in the base for calculating salaries of a total of 3.5 percent and the gradual introduction of a meal allowance, which would reach 50 euros per month by the end of the year. Ćorić considers this a realistic offer, aligned with the possibilities of the state budget.

An agreement has not yet been reached, however. The public service trade unions rejected the offered increase in the base and initiated a mediation procedure, while the state service trade unions still need to consider the offer in their bodies.

further spending on defence

Speaking about increased defence expenditure, Ćorić said that economic results enable higher budget revenues and expenditures, which is why it was not necessary to reduce funds for other sectors in order to finance security investments. Around 1.5 billion euros is envisaged for defence in the budget proposal for 2027, and the minister confirmed that spending should continue to grow due to the obligations Croatia has assumed within NATO.

At the same time, the Government plans to keep the general government deficit at the level of 2.9 percent of GDP and to continue reducing the share of public debt. Ćorić emphasised that stable public finances and the rise in Croatia’s credit rating enable more favourable borrowing conditions. As an indicator of citizens’ confidence in government securities, he singled out the latest issue of one-year treasury bills, in which the desired amount of one billion euros was reached after only five days. The minister also expects that a budget rebalancing could follow after the summer of 2027, but he does not foresee major changes compared to the current plans.

World.title: Seismic Stations Cover All of Croatia for the First Time
World.content:
November the 16th, 2026 – Seismic stations cover all of Croatia for the first time ever, with 125 stations currently measuring earthquakes, and a further 55 planned.

As part of the much wider EU CROSSNET project, Croatia has installed 125 seismic stations and plans another 55, which would bring the network to around 180 stations. Zrinka Gabelica Toplek reports for Poslovni that project leader Tomislav Fiket emphasised that for the first time, the entire country is now covered from Ilok all the way down to Cavtat. He did however duly warn that further implementation depends on the employment of nine young experts.

rapid warning systems

CROSSNET modernises and significantly expands the system for monitoring seismic activity in Croatia. A dense network of stations enables more precise determination of the location and magnitude of earthquakes, faster data processing and better information for the public and the competent services. At the conference “From the 1880 earthquake to the modern seismic network – how we monitor ground shaking today”, held to mark the 146th anniversary of the great Zagreb earthquake, Fiket said that the general public, wherever they live, should now be able to receive equally high-quality information.

“For the first time in history, all of Croatia has been successfully covered by seismic stations. It’s extremely important to us that every single person, wherever they live, has the opportunity to receive equally high-quality information,” Fiket emphasised. Earthquakes can’t be predicted, but rapid warning systems can react after the arrival of the first, non-destructive wave. A dense network of stations makes it possible to send a warning to citizens before the arrival of the destructive second wave, which can reduce the number of victims and the extent of damage. Data from the stations arrives at the central system in near real time, and people can also follow 24-hour records of the seismic stations and an interactive earthquake hazard map.

a 13.6 million euro project

The CROSSNET project is otherwise worth around 13.6 million euros. Of that, 75 percent is financed by the European Union through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), and 25 percent comes from the state budget itself. It was launched back in November 2021 and was supposed to finish at the end of June, but has been extended until the 31st of December 2026 because the employment of nine young experts participating in its implementation has not been secured.

The problem arose after the financing of the Seismological Service of the Republic of Croatia was transferred from the state budget to programme contracts of the Faculty of Science (PMF) at the end of last year. “Those nine jobs were missed in the negotiations and were not negotiated,” Fiket said, emphasising that the Faculty of Science was supposed to ensure the employment of these experts, but this has not been done so far.

World.title: Ryanair Set to Increase Number of Flights from Zagreb Airport
World.content:
November the 16th, 2026 – The hugely popular Ryanair is set to increase its number of flights from Zagreb Airport, with 14 flights per week on one of the most frequented routes.

The Irish low-cost airline Ryanair plans to increase the number of flights on a series of routes from Zagreb during the summer season of 2027, Ex-Yu Aviation News reports. Passengers travelling from Zagreb will therefore have more flights available to some of the most popular European destinations.

london, malta and palma de mallorca

Poslovni reports that the biggest changes concern the routes to London (Stansted Airport) and Malta, on which there will be two daily flights, meaning that Zagreb and London Stansted will be directly connected a whopping 14 times a week. The number of flights to Palma de Mallorca is also increasing, which will be connected to Zagreb every single day. There will be eight flights a week to Basel, and six flights a week to Dublin and Paris (Beauvais Airport). Five flights a week are planned for Cypriot Paphos, while Alicante, Corfu and Naples will each have four weekly flights.

a temporary suspension of zagreb-eindhoven flights

Ryanair will continue to fly during the summer season of 2027 on the new Zagreb – Warsaw (Modlin Airport) route, which began operating on the 26th of October this year. On the other hand, flights between Zagreb and the Dutch Eindhoven will be temporarily suspended from the 1st of February to the 19th of July 2027. The reason is extensive runway works and infrastructure modernisation at Eindhoven Airport. Flights on that route should resume on the 19th of July.

popular destinations among croatian travellers

Croats like to travel to neighbouring Italy, as well as to Spain and Greece, whether for a summer holiday, a short break or a weekend trip. That is why among the new reinforcements in Ryanair’s already packed Zagreb Airport schedule the flights to Naples, Mallorca, Alicante and Corfu could be particularly interesting going forward. Malta is also becoming increasingly popular among Croatian tourists, while London and Paris have been attractive for city breaks and shorter trips for very many years.

World.title: Croatia Clinch Third in Nations League Group and Pot 1 for Euro Qualifiers
World.content:
Croatia beat Czechia 2-1 at the Opus Arena in Osijek on Sunday night to finish third in League A Group 3 of the Nations League. The win secures a play-off to stay in the competition’s top tier and a place in Pot 1 for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw.

Croatia hosted the Czech Republic at Osijek’s Opus Arena on Sunday night in the sixth and final round of the Nations League group stage. The match was a fight for third place in the group, which brings a play-off to stay in the Nations League’s top tier and a place among the top seeds in qualifying for Euro 2028.

Lineups

Croatia: Livaković; Stanišić, Vušković, Ćaleta-Car, Gvardiol; Modrić, Kovačić; P. Sučić, Baturina, Perišić; Beljo

Czech Republic: Kinský; Coufal, Zima, Vlček, Sláma; Červ, Král; Hopi, Sadílek, Kabongo; Hložek

Croatia could not have asked for a better start. Inside two minutes, Kovačić carried the ball upfield and found Beljo, who skilfully held off the Czech defenders and laid the ball off to an unmarked Perišić. Back from suspension, he finished from the edge of the box for 1-0!

The first chance for the Czech Republic came in the 9th minute, when Coufal’s cross from the right found Hopi, who could not hit the target. The winger’s next effort a minute later was blocked. Croatia broke well in the 15th minute, moving the ball from Stanišić to Perišić, whose cross was blocked behind for a corner.

The visitors began to press high. In the 17th minute, Perišić chested a Král cross back to Livaković from inside the box, but Czechia won the ball back, and Hložek fired over from 18 meters. Ćaleta-Car dealt well with another play into the box three minutes later, as Croatia struggled to create anything more.

Perišić shot wide from distance in the 21st minute, and Modrić headed away another Král cross two minutes later. Croatia then began to string passes together, though one neat move ended with Petar Sučić penalized for a foul in attack as he tried to dribble past a defender.

In the 26th minute, Stanišić combined with Perišić and crossed from the right, and Zima almost turned it into his own net before the ball deflected off his head for a corner. Ćaleta-Car found space but could not convert his volley.

By the half-hour mark, Croatia were keeping the ball. Perišić went down in the box after a challenge from Sláma in the 29th minute, but the referee did not call a penalty.

Croatia should have doubled their lead in the 37th minute. Baturina won the ball in midfield and found Sučić, whose first pass for Perišić was cut out, but the ball came back to him, and he played it right to Beljo, whose shot from the top of the box was blocked.

An even better chance followed three minutes later. Modrić swung in a corner, Vušković headed it on to Beljo, unmarked, but the striker got in a tangle and could only poke a back-heel at Kinský. Gvardiol’s follow-up went straight at the goalkeeper.

Neither side made changes at the break. In the 47th minute, Perišić crossed from the right, and the ball struck Sláma’s hand, but it was not deemed a handball and Croatia were awarded a corner. A minute later, Baturina and Vušković headed the ball on to Beljo, who was in a good position but lost control and went down after a challenge with the Czech goalkeeper. The incident was briefly checked, but no penalty was given.

In the 50th minute, Croatia broke quickly, and Beljo laid the ball off for Sučić, who cut inside, beat his defender and fired from a tight angle into the side netting.

The Czechs responded in the 51st minute, when Hložek headed wide from a Coufal cross. Croatia then let another promising chance slip four minutes later, as Baturina found Beljo, whose poor first touch allowed Vlček to clear. In the 56th minute, Hložek intercepted a loose pass from Sučić intended for Kovačić, and Hopi shot off target.

Baturina worked space in a tight area in the 58th minute and shot from 18 meters, but Kinský saved comfortably. Croatia’s best chance of the half came in the 61st minute. Kovačić and Sučić exchanged a one-two that opened up the Czech defense, but Kovačić’s low shot went straight at Kinský.

Bilić then made a double change in the 63rd minute, bringing on Matanović and Marco Pašalić for Beljo and Kovačić. In the 67th minute, Gvardiol crossed from the left and the ball reached Baturina on the far side, but his shot was blocked by Prebsl.

Modrić tried his luck in the 70th minute with a low shot, but Kinský saved. In the 71st minute, Stanišić was booked after protesting a foul.

A minute later, Matanović brushed off a Czech defender, burst into the box and shot towards the near left corner, but Kinský saved again. Bilić then brought on Majer for Baturina in the 73rd minute. Croatia almost profited from a Czech error in the 75th minute, when Kinský came out of his area and lost the ball. Matanović carried it forward but could not get a shot away.



Croatia kept pressing for a second goal. In the 78th minute, Majer won the ball and fed Perišić, whose cross for Matanović was cut out by Prebsl. By now Czechia were barely in the game, but Croatia still could not find the goal to make it safe.

Modrić picked out Marco Pašalić with an excellent long ball in the 80th minute, but the winger went too early and was caught offside.

Then, out of nowhere, the Czech Republic equalized. In the 84th minute, Hložek shot from the top of the box, and the ball took a deflection off a Croatian player on its way past Livaković for 1-1.

Croatia’s answer came three minutes later. Vušković worked hard to get the ball to Majer on the left side of the box, cut inside slightly and finished to restore the lead at 2-1 in the 87th minute.

Croatia saw out the remaining minutes to win 2-1 and finish third in League A Group 3. The result secures a play-off to stay in the Nations League’s top tier and a place in Pot 1 for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw. The two worst third-placed and two best fourth-placed national teams from the top-tier Nations League groups will play against the four runners-up from League B. The first legs will be played from March 25-27, with the return legs from March 28-30.

World.title: The Place in Croatia Where a Doctor Once Prescribed Wine
World.content:
November the 14th, 2026 – There’s a beautiful house in Croatia that looks as if it’s rising from the sea, and the doctor who lived there used to prescribe both aristocrats and prisoners wine there.

The beautiful Brijuni islands are an unusual Istrian archipelago. They were once a favourite destination of European aristocracy and the place where Josip Broz Tito hosted statesmen from around the world. Ivana Vasarevic reports for Putni kofer that on Veliki Brijun specifically, right next to the harbour where tourist boats dock, there’s a particularly interesting building. It looks as if it is rising right out of the sea, it’s over 120 years old, and for decades a doctor lived there who took care of the health of the island’s guests. It’s known as the Boat House (Kuća za brodice) and it is at the heart of a story that takes us back to the era when the Brijuni islands were one of the most elegant resorts on the entire Adriatic coast.

THE ONLY COMPLETELY PRESERVED ART NOUVEAU BUILDING ON VELIKI BRIJUN

Johann SUHM

It all began back at the end of the 19th century, when the Austrian industrialist Paul Kupelwieser purchased Brijuni and decided to turn the area into a luxury tourist destination. That’s when the Boothaus, or Boat House, was also constructed. In 1901, Kupelwieser engaged the young Viennese architect Eduard Kramer, a pupil of the famous Otto Wagner, to design an apartment above the existing boat storage. The building was completed in 1902 and is considered the only completely preserved Art Nouveau building on Veliki Brijun. The ground floor of the House boasts four large arches facing the sea and once served for storing boats. Above it is the residential floor with a spacious balcony and an elegant wrought-iron railing, while on the land side a winding staircase leads to the former apartment. It is also worth noting that the attractive Boat House was the first building of civil purpose on the island built using reinforced concrete.

DOCTOR OTTO LENZ EVEN PRESCRIBED WINE WITH IRON TO HIS PATIENTS

From 1903 to 1938, it was the home and workplace of doctor Otto Lenz, who settled on Brijuni with his wife and son. His task was to take care of the health of the resort’s guests, and in the house he set up a surgery and a well-equipped pharmacy. He received patients every day from 10 to 12 o’clock. Among them were distinguished and wealthy visitors to Brijuni, but also convicts from the prison in Koper who worked on the construction of the island’s hotels.

In Lenz’s pharmacy one could obtain tonic syrups and preparations against headache, rheumatism, colds, fainting and seasickness, and the doctor also prescribed wine with iron to his patients! This preparation was used to stimulate the appetite, strengthen the nerves and improve the blood count. The original glass bottles for medicines, found during diving and cleaning of the Brijuni harbour, are today exhibited precisely in the Boat House.

THE LENZ COUPLE LEFT THE BRIJUNI ARCHIPELAGO IN 1938 AND MOVED TO OPATIJA

Thanks to the notes of the doctor’s wife Maria, who in 1956 handed over her memories to the archive of the Brijuni Administration, it was possible to reconstruct the former purpose of the rooms. Thus we know that their house had a kitchen, bedroom, salon, maid’s room and waiting room. Maria was a musician, so music was also an important part of the family’s everyday life. An interactive museum exhibition has been arranged in the house where you can listen to music from that time, and as you pass through the former kitchen, the sounds of dishes can be heard that evoke the everyday life of the Lenz family. The Boat House was their home for more than three decades. The couple eventually left the archipelago in 1938 and moved to Opatija on the mainland.
