World.title: What Can Croatia Do to Slow the Warming of the Adriatic Sea?
World.content:
November the 15th, 2026 – Croatia should be deeply concerned about the warming of the Adriatic Sea, but what can actually be done about it right now? Quite a lot, as it happens.

The Mediterranean is one of the world’s hot spots when it comes to damaging climate change, and the Adriatic in particular is among the seas where average and extreme surface temperatures are rising the fastest. Nenad Jaric Dauenhaur reports for Index that the surface of the world’s oceans has warmed by about 1 °C since the end of the 19th century. In the southern Adriatic specifically, the warming trend of the upper 20 metres of the sea has, in places, reached about 3 °C per century. The Adriatic is a semi-enclosed sea, and its shallow north is particularly sensitive to warming. But changes are also visible in the depths. A study published this autumn showed that the acceleration of warming of deep waters is particularly pronounced in the southern Adriatic.

The consequences are also felt on land, or in the air. The air in the Mediterranean has been warming faster than the global average since the 1980s. At the beginning of the 2020s the average air temperature in the region was about 1.5 °C higher than in the pre-industrial period. Heat waves are becoming more frequent and more intense, the risk of droughts and fires is rising, and extreme heat increases mortality, especially among the elderly. Droughts in turn reduce water reserves and threaten agriculture.

the limits of coastal protection

Nicolas Entrup, director of international relations at the organisation OceanCare, revealed that the coast can be protected from floods and sea-level rise, which is a matter of adaptation, but that such measures will not stop the main cause, which is warming. “We must do everything to limit its scale, and we can only do that if we reduce emissions faster,” he adds.

extensive economic damage

According to an estimate by the World Bank, damage from climate change in Croatia from 1980 to 2021 averaged around 0.7 percent of GDP annually, with tourism, agriculture and forestry being the most affected. Croatia, Entrup says, can introduce some measures immediately, and can achieve a greater effect if it manages to actually agree on some common rules with its neighbours. This is where OceanCare comes into the picture. OceanCare is a Swiss non-governmental organisation that deals with the protection of marine species, underwater noise, plastic pollution and the impact of fishing on the sea. It has special consultative status with the UN Economic and Social Council, is accredited for UN climate negotiations, and this year co-organised a discussion on the de-carbonisation of the Mediterranean in the European Parliament.

Mediterranean countries agreed in 2025 on a common framework for adaptation to climate change, but emissions in the region, according to OceanCare, continue to rise. Ahead of the UN climate conference COP31, which is being held from 9 to 20 November in Antalya, Turkey, the organisation called on them to draw up a joint emissions reduction plan within the framework of the Barcelona Convention. It would be the first such plan within any of the world’s conventions on regional seas.

According to an analysis by the Basque Centre for Climate Change prepared for OceanCare, if emissions remain at the current level, the Mediterranean will by 2035 already have exhausted its share of the remaining global carbon budget. That budget represents the total amount of CO₂ that the world can still emit while aiming to keep long-term global warming below 2 °C relative to the pre-industrial period. The analysis estimates that from 2030 to 2050 emissions should be reduced by around six percent per year. Earlier cuts would ease the pressure after 2030.

croatia will have the opportunity to make history in 2027, but will it take it?

OceanCare is calling for countries to start reducing emissions immediately, to stop exploration of new oil and gas deposits at sea, and to fairly share the remaining carbon budget. Entrup stresses that Turkey and the countries of North Africa must also participate in the agreement. He sees an opportunity at the meeting of the parties to the Barcelona Convention in Croatia in December 2027. “Croatia will then have the opportunity to make history,” he emphasises.

immediate measures that can be taken in croatia

One measure that states, according to Entrup, could introduce immediately is mandatory slowing of vessels. “Just like when you drive a car, the faster you go, the more fuel you use. When a ship sails more slowly, it emits fewer greenhouse gases and pollutants and creates less underwater noise. Slower sailing also reduces the risk of collisions with endangered whales. Even one or two knots less can significantly reduce emissions if the measure is applied to a large number of ships,” Entrup claims. Limits could differ according to vessel category, while common rules for the entire Mediterranean should ensure equal conditions for all shipowners.

Shipowners must also know which fuels they will be able to count on before investing millions in new ships. The International Maritime Organisation has set a goal of net-zero emissions around 2050, with intermediate targets for 2030 and 2040, but has postponed the adoption of concrete measures. “Nobody wants to risk such an investment if they do not know what conditions will apply in ten or fifteen years,” Entrup says. Among the countries that oppose a faster abandonment of fossil fuels, the USA, Russia and Iran particularly stand out.

are there any good examples?

Colder seas often abound in plankton and fish, especially where the mixing of water brings nutrients from the depths to the surface. Warmer seas can mean less fish and a different composition of catches, Entrup warns.

“Tropical species can displace native ones, and among the newcomers in the eastern Mediterranean there are also poisonous species. Intensive fishing further burdens the sea,” he warns. As an example of a measure that has proven useful, Entrup cites the Jabuka Pit between Croatia and Italy. There, in 2017, certain forms of fishing were restricted in order to allow the recovery of populations of hake, Norway lobster and other species.

“When you protect an area, the fish stocks can recover. Fishermen see that in their nets,” he says. OceanCare is calling for a ban on bottom trawling, starting with protected marine areas. Dragging heavy nets along the bottom damages habitats and consumes a lot of fuel, and the organisation also warns of the possible release of carbon from the sediment.

what could croatia do, and how can the eu remain competitive?

Entrup proposes that Croatia gradually phase out existing oil and gas exploitation at sea and stop issuing new permits. As examples of countries that have stopped new exploration he cites France, Portugal and Spain. OceanCare warns that seismic surveys, among other things, create strong underwater noise that can harm marine animals over a large area, because noise is transmitted more strongly through water than through air. Asked how the EU specifically can remain competitive while the USA wants to expand drilling and Russia relies significantly on energy exports, Entrup replies that it is precisely dependence on fossil fuel imports that endangers Europe and exposes it to price spikes. As examples he cites the Russian war against Ukraine and the war involving Iran. In the transition to sun and wind he sees an opportunity for greater energy security and new jobs.

renewable energy and the plague of data centres

In addition to investment in renewable sources, Entrup also advocates more efficient equipment and incentives for energy saving. “If production from renewable sources grows, but total consumption grows at the same rate, the share of renewables will not increase,” he says.

Asked about plans for a huge data centre in Topusko in Croatia, he said he does not know the details of the project, but that powering it with additional quantities of gas would be contrary to the energy transition. The cost of delaying emissions reductions is already visible, Entrup says, from summer fires in Spain, Greece and France to coastal damage and water shortages that affect agriculture. “We are already feeling the consequences now. What will it be like in ten years if warming continues? We need to act together, as neighbours. We are all in the same boat,” he concluded.

World.title: Austria Claims Croatian Police Beats Migrants
World.content:
November the 15th, 2026 – Austria has claimed that Croatian police have been beating migrants. Interior Minister Davor Božinović has since responded.

Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Davor Božinović stated that the Croatian police have no information that would confirm claims about the alleged beating of migrants by Croatian police officers. Index reports that he also said that they have not received any official information on the matter from the competent authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

“We learned about these allegations from the media and the police immediately took steps to check whether they have any information about this incident. We do not have such data, nor have we received any official notification from the Bosnian authorities, primarily the police, with whom we are in constant contact,” Božinović said.

constant migratory pressure

He emphasised that migratory pressures on the Croatian border have not stopped and that the police prevent an average of up to 90 people every day from attempting to enter Croatia illegally. In doing so, they act in accordance with national and international regulations.

“The Croatian police protect the Croatian and external border of the European Union 24 hours a day. The migratory wave has not subsided, and our police officers prevent illegal entries on a daily basis, while consistently respecting the law,” the minister stressed. Božinović also warned of the problem of violence among migrant groups in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He stated that the latest information they received from the Bosnian police related to armed criminal groups within the migrant population.

are there armed criminal groups among the migrants?

“The Croatian police have been warned about the possibility of them crossing onto our territory, which has not happened. The Bosnian police later found automatic weapons and pistols in their improvised shelters,” he said. He emphasised that there are known patterns of violence by criminal groups against migrants, but that these circumstances cannot automatically be linked to the specific case. “I am not claiming that this happened in this case because we do not yet have established facts. However, we know that such patterns of violence exist and that is why we are very carefully monitoring the security situation on the border,” he said.

Božinović stated that the Croatian police will continue to decisively combat migrant smuggling and protect the Croatian and external border of the European Union, while consistently respecting the law.

World.title: Photos: Truck crash jams outbound traffic on Tallinn's Tartu maantee
World.content:
A truck crashed into a lamppost on Tartu maantee and got stuck under an overpass Monday afternoon, disrupting outbound traffic at a busy Tallinn junction ahead of rush hour.

Two outbound lanes on Tartu maantee have been closed due to the crash, backing up traffic near Ülemiste, T1 and Sikupilli shopping malls, Ülemiste train station and Tallinn Airport.

Police received a report of a crash at around 2:30 p.m. on Monday.

Initial information suggests the truck and its trailer struck part of the overpass, bringing down an overhead road sign gantry onto the roadway.

The driver, a 37-year-old man, was sober and licensed to operate the vehicle. No one was injured in the crash.

Police at the scene have been redirecting traffic via Peterburi tee.

Traffic along and around Tartu maantee in Tallinn following a crash on Monday afternoon. November 16, 2026. Source: Waze/screenshot

World.title: Mayor: Narva fears humanitarian and economic consequences of the border closure
World.content:
Narva Mayor Jaan Toots (Center Party) says that if the Estonian-Russian border is completely closed, border controls should also be reinstated on the Latvian border.

He also calls on the government to allow humanitarian crossings for Estonian residents who still have relatives in Russia.

In an interview with ERR in Narva on Monday, Toots said he learned about the government's plans to completely close border crossings with Russia starting December 1 from the news. According to him, the interior minister had previously discussed possible border closure scenarios with him, but city authorities were not informed in advance about a specific decision.

Russian flag at Ivangorod Fortress, opposite of Narva at the Estonian-Russian border. Source: Sergei Stepanov/ERR

Toots has several concerns

Toots highlighted three main concerns related to the potential closure of the border.

The first concerns security. In the mayor's view, if the authorities consider the threat serious enough to close the border with Russia, they should also restore controls on the Estonian-Latvian border. He noted that recent incidents involving illegal border crossings were linked to people arriving from the Latvian side.

The second concern is humanitarian. Jaan Toots believes it is necessary to find a way to allow Estonian residents to travel to Russia when they need to visit elderly relatives, attend funerals, or deal with other urgent family matters.

The third concern is economic. According to the mayor, closing the border could further harm employment in Narva, since border guards and customs officers are mostly local residents. In addition, the city could lose some tourists from Finland, Latvia, and other countries who have used local hotels and restaurants.

Jaan Toots said he has already contacted the interior minister and intends to present his arguments to him. The issue was also discussed at the morning meeting of the leadership of the Center Party, where the mayor of Narva serves as a vice chairman.

Asked about the future of the project to build a shelter for people waiting at the border crossing, for which funding has been allocated in the city budget, Toots replied: "Everything is on hold now."

Urbo Vaarmann. Source: Sergei Stepanov/ERR

Vaarmann: Estonian state should support the affected region

Narva City Council Chairman Urbo Vaarmann said that if the border is closed, he expects the government to provide support to Narva residents and local businesses.

According to Vaarmann, Narva and the whole of Ida-Viru County must remain places where people feel confident visiting, living, and investing.

"The announcement of the border closure may cause visitors and investors to reconsider their plans. Therefore, the state must help maintain confidence in our region, support local businesses, and attract new investments," Vaarmann said.

The chairman of the Narva City Council stressed that the assessments of Estonia's security agencies must be taken seriously. At the same time, he noted that the state has a duty to protect people and prevent security threats, and that responsibility also includes having a concrete plan for supporting the region most directly affected by such decisions.

"Our people must feel that the state stands by them. That means a safe hometown, jobs, warm homes, and affordable utility bills," he added.

The Estonian government announced its intention to close all border crossing points with Russia from December 1 following the attempted arson attack on defense company Threod Systems in Viimsi on November 14. According to the Internal Security Service (ISS), the attack was organized at the direction of Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU. Eight Latvian residents were detained on suspicion of involvement in preparing the attack.

World.title: Professor: New power generation should accompany data center construction
World.content:
Large data centers planned for Estonia could end up consuming a significant share of the country's electricity, says Mart Landsberg, a professor at Tallinn University of Technology. The most important question is how much added value can be created with that energy.

Professor Landsberg pointed to two data centers planned in Estonia, one near Tallinn in Hüüru and another in Risti. Both are designed to have a capacity of roughly 200 megawatts.

For comparison, Estonia's peak electricity demand during this past winter's highest-demand hour was about 1,700 megawatts. A single 200-megawatt data center would therefore account for more than 10 percent of that figure. In terms of annual electricity consumption, such a facility could use approximately 1.3 to 1.6 terawatt-hours of electricity, equivalent to roughly 20-25 percent of Estonia's annual electricity consumption.

"What matters about energy is not where it comes from or how much it costs. What matters is how much added value we can create with that energy," Landsberg said.

According to him, even cheap and clean energy may bring limited benefits to society if it is used for low-value-added activities. Conversely, more expensive energy can make economic sense if it generates sufficient wealth and raises people's incomes.

Landsberg said data centers differ from many current industrial and household consumers because their electricity consumption does not depend as heavily on whether conditions are warm or cold. As a result, they can be valuable customers for the electricity system because their demand is more stable.

At the same time, he noted that a growing share of electricity system costs consists of fixed costs, while the cost of the electricity itself, such as the wholesale market price, makes up an increasingly smaller share of total expenses.

Eestisse rajatava AI-tehase Nebius andmekeskus. Autor/allikas: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"Energy itself no longer costs very much, but capacity and access to energy are worth their weight in gold," Landsberg said.

The problem, according to Landsberg, is that electricity consumption among households and commercial customers in Estonia is growing while industrial electricity consumption is declining. This means there are fewer consumers helping to share fixed network costs, potentially shifting a larger burden onto households and businesses.

For that reason, he said the impact of data centers on electricity costs for Estonian consumers cannot be viewed as purely positive or negative. The overall cost of energy supply must be considered, along with the broader economic benefits data centers bring to society.

Important factors include the jobs created, tax revenue generated and the extent to which data centers use goods and services produced in Estonia. Landsberg cited local industry as an example of a sector that could benefit from new opportunities created by data center development. In his view, the presence of local data centers could also support product development by speeding up innovation processes and creating competitive advantages for companies.

Data center connection requests exceed Estonia's current electricity demand

Asked whether Estonia's electricity system is prepared for the addition of several large data centers, Landsberg said everything depends on how quickly and on what scale those projects are implemented.

He referred to data from Elering showing that Estonia's current peak demand is around 1,700 megawatts, while connection requests from data centers and other large consumers total approximately 3,000 megawatts.

If all of those projects were realized simultaneously, the resulting change would be enormous and could not immediately be accommodated by the existing electricity system. However, connection requests do not automatically translate into completed projects. Landsberg cited Finland as an example where, according to him, there are far more interested developers than signed connection agreements.

In addition, data centers are typically built in phases rather than all at once. One module is completed first, followed by the next. For that reason, development of the electricity system and the regulatory environment must keep pace with project development.

Landsberg argued that investments in electricity networks required for data center projects should not be borne solely by other electricity consumers. Data centers themselves should shoulder a larger share of those costs.

New power generation should accompany data center development

One of the biggest questions, Landsberg said, is how to avoid a situation in which new data centers push up electricity market prices by introducing major new demand that competes for existing generation capacity.

That effect could be reduced by requiring data center developers to ensure additional electricity generation capacity alongside their projects. This could take the form of building their own power plants or entering into long-term agreements that support the development of new generating capacity.

Landsberg pointed to a regulatory change currently being discussed in the Finnish parliament that would require data centers seeking grid connections to ensure additional electricity generation capacity on a long-term basis.

"If done intelligently, data centers could certainly help drive the construction of new power plants," he said.

In his view, it is not enough to rely on market forces alone and assume new generating capacity will automatically appear in response to increased demand. Appropriate mechanisms need to be designed in advance.

"Landsberg estimated that the average lifespan of computing equipment may be around five years or slightly longer."

As one example, he highlighted plans for the Risti data center, where the project is being developed alongside solar and wind generation as well as battery storage. Power purchase agreements and other obligations may also form part of the solution.

According to Landsberg, the goal should be to ensure that existing electricity consumers benefit rather than lose out from the arrival of data centers.

He also noted that the investment horizons of data centers and power plants differ significantly. Power plants are long-term investments. Wind farms typically have a lifespan of around 20 years, while nuclear power plants can operate for about 60 years.

Data centers, by contrast, have shorter investment cycles because the computers they use require relatively frequent replacement. Landsberg estimated that the average lifespan of computing equipment may be around five years or slightly longer.

This means that if energy costs rise significantly, a data center could relatively easily decide to relocate elsewhere. If the project also includes investments in power generation or energy infrastructure, however, lasting value remains in Estonia even if the data center eventually leaves.

Data centers require a continuous electricity supply, which means their operations cannot rely directly on the variable generation of wind and solar energy. According to Landsberg, one solution is battery storage, which can store energy from wind and solar power and release it when data centers need it. Batteries can help manage fluctuations within and between days.

The unresolved issue remains seasonal fluctuations. Estonia receives little sunlight during winter, raising the question of how electricity generated from solar energy in summer can be stored for winter use.

"At the moment, we do not have a better solution than fossil-fuel power plants, such as gas-fired plants, which can cover the shortfall during winter peak demand periods," Landsberg said.

Over the longer term, he sees an important role for hydrogen, both in hydrogen production and in converting hydrogen back into electricity.

Landsberg said Estonia's strengths include favorable offshore wind conditions and a relatively cool climate that provides efficient cooling conditions for data centers. Combined with hydrogen technology, these advantages could form one of Estonia's future growth engines.

Greenergy data center in Hüüru, Harju County in northern Estonia. Source: Tõnu Tunnel/Greenergy

Waste heat use depends on nearby demand

Data centers also produce waste heat that can potentially be reused. According to Landsberg, successful utilization depends largely on whether a sufficiently large heat consumer is located nearby.

He compared two planned Estonian projects: the data center in Hüüru and the planned facility in Risti. Because of its proximity to Tallinn, it will likely be easier to find a major heat user for the Hüüru project.

At the same time, utilizing waste heat requires additional investment, creates additional risk and lengthens project timelines for developers. This can increase costs and delay completion.

As a result, developers must determine whether potential revenues from selling waste heat outweigh the added costs and risks.

Landsberg said that while waste heat utilization may make perfect sense from society's perspective, what is optimal for society is not necessarily optimal for developers. In his view, the state can help by designing a regulatory framework that ultimately delivers the most cost-effective outcome for consumers.

Estonia must learn to capitalize on the electric age

More broadly, Landsberg argued that the world has entered the electric age.

According to him, the International Energy Agency has highlighted the growing shift toward electricity as the dominant form of energy consumption. In the coming decades, key technologies will increasingly be those powered by or connected to electricity.

Estonia's challenge, he said, is determining how to extract as much economic benefit as possible from this transformation. If the country fails to keep up, it may find itself among the losers. If it uses new opportunities wisely, however, it can increase both national and societal prosperity.

Landsberg compared current technological developments to the Industrial Revolution.

"If the first Industrial Revolution centered on transferring physical labor to machines, then the next Industrial Revolution now underway is about transferring intellectual labor to machines. The question for us is whether we want to be among the winners or the losers in this revolution. Energy exists to do work on behalf of people," Landsberg said.

World.title: Foreign Ministry summons Russian chargé d'affaires
World.content:
Estonia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has summoned Russia's chargé d'affaires to express its strong condemnation of the attempted arson attack carried out against defense industry company Threod Systems on Saturday night.

According to the Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS), the act of sabotage was ordered by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said that Vladimir Putin has failed to achieve his objectives in the war of aggression against Ukraine and is now increasingly seeking to sow uncertainty among Ukraine's allies.

"Through various acts of sabotage, Russia aims to spread fear, divide our societies, and distract attention from supporting Ukraine," Tsahkna said.

"Estonia is, however, a difficult target for this type of inluence activity. We have many years of experience in detecting and preventing Russian sabotage, businesses are aware of the risks, and authorities act swiftly and decisively. The saboteurs who targeted Threod Systems have been detained and the threat has been eliminated," the foreign minister added.

According to Tsahkna, Russia's hostile actions come at a cost.

"We are preparing to close all road border crossing points between Estonia and Russia to vehicles and pedestrians starting on December 1. Together with our allies and partners, we will continue exposing and countering Russian influence activities. Nor will our pressure on the aggressor diminish. Just today, the European Union added 150 individuals and entities to its sanctions list. We will continue working to strengthen sanctions, tighten visa restrictions, and increase support for Ukraine, especially ahead of the coming winter," Tsahkna said.

Representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs also strongly condemned Russia's large-scale drone and missile attacks against Ukraine in recent weeks.

Over the past week alone, Russia has launched more than 2,300 drones at Ukraine.

The primary targets of these attacks have been civilian infrastructure, including critical infrastructure, hospitals, educational institutions, shopping centers, residential buildings, warehouses, and ports. During the past week alone, 55 people have been killed and 371 injured.

World.title: Auditor general: Pension hikes won't hinge on state budget being passed
World.content:
Pensions in Estonia will rise next year even if the Riigikogu fails to pass the 2027 state budget in December, says Auditor General Janar Holm.

Holm rejected claims by governing politicians that pensions and pay raises for senior public officials would be jeopardized if the budget is not approved.

Speaking on Vikerraadio's "Uudis+" on Monday, Holm explained that pensions are indexed each year on April 1 under the State Pension Insurance Act, making the annual increase a legal obligation independent of the state budget.

"To the best of my understanding, the pension amount does not depend on whether the state budget is adopted," he said.

The same applies to pay increases for senior public officials because those are also required by law. However, planned raises for teachers could be affected, as they are not statutory obligations and cannot be distributed without an approved budget.

"But as far as pensions are concerned, based on my understanding, I'd say that pensions are clearly a statutory expense and do not hinge on the passage of next year's state budget," Holm reiterated.

State won't grind to a halt

Holm explained that if the Riigikogu doesn't pass the 2027 budget, the Estonian government will have to use the previous year's budget as its basis, checking whether each expense was included and limiting monthly spending on it to one-twelfth of the amount allocated for that purpose in the previous year's budget.

He said that could affect investments, while new spending not included in the previous year's budget would not be able to go ahead until the new budget is approved.

If the budget bill allocates less for a particular expense than the previous year's budget, he added, spending must also stay within the lower proposed amount.

"The budget should still be passed, as the state operates on the basis of that budget," the auditor general said, but emphasized that the country will not grind to a halt if the Riigikogu doesn't pass it in time.

The Constitution and other laws, he noted, provide various mechanisms for handling such situations.

World.title: Saaremaa shipyard to launch largest Estonian-built warship
World.content:
An experimental 45-meter military vessel will be launched at the Baltic Workboats shipyard on Saaremaa on November 18.

EUROGUARD will be the largest military vessel built in Estonia since the restoration of independence. The project is led by Estonia and involves ten European countries and 27 industrial partners, said Ahto Pärl, member of the management board of Baltic Workboats AS.

Its total budget is €95 million, with €65 million provided by the European Defense Fund.

The ship has been developed as an experimental platform for the next generation of European naval vessels. The design includes capabilities for autonomous navigation and remote operation from shore.

The vessel is intended for maritime surveillance, mine countermeasure operations, protection of critical infrastructure, and search-and-rescue missions. It is designed to travel at a speed of at least 20 knots, has a range of at least 2,000 nautical miles, and can remain at sea for up to 10 days.

World.title: Kaspar Viilup: Pop culture wave of "GTA VI" will be felt for a long time
World.content:
The new "Grand Theft Auto" video game, more than a decade in the making, is just days away, and while the Estonian media still struggles to cover gaming as thoroughly as it should, the impact of this pop culture tidal wave can hardly be overstated, Kaspar Viilup writes.

If we try to briefly explain the phenomenon behind this video game, the most important foundation is its long history. Just like "Super Mario" or the legendary fighting games "Tekken" and "Mortal Kombat," "Grand Theft Auto," which first appeared nearly 30 years ago, has been a part of several generations' childhoods. Fathers have introduced the game to their sons and those same sons may now have children of their own, opening the door for them to this vast criminal underworld where players are given free rein to decide what kind of experience they want to have.

So at this point, we're not simply talking about a single game, but decades of expectations and experiences, nostalgia and anticipation, built up layer by layer. Add to that the fact that fans have had to wait more than a decade for a new installment and the fire has been continually fueled. Developer Rockstar Games is well aware of this, too, because although previous installments have also been massive undertakings, the scale is now on an entirely different level: Analysts estimate that the game's budget could reach $1.5 billion, while first-week sales revenue could climb as high as $5 billion. Yes, I know those numbers sound completely unrealistic, but that's precisely the kind of absurd, mind-boggling scale this game operates on.

Another key to understanding "Grand Theft Auto" is its lack of boundaries: Almost everything you can do in the game is either irrational or illegal, from stealing cars and recklessly speeding through the streets to engaging in mindless violence. While it's also possible to follow the game's storyline, my experience, and probably that of many others, has always been about seemingly aimless wandering. I vividly remember, for example, that my first encounter with country music as a teenager came while driving an SUV along rural roads in "Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas," with Hank Williams playing on the car radio. Once you've had a taste of that kind of escapism, you want to experience it again.

In other words, excitement over what this new release will bring has reached fever pitch and there's even widespread talk that when the game comes out, many people around the world will suddenly fall ill and fail to show up for work. In Estonia, however, the biggest challenge will be how the media manages to cover it all. Although "Disco Elysium" provided an initial trial by fire for more conservative publications that would otherwise run in the opposite direction at the mere mention of video games, its impact wasn't particularly long-lasting. When ZA/UM studio's new game "Zero Parades" was announced, everything had been forgotten and the silence in the Estonian media was deafening.

So I'll proudly get the ball rolling: Don't be afraid to talk about "Grand Theft Auto." It's perfectly fine to risk looking foolish and ask people who know more about it for help, because chances are there are at least a handful of people among your friends or even family members who will spend the coming days and weeks glued to their television screens, eyes darting back and forth. Even the major Hollywood studios know this, having pushed their biggest movie releases as far away from the "GTA" launch as possible, with the new "Hunger Games" movie the only one brave enough to remain. We'll see how these two giants fare against each other, but I can predict the outcome with considerable confidence: "Grand Theft Auto VI" will emerge victorious and we'll still be feeling its ripple effects at the end of this year and into the beginning of next year, perhaps even longer.

World.title: Kaja Kallas' role in Ukraine peace talks unclear
World.content:
Responding to an ERR question about her inclusion in Europe's negotiating team, Kaja Kallas said the decision was up to European Union leaders and that she would continue working on the substantive issues in the negotiations regardless.

Last week, European Union leaders agreed that Europe would be represented in Ukraine peace talks by the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and EU institutions. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the institutions would be represented by European Council President António Costa and either Ursula von der Leyen or Kaja Kallas from the European Commission.

I was a little unclear about the new agreement, specifically who will speak on behalf of the European Union and represent Europe. Will it be António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen, or will you also be involved?

It was the leaders' wish that António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen would be the ones involved, alongside the five countries.

After all, I meet with foreign ministers every month. I have the European External Action Service, which has experts on Russia and previous agreements. That expertise is also needed in these negotiations. So we are working on the substance, even if the format was decided on Friday.

Still, you have been very outspoken on Russia. Should we now be concerned that the European Union is unwilling to speak as clearly on these issues as you have? Is the European Union reluctant to choose the people who would present its positions in the clearest possible terms?

The European Union consists of 27 member states and representatives of those 27 member states, all of whom come from democracies, so to speak. That is why I think the work you do in the media is also very important — asking those negotiators questions at every opportunity. Of course, we do the same.

For example, when Russia has put forward various demands, have you asked for anything in return? If someone comes along saying sanctions must be eased, which is obviously in Russia's interest, what do we get in return?

Right now, we see that Russia has presented its maximalist demands, some of which are completely absurd. Together with the foreign ministers, we have prepared Europe's maximalist demands. Yes, you could say that some of those are also absurd, but they actually reflect two things.

First, they reflect the fact that Russia is the aggressor in this conflict. They also reflect the pressure being placed on Ukraine, for example, when it comes to limiting the size of its military. The problem, after all, is the size of Russia's military, not Ukraine's. We are trying to keep the focus on these substantive issues and we hope the free media will do the same.

A quick question about Estonia as well: There was an attempted arson attack on a building belonging to defense industry company Threod over the weekend. What is the European Union doing to support Estonia in this situation?

We will, of course, discuss all these hybrid attacks today. I also feel that the word "hybrid" is far too mild and that we should actually describe these attacks more specifically for what they are. Naturally, we will also propose various sanctions in response.

World.title: Saudi Arabia promotes cooperation as key to growth of the Paralympic Movement
World.content:
RIYADH: Cooperation is the key to the development of Paralympic sports, the head of the Saudi Olympic and Paralympic Committee said after attending the 2026 International Paralympic Committee Membership Gathering in Berlin.

The three-day event, which took place just weeks after Team Saudi’s record-setting showing at the Asian Para Games in Japan last month, brought together national Paralympic committees, international federations, regional organizations and Paralympic leaders from around the world under the theme “Coming Together: A Call to Action.”

The Saudi delegation was led by the CEO and secretary-general of the Olympic and Paralympic Committee, Abdulaziz Baeshen, and included the Paralympic affairs advisor, Fahad Al-Qabaa, and Paralympic equestrian athlete Ahmed Al-Sharbatly.

Panels and workshops during the event, which concluded on Nov. 9, focused on the International Paralympic Committee’s strategic plan for 2027-2030 and cooperation between member organizations. Delegates also discussed governance, funding and support mechanisms, the latest developments in sport classification, and preparations for 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles. Other topics included ways to expand opportunities for participation among persons with disabilities, and the development of technical and administrative capabilities.

Baeshen said international partnerships were central to Paralympic development: “The continued growth of the Paralympic Movement relies on strong partnerships and knowledge exchange.

“Building on Saudi Arabia’s progress in developing Paralympic sport, we remain committed to sharing our experiences and learning from others to further develop Paralympic sport in the Kingdom and contribute to the continued advancement of the movement worldwide, while creating greater opportunities for athletes.”

This progress in the development of Paralympic sport can be seen in the growing successes of Saudi athletes since the Kingdom integrated the administration of Olympic and Paralympic sports under a single organization in 2021 to ensure equal attention and support.

Most recently, Team Saudi fielded 41 athletes in eight sports at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games in October, who came home with 17 medals, including eight golds, nearly twice as many as the nine won in Hangzhou in 2022.

World.title: Children’s book fair in Homs promotes reading, nurtures young talent
World.content:
HOMS: The Homs Culture Directorate launched its children’s book fair on Sunday, offering young visitors a range of books, interactive activities and creative workshops to encourage reading and develop literary talents.

The fair, organized to mark World Children’s Day and Book Week, runs to Nov. 19. It features educational and entertaining books and stories, and learning materials and competitions designed to encourage children to read and explore their interests.

Farah Alfa, head of the directorate’s children’s section, said the event brings together storybooks and educational materials, alongside interactive workshops and competitions. Awards are to be given for the best original story and the best story cover design at the fair, she said.

Alfa said the main aim was to encourage children to turn to books instead of smartphones to help raise a generation of readers.

Rana Jabr, coordinator of the Arab Reading Challenge in Homs, said the body’s corner at the fair provided a five-day program introducing children to the competition; reading and discussing books; holding debates among participants; and sharing messages of encouragement.

The corner features a Reading Challenge Tree, where visitors can write down the titles of books they have read and the knowledge or lessons they gained from them.

Jabr said the event also provided an opportunity to meet parents and explain the importance of reading, while encouraging them to buy books for their children.

Young visitor Zainab Al-Kurdi said she was delighted by the fair, particularly the children’s corner where stories and games caught her attention and introduced her to new books and novels.

The mother of Shaghaf Mualla, who is taking part in this year’s reading challenge, said the fair offered a wide selection of scientific and cultural books that helped broaden children’s knowledge. She added that her daughter had already benefited from the books on display.

The opening day featured the launch of a five-day short-story-writing workshop led by writer and activist Firas Al-Najjar and aimed at children aged 7 to 14. The workshop looked to develop their writing, expression and independent-thinking skills.

Al-Najjar said the sessions sought to nurture children’s literary potential and develop their appreciation of beauty. He stressed the importance of cooperation among cultural, educational and social institutions to help restore children’s creative spirit, particularly in a society emerging from a devastating war.

He called for more courses and programs to encourage young people to write and think freely, adding that the Syrian Arab Republic had a long tradition of creativity and its children should have opportunities to express themselves.

Children’s book fairs across Syria bring books closer to younger generations by combining reading with interactive and creative activities, helping to make books a regular part of children’s lives.

World.title: Syria’s peanut growers hit by declining yields, rising production costs
World.content:
DAMASCUS: Syria’s peanut production this season is expected to reach 17,970 tonnes from 6,256 hectares, according to the Agriculture Ministry.

The Al-Ghab region in Hama accounts for the largest share of cultivated land. However, declining yields, rising production costs and a shortage of specialized harvesting equipment continue to hamper the sector’s development and its potential to become a strategic agricultural commodity.

Peanuts improve soil fertility through nitrogen fixation, supply raw materials for food industries and provide livestock feed. Expanding cultivation and processing could also create opportunities for small businesses, generate higher value products and improve farmers’ returns.

Ali Youssef Diab, supervisor of the peanut group within the Family Projects Group, said that cultivation began with selecting healthy seeds and keeping them in their shells until planting.

Farmers prepare the land through plowing, soil conditioning and fertilization. The optimal planting period extends from early April to May 10, after the risk of spring frost has passed. Planting in March could weaken germination, Diab said.

The crop requires temperatures of 20-25 degrees Celsius during germination and flowering, along with adequate moisture and warm soil.

In coastal areas, peanuts can also be grown as a second-season crop after the wheat and barley harvest in late June and early July, although yields are lower than during the main season.

The crop’s yellow flowers develop above ground before slender stems extend into the soil, where the pods and seeds form. Proper harvesting and drying are essential to quality.

Farmers examine field samples to ensure the pods have matured and the seeds have turned brown.

Kazem Ali, a peanut grower in Al-Ghab, said that farmers relied mainly on rainfall during the main growing season, supplementing it with groundwater when necessary.

After harvesting, traders purchase the crop directly from farmers’ homes or storage facilities before transporting it to shelling facilities for sorting and processing.

Diab said that three main peanut varieties were traded in the Syrian Arab Republic: the Turkish variety, known as Virginia, which produces large, elongated pods, the local variety, characterized by smaller pods and thinner shells, and improved varieties, including Al-Sahel and Giza, imported from Egypt.

The improved varieties offer higher yields and more uniform seed sizes, making them suitable for mechanical shelling and the production of peanut butter and halva.

Peanuts are used in roasted snacks, confectionery, chocolate, halva, nougat and peanut butter. Their seeds contain 45-50 percent oil, which can be extracted for vegetable oil production.

The resulting press cake can be used in animal feed. The foliage provides feed for cattle and sheep, while outer shells can serve as heating fuel and plant residues can be converted into organic fertilizer.

Despite these applications, the shortage of specialized processing facilities limits demand and the development of additional uses. Local consumption remains largely concentrated on peanuts sold for direct consumption or roasting.

Production expenses include land preparation, seeds, fertilizers, fuel, pesticides, harvesting and crop protection.

Farmers also face water shortages and drought, while the lack of specialized mechanical harvesting equipment increases costs.

Regular field monitoring is necessary to control pests and diseases, including stem rot, worms and red spider mites. Other threats identified by the Agriculture Ministry include green caterpillars and powdery mildew.

Harvesting presents additional difficulties because peanuts must be dried under sunlight, making autumn weather an important factor in crop quality and safety.

Diab said that yields before 2000 ranged from 500 to 700 kg per dunam (1,000 sq. meters), encouraging farmers to expand cultivation. In some areas, peanuts replaced cotton and sugar beet.

But average yields had since fallen to about 300-400 kg per dunam, he said.

Ali reported a similar decline. His production has fallen from about 600-700 kg per dunam five years ago to about 250 kg this season.

Despite lower productivity, farmers continue cultivating peanuts because traders buy the harvest directly at production sites and pay in cash.

However, growers can face pressure to accept lower prices to cover seasonal expenses.

The Al-Ghab Plain in western Syria is the country’s main peanut-growing area, accounting for about 40 percent of cultivated land, while Idlib accounts for 18 percent, according to Agriculture Ministry figures published in October.

The ministry said that the area planted with peanuts had remained almost unchanged from the previous season.

Maher Al-Dajj, the ministry’s director of plant production, said yields could reach 3-4 tonnes per dunam under favorable conditions and increase further with improved agricultural services and crop management.

This potential yield estimate differs from the actual yields reported by Diab and Ali, reflecting the distinction between favorable growing conditions and production achieved in the fields.

Marketing difficulties also constrain the sector. Traders’ influence over prices, fluctuating market conditions and a shortage of reliable sales outlets leave farmers exposed to changes in supply and demand, creating uncertainty over their returns.

Agricultural extension units monitor fields from planting through harvesting and provide technical advice on crop management, according to the ministry.

Agricultural development expert Akram Afif said that expanding peanut processing could create opportunities for small and family-run food businesses, generate higher value products and provide employment.

But high production costs, difficulties securing financing, fluctuating selling prices and traders’ influence over prices continued to constrain farmers’ returns and their ability to maintain or expand cultivation, he said.

Using crop residues to feed cattle, sheep and goats would help integrate peanut cultivation into a broader agricultural and food production chain, he said.

Diab said that bacterial nodules on peanut roots fixed atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility and benefiting subsequent crops, including wheat and winter vegetables.

Developing the sector required improved agricultural services, better access to irrigation, reliable supplies of production inputs and specialized machinery for harvesting, sorting and drying peanuts, he said.

Establishing food-processing and oil-extraction facilities would also reduce reliance on selling raw produce, increase its added value and improve farmers’ economic returns, he said.

World.title: DP World ILT20 wildcard picks add star quality to Season 5
World.content:
DUBAI: The six DP World International League T20 franchises have named their wildcard picks for Season 5, adding even more firepower to squads that already feature some of the biggest names in T20 cricket.

Abu Dhabi Knight Riders have brought back Andre Russell, Desert Vipers have signed Tom Curran, Dubai Capitals have added Sam Billings, Gulf Giants have picked Akeal Hosein, MI Emirates have named Kieron Pollard and Sharjah Warriorz have signed Tim Seifert.

The wildcard picks give each franchise a boost before the season gets underway, with Desert Vipers taking on MI Emirates in the opening match in Dubai on Saturday, Nov. 21.

West Indies all-rounder Russell has played only for the Knight Riders in the DP World ILT20 (38 appearances). He made history in Season 4, when his 500th T20 wicket, against Desert Vipers, made him the first player to reach 5,000 runs, 500 wickets and 500 sixes in the format.

England all-rounder Curran is a familiar face at the Vipers, now the defending champions. He played for the franchise in the inaugural season of the league, when they reached the final. Curran also featured for the Gulf Giants in Season 2 of the competition. Across both seasons, he has 14 wickets and 307 runs in 16 appearances.

England wicketkeeper-batter Billings captained Dubai Capitals to their maiden DP World ILT20 title in Season 3. He played in the final in each of the league’s first three seasons, first with Desert Vipers in Season 1 and then as Dubai Capitals captain in Seasons 2 and 3, and will captain the franchise again this season. The 35-year-old averages 30.9 with 649 runs in 29 appearances in the league.

West Indies left-arm spinner Hosein has taken 21 wickets in 29 DP World ILT20 appearances for Abu Dhabi Knight Riders and MI Emirates (two seasons), with best figures of 4/23. He will spearhead a strong Carribean bowling attack at the Giants, comprising Alzarri Joseph, Shamar Joseph and Alick Athanaze.

World.title: Saudi Arabia’s Fatima Al-Ammari to face Lebanon’s Anna Wakim at PFL MENA 12
World.content:
RIYADH: Saudi Arabian MMA fighter Fatima Al-Ammari returns to the cage to face off against Lebanon’s Anna Wakim on Friday, Dec. 11, as part of the PFL MENA 12, as reported by Asharq Al-Awsat.

The event will be hosted by Dhahran Expo in Alkhobar, bringing together two champions with a background in Thai boxing.

The Professional Fighters League announced that the fight would be held as part of the women’s amateur fights at a weight division of 139 pounds (63 kg); Al-Ammari enters the fight looking for a second victory after securing her first on debut in the PFL.

The Saudi fighter has a record of four Saudi championship titles in Muay Thai and also in boxing, an experience she seeks to bring into the cage in Alkhobar.

In contrast, Wakim will be having her first experience in mixed martial arts, relying on her background as a Lebanese champion in Muay Thai and Wushu Sanda to begin a new phase in her career.

The shared combat background of the two fighters gives the confrontation a unique character, with Al-Ammari looking to continue her winning streak and Wakim seeking a successful debut.

World.title: Syrian authorities reopen 841 km of roads in war-hit Aleppo
World.content:
LONDON: Authorities in the Syrian Arab Republic have reopened 841 km of roads and removed barriers and trenches across areas of Aleppo’s countryside that were affected by civil war.

The work was carried out as part of the Echo of Resilience 2 project, which encompasses 255 cities, towns and villages and aims to restore access to farmland and revive economic activity, the Syrian Arab News Agency reported.

Aleppo and its surrounding countryside were the scenes of brutal fighting between armed rebels and forces loyal to the Bashar Assad regime during the conflict that ran from 2011 to 2024.

The region is crossed by the M4, running east and west, and M5, north and south, motorways.

Farmers have welcomed the removal of wartime barriers and reopening of roads, giving them easier access to their land after years of restrictions and lengthy detours.

Khaled Ali al-Hassan said that before the routes were reopened he had to take a detour of more than 6 km to reach his fields.

Teams from the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management and Ministry of Defense are involved in the Echo of Resilience 2 project.

The latest areas to be cleared include the town of Manbij and Shijraz village, north of Azaz town.

World.title: Saudi FM discusses regional developments with Qatari, Egyptian counterparts
World.content:
RIYADH: Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan held separate phone calls with his Qatari and Egyptian counterparts on Monday, the Saudi Press Agency reported.



Prince Faisal and Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani discussed current regional developments and efforts aimed at de-escalation and maintaining security and stability in the region.



The Kingdom’s foreign minister and Badr Abdelatty reviewed Saudi-Egyptian relations and explored ways to strengthen and develop them across various fields.



They also discussed current regional developments, emphasizing the importance of continued coordination and consultation, and supporting diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalation.

World.title: iMENA completes $214m capital increase to fuel regional expansion
World.content:
JEDDAH: Saudi Arabia-based technology group iMENA has completed a capital increase of SR802 million ($214 million) to support its next phase of growth in the Kingdom and other Middle Eastern and North African markets.

The announcement was made during the Digital Entrepreneurship Majlis, held under the patronage of Minister of Communications and Information Technology Abdullah Al-Swaha and Minister of Investment Fahad Al-Saif.

Growth strategy

Completed in two tranches, the capital increase will strengthen the group’s financial position and support investments in Saudi Arabia, while enabling the expansion of its digital platforms and operations across the region.

iMENA Chairman Nasir Al-Sharif described the capital increase as a milestone in the group’s efforts to build technology businesses that address the evolving needs of regional markets.

He highlighted the opportunities created by Saudi Vision 2030 for technology companies to grow and expand, reaffirming iMENA’s commitment to supporting the development of the digital economy and generating sustainable value for shareholders and the markets in which it operates.

iMENA CEO Sara Al-AlShaikh said the group’s priorities in the next phase would include strengthening integration across its businesses and leveraging their technological capabilities, data and expertise to accelerate growth and improve competitiveness.

She added that Saudi Arabia would remain central to this strategy, with the group seeking to expand its presence and investments in the Kingdom and strengthen its role as the operational base for regional expansion.

Regional footprint

iMENA operates digital platforms across classified advertising, automotive commerce and mobility services, including OpenSooq, SellAnyCar and Jeeny.

Its platforms serve more than 100 million users across over 20 countries in the Middle East and North Africa.

The group’s investor base includes Sanabil Investments and several Saudi institutional investors, which have supported its growth and business expansion.

The announcement at the Digital Entrepreneurship Majlis highlights the initiative's role in connecting entrepreneurs with investors, showcasing investment opportunities in technology businesses and supporting the growth of the digital economy in line with Saudi Vision 2030.

World.title: Zaidi invites German firms to invest in Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi met with Germany’s Federal Minister for Economic Cooperation and Development, Reem Alabali-Radovan, and her accompanying delegation in Baghdad on Monday, November 16, 2026, renewing his call for German corporations to enter the Iraqi market and participate in major infrastructure and industrial projects.

According to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Media Office, discussions centered on expanding bilateral cooperation across economic, commercial, and investment sectors. Al-Zaidi emphasized the depth of Iraqi-German ties and underscored that the federal government is prepared to grant extensive incentives and administrative facilitations to streamline operations for foreign investors entering Iraq.

Highlighting Iraq’s strategic push to build a diversified, non-oil economy, the Prime Minister pointed to the flagship Development Road Project as a primary catalyst for bilateral partnership, noting the substantial commercial opportunities embedded in its planned industrial and economic cities along the transit corridor.

For her part, Minister Alabali-Radovan reaffirmed Berlin’s backing for the Iraqi government’s reform and development agenda, expressing Germany’s readiness to expand joint initiatives across key priority sectors:

Climate, Environment & Agriculture: Expanding technical and developmental cooperation to address environmental stress, climate resilience, and sustainable agricultural modernization.

Institutional Development Financing: Moving forward with signing a formal Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) linking Iraq with the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ) and the German Development Bank (KfW) to anchor long-term bilateral projects.

The Baghdad meeting builds directly on Prime Minister Al-Zaidi’s official visit to Berlin in mid-September 2026, where he held talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to deepen European trade ties and attract German industrial investment into Iraq.

World.title: Iraq seeks implementation of land transport deals with Jordan, Egypt
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is moving toward the early implementation of land transport agreements with Jordan and Egypt to boost regional trade and cross-border movement.

Iraqi Transport Minister Wahab al-Hassani announced the push two weeks ago during a regional transport summit in Alexandria, Egypt.

Al-Hassani confirmed that Baghdad has finalized several land transport agreements with Amman and Cairo that are expected to enter into force soon.

The announcement took place during the 39th session of the Arab Transport Ministers Council, which was held at the Arab Academy for Science, Technology and Maritime Transport in Alexandria.

The deals build upon a previously signed memorandum of understanding between the Iraqi and Egyptian transport ministries covering the overland movement of both passengers and goods.

Earlier in August 2026, Iraq and Egypt also reached a specific agreement allowing empty Iraqi cargo trucks to re-enter Egyptian territory.

Officials emphasized that activating these corridors is a priority to protect trade flows amid ongoing regional disruptions.

Alongside the deals with Jordan and Egypt, al-Hassani highlighted Iraq’s broader push to establish itself as a regional transit hub through the country’s strategic project of the Development Road.

The strategic corridor spans 1,200 kilometers from the al-Faw Grand Port in the southern province of Basra to the Turkish border, combining new highway and railway networks.

World.title: Baghdad launches crackdown against Kataib Hezbollah
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has launched a major crackdown against the Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah over an illicit oil-smuggling network operating in its stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhr.

Iraqi officials estimate the scheme has stolen hundreds of millions of dollars from the state since 2021, with monthly illicit revenues reaching up to $30 million.

Investigators uncovered concealed pumping equipment inside hangars and a hidden oil refinery in Jurf al-Sakhr, located about 50 kilometers south of Baghdad.

The network illegally tapped into strategic pipelines—including a 26-inch pipeline carrying at least 200,000 barrels per day—to siphon crude oil onto tanker trucks.

Following the investigation, al-Zaidi dismissed nine senior security and oil-sector officials and referred suspects to the judiciary.

Those removed include the Babil provincial police chief, local intelligence and security commanders, and the director of the state-run Oil Pipelines Company.

According to Reuters, al-Zaidi has ordered senior military and security commanders to deploy additional forces around Jurf al-Sakhr. Troops are preparing to enter the militia-controlled town, raising the risk of direct armed confrontation.

Kataib Hezbollah has denied the smuggling allegations, claiming the storage tanks and workshops found by investigators were used to fuel military equipment. The group characterized the government probe as a campaign of “blackmail” designed to force it to surrender its weapons.

The crackdown comes amid heightened US pressure on Baghdad to curb Iranian influence and illicit oil networks in Iraq, following US sanctions imposed earlier this year on Iraqi officials and militia-linked entities.

World.title: Iraq orders nationwide ban on Telegram due to security concerns
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi authorities ordered on Wednesday a nationwide ban on the Telegram messaging application due to security concerns, regulatory violations, and the platform’s failure to address unlawful content, incitement, and extremism.

According to the Iraqi Communications and Media Commission (CMC), the directive was issued by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, providing the platform with 30 days to comply with national laws.

Reports mentioned that Telegram failed to comply with Iraqi laws and regulatory requirements. The CMC cited national security concerns, cybercrime, hate speech, extremism, and incitement to violence and unrest.

The CMC gave Telegram’s operator 30 days to regularize its legal status and cooperate with Iraqi authorities on content moderation. Officials have not yet specified the exact technical steps required or whether the block will be lifted early if the company complies.

The announcement comes on the same day Jordan banned Telegram over similar concerns regarding extremism and national security.

In April 2026, Iraqi authorities suspended Telegram. On May 9, the CMC lifted the ban after Telegram’s management promised to abide by national laws and user safety requirements.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate rises to 1,710 dinars in Iraq’s parallel market
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The US dollar exchange rate continued to rise for the second day in Iraq, reaching 1,710 Iraqi dinars per US dollar.

Currency exchange activity in the parallel markets of Baghdad, Basra, and Erbil saw a fresh surge on Monday morning, with expectations of further increases throughout the day’s trading.

The volatility in the parallel market is attributed to the delay in approving the general budget for the 2027 fiscal year, which resulted from disagreements between the federal government in Baghdad and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) regarding the allocation of funds within the budget.

In the proposed federal general budget for the 2027 fiscal year, the Iraqi government has set the exchange rate for the US currency at 1,500 Iraqi dinars per US dollar, compared to the 1,320 dinars per US dollar used in the budgets of the previous four years.

Approximately 94 percent of Iraq’s total currency is held outside of banks, with only six percent remaining within the banking system, according to data released by the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) on Wednesday.

This figure represents the amount of cash in circulation among the general public relative to the liquidity held within banks.

World.title: Iraq will not be held hostage: PM takes on Iran-backed corruption
World.content:
Baghdad – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials on Saturday, following an investigation into allegations of oil smuggling in the Jurf Al-Sakher area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group.

Baghdad faces mounting US pressure to rein in Tehran-backed armed groups and curb Iran’s influence, a difficult task in a country long caught between its two key allies, the US and Iran.

Zaidi, who came to power with US blessing, had launched earlier this week a probe into oil smuggling in the Jurf Al-Sakher area — a stronghold of Kataeb Hezbollah, which Washington designates a terrorist organization — in Babylon province, south of Baghdad.

“In light of the investigation’s findings,” Zaidi “ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary,” his military spokesman Sabah Al-Numan said, without identifying the suspects.

The premier “also ordered the dismissal” of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babylon province, an interior ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the oil ministry.

Numan did not elaborate on the role of the sacked officials in the alleged smuggling operations.

A committee investigating the allegations entered Jurf Al-Sakher on Friday, accompanied by members of Kataeb Hezbollah.

On Wednesday, the state news agency INA reported that “intelligence documents” containing satellite images “showed crude oil and oil-derivatives smuggling operations carried out by an armed faction” in Jurf Al-Sakher, accusing the unnamed faction of tapping into a pipeline there.

According to Numan, the investigating committee “confirmed the accuracy” of the information.

Tensions have mounted between Zaidi and Kataeb Hezbollah since the prime minister, who enjoys close relations with the US, vowed to ensure that armed factions would hand over their weapons to the state.

While some groups said they would disarm, other powerful factions, mainly Kataeb Hezbollah, refused to do so.

Senior Iraqi politicians previously told AFP that Zaidi had repeatedly said he was ready to “confront” groups if they do not disarm.

Kataeb Hezbollah has recently issued several sharp statements against the prime minister, accusing him of corruption and threatening his government.

A senior Iraqi politician told AFP that “it has become personal” between Zaidi and Kataeb Hezbollah, adding that political leaders were working to defuse tensions.

Washington has accused Iraqi armed groups of involvement in oil smuggling. It has also sanctioned Iraqi officials and entities for blending Iraqi and Iranian oil or selling Iranian oil as Iraqi to help Tehran evade sanctions.

Pro-Iran armed groups have long targeted US interests in Iraq and stepped up their attacks in support of Tehran during the Middle East war.

World.title: UN to debate rules for ‘killer robots’
World.content:
Geneva – Countries will debate whether to start talks on binding rules for autonomous weapons systems — dubbed “killer robots” by critics — at the UN from Monday, as concerns grow about their increasing use on the battlefield.

Warfare is undergoing a radical transformation as armies seek to capitalise on the boom in artificial intelligence to boost their fighting abilities by identifying and striking targets more quickly and more accurately.

But a chorus of voices, from campaigners to UN chief Antonio Guterres and Pope Leo XIV, have warned against the dangers of handing the power of life and death to fully autonomous machines.

“The need to regulate autonomous weapons has taken on new urgency” with developments in artificial intelligence, said Laurent Gisel, head of the Weapons and Conduct of Hostilities Unit at the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

Russia has reportedly used fully autonomous drones to deadly effect in its war on Ukraine, while Ukraine’s own defence industry is pushing to develop autonomous “drone swarms”.

Human Rights Watch said the meeting in Geneva this week of the UN’s Review Conference of the Convention on Conventional Weapons (CCW) would leave civilians “dangerously exposed” if it failed to act decisively.

The meeting will bring together 128 countries to decide whether to open negotiations on legally binding rules.

– ‘Carefully cultivated ambiguity’ –

But while many states are in favour of tighter rules, as with other advanced military capabilities such as nuclear weapons, countries that have acquired the technology are reluctant to have their hands tied.

At the UN General Assembly last month, 163 states adopted a resolution calling for negotiations on rules governing autonomous weapons.

Five countries voted against — the United States, Russia, Belarus, Israel and North Korea, which last week boasted of a new AI-enabled torpedo system.

Nine abstained, including Iran, Saudi Arabia and China, which has maintained a “carefully cultivated ambiguity”, said Laure de Roucy-Rochegonde of the French Institute of International Relations.

Washington has proposed a five‑year process to develop a non‑binding instrument, while NGOs and the ICRC are advocating for a one‑year timeline.

In 2023, Guterres and ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric Egger called on states to ban autonomous weapons before 2026.

The ICRC is calling for a ban on two categories of autonomous weapons: so‑called “unpredictable autonomous weapons” and those designed or used to directly target humans.

Given the opposition from leading international powers, observers say it looks unlikely agreement will be reached this week to start talks on binding rules.

World.title: The 10 biggest stock market IPOs
World.content:
Washington – Anthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot, is set to start trading on Wall Street on Thursday.

The offering could raise as much as $64.4 billion, which would make it the second-largest IPO in history.

Here is the ranking of the 10 largest IPOs on record, in terms of funds raised. The figures leave out extra shares that underwriters can buy after the sale:

SpaceX — $75 billion. The rocket and AI company listed on the Nasdaq in June 2026, raising almost three times the previous record.

Saudi Aramco — the Saudi oil giant raised $25.6 billion on the Riyadh stock exchange in December 2019.

Alibaba — at $21.8 billion, the Chinese e-commerce giant made its debut on the New York Stock Exchange in September 2014.

SoftBank Corp — $21.3 billion on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in December 2018.

AgBank — $19.2 billion. Chinese lender Agricultural Bank of China listed on the Shanghai and Hong Kong stock exchanges in July 2010.

ICBC — $19.1 billion. Another Chinese bank, Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, also opted for Hong Kong and Shanghai in October 2006.

NTT Mobile — $18.1 billion. The Japanese mobile operator was listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in October 1998.

Visa Inc — $17.9 billion. The American credit card network made its New York Stock Exchange debut in March 2008.

AIA Group — $17.8 billion. This Asian subsidiary of American insurer AIG arrived on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in October 2010.

Enel — $16.5 billion. The Italian energy giant, whose shares trade in Milan and New York, made its stock market debut in November 1999.

World.title: ‘Papa would be proud of you’: Son Rahul Gandhi gets emotional at Sonia’s memoir launch
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

leader

got emotional while speaking about his mother,

, at the launch of her memoir,

Belonging: A Journey of Love

, recalling her courage, resilience and the personal tragedies she has faced over the years.

Speaking at the event, Rahul said the book offered a glimpse of his mother before the death of his father, former Prime Minister

Rajiv Gandhi

. He said Sonia had gone through several difficult phases in life but had never allowed them to break her spirit.

âI have never seen her scared. I have never seen her back down,â Rahul said, praising her strength. He also revealed that Sonia was a four-time cancer survivor, adding that she often played down the seriousness of her health struggles.

Meanwhile, BJP leader Captain Amarinder Singh, who was also present at the launch, praised the book. He said, âIt is a wonderful book; I read it... It is a very well-written book.â

Asked whether he would rejoin the Congress, Singh ruled it out, saying, âNo... Sonia Ji came to my book launches also, so I am very happy to come to the launch event of her memoir.â

World.title: Theatre commands are operational imperative, will be implemented soon: CDS; says Agnipath reforms not rollback
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General NS Raja Subramani on Monday said the creation of Integrated Theatre Commands (ITCs) is an âoperational imperativeâ rather than an administrative requirement and that all three services are on the same page and that the country will soon see its rollout.

The CDS also noted that the revision to the Agnipath scheme does not mean a ârollbackâ and its critics are âtrying to confuseâ the public.

Speaking at the ANI National Security Summit, General Subramani explained why integrated command structures are indispensable for future conflicts as such warfare goes beyond traditional boundaries. âOperation Sindoor has aptly proved that multi-domain operations are the need of the hour,â he said.



IAF chief Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, who accompanied the CDS at the summit, also vouched for theatre commands and dispelled perceptions of institutional resistance by describing air power as âthe glueâ that will bind jointness, integration, and theatreisation together.

Gen Subramani said, âWe are not only going to fight on land, air and sea, but also sub-sea, cyber, electronic warfare, spectrum, space spectrum as well as the cognitive spectrum."





Clearing the doubts about the Agnipath scheme reforms, Gen Subramani said, âWhen we started the Agnipath scheme four years ago, it was already decided that the scheme would be reviewed from time to time, keeping in mind its efficacy. Patthar ki lakeer nahi hai (not a line carved in stone), only stupid people do it like that and people who don't want to change it do it like that. Whatever changes have been made have been made after a lot of review and study, on the recommendation of the defence forces.

Those who are trying to confuse and are saying wrong things. Yeh sab galat hai.â

âI should make it clear that Agniveers will be absorbed in the forces after 4 years and 6 years as regular soldiers. It all depends upon when they want to join the forces permanently,â Gen Subramani said
