World.title: Cultural activists protest at Thiruvananthapuram Corporation over denial of permission to Manaveeyam Veedhi event
World.content:
Following the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led Thiruvananthapuram Corporation’s denial of permission for a cultural programme at Manaveeyam Veedhi featuring singer Pushpavathy, a group of cultural activists representing various organisations at Manaveeyam staged a protest at the Corporation office on Monday. Dramatic scenes were witnessed as the activists who gheraoed the Corporation Secretary ahead of the council meeting were forcibly detained by the police. The police dragged out of the Corporation office the six activists, including veteran theatre artist D. Raghoothaman, Vinod Vaisakhi, S.Rahul, K.G.Suraj, Diya Sana and S.S.Deepu. Condemning the police action, CPI(M) State Secretary M.A.Baby posted in X that Mayor V.V. Rajesh and the BJP-run Corporation are attempting to erase a venue that offered a space for cultural expression of all hues and colours, a pluralistic space at the heart of Keralam’s capital that has been accessible to the public for the last 25 years and is an integral part of the democratic culture of the city. “I was myself a part of the inaugural event held on October 22 as part of the silver jubilee celebrations of Manaveeyam Veedhi. It is highly unfortunate that the State government is using the police machinery to crack down on those who are questioning the BJP’s attempt to capture public institutions and democratic spaces in the State. The people of Keralam will resist all such efforts. Our streets will continue to sing the songs of freedom,” said Mr.Baby, during whose tenure as the State Culture Minister that Manaveeyam was conceived as a cultural corridor in 2001.

According to K.G. Suraj, secretary of the Manaveeyam Theruvidam Cultural Collective and Street Library, the group had approached the Secretary to know the reasons for denial of permission. “The Secretary showed us that he had cleared our application for permission for the event. However, it remained pending with the Mayor for days, since he didn’t want the event to happen. However, clearance has been accorded to events of the BJP as well commercial programmes,” he said. On Sunday, an event titled Nammude Manaveeyam, Nammude Shabdam was organised at Manaveeyam in defiance of the Corporation, with musicians, actors, political leaders and common people joining in for an evening of protest music. Cultural Affairs Minister P. C. Vishnunadh had on Saturday urged the Corporation to reconsider its decision to deny permission for the music concert featuring singer Pushpavathy at Manaveeyam Veedhi. Mayor V. V. Rajesh had said he had never heard of singer Pushpavathy. Mr. Rajesh said the State government had entrusted the Corporation with maintaining Manaveeyam Veedhi as it was renovated using funds under the Smart City Mission. He said there should be official records with the Corporation if a committee had been formed to organise the silver jubilee celebrations of Manaveeyam Veedhi. CPI(M) leaders have maintained that the Manaveeyam Veedhi is a road under the Public Works Department (PWD) and that its management rights have never been transferred to the Municipal Corporation.

World.title: Cyclonic Storm Akvan forms over the Bay; CM tells officials to take precautionary steps
World.content:
The deep depression over southeast and southwest Bay of Bengal has intensified into a Cyclonic Storm ‘Akvan’ on Monday evening, and is moving north-northwestwards towards the A.P. coast at 10 kmph.

According to the obsevations made by the India Meteorological Department (IMD), at 5.30 p.m., the storm was centred over the central parts of south and westcentral Bay of Bengal, which is about 610 km east of Chennai of Tamil Nadu, 630 km northeast of Trincomalee of Sri Lanka, 660 km southeast of Machilipatnam and 670 km south-southeast of Visakhapatnam of Andhra Pradesh and 790 km south of Gopalpur of Odisha.

The storm may continue to move north-northwestwards and intensify into a Severe Cyclonic Storm over westcentral Bay of Bengal by Tuesday evening and may cross the A.P. coast around noon on November 20, as a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm, with windspeed gusting to 145 kmph, similar to that of Arnab. The rainfall activity may begin in the State from November 18, becoming very heavy on November 19 and 20.

The IMD said that the probable landfall location could be anywhere between Nellore of SPSR Nellore district and Tuni of Kakinada district. The current weather models indicate the movement of the system towards Machilipatnam.

This time, too, Central A.P is likely to be affected. The districts of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema, Kakinada, East Godavari, West Godavari, Krishna, NTR and Guntur have been put on alert, as very heavy to extremely heavy rainfall is expected in these distrcts on November 19 and 20. Except for Krishna and NTR, the other districts bore the brunt during Arnab and Murasu too. Most of these districts are known for rich cultivation of paddy.

As the State prepares for yet another cyclonic storm, third in less than a month, Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu reviewed the situation from the Secretariat on Monday and instructed officials to take all necessary precautionary measures. He also instructed officials to take necessary steps to divert floodwaters resulting from heavy rainfall into reservoirs to ensure effective water management, since the State still has an overall rainfall deficit of 27.2%.

Both Arnab and Murasu brought very heavy rainfall to northern and central parts of the State, while Rayalaseema continues to remain parched with a few districts reporting deficits of more than 50%.

The Deep Depression over SE & adjoining SW BoB intensified into Cyclonic Storm "Akvan" and lay over central parts of South & adjoining Westcentral BoB at 1730 IST of 16 Nov, about 610 km E of Chennai. Likely to intensify into SCS by 17 Nov evening and VSCS by 19 Nov morning. https://t.co/Lidf8uWved — India Meteorological Department (@Indiametdept) November 16, 2026

Alert for all coastal districts

Since the wind over southeast and southwest Bay of Bengal and also along the coast may increase gradually from the morning of November 17, the Fisheries department has issued an alert for 12 coastal districts covering the State’s 1,053-km coastline.

Of the 30,808 fishing boats in the State, 30,635 had returned safely to shore by 10 a.m. on November 16, while efforts were under way to bring back the remaining 173 boats.

World.title: Six Liangmai Naga civilians laid to rest in Manipur 187 days after abduction, killing
World.content:
The bodies of six Liangmai Naga civilians were laid to rest in Manipur’s Kangpokpi district on Monday (November 16, 2026), 187 days after they were abducted and subsequently killed almost a month later.

The family of the deceased and Naga organisations had refused to claim the bodies — kept at the mortuary of the Jawaharlal Nehru Institute of Medical Sciences in Imphal since June 10 — until their demands were met.

One of the main demands of the Naga civil bodies was the abrogation of the 2008 Suspension of Operations agreements with 25 Kuki-Zomi armed groups. The UNC and the families agreed to accept the bodies after receiving assurances of justice at a tripartite meeting involving the Union government, the Manipur government and Naga organisations in Guwahati on September 26, and after the completion of a safer alternative road for the people of Konsakhul village.

The families received the bodies on Monday and transported them to their home village of Konsakhul in the Kuki-dominated Kangpokpi district for the final rites. People from various communities gathered for the funeral.

‘Darkest day in State’s history’

Speaking at the funeral, United Naga Council (UNC) president N.G. Lorho said May 13, 2026, would remain the darkest day in Manipur’s history.

“On that day, six Naga men were killed, mutilated, and dismembered at Leilon Vaiphei village by KNF-P (Kuki National Front-Presidential), Kuki militants, and Leilon villagers. Their bodies were treated in a manner that brings shame to the State of Manipur and to India before the whole world,” he said.

He also noted that the funeral underscored the unity of the Nagas and other indigenous communities of Manipur.

“Our land is being invaded and ravaged. Our people are being killed, displaced, and terrorised. If this incursion is not stopped, the very existence, identity, and future of the indigenous people of Manipur will be at stake,” Mr. Lorho said.

The UNC, Manipur’s apex Naga organisation, urged the Centre to immediately end the “policy of appeasement and protection of militant groups” carrying out attacks and killings, and to fulfill its constitutional and moral responsibility to protect the lives, land, and identity of indigenous people.

What triggered abductions

The killing of three Thadou church leaders in an ambush in Kangpokpi district on May 13 prompted a series of abductions. The Thadous are divided over their Kuki identity.

Altogether 48 people — 28 Kukis and 20 Nagas — were abducted within hours of the ambush. Eighteen of the 20 Nagas were abducted from Leilon Vaiphei village.

After security forces brokered a hostage-exchange deal, Nagas released 14 of the 28 Kuki captives, while Kukis freed 14 Nagas on May 15. The Nagas set free included 12 of the 18 abducted from Leilon Vaiphei.

On June 9, Nagas released the remaining 14 Kukis, but the six abducted Nagas remained untraced until security forces recovered their bodies on June 10

World.title: Bengaluru leads country in voluntary disclosure of foreign assets
World.content:
Bengaluru has emerged as the leading centre in the country for voluntary foreign asset disclosures under the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers-Disclosure Scheme (FAST-DS) 2026, accounting for 217 applications out of 1,026 Form 1 submissions received across various Principal Chief Commissioner of Income Tax jurisdictions as of October 20.

Disclosing the figures at an outreach programme organised by the Bangalore Chamber of Industry and Commerce (BCIC) here on Monday, Manjit Singh, Chief Commissioner of Income Tax (TDS), Bengaluru, said the city’s response was significantly ahead of other jurisdictions, reflecting growing awareness among taxpayers about foreign asset reporting requirements.

The outreach programme focused on creating awareness about FAST-DS 2026, which provides eligible small taxpayers with a one-time, faceless opportunity to disclose previously undeclared foreign assets or foreign-sourced income within prescribed thresholds and obtain relief from penal and prosecution consequences under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015, subject to the scheme’s conditions. The scheme, which opened on August 16, 2026, will remain available until December 31, 2026.

While delivering the keynote address, Mr. Singh said, “Bengaluru is the highest with 217 forms, while others are far away. The Income Tax Department had undertaken extensive outreach initiatives, including engagement with approximately 267 companies whose employees could potentially benefit from the scheme.”

Online awareness programmes have also been conducted to explain the disclosure requirements and encourage eligible taxpayers to come forward, he noted. Mr. Singh also observed that overseas travel and foreign financial exposure have become increasingly common among professionals and businessmen. Inadvertent omissions in reporting foreign assets could expose taxpayers to penalties or notices at a later stage, making timely voluntary disclosure particularly important.

“As Indian businesses and professionals become increasingly integrated with the global economy through overseas investments, ESOPs, foreign bank accounts, and cross-border transactions, international tax reporting has become both essential and complex,” commented K. Ravi, President, BCIC.

Many small taxpayers and returning professionals inadvertently overlook reporting overseas holdings, often without any intention of evading taxes; however, FAST-DS 2026 provided a timely opportunity to regularise such omissions, he pointed out.

I-T dept seeks inputs

According to Mr. Singh, the Income Tax Department has been seeking industry inputs on digital economy taxation. The tax administration must evolve with emerging digital platforms, content creators, and new business models, he said, adding that a committee has been constituted in his office to engage with stakeholders and seek suggestions on simplifying tax compliance.

World.title: Third American aircraft carrier arrives in West Asia as Trump keeps options open in Iran war
World.content:
The USS Theodore Roosevelt has arrived in the West Asia, once again bringing the total number of U.S. aircraft carriers in the West Asia to three — an unusually high number.

A U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations, on Monday (November 16, 2026) confirmed the carrier’s arrival in the region.

It brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as President Donald Trump has kept his options open during the more than 8-month-old Iran war.

The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September.

The Theodore Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as scores of smaller navy ships, that are in the region maintaining a blockade of Iranian shipping. The H.W. Bush arrived in the region in April while the George Washington arrived in August.

According to the Navy, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes three aircraft carriers as well as 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship.

World.title: Census portal lists ‘ISKCON’, ‘Tantric’, ‘Gorak Nath’ among 287 ‘other’ religions; removes menu later
World.content:
Going by the government's initial classification of “other” religions in the self-enumeration portal for the Population Enumeration phase of Census 2027, ‘ISKCON’, ‘Ramakrishna Paramahans’, ‘Sanatan’, ‘Shri Ram’, ‘Shri Krishna’, ‘Balmiki’, ‘Ramdev’, ‘Bishnoi’, ‘Sarna’, ‘Tantric’, ‘Yogi’, ‘Shia’, ‘Sunni’, ‘Methodist’, and ‘Pentecostal’, are among the religions practised in the country.

While these were among 287 options given under the ‘Others’ category for the question pertaining to the respondent's religion in the self-enumeration portal that went live on Monday (November 16, 2026) for four poll-bound States, the drop-down menu with these options was removed later in the day after The Hindu raised a query with the Union Ministry of Home Affairs regarding the classification.

Along the same lines as the previous Census exercises, there are seven main categories in the religion column: Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, and Others. In a first, the 'Others' category had been expanded into at least 287 further options, many of which have previously been classified by the Indian government as sects within the six major religions or as respondents’ entries in the “other religions and persuasions” category in the 2001 and 2011 Censuses. The drop-down menu also had several options that had not been recorded before, such as ‘ISKCON’, ‘Ramakrishna Paramhans’, ‘Ramdev’, ‘Khalsa’, ‘Tirupati Balaji’, ‘Gorak Nath’, ‘Basaveshwara’, ‘Baldev’, ‘Devi Maa’, ‘Devi Bhakt’, and ‘Dev Samaj’, among others.

‘Predictive text entries’

After the removal of the drop-down menu, a representative of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India (RG&CCI) said that, apart from the six major religions, there is the ‘Others’ category in which the “respondent is free to write any other religion as in previous censuses.” The official also said that it was “incorrect to say the mentioned terms have been shown as other religions”.

However, a government official told The Hindu that the list of options had been prepared as "predictive text entries" for the 'Other' religions category to help enumerators fill in the forms without “spelling variations and mistakes” when a respondent mentions any faith other than the six major ones. Giving an example, the official explained that if a respondent said they were a follower of ISKCON, the predictive text list would complete the entry without spelling variations or mistakes. How these appeared as options in a drop-down box is being inquired into, the official said.

The self-enumeration portal (se.census.gov.in) went live on Monday (November 16, 2026) for the States of Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Goa, and Punjab, where elections are scheduled to be held in 2027. For the rest of the country, the portal will open in January 2027.

A retired Census official told The Hindu that the options in the now-removed drop-down box were “strange”, particularly because there is no previous data to compare them with. The retired official also said that these entries appeared to be sects or movements within major religions. In 2001 and 2011, the tables on classified sects within major religions and respondents’ entries in the ‘other religions and persuasions’ category were tabulated later, after the enumeration was completed.

Before the drop-down box under the other religions category was removed, a government official in Uttar Pradesh, who provided training to Census enumerators, said, “The instructions are to record religion from the six mentioned categories. If a respondent chooses the ‘Other’ category, they can pick from the specified drop-down box with more than 280 names, and if the preferred religion’s name is not there, they can enter the name and it will be recorded as is."

There has been a sustained movement by tribal communities in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and West Bengal, calling for a separate religion column for Adivasi faiths, which they asserted was different from Hinduism.

Many firsts

The current Census, which has been delayed by six years with the last one having been conducted in 2011, is being referred to as the first digital Census. It is also the first to enumerate caste and the first to allow self-enumeration. The Office of the RG&CCI has decided to use an open column for caste enumeration despite demands and protests for a drop-down box of all castes. The government’s justification for using an open column was that there was no single available list of all castes, apart from the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes lists.

The RG&CCI had on August 14 notified a set of 40 questions to be asked during the Population Enumeration phase of Census 2027, which included 13 new questions or data fields that were not part of the Census 2011 questionnaire.

The questions that have been added for the first time are spouse’s name, nationality, father’s particulars and mother’s particulars, digital literacy, permanent residential address, place of Covid-19 vaccination, number of bank accounts, passport number, driving licence availability, and mobile, Aadhaar and voter ID numbers, if available.

World.title: Library room for women advocates inaugurated
World.content: A library room with additional facilities for women advocates was inaugurated on the Madurai District Court campus here on Monday. The Administrative Judge of the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court Justice P. Velmurugan inaugurated the facility in the presence of the Madurai Principal District and Sessions Judge M. Sai Saravanan, Chief Judicial Magistrate K. Selvapandi, Madurai Bar Association president A. Baskaran, secretary S. Mohan Kumar, treasurer S. Rajamohan and others.

World.title: Tourism Minister honours artists with awards in Kanniyakumari
World.content:
Tourism Minister S. Rajesh Kumar has honoured artists by presenting awards on behalf of the Department of Art and Culture at an event held in Midalam on Monday.

The Tamil Nadu government presents ‘Kalai Ilamani,’ ‘Kalai Valarmani,’ ‘Kalai Sudarmani,’ and ‘Kalai Nanmani’ awards every year to encourage young and senior artists and recognise their contributions to the field of art and culture.

The Minister presented awards along with cash prizes to the recipients and congratulated them.

At the event, he distributed pattas and welfare assistance to the beneficiaries on behalf of the Revenue and Disaster Management. Mr. Rajesh Kumar has handed over natham housing pattas to 37 beneficiaries. He also distributed a Community Investment Fund of ₹7 lakh to six Women Self Help Groups (SHGs).

In addition, he distributed various welfare assistance under agriculture, horticulture, animal husbandry and Adi Dravidar and Tribal Welfare departments.

Kanniyakumari District Collector M. Prathap, District Revenue Officer M. Velumani and other officials were present.

World.title: Mephedrone & hybrid ganja seized from Thar near Vadodara hospital, 2 held: Police
World.content:
A LATE-NIGHT “contraband delivery” bid near the maternity wing of the SSG Hospital in Vadodara led to the arrest of two youths travelling in a Mahindra Thar with mephedrone and hybrid ganja, after the Local Crime Branch (LCB) Zone 2 team and Raopura police intercepted the vehicle in the early hours on Monday.

The police seized six grams (gm) of mephedrone, eight gm of hybrid ganja, two mobile phones, cash and a digital weighing scale, along with the vehicle, taking the total value of the seized goods to Rs 16.005 lakh. Police identified the accused as Aman Shahid Memon (23) and Shafin Raza Rizwanali Sarani (21) – both residents of Vadodara city.

World.title: Bajrang Dal men ‘stormed’ sacred site alleging cow slaughter. Now, Odisha tribals threaten stir
World.content:
The alleged desecration of a religious site of the Santhal community in Odisha’s Keonjhar district over allegations of cow slaughter during a ritual last month has turned into a political flashpoint in the state.

While the Biju Janata Dal (BJD) on Monday announced its support to the protest called by the tribal community on November 18, the VHP has slammed the arrest of five Bajrang Dal activists last week in connection with the incident.

Calling the arrests “arbitrary”, the VHP sought intervention of Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi in the matter. Keonjhar is the home district of the CM.



The tribal community said it would hold a massive protest on Wednesday demanding the arrest of the other accused in the case.

World.title: Sachin Tendulkar donates 25 bats, and the stories that came with them
World.content:
“I’ve said that it (the cricket bat) is an extension of my body. So, I’m giving you a part of my body. Please take care of it.”

For Sachin Tendulkar, a cricket bat was never just equipment. It was a companion through a 24-year career, a source of runs and, at times, reassurance. The 25 bats he handed over to the MCA Sharad Pawar Cricket Museum on Monday, in the presence of MCA president Ajinkya Naik, told the story – from an unexpected childhood gift to the bat he used in his final Test innings against West Indies at Wankhede Stadium in 2013.

Titled Batography, the collection is more than a display of memorabilia. Each bat marks a moment in Tendulkar’s journey and offers a glimpse into his personal choices and beliefs. His association with bats began when he was five, after his sister brought him one from Kashmir.



“My sister Savita Tai had gone on a trip to Kashmir. I was expecting her to bring back walnuts, apples and other things. But when she gifted me a cricket bat instead, I was absolutely delighted. From then on, that bat accompanied me everywhere,” he recalled at a fireside chat on Monday.

His brother Ajit and coach Ramakant Achrekar later helped him get his first season-ball bat: a full-size Symonds, heavy for a 12-year-old.

“In 1985, I received my first leather-ball bat. I had gone with Achrekar Sir, and the moment I saw a particular bat, I liked it and decided that I wanted that one. From the sixth standard onwards, I started concentrating seriously on cricket. My elder brother spoke to my father, who then bought me a separate bat. It was a full-sized bat and quite heavy for my age, but I was determined to have that particular bat.”

As an adult, his choices also reflected the values he carried from home. During the 1996 World Cup, Tendulkar played with a sponsorless bat because his family had decided he would not promote alcohol or tobacco.

“At home, we had decided – the whole family had decided – that I would never promote alcohol or tobacco,” he said. “I ended up playing for close to two years without any sticker on my bat.”



A foreign sports brand offered him a deal during the tournament. But having already played two matches without a sticker, including a hundred against Kenya, Tendulkar was reluctant to change anything.

“I said, ‘No. I’m slightly superstitious now. With the blank bat, it was priceless to score those runs. We’ll talk after the World Cup is over.’ Right now, the whole World Cup, I’m going to play with a blank bat.”

Another bat had an unusual journey into his collection. In 2009, Soni Kohli showed him a bat in Mohali that had been made for former India spinner Sunil Joshi. Tendulkar liked it, and it was delivered as the team bus was leaving for the Hyderabad match against Australia.

“I hadn’t played a single ball with it. I took it out and played with it in the match. A brand-new bat,” he said.



The bat soon became a favourite. He used it to score 175 against Australia in Hyderabad and the first-ever ODI double century against South Africa in Gwalior. Tendulkar called it the “super bat”.

Tendulkar also recalled his father’s advice about what a cricket bat meant to a player, urging him to keep the equipment close to him.

“My father used to say that you should keep your things close to you. That includes your talent. It’s a God’s gift. So you have to keep it close and worship it,” he said. “Why should you throw a bat? What are you going to achieve? Why disrespect your gift?”

The collection also included his first helmet, Mumbai’s Ranji Trophy jersey, the India jersey and helmet from his 200th Test, and the sheet of paper on which he wrote the points for his farewell speech at Wankhede Stadium.

World.title: From new bus services to beautification: Delhi gears up to host India Biennale ’26
World.content:
With preparations underway for the 108-day India Biennale 2026, the Delhi government has directed various departments to draw up time-bound action plans for traffic management, transport connectivity, sanitation, beautification and visitor facilities across more than 22 heritage sites and cultural institutions in the Capital.

At a meeting chaired jointly by Union Culture and Tourism Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta at the CM’s Janseva Sadan on Monday, departments were asked to work in coordination to ensure the smooth organisation of the event, scheduled from December 4, 2026, to March 21, 2027, officials said.



Gupta directed that the Secretary of the Urban Development Department be appointed as the nodal officer, with senior liaison officers in each department to monitor preparations.

World.title: RBI reiterates demand for listing of Tata Sons
World.content:
A senior RBI official on Monday reiterated the central bank’s demand that Tata Sons, the holding company of the salts-to-software conglomerate, be listed as per existing regulations.

Writing in response to an October 6 communication from Tata Sons Pvt Ltd (TSPL), a Deputy General Manager in the Department of Regulation advised the company to comply with all applicable rules for Upper Layer Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFC-UL), including the listing requirement.

“While specific guidance has not been sought on any particular regulation/ guideline/ direction, from the discussion in the Board regarding listing, it seems the guidance is perhaps with respect to the same,” the letter says.

Emails sent to Tata Sons and RBI did not elicit an immediate reply.

World.title: ‘People want clarity’: Maharashtra CM Fadnavis asks Amit Shah to expedite Ajit plane crash probe
World.content:
Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis on Monday said he had requested Union Home Minister Amit Shah to expedite the investigation into the plane crash that killed former deputy chief minister Ajit Pawar, stating that the report should be made public at the earliest to address questions and suspicions surrounding the incident among people in Maharashtra.

Speaking at a ceremony to unveil a bust of Ajit Pawar at the Pune Zilla Parishad, Fadnavis said that nearly 10 months had passed since the crash and that a detailed investigation was underway, involving representatives from the United States and other countries. He said Shah had assured him that he would personally look into the matter to ensure that the investigation report was released as soon as possible.

“Following the untimely passing of Ajit Pawar, there are questions among the common people of Maharashtra about whether it was an accident or whether someone was behind it. People want clarity and the truth to come out. I have requested Amit Shah to ensure that the investigation report is released as soon as possible,” Fadnavis said.



Also Read | Ajit Pawar death: Rohit accuses Fadnavis of shielding plane company owners

He added that the findings would help establish whether the incident was merely an accident or whether someone was responsible for it. “If someone is involved, we should be able to hang them. And if it was a mere accident, the anger among the people of Maharashtra should at least be eased,” he said.

Fadnavis said Ajit Pawar’s presence had been a strong support for the state government and that his absence was particularly felt amid the prevailing drought conditions in parts of Maharashtra. “If he were here, he might have fought this battle against drought very well,” he said.

The Chief Minister was speaking at the unveiling of Ajit Pawar’s bust at the Pune Zilla Parishad, an institution with which the late leader had a long association. Union Home Minister Amit Shah unveiled the bust in the presence of Fadnavis, Deputy Chief Ministers Eknath Shinde and Sunetra Pawar, Union Minister of State for Civil Aviation Murlidhar Mohol, NCP (SP) Lok Sabha MP Supriya Sule, Ministers Chandrakant Patil and Dattatray Bharne, Maharashtra BJP chief Ravindra Chavan, among others.

Recalling Ajit Pawar’s contribution to the Pune Zilla Parishad, Fadnavis said he had played a significant role in shaping the institution’s functioning and that seven to eight leaders had emerged from the organisation under his guidance.



Describing him as a disciplined leader with a strong understanding of administration and a visionary outlook, Fadnavis said Ajit Pawar was known for his straightforward approach and firm convictions.

“If he believed in something, he would stand firmly behind it. If he disagreed, he would make his stand equally clear,” Fadnavis said.

Highlighting his administrative capabilities, Fadnavis said that even while presenting several state budgets as Finance Minister, Ajit Pawar had maintained fiscal discipline despite challenging economic circumstances. He also emphasised the late leader’s focus on the proper utilisation of public funds, quality of work and ensuring that development projects achieved their intended outcomes.

Recalling his work routine, Fadnavis said, “Ajit Pawar would be ready for work by 6 am and begin official duties by 7 am, often reaching the state secretariat by 8 am to ensure that files and other matters were cleared promptly.”



“Sometimes, we would joke about what would happen to our officers and whether they would have to work for 24 hours. Ajitdada would start working early in the morning, I would begin my work after him, while Eknath Shinde would work late into the night. Ajitdada never compromised on his discipline, something rarely seen in politics,” he said.

Fadnavis added that Ajit Pawar’s influence could be seen in several development projects across Maharashtra. While he appeared stern, he had deep affection for those close to him and was always willing to stand by them, he said.

NCP (SP) MP Supriya Sule, who was also present at the event, while talking to the media, said, “Ajit Pawar had made significant contributions to the development of Pune and Maharashtra.” Recalling his association with the Pune Zilla Parishad as the district’s guardian minister, she said he shared a close bond with the institution and the people associated with it. “I thank the Pune Zilla Parishad for building his bust,” Sule said.

When asked about the absence of senior NCP leaders, including Praful Patel, Sunil Tatkare, Chhagan Bhujbal and Hasan Mushrif, among others, Sule said she had attended the programme as a guest and was unaware of the reasons for their absence.



Minister Dattatray Bharne, speaking to reporters after the ceremony, also said that the confusion surrounding the plane crash should be cleared soon and that the actual reason behind the incident should be made known to the public.

Asked about the absence of senior NCP leaders, Bharne said, “The programme was organised by the Pune Zilla Parishad and was not a state-level event. The Zilla Parishad president and members had invited political leaders from Pune,” he said.

World.title: ‘Best sleep of my life’: Ashwin opens up on dismissing Jos Buttler in IPL 2019
World.content:
R Ashwin got embroiled in a controversy in IPL 2019 in a match between then Kings XI Punjab and Rajasthan Royals when he mankaded RR’s Jos Buttler. The incident had raised a lot of controversy on fair play. Since then, the controversy has always followed Ashwin everywhere and he recently opened up on it in a chat with former India batter Aakash Chopra.

“In that game, Rajasthan Royals had an edge. I was the captain of Kings XI. I had done the run out and my team got upset. I called everyone and said these people were disturbed. I knew in the next three days, I would have to listen to everyone give their opinion on the run out. But I would handle it. Our task was to win the game and that we won. If Buttler’s run out gives us the victory and 2 points, why shouldn’t we take it?,” Ashwin said in the Baith and Bol show on Chopra’s YouTube channel.

World.title: How excess vitamin B6 can do more harm than good: ‘Especially without medical supervision’
World.content:
Vitamin B6, or pyridoxine, is an essential nutrient that supports brain development, nerve function, neurotransmitter production, and red blood cell formation. However, Dr Atampreet Singh, Director, Neurology, ShardaCare – Healthcity, says, “Consuming it in excessive quantities, for a prolonged period of time, particularly through high-dose supplements, can become harmful to the nervous system.”

“It can also damage the peripheral nerves, a condition known as peripheral neuropathy,” he adds.

DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine.



What causes vitamin B6 toxicity?

Many people unknowingly consume more than the recommended amount because this is present in several products, including multivitamins, B-complex supplements, energy drinks and certain health supplements. When these sources are combined, the overall intake can exceed safe limits.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
