World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019255/China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
World.title: China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019255/China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
World.content:
SHANGHAI — When prospective clients contacted Li Shuping’s medical companion agency in Shanghai, their first question often had little to do with the hospital visit they were arranging.

“Patients used to ask first whether we were individuals or a legitimate agency,” Li tells Sixth Tone. Patients hire her company, Qingbeihu, to send a trained companion with them to hospital, helping with appointments, consultations, and paperwork.

The agency opened in September 2025, when almost anyone could advertise the same service on social media. And with people aged 60 or older accounting for 23% of China’s population by the end of 2025 and 59 million forecast to need care by 2030, more families were turning to companions to guide elderly relatives through hospital visits.

But written contracts were often absent, leaving services and fees unclear. Some patients faced unexpected charges once a visit was underway, with little recourse if they disputed them, prompting calls for tighter oversight.

But since Shanghai announced new rules for medical companion services effective July 1, Qingbeihu has received more inquiries, Li says. “Orders are growing steadily, and prospective clients seem more willing to trust the service.”

The rules cover medical companion services for Shanghai residents aged 60 and older and set requirements for worker qualifications, pricing transparency, and written contracts. They also require companions to wear identity badges, provide public lists of qualified agencies, and define responsibilities that include helping patients communicate with doctors and offering psychological support.

More recently, a national standard that took effect Nov. 1 covers medical companion services for patients of all ages across China. It also sets limits on what companions can do, prohibiting them from giving medical advice or making treatment decisions on patients’ behalf.

Following Shanghai’s new rules, Li says Qingbeihu now uses written risk and privacy agreements with patients and companions, as well as accident insurance for companions. For elderly clients unfamiliar with digital services, the agency also provides paper consent forms before a visit.

“Elderly people are very willing to have young people accompany them to seek care — it is also a kind of emotional support,” Li says.

For Qingbeihu’s six full-time companions, all under 30, the working day often begins as early as 5 a.m.

Patient work

By the time Li Suyu, not related to Li Shuping, meets a patient at the hospital around 7:30 a.m., she has already asked about their medical history, drug allergies, and mobility. She then checks registration details and organizes medical records and examination reports before the hospital opens at 8.

Once consultations begin, the 22-year-old accompanies patients to see their doctors, records treatment plans and prescribed medications, and arranges any examinations ordered. She also keeps family members informed and, after the visit, helps patients keep track of follow-up appointments and medication reminders.

In the afternoon, she takes patients for blood tests or ultrasounds, then collects their reports and mails them out. She often handles about 28 bookings a month, with as many as four on a busy day, each lasting two to four hours. At Qingbeihu, a two-hour booking costs 188 yuan ($26), while four hours of surgery accompaniment costs 360 yuan.

Li previously worked in sales and became interested in medical companionship after accompanying a family member to hospital and struggling with some of the procedures herself.

“I had no medical background, so even understanding the doctors’ terminology was difficult at first,” she recalls. When she encountered unfamiliar terms, she consulted more experienced colleagues.

At Qingbeihu, training covers first aid, hospital procedures, and organizing patient records. Companions also attend training at a Red Cross first-aid center and must pass an assessment organized by the Shanghai Association of Elderly Care Services and Aging Industry to obtain a medical companion certificate.

Much of the initial training is theoretical. Even after certification, newcomers must shadow experienced colleagues before taking bookings on their own.

“Many elderly patients become anxious in crowded hospitals, especially when they don’t know their way around,” Li says. She learned to calm them through conversation or small gestures, such as offering a bottle of water or some snacks.

One elderly patient with mid- to late-stage cancer initially refused to engage with her. He believed his illness was incurable and saw little point in spending money on treatment.

Li began talking to him about his family, listening as he spoke about his grandchildren. As he grew more comfortable with her, she encouraged him to continue treatment, reminding him that his relatives wanted him to recover. Li says he eventually agreed to cooperate with treatment.

Ma Xunru, a 60-year-old Shanghai retiree, had reservations when she hired a medical companion while her daughter was away on a business trip. She needed to visit a hospital for dizziness and cervical spine problems but worried that the companion might not be professional.

The crowds at the top-tier hospital made her dizziness worse. But her companion arranged appointments with two departments so she could see the doctors and complete the necessary examinations. Ma says that if she had gone alone or with her daughter, they would have registered with only one department.

“It was such a relief to have the companion with me. Otherwise I wouldn’t have known where to go,” Ma says. She now plans to use the service again.

“I think in the future I’ll ask my daughter to book a companion as well, so that I don’t need to bother her, since she’s busy with her work and life.”

Doctor’s orders

When Wang, a rehabilitation doctor in Shanghai, needed someone to accompany her for a gastroscopy, she hired a medical companion. Most of her friends were doctors, too, and asking one of them to come along would have meant rearranging a hospital shift.

She expected help preparing for the procedure and someone to talk to while she waited. “When taking the order, they only asked what time and where. And they were on their phone the whole time,” she recalls.

The experience helped prompt Wang, 25, to establish Zhuoyu Health with Zhou, 30, a gynecology and reproductive medicine doctor. Both asked to be identified only by their surnames.

Both had seen elderly patients struggle with hospital equipment such as self-service machines. Zhuoyu now has more than a dozen part-time companions drawn from rehabilitation, gynecology, anesthesiology, and the medical device industry.

Wang and Zhou found that questions they considered straightforward could leave patients at a loss, from what to do if they lost their ID card at a hospital to how to prepare for a CT scan. During consultations, they also help patients ask questions they might otherwise overlook and, afterward, understand their doctors’ instructions.

Wang’s first booking, in early June, involved an elderly woman whose health had suffered, she says, from using folk remedies during a long illness.

Before the visit, Wang and the woman’s son-in-law reviewed her medical records and the remedies she had been taking. With heavy rain that day, Wang rented a wheelchair for her. During an echocardiogram, she helped the woman adjust her clothing and explained each step.

Wang admitted to the family that she was handling her first booking. “I was very nervous taking my first order, and the patient’s family comforted me instead,” she recalls.

Zhou encountered a different problem while accompanying an elderly woman with poor hearing and limited Mandarin for a contrast-enhanced CT scan. The patient struggled to follow instructions requiring specific movements, and her anxious daughter began scolding her.

Zhou took the woman out of the examination room and explained what she needed to do. The second attempt went smoothly. “She wasn’t being uncooperative. She genuinely didn’t understand what she was supposed to do,” Zhou recalls telling the daughter.

Yang Hanxue, 25, decided to become a medical companion after seeing elderly people living alone and out-of-town patients struggle through hospital visits while she was working as a nurse.

Now at Qingbeihu, she adjusts her approach to different patients, explaining delays to those who are anxious, listening to those who want to talk, and keeping small talk to a minimum with people wary of the service.

Yang recalls a family wanting an elderly relative to undergo a full set of examinations, although the patient might not have been able to tolerate them. In such situations, she says, companions should remain neutral, relay the doctor’s advice, help families raise questions during consultations, and work toward an arrangement that accounts for the patient’s condition and the family’s wishes.

“Many people don’t understand this profession and mistakenly think we are experts, consulting us on how to treat illnesses,” Yang says. She tells patients and families to follow their doctor’s advice rather than offering treatment recommendations herself.

Wang recalls a patient who fell into a deep coma. The family eventually decided to discontinue treatment. Wang and Zhou say companions should not influence such decisions, but can offer support to relatives struggling with the choices they face.

Despite being a practicing doctor, Wang believes the boundaries of medical companionship need to be more clearly defined, particularly when patients ask companions to weigh in on treatment decisions.

“Patients often ask me, ‘The doctor recommended this — should I do it? Should I keep taking this medicine?’” she says.

Contributions: Marianne Gunnarsson; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A trained medical companion explains prescribed medication to an elderly couple at a traditional Chinese medicine hospital in Beijing, May 22, 2025. Jade GAO/AFP/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.title: Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.content:
A pair of Chinese noodle shops serving free meals sparked debate this week after their popularity reportedly disrupted neighboring shops’ business.

“Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop,” which opened two outlets last month in the densely populated Jiangning and Yuhuatai districts of Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, offers only one dish: noodles with braised vegetarian chicken and shiitake mushrooms. Each restaurant has around 50 seats, and since opening have been frequented mainly by middle-aged and elderly customers, according to domestic media.

Jiangning is home to a large migrant worker population, while Yuhuatai has the city’s largest public housing project. Signs outside the restaurants read, “A bowl of pure intention, with no fixed price; three meals a day, offered with warmth to those in need.”

The owner, surnamed Zhang, told domestic media he opened the shops for two reasons: promoting vegetarianism and charity. He said he had previously donated to charities and operated low-cost vegetarian restaurants but found that offering free noodles was the most effective way to achieve his philanthropic goals.

The two shops have served more than 1,000 bowls of noodles each day, Zhang said. He added that he had initially planned to open 10 stores, each serving 500 bowls a day, but demand had exceeded his expectations.

“Our idea was simple: get more people to come eat,” he said.

The topic has garnered more than 10 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many questioning whether the measures can genuinely help those in need.

Asked what they thought about the initiative, a local resident told domestic media, “It’s both good and bad. The good thing is that people who are genuinely struggling can come here to get a meal and meet their basic needs. The bad thing is, how can you tell who has money and who doesn’t?”

Other users suggested requiring customers to show their ID cards to exclude locals and help migrant workers.

In an interview with domestic media, Zhang rejected the idea of screening customers. “We want to give people facing difficulties a sense of dignity and respect,” he said.

Domestic media reported that one nearby restaurant’s daily revenue had fallen from 3,000 yuan ($450) to just a few hundred yuan. Another shop owner said he was considering not renewing his lease over concerns about declining customer traffic.

However, some shop owners said customer traffic along the street had already fallen after the relocation of several nearby factories. Others said the free noodle shops had not significantly affected their business.

Zhang told domestic media that affected business owners could work at his stores if they were willing.

He added that the two shops could lose up to 10 million yuan a year. The stores do not have payment QR codes, and he has also turned down donation offers from friends.

The shops have reportedly recently installed barriers to keep lines orderly and stopped providing noodle refills and napkins to discourage those who don’t truly need help from taking advantage of the offer.

Authorities told domestic media they had found no evidence that the restaurants were providing free meals as a publicity stunt. Local authorities also said they had visited the shops to check food safety compliance and help maintain order among customers queuing outside.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Crowds gather at a “zero-yuan noodle shop” in Nanjing, Jiangsu province, October 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019244/What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
World.title: What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019244/What a Lost City Can Tell Us About Chinese Civilization’s ‘First Draft’
World.content:
Fufeng County, some 110 kilometers west of the northwestern Chinese city of Xi’an, is best known for its stunning Tang dynasty (618–907) relics, unearthed from an underground crypt beneath Famen Temple in the late 1980s.

But ask a Chinese archaeologist about Fufeng, and they’ll likely point you in another direction: toward a quiet cluster of more than 20 villages located along the border with neighboring Qishan County. There, hidden beneath unassuming farms and village houses, lies what a growing number of experts believe was the first capital of the Western Zhou (1046–771 BC) — one of China’s earliest and most important dynasties.

Known as Zhouyuan — literally “The Plains of Zhou” — its excavation sites have produced some of China’s most famous bronze ritual vessels. In the 1940s, those discoveries led archaeologist Shi Zhangru to survey the area and eventually propose that this was Qiyi, the center of Zhou culture before the Zhou toppled the Shang dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BC).

In the decades that followed, archaeologists worked on the site sporadically, uncovering large rammed-earth building foundations, cemeteries, craft workshops, bronze hoards, and oracle bones, all dating to the Zhou period.

Yet planned, continuous excavation at Zhouyuan began only at the turn of the 21st century, when the Institute of Archaeology at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, and Peking University’s School of Archaeology and Museology formed a joint team to systematically explore the site.

Why the delay? Part of the problem was historiographical. Chinese scholars have long relied on written texts to locate historic sites, and for more than 2,000 years historians placed the Western Zhou capital dozens of kilometers away, in a place called Fenghao, near Xi’an.

This drew attention and resources from other sites in the region, including Zhouyuan. But over the past decade or so, the joint archaeological team at Zhouyuan has made a string of breakthroughs that suggest Shi Zhangru’s near-century-old hunch might be right — and possibly even show that Zhouyuan, not Fenghao, was the Western Zhou’s first capital.

“Modern excavations are revealing more and more contradictions between the archaeological record and traditional accounts,” Cao Dazhi, a Peking University-based archaeologist and co-leader of the Zhouyuan team, wrote in a 2023 paper. Cao’s analysis attracted widespread attention in China for arguing that Zhouyuan was the Zhou capital, while the Fenghao region was merely an important hub and site of the royal hunting grounds.

But the dispute over ancient capitals may not be the biggest revelation to emerge from the Zhouyuan excavations.

While the exact significance of the discoveries remains a matter of debate even within the team, mounting evidence suggests the Zhou capital’s population was far more diverse than previously thought. In addition to the core Zhou population, it was home to large numbers of conquered Shang, as well as migrants from the northwest and south.

That matters because, over time, the Zhou would establish a very different political and moral order from the Shang, one combining military power with ritual, moral claims to legitimacy, and the incorporation of conquered peoples. This order would help shape Chinese political culture for the next 3,000 years, but where did it come from? And could the answer lie in the palaces, streets, and workshops of Zhou’s most prominent early settlement?

“Sweet as sugar”

Zhouyuan was founded by a people on the move.

According to legend, an ancestor of the Zhou people had served as an agriculture official under the Xia — a legendary state traditionally regarded as China’s first dynasty — and the clan made its living farming the land north of what is now Xi’an.

After the Xia declined, the clan lost its fief. For most of the Shang, the Zhou wandered from place to place.

Finally, around the 12th century BC, their leader Gugong Danfu set out with his people in search of a land where they could finally settle and prosper.

“Mian,” a poem from the “Book of Songs,” China’s oldest surviving poetry anthology, tells this story in just 400 characters: After a long journey, the Zhou arrive at a place called Mount Qi, where they find wild herbs “sweet as malt sugar.” They carve a turtle shell for divination, and the resulting oracle tells them to settle there.

Laborers toil under the direction of officials, stretching cords to mark straight lines and raising frames to tamp the earth. Soon, “a hundred walls rise together.” Ancestral temples, palaces, and homes are built, roads are laid down, and the local barbarian tribes, awed by the magnificent new city, can only flee in disarray.

The claim that Zhouyuan’s wild grass tasted as sweet as sugar may be poetic license, but modern archaeological discoveries support the outlines of the story. Archaeological and environmental evidence suggests that the region offered favorable conditions for early agriculture, with fertile loess soils and plentiful rainfall.

That supported the Zhou as they developed a mixed agricultural system dominated by millet and, later, wheat. The region’s abundance is reflected in the contents of a predynastic Zhou storage pit — a kind of primitive refrigerator with walls plastered in straw-tempered mud — containing some 500 apricot pits, more than 150 melon seeds, and a handful of plum pits, some still glossy after 3,000 years.

But the crucial evidence for Zhouyuan as the site of the Zhou’s foremost settlement only came in 2020, with the discovery of a building archaeologists call Wangjiazui No. 1. Covering more than 2,500 square meters, the compound is divided into front and rear sections, with a front courtyard framed by gatehouses, side chambers, and a front hall. In the rear lies another courtyard, surrounded by a hall, side chambers, and a back chamber.

It’s a structure of truly royal proportions, and Wangjiazui No. 1 quickly caught the attention of the archaeological team. “Ever since Shi Zhangru proposed in the 1940s that Zhouyuan was where Gugong Danfu migrated, the bronze hoards and large building foundations unearthed here have steadily reinforced that judgment — but hard proof of a high-ranking predynastic building was always missing,” Chong Jianrong, director of the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, tells Sixth Tone. “Large rammed-earth foundations are the most direct indicator of a settlement’s rank: Only a settlement with capital-level political functions could build such a structure. Wangjiazui No. 1 provides that key evidence.”

Based on stratigraphy and radiocarbon dating, the team confirmed that the building dated to the predynastic Zhou period, before the conquest of Shang, thereby verifying the existence of a “central settlement” within the Zhouyuan cluster. Wangjiazui No. 1’s size and clearly defined layout are unmatched among predynastic finds, and archaeologists were also able to trace a belt of predynastic structures stretching over 150 meters from north to south — evidence of a deliberately planned settlement that was developed continuously, rather than a temporary encampment.

Yet even the grandest predynastic building at Zhouyuan pales next to contemporary Shang architecture: the No. 1 palace at the Shang city of Huanbei, built at least a century earlier, covers some 16,000 square meters — six times the size of Wangjiazui No. 1.

The gulf in scale reflected a gulf in power. In the 12th century BC, the Shang were a powerful empire built on violence and tight state control, with formidable armies, complex cities, and impressive industry.

The Zhou, meanwhile, were still a small tribe on the distant fringes of the Shang cultural sphere. But after centuries of wandering, they had finally found land to farm and walls to call home. And within a few generations, their roles would flip as the Zhou destroyed the Shang and conquered the Chinese heartland.

A melting pot

In early 1046 BC, on a plain in what is now the central province of Henan, the Battle of Muye — a clash that would transform the course of Chinese history — was about to begin.

According to traditional accounts, Ji Fa, Gugong Danfu’s great-grandson, led a coalition of allied tribes numbering fewer than 50,000 men. Opposing them was a Shang army said to number hundreds of thousands. Yet despite its supposed numerical superiority, the Shang force offered little resistance, and its defenses collapsed almost immediately. The decisive battle was over in a single day — and with it, nearly six centuries of Shang rule.

Zhou’s conquest of Shang greatly expanded their territory. To administer their new lands, the Zhou established two capitals. One was Luoyi, near present-day Luoyang in Henan. Close to the conquered Shang heartland, it was intended to keep watch over Shang remnants and the eastern lords.

For centuries, the other was believed to be Fenghao, in what is now Xi’an’s Chang’an District, roughly 90 kilometers from Zhouyuan as the crow flies.

But recent finds at Zhouyuan have uncovered hard evidence against that view: in particular, the presence of a walled city of about 1.75 million square meters, with a palace complex at its core.

The palace lies at the exact center of the city’s northern half, says Cao, the Peking University archaeologist whose article kickstarted the Fenghao-Zhouyuan debate. Covering roughly 500,000 square meters, it is the largest and best-preserved pre-Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) palace complex ever discovered.

A comprehensive coring survey in 2023 revealed buildings across almost the entire site. Roads crisscross the area: the avenue leading into the city was paved with a foundation of large stones topped with soil and gravel, not unlike a modern gravel road. And in the moats outside the palace city’s walls, archaeologists found oracle bones used in royal divination.

“By comparison, no city walls have yet been found at Fenghao,” Cao says. “In fact, Zhouyuan’s remains of every kind are richer than Fenghao’s: more people, more nobles and officials, more wealth.” He adds that a building he is currently excavating is the largest structure ever found from the Western Zhou.

Inside the palace district, members of the royal house would have enjoyed the highest luxuries the age could offer. Beyond the palace walls, the settlement hummed with industry. Archaeologists have identified 61 craft production sites within the settlement, which produced bronzes, bone objects, pottery, jade ware, and lacquered wood.

Notably, many of the laborers staffing these workshops were not from the Zhou. Strontium isotope analysis of human bones and teeth from sites across the Yellow River basin found that populations at predynastic Zhou and Western Zhou sites were among the most heterogeneous on record in China, pointing to large-scale migration to Zhouyuan.

The influx began even before the conquest of Shang, says Chong of the Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology. He identifies two early waves of migration: people associated with the Nianzipo culture to the north, whose graves featured distinctive vertical shafts, followed by people associated with the Liujia culture to the west, who used catacomb-style tombs.

Once the Western Zhou was established and Zhouyuan became a dynastic capital, people and cultural influences converged there from every direction — including the Chu from the south and the Qin from the west. Two shell carvings of human heads unearthed in 1980 feature high-bridged noses and deep-set eyes reminiscent of depictions of the Saka, a Scythian-related people of the Eurasian steppe — a hint that even more distant groups may have lived at Zhouyuan.

But the largest group of migrants came from the east: the conquered people of the Shang. In fact, the Shang may have been the city’s second-largest demographic after the Zhou themselves.

“The population structure of Zhouyuan was highly complex, and the available material doesn’t yet support precise ratios,” Chong tells Sixth Tone. “But what is certain is that, while the Zhou formed the ruling core, other groups from the northwest and south were integrated in different ways; and Shang remnants were a major group of considerable size.”

Learning from the conquered

So why were so many Shang people living in the Zhou capital?

Immediately after their victory at Muye, the Zhou were faced with a challenge: how to integrate this distant power center into their new state. They moved quickly to extend their rule east, building Luoyi to strengthen their position in the Shang heartland, while planting their agents and allies at strategic points throughout the new territory.

They also pursued a deliberate strategy of breaking up the close-knit Shang clans and resettling them across their empire.

It must have been a colossal undertaking. At its peak, the Shang capital alone is estimated to have had a permanent population in the hundreds of thousands. But in the eyes of the Zhou rulers, the effort of relocating large numbers of people hundreds of kilometers was worth the trouble. Not only did it allow them to keep a close eye on their new subjects, but it also made a powerful political statement: the remnants of the fallen dynasty had fully submitted to the Zhou order.

Then there were the practical reasons for the relocation: Archaeological finds suggest that Zhouyuan’s new Shang residents clustered around the city’s workshops, where they would have put their technological know-how and skills to work for their new rulers.

“In the predynastic period, bronze casting across the Guanzhong region (surrounding Zhouyuan) was scarce, and only very simple vessels could be made,” Cao tells Sixth Tone. “Then, at a certain point, large numbers of exquisite bronzes suddenly appear, essentially identical to late Shang products.”

Scholars such as Cao speculate that this sudden shift was connected to the Zhou bringing Shang artisans — along with bronzes seized in war — back to Zhouyuan.

Bronze was just one of many crafts and cultural practices the Zhou learned from the Shang. Li Xueqin, the late chief scientist of the state-sponsored Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project, compared the oracle-bone inscriptions of Yinxu and Zhouyuan and found them “more alike than different” — evidence of continuity in the writing system and divination practices across the two dynasties.

Song Jiangning, who heads the CASS Institute of Archaeology’s Zhouyuan project, argues that several early Western Zhou buildings imitate Shang architectural forms, and believes that their designers were most likely Shang people.

The evidence suggests the Zhou allowed these people to maintain many of their cultural practices. Excavations at multiple Zhouyuan workshops show that Shang people carried on key traditions, including burying their dead close to home and organizing production around clan lines.

Production and daily life were concentrated within the workshop quarters; the dead were buried there in their clan’s customary way; and children inherited the family trade. In other words, the Zhou rulers treated them with relative leniency — especially in contrast to the Shang’s own brutal treatment of outsiders, as attested by the large numbers of human sacrifice victims unearthed at the former Shang capital.

“The archaeological material tells us that the early Western Zhou inherited many Shang practices across the board — crafts, writing, architectural layouts, and even the ‘hereditary artisan clan’ mode of organizing production,” Chong tells Sixth Tone.

Running dry

As Zhouyuan attracted more and more people, its workshops continued to grow, eventually outpacing the city’s initially planned borders.

Toward the end of the Western Zhou period, the dynasty established a new, far larger settlement southeast of the original city, roughly tripling Zhouyuan in size and turning it into the largest known Chinese city of the Western Zhou. Excavations have uncovered walls and gates on a scale unprecedented for the pre-Qin period. It was a clear display of power and order.

Yet the city’s residents had little time to enjoy their magnificent new metropolis. In 771 BC, after 275 years of rule, the Western Zhou fell. Nomadic tribes from the west invaded the Guanzhong Basin, and King Ping fled east with his lords to the dynasty’s second capital of Luoyi. The Zhou would survive as the Eastern Zhou, but royal power quickly declined, and China descended into centuries of conflict and war.

Curiously, archaeologists have found almost no Eastern Zhou artifacts at Zhouyuan.

That might seem natural enough: after all, Zhouyuan was no longer the capital. But experts say it is highly unusual. “Think about it,” Song Jiangning of CASS tells Sixth Tone. “Chinese history is full of cities — Xi’an, Nanjing, Hangzhou — that were once capitals and later weren’t. When a city loses capital status, the royals and officials leave, sure. But do ordinary people leave? No. They go on with their lives. Zhouyuan is different. After the Western Zhou, the people of that city disappeared almost completely.”

The bronze hoards found densely packed across the site suggest the city’s abandonment was sudden.

“Picture the scene: the city suffers a sudden disaster, and the noble families must flee with the royal house,” Cao explains. “Their bronzes are incredibly precious — and far too heavy to carry — so they hastily dig pits and stash them away. The density of bronze hoards at Zhouyuan makes it easy to picture the rows of aristocratic mansions that once stood here, and the panic of their owners’ flight.”

But what exactly was the catastrophe? Many historians attribute the city’s fall to invasions by groups from the west. Song, however, wonders whether the city succumbed to something deadlier than war.

“Down through the ages, cities have generally met one of two fates,” he says. “The first is ‘rise and decline’: once a capital, then no longer; once prosperous, then decayed. That kind of story is common, and behind it are human factors.”

“The second fate, less common, is ‘life and death,’” he says. “Liangzhu died, Shimao died, Taosi died, the capitals of the 36 states of the Western Regions almost all died. Perhaps that is what happened to Zhouyuan. The death of a city means its people simply could no longer live there — and behind that usually lie forces of nature.”

For years, Song has studied the relationship between Zhouyuan’s water resources and its urban planning, hoping to crack the mystery of the city’s disappearance. Zhouyuan sits on a loess tableland, and its inhabitants drew water from two rivers descending from the mountains. To secure a sufficient, stable supply, they built a hydraulic system covering more than 30 square kilometers — enormous in scale and remarkably complex and refined in design.

For a time, the artificial canals worked well. But rivers rushing down from the mountains continually cut deeper into their channels; as the water levels fell, the canals had to be dug ever deeper, and at ever greater cost. Meanwhile, Zhouyuan kept expanding, and the demand for water kept growing.

To make matters worse, sediment analysis suggests that the city’s water-management authorities maintained the system diligently in the early Western Zhou, but grew lax in the middle period, and had ceased to function entirely by the dynasty’s collapse.

Although the evidence is inconclusive, water scarcity may be one reason Zhouyuan was abandoned. The same may have happened to several large Western Zhou dozens of kilometers to the west.

To Song, the quest to understand how Zhouyuan collapsed is almost as important as the answer itself. “To attend to one thing is inevitably to neglect another — and on that, we are no different from the ancients,” he says. “What the ancients did is done and cannot be redone. But we can study them, assess them, and learn from them. Zhouyuan is a modern-day revelation — how it rose, prospered, and died.”

A new order

The death of Zhouyuan was a catastrophe for the nobles and commoners who called it home. For archaeologists today, it has proven an unexpected gift.

One need only compare it with Luoyi — modern-day Luoyang — the Zhou’s eastern capital. Celebrated in China as the “ancient capital of thirteen dynasties,” Luoyang has served as a seat of power longer, and for more dynasties, than almost any other city in China. But that very longevity is the archaeologist’s headache: wave upon wave of construction has left cultural layers piled one atop another, making dating unearthed remains a thorny task.

Zhouyuan is different. No major city has stood there since the Western Zhou. The land has been farmed for nearly 3,000 years, and remains so today.

For China’s archaeologists and historians, that is rare good fortune, especially given that Zhouyuan may contain the answer to one of the longest-standing riddles in Chinese history: How China transitioned from the Shang to the Zhou, whose focus on ritual, order, and moral justifications for rule would shape future Chinese states for millennia.

Over a hundred years ago, the renowned scholar Wang Guowei called the Shang-Zhou transition “the most drastic transformation in Chinese politics and culture.” In essence, it shifted the basis of political order — from sacrificial ritual to political ethics. The Shang revered gods and ghosts, seeking to appease them with elaborate sacrifices, including human sacrifice; the Zhou, while not immediately breaking from Shang practices entirely, set out to build an alternative justification for their rule.

Historians have read this shift in many ways. According to one widely shared view, the Shang placed their faith in divination and sacrifice, trusting that so long as the rituals never lapsed, their ancestors and the spirits would protect them.

The Zhou advanced a different argument: Heaven favored virtue, and political legitimacy depended on the moral conduct of the ruler. Through the patriarchal clan system and the strategic allocation of titles and fiefs, they wove political and ethical order into a single fabric.

Dynasties rose and fell over the nearly 3,000 years that followed, and the machinery of government was rebuilt many times — but the Zhou ideal of “governing through virtue” endured. “By the Western Zhou, Chinese civilization had its ‘final draft,’” says Song.

Now, archaeologists can look for the physical evidence of that transition. The numerous tombs of Shang survivors found around Zhouyuan’s craft workshops, for instance, reveal a dynasty that inherited Shang culture and technology on a massive scale even as it labored to build a new ethical and moral order — one that could legitimize Zhou rule while incorporating conquered peoples and other groups.

“What did not change between Shang and Zhou dwarfs what did,” says Chong. “But that is precisely why we focus on the change — on how the Zhou built the ritual order that would define Chinese political culture for the next 3,000 years.”

(Header image: Visuals from Shaanxi Academy of Archaeology, reedited by Fu Xiaofan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: Making P-pop history: SB19, BINI nominated for 2027 Grammys
World.content:
The two P-pop groups are nominated under the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category

MANILA, Philippines – History is made as P-pop groups SB19 and BINI are nominated for the 69th Grammy Awards.

The Recording Academy announced on Monday, November 16 (Manila time), that the two Filipino music acts were nominated under the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category.

SB19 received a nomination for the song “VISA,” while BINI was nominated for “Unang Kilig.”

“From the Philippines to the world, thank you for believing in SB19 and standing with us as we carry Filipino music to the global stage!” SB19 said about its nomination.

“A historic moment for OPM, for Filipino music, and for everyone who believes in them. The girls are making history, and we couldn’t be prouder! Thank you to everyone who continues to support us!” BINI wrote.

Under the Best Asian Pop Music Performance category, SB19 and BINI are joined by fellow nominees, K-pop girl groups IVE (“BANG BANG”) and KiiiKiii (“404 (New Era)”), Japanese soloist LiSA (“Yes”), and Japanese kawaii metal band BABYMETAL and American rock outfit Polyphia (“Sunset Kiss”).

SB19 and BINI’s nominations come at a time when the two groups have achieved several major milestones all year.

BINI became the first-ever homegrown Filipino music act to perform at the 2026 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival in April, while SB19 later achieved the same feat in July at Lollapalooza in Chicago.

SB19 will also be heading to Coachella in April 2027. Their inclusion in the lineup was just announced on November 11.

BINI, meanwhile, just wrapped up their 2026 BINI Signals World Tour in Taiwan on November 15. – Rappler.com

World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The global energy crisis, food security, and transnational crime are among the top issues on the table as Southeast Asian leaders and their allies converge in Manila.

The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for 2026, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from Sunday, November 15, to Tuesday, November 17.

Aside from leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, other world leaders will be in attendance, including United States President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is embarking on a state visit to the Philippines before the summit.

During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

World.title: Climate advocates at COP31 urge probe into mass arrests at ASEAN protests
World.content:
PAX SILICA PROTEST. Militants gather at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila on November 15, 2026, to protest the proposed Pax Silica initiative and US President Donald Trump's visit to the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Pax Silica, a key issue in the ASEAN protests, is opposed by many environmental and climate groups as well

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino climate justice and environmental advocates present at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, are urging an independent probe into the mass arrests of people who joined the protests against the ASEAN Summit back in Manila.

“Whether at COP31 or the ASEAN Summit, the government cannot speak of a peoples-centered future while treating their voices as a security threat,” read the groups’ statement released Monday, November 16.

They demanded “an independent, transparent and immediate investigation into the arbitrary mass arrests and illegal detention.”

Climate justice activists underscored the link between the fight for the planet and for human rights and democratic freedoms.

“We stand in solidarity with the victims of this police brutality, their families, and the communities demanding accountability,” they said.

A key issue in the ASEAN protests is the Philippines’ participation in the United States’ initiative Pax Silica

— a red flag for environmental groups for its components of building data centers and processing critical minerals.

The groups called on the government to “reject the Pax Silica initiative and all related projects affecting ancestral domains, respecting the right of affected indigenous peoples to free, prior, and informed consent.”

Some of the climate organizations listed as signatories in the statement have members or allies who were arrested in the protests in Manila.

The 49th ASEAN Summit, hosted by the Philippines, opened on Sunday, November 15. Hundreds who massed up for the protests in Metro Manila on Sunday were arrested. Nearly 300 people, delegates of Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan opposing the expected visit of US President Donald Trump, were arrested in Muntinlupa.

There were also arrests in Bulacan, Liwasang Bonifacio, Malate Church, and Welcome Rotonda in Quezon City, according to various local environmental and human rights groups.

“This is one of the largest mass arrests by the PNP (Philippine National Police) in recent years,” the International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines noted. The network has started a donation drive for legal funds to support those arrested.

Even before the opening of the ASEAN Summit, thousands of students had already walked out and marched on the streets.

Meanwhile, Bishop Gerry Alminaza, climate champion of the Catholic Bishops Conference of the Philippines, called on the government to “stop criminalizing the poor.”

“It is unconscionable that the poor are met with police violence when they should be met with justice, protection and action,” Alminaza, who was also in Turkey for the climate summit, said in a separate statement on Monday. – Rappler.com

World.title: Lawmakers, groups slam November 15 arrests: Where is maximum tolerance?
World.content:
ASEAN PROTEST. Police arrest a protester in Liwasang Bonifacio during the opening of the ASEAN Summit in Manila, on November 15, 2026.

'Where is the maximum tolerance expected of police officers and their respect for freedom of speech and expression in these arrests?' asks Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima

MANILA, Philippines – Several personalities and groups raised concerns over the massive arrests of activists and media workers during Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Pax Silica-related protests in Metro Manila on Sunday, November 15.

Progressive group Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (BAYAN) condemned the arrests, saying that they contradict the statement of Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Nartatez Jr.’s claim that the summit’s opening was “generally peaceful.”

“It is the police who were caught on camera kicking down arrested protesters in Manila, manhandling Lakbayan delegates in Sucat, and torturing the detainees by threatening to handcuff those who refuse to have their mugshots taken. They acted like criminal thugs who ordered the throwing of human waste at the Liwasang Bonifacio to discourage people from gathering in the park,” BAYAN said on Monday, November 16.

“The police should also explain the use of deadly weapons such as nails and ice picks in puncturing the tires of the truck to be used for the protest in Manila,” the group added.

As of Sunday, the Manila Police District said at least 11 protesters were arrested by the police in Liwasang Bonifacio.

Most of the arrests in Metro Manila happened in Muntinlupa, where PNP nabbed 276 individuals. They were from Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan, who were heading to Liwasang Bonifacio to join other groups that protested against Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump’s expected arrival.

Some student journalists were also among those arrested.

Mamamayang Liberal Representative Leila de Lima questioned the PNP’s supposed observance of maximum tolerance and respect for freedom of expression. She called for an investigation into the reported violence and alleged denial of detainees’ access to lawyers and family members.

“Where is the maximum tolerance expected of police officers and their respect for freedom of speech and expression in these arrests?” said De Lima.

“We strongly condemn these arrests and the disregard for protesters’ rights. We demand a thorough investigation into the reported unlawful acts committed by the arresting officers and that those responsible be held accountable. All protesters who have been illegally detained must be released immediately!” she added.

On Sunday, several progressive groups gathered outside Camp Bagong Diwa, Taguig City, to denounce the arrests.

“Pinapakita ng pag-aresto sa humigit-kumulang tatlong daang Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan kung kaninong interes ba talaga nagsisilbi ang rehimeng US-Marcos. Sa pagbisita ni Trump, pinapakita talaga na nasa interes ng mga dayuhang bansa ang interes nila,” human rights advocate Charm Maranan said.

(The arrest of almost 300 people of Lakbayani ng Timog Katagulan shows where the interest of the US-Marcos regime truly lies. With Trump’s visit, it just shows that their interest lies in a foreign country.)

The Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan protest march kicked off in Los Baños, Laguna, on November 12, with progressive groups led by BAYAN Timog Katagalugan.

Throughout the march, activist groups and alternative media outlets reported multiple instances of harassment from the police. This included blocking the march’s path, allegedly sabotaging the protest vehicles’ tires, alleged violent manhandling of arrested protesters, and denial of the Commission on Human Rights and lawyers’ entry to police stations.

Call for accountability

“Malinaw na ginagarantiya ng Saligang Batas ang kalayaan nating magpahayag at mapayapang magtipon. Ang kakayahan ng mamamayang pumuna at manawagan ng pagbabago ang patunay na buhay ang ating demokrasya,” said Akbayan Representative Chel Diokno.

(It’s clear that the Constitution guarantees our freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. The ability of the citizens to redress their grievances and call for change is proof that our democracy is alive.)

Meanwhile, the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) demanded the immediate release of individuals detained for participating in or covering the protests. The group also appealed to fellow lawyers to provide legal assistance to those arrested, calling on them to “help secure the freedom of the arrestees.”

“While we have already dispatched quick reaction teams to assist the detainees, we need more lawyers to assist them. And we are calling [on] our people’s lawyers to once again rise to the occasion. Our brave clients need brave lawyers,” said NUPL president Ephraim Cortez.

Karapatan secretary general Cristina Palabay also pushed for accountability from police personnel and officers involved in the reported assaults.

“Protestors must be immediately released,” Palabay asserted, urging authorities to guarantee the arrested’s access to legal counsel, relatives, and medical assistance while in custody.

On a similar note, the National Union of Journalists of the Philippines also pressed authorities to stop the violence against media workers, noting the importance of peaceful assembly and press freedom.

“Journalists must be allowed to exercise their duty to cover public events, document abuses, and report the stories of those who take to the streets,” the union stated. – Ren Enano and Rhen Peñada/Rappler.com

Rena Eñano and Rhen Peñada are Rappler volunteers. Eñano is a senior literature student from Ateneo de Manila University, while Peñada is a third-year information technology student from Polytechnic University of the Philippines Sta. Rosa, Laguna Campus.

World.title: [Vantage Point] Clark’s billions demand public accounting
World.content:
Joshua Bingcang’s move from BCDA to PEZA leaves unanswered questions over Clark International Airport’s concession returns and asset valuations, alongside procurement, financing, and tax issues surrounding the New Clark City sports complex. While leadership changes neither prove wrongdoing nor absolve officials, true accountability demands opening the books to show whether taxpayers secured a fair bargain.

Joshua Bingcang’s transfer from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) to the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA) leaves a massive public accounting unfinished.

BCDA. Former Bases Conversion and Development Authority president and CEO Engineer Joshua Bingcang, in Makati City on March 9, 2026. Rappler

While his successor Ariel Nepomuceno now inherits the institutional duty to explain BCDA’s transactions, a simple changing of the guard does not settle the questions raised by state auditors and government agencies on how government funds were handled.

Establishing public accountability begins with examining the roles officials actually held. BCDA’s 2023 annual report identifies Bingcang as New Clark City’s overall project manager during his tenure as senior vice president, placing him in charge of business strategies and construction oversight.

He also chaired the special bids and awards committee for Clark airport operations and maintenance. While holding these positions does not prove personal wrongdoing or confirm his sign-off on every specific transfer or payment, it squarely justifies scrutinizing the recommendations he made while steering these multi-billion-peso ventures.

An airport concession is worth far more than the terminal it operates, just as a sports complex costs more than its concrete and steel. At Clark, a true public accounting must capture the land, commercial contracts, financing obligations, and tax responsibilities underpinning the infrastructure. Official records raise pointed questions about these contributions, making documentary transparency all the more essential.

Play Video

Consider the 25-year concession for Clark International Airport, operated by the Luzon International Premiere Airport Development Corp. (LIPAD). Bringing together Philippine corporate and aviation players—Filinvest Development Corp., JG Summit Holdings Inc., and Philippine Airport Ground Support Solutions Inc.—alongside Singaporean expertise via Changi Airports Philippines, LIPAD manages a vast commercial footprint.

According to the Clark International Airport Corp. (CIAC), the concession covers 759 hectares and includes 110 transferred lease agreements. Although these figures describe operating coverage and transferred contracts rather than an outright sale of state land, existing tenants and leases carry substantial economic value that the government’s returns must accurately reflect.

BCDA maintains that the government receives an 18.25% revenue share plus P500 million annually for 20 years—a P10-billion stream before discounting or examining contractual qualifications. Yet numbers in isolation tell an incomplete story. Without weighing those receipts against the commercial rights transferred, investment obligations, and retained public risks, it is impossible to establish whether taxpayers secured a favorable bargain or an undervalued concession.

Audit issues

Underlying asset valuations complicate the picture further. A CIAC audit-action report describes separate negotiations over assigning assets to BCDA for the LIPAD concession. In June 2025, BCDA reported that 40 buildings valued at P934 million were already recorded in its books—a move CIAC said occurred without its knowledge, prompting it to contest BCDA’s recording of the passenger terminal and crash-fire-and-rescue buildings that CIAC itself financed.

Meanwhile, seven other buildings worth approximately P478 million were excluded from the proposed assignment after CIAC clarified it did not own them under existing leases. By September 2025, BCDA’s recommended P263.73-million assignment figure stood sharply against the P777.12-million net book value under CIAC review.

Different asset coverage and accounting treatments might explain those figures without establishing a financial loss, and asset assignment to BCDA must be distinguished from LIPAD’s operational use, but the public deserves a reconciled ledger.

BCDA and the SEA Games controversy

SEA GAMES. New Clark City’s athletic stadium built for the 30th Southeast Asian Games in 2019. Rappler file

The Southeast Asian Games sports facilities at New Clark City present a distinct set of questions involving a different partner and agreement. While the Philippine Competition Commission confirmed that Malaysian firm MTD Capital Berhad’s unsolicited proposal went through a competitive challenge, and BCDA’s financial statements show that government acquisition of the facilities—with an option to shorten repayment—was contemplated by the agreement, acquisition alone establishes no improper buyback. (Read Rappler’s special report on this controversy by clicking these links below:

However, the Commission on Audit (COA) questioned the procurement route itself, finding that sports facilities originally conceptualized by BCDA were negotiated into an unsolicited proposal, granting MTD an “undue advantage.”

BCDA disputed this finding, defending the integrity of its Swiss challenge. Resolving these competing positions requires opening up to public view the original proposal, negotiated changes, and challenge documents. (Read more stories on the SEA Games controversy by clicking these links below:

The financial breakdown also warrants closer inspection. BCDA’s published figures put total payment at P9.539 billion: P8.510 billion for the sports facilities, P579 million in financing costs, and P450 million in ICT (Information and Communications Technology) variations.

These additions are not all interest or automatic evidence of overpricing. BCDA defended a 7.5% financing rate under an arrangement where savings below that benchmark would be shared 90:10 between the government and MTD. Settlement records should verify actual borrowing costs and confirm whether any credited savings materialized.

Tax compliance adds another unresolved thread. An audit done in 2020 recorded payments of P5.145 billion in December 2019 and P4.394 billion in April 2020, flagging P343 million in taxes withheld but not remitted to the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), alongside P274.613 million in required withholding taxes never deducted from the later payment. Management explained that the venture was not yet fully incorporated or BIR-registered while anticipating PEZA tax incentives, citing missing incorporation approvals and promising a resolution in 2021.

Auditors maintained that the withholding obligation still applied. Instead of relying on unsupported assertions of continuing nonpayment, the relevant focus today should be what registrations, remittances, and corrective actions actually took place afterward.

Legal developments offer no shortcuts to accountability. An earlier complaint involving then-BCDA chief Vince Dizon and others was dismissed for insufficient evidence in December 2021, a ruling the Ombudsman announced it would review in July 2026. (READ: NBI probes 2019 SEA Games: What we know so far)

Neither development establishes liability for Bingcang, who became BCDA president in 2023—well after the original award and payments. Individual responsibility cannot be inferred from a job title alone. It requires tracing the documentary record to identify who proposed each arrangement, evaluated its financial terms, and authorized its implementation.

Ultimately, an institution’s account of benefits must be tested against its contractual commitments and actual receipts, payments, and recoveries. Both the airport and the sports facilities must be assessed through their separate contracts and documented obligations. (READ: Auditors flag P290-M Clark air traffic control tower project delays, cost overruns)

Publishing reconciled asset schedules, procurement justifications, financing calculations, and tax resolutions would allow the public to evaluate these bargains for themselves.

The real test is whether the government can demonstrate that it properly valued its contribution, obtained adequate returns, and enforced the protections written into its agreements. – Rappler.com

World.title: SC declares parts of Magna Carta of Seafarers unconstitutional.  So what?
World.content:
The SC voids the rule that requires seafarers who had already won their labor disputes to post a bond or payment, while their shipowners or agencies are appealing the victory before a court

The Supreme Court (SC) has declared unconstitutional a provision in the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers. Groups had previously criticized the provision as discriminatory because it requires seafarers who initially win in cases to post a bond while their shipowner or manpower agency is appealing the decision.

The High Court likewise voided other provisions in the law and other issuances related to it.

In a decision penned by Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh, the High Court en banc partially granted the five consolidated petitions challenging the legality of Republic Act (RA) No. 12021, or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers. The petitions likewise questioned certain provisions of the law’s Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR), as well as related government issuances.

Petitioners include labor lawyer Sonny Matula, several seafarers, labor organizations, and maritime educational institutions.

“The Court emphasized that although the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers was enacted to advance the welfare of Filipino seafarers, all legislative measures must conform to the Constitution. The law therefore remains valid and enforceable, except for the provisions expressly declared unconstitutional or void,” said the ruling penned by Singh.

Signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in 2024, the Magna Carta clarifies the rights of Filipino seafarers — just working conditions, right to organize, and freedom from discrimination.

Bond payment is unconstitutional

The ruling voided the law’s Section 59 or the requirement for Filipino seafarers who had already won their labor disputes to post a bond or payment, while their shipowners or agencies are appealing the victory before courts. The bond requirement was supposedly meant to ensure restitution or monetary reward, should the case be subsequently reversed or modified.

Groups challenged this because the only chance for seafarers to be reimbursed for the bond they post is if they win their case.

The High Court sided with the petitioners and ruled that this bond requirement violates due process and equal protection clauses under the 1987 Constitution.

The SC said this rule imposes a financial burden on seafarers seeking to enforce favorable labor judgments, and subjects them to a disadvantage “not similarly imposed on other workers.”

“While recognizing the State’s interest in preventing ambulance chasing and protecting the maritime industry against unrestituted awards, the Court found that these objectives did not justify the challenged restriction on the execution of monetary awards,” said the SC.

The SC also declared unconstitutional the authorization to use the Department of Migrant Workers’ (DMW) Agarang Kalinga at Saklolo Para sa mga OFW na Nangangailangan (AKSYON) Fund to pay for the bond premiums. The High Court said this mechanism failed the constitutional requirement that public funds should be used for a public purpose, as found under Section 29(1), Article VI of the 1987 Constitution.

“Sections 4 and 5, Rule III of Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) Department Order No. 247, Series of 2025, were likewise declared unconstitutional and void insofar as they implemented the bond requirement,” the High Court added.

Play Video

“Great, at last, our petition was resolved by the SC. This a good news. This is victory for workers especially the seafarers,” Matula told Rappler.

“We argued [that Section 59] is discriminatory. It violates the equal protection clause of the 1987 Constitution because land-based workers do not face this requirement. We also contend that it creates an unfair financial burden on sick, injured, or unemployed seafarers,” he added.

More unconstitutional rules

The SC also struck down Section 60 of RA No. 12021, as well as Section 4 of RA No. 10706, or the Seafarers Protection Act. The High Court said these provisions regulated the practice of law, which is a violation of Section 5(5), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution.

Petitioners challenged these sections because they regulate lawyer-seafarer contracts and cap contingent legal fees at 10%.

“Petitioners argue that this rule (Section 60) usurps the exclusive constitutional power of the Supreme Court to regulate the practice of law and may restrict seafarers’ access to competent legal counsel,” said Matula.

The SC explained that while the legislative department may create laws to protect seafarers from lawyers’ alleged abusive practices like ambulance chasing, among others, the regulation of lawyers’ professional conduct and the practice of the law remains under the High Court’s exclusive authority.

Ambulance chasing refers to the practice of lawyers of soliciting professional employment.

Apart from the said provisions, the SC also declared unconstitutional Section 1, Rule XXII, of the law’s IRR. This is because it applies Section 59 to monetary rewards from complaints filed on or after the magna carta’s effectivity.

“The Court found that the implementing provision contravened Section 94 of the law, which expressly preserves the rights, privileges and benefits previously enjoyed by Filipino seafarers before its effectivity. It reiterated that administrative regulations must conform to the statute they implement and cannot diminish rights expressly preserved by law,” said the SC.

On maritime education

Meanwhile, the Court denied the challenge to the law’s Sections 75, 76, and 78, because it said they do not violate constitutional guarantee of academic freedom.

Section 75 – States that the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) has jurisdiction over maritime education in the country.

Section 76 – Requires shipboard training for international maritime degree programs. MARINA determines the applicability of the training, including the duration.

Section 78 – Requires maritime higher educational institutions offering international maritime degree programs to have their own training ships, simulators, or related technologies. This also requires them to enter into agreements with local or international shipping companies, shipowners, or agencies for the shipboard training program of students or cadets.

The Philippine Association of Maritime Institutions, Inc. and other maritime educational institutions questioned these provisions before the SC.

In its ruling, the SC said academic freedom ensures the autonomy of higher educational institutions, but this freedom does not exempt them from reasonable regulations.

“[The Court] found that the challenged provisions established minimum regulatory standards intended to ensure the quality of maritime education, the competency of Filipino seafarers, and compliance with applicable international maritime standards. Particularly, the requirements relating to enrollment and available shipboard training opportunities were considered reasonable measures to address the availability of practical training for maritime students,” said the SC.

“The prohibition against charging tuition or matriculation fees for shipboard training conducted by third party providers was likewise sustained as a measure against unjustified charges,” it added.

The petitioners also questioned the legislative process leading to the magna carta’s passage. But the SC denied this specific challenge and upheld the procedural validity of the law.

It found that Congress complied with the constitutional requirements in passing a law, such as the three-reading rule under Article VI of the Constitution.

“The Court likewise upheld the President’s Certification of Urgency and recognized the authority of the Bicameral Conference Committee to reconcile differences between the House and Senate versions of the proposed legislation,” the SC added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Police deny releasing suspects’ sketches in Basilan judge’s ambush
World.content:
Zamboanga City Mayor Khymer Olaso announces a P2-million reward during a press briefing at City Hall on Thursday, Nov. 12, for information leading to the arrest of the gunmen behind the killing of Isabela City Regional Trial Court Judge Joseph Wee Sit in Barangay Tumaga. Photo by Zamboanga City LGU Information Office

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – Police authorities in Western Mindanao on Monday denied releasing cartographic sketches of the suspects in the deadly ambush of Judge Joseph Wee Sit, warning the public against sharing unverified materials circulating online.

In separate advisories issued on Nov. 16, both the Police Regional Office 9 (PRO-9) and the Zamboanga City Police Office (ZCPO) refuted claims that official composite illustrations of the perpetrators had been made public.

“The Police Regional Office 9 clarifies that it has not released or issued any cartographic sketch pertaining to the suspects in the murder of Hon. Judge Joseph Wee Sit,” PRO-9 said in a statement.

Article continues after this 

Echoing the regional headquarters, the ZCPO stressed that it neither published nor disseminated any cartographic images tied to the ongoing probe into the killing of the judge.

Both police offices urged netizens and the general public to exercise vigilance, verify information strictly through official law enforcement channels, and refrain from spreading fake news that could sow confusion.

PRO-9 reiterated its commitment to providing the public with accurate and verified updates as the investigation into Wee Sit’s killing progresses. /ms

World.title: 2 nabbed, P260,000 ‘smuggled’ cigarettes seized in Surigao del Sur
World.content:
Police inspect P260,000 worth of suspected smuggled cigarettes seized during an operation in Tandag City, Surigao del Sur, on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Photo by PRO-13

SAN FRANCISCO, Agusan del Sur — Police arrested two individuals, including a minor, and seized 400 reams of suspected smuggled cigarettes valued at P260,000 following a high-speed chase in Tandag City, Surigao del Sur, on Sunday, Nov. 15.

Brig. Gen. Rolindo Suguilon, director of the Police Regional Office in Caraga (PRO-13), identified one of the suspects as alias “Abdul,” 45, a businessman from Barangay Villa Kananga in Butuan City, and his companion, a 16-year-old boy.

According to a police report, joint operatives from the Surigao del Sur Provincial Intelligence Unit, Tandag City Police Station, and the 2nd Surigao del Sur Provincial Mobile Force Company flagged down a Mitsubishi Mirage along the national highway in Barangay Buenavista.

Article continues after this 

Instead of stopping, the driver sped off, prompting a police pursuit.

Upon reaching Purok Papaya in Barangay Salvacion, the fleeing car collided with a three-wheeled utility vehicle locally known as a bao-bao. The impact caused several boxes of cigarettes to spill onto the road.

The two suspects attempted to flee on foot after the crash, but pursuing officers quickly cornered and arrested them.

Both suspects sustained injuries from the collision and were taken by personnel from the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office to the Adella Serra Ty Memorial Medical Center for treatment.

Aside from the getaway vehicle, police confiscated 400 reams of Casablanca cigarettes with an estimated market value of P260,000.

Article continues after this 

“PRO-13 remains steadfast in its campaign against smuggling and the proliferation of illicit tobacco products in the region. We will continue to strengthen our intelligence-driven operations and work closely with our partner agencies to ensure that individuals involved in these illegal activities are held accountable,” Suguilon said in a statement.

The suspects and the confiscated items were placed under the custody of the Tandag City Police Station for proper disposition.

Article continues after this 

Police said charges for alleged violation of Republic Act No. 10643, or the Graphic Health Warnings Law, are being prepared against Abdul, while the 16-year-old suspect will be turned over to local social welfare authorities. /ms

World.title: Clark segment of North-South Commuter Railway to be operational by 2029
World.content:
Transport Secretary Vince Dizon inspects the North-South Commuter Railway project in Clark, Pampanga on Monday, November 16, 2026. (Photo by DOTr/Facebook)

MANILA, Philippines — Commuters can look forward to a shorter travel time from Makati City to Clark International Airport as the Clark station of the North-South Commuter Railway (NSCR) is expected to be operational by 2029, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said on Monday.

“Lampas ng kaunti sa term ng pangulo pero ang importante, matatapos tayo na by 2029 from Makati hanggang dito sa Clark, tapos na,” Dizon said as he led the inspection of the NSCR project segment construction at the Clark Freeport Zone in Pampanga.

(It will exceed a little more than the president’s term, but what’s important is that the Makati to Clark segment will be finished by 2029).

Article continues after this 

Dizon said the completion of the Clark segment will improve connectivity for passengers who will be using the airport for their travels. He added that the project, once completed, is seen reducing travel time from Makati City to Clark International Airport from almost two hours to less than an hour.

READ: North-South Commuter Railway full operations moved to Q3 of 2033

The Clark segment is part of the 147-kilometer North-South Commuter Railway Project that will connect Metro Manila to Pampanga and Laguna.

Dizon also said that the Valenzuela-Malolos, Bulacan segment will be operational before the term of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ends in 2028. He added that the travel time in this area may be reduced from almost two hours to approximately 40 minutes.

According to him, the railway project would provide both mobility and convenience to commuters.

Article continues after this 

“Maraming sasakyan din ang mababawas sa NLEx (North Luzon Expressway) kasi imbes na magsasakyan, makakatipid sa gasolina, oras, at gastos. Para hindi na magsasakyan, magtren na lang. Napakaganda nito pag natapos,” he added.

(NLEx will see less cars because instead of using their vehicles, people can save more on gasoline, time, and money. They will just ride the train instead. This will be very nice once this is finished.)

Article continues after this 

READ: Lawmakers, JICA join inspection of North-South Commuter railway

Dizon said the Department of Transportation will prescribe the fares for the train line.

Meanwhile, Dizon acknowledged the delay in the construction of the project, which began in 2020.

He noted that right of way acquisition for the SM Clark to Angeles station is now at 90 percent, while the acquisition rate for the San Fernando station is at 60 percent.

“Matagal nang delayed to but wala na akong magagawa doon. I cannot bring back the past so we just have to move forward,” he stressed.

World.title: Yangon Condo Raid Reveals Myanmar’s Cyber Scam Sector Thriving in Commercial Capital
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime says it has arrested 106 suspected online scammers in Yangon, signaling the country’s cyber-fraud epidemic has spread from the lawless borderlands to its largest city.

The regime announced Saturday that its forces raided Golden River Residence Condo in Yangon’s Thaketa Township on November 12, arresting 52 Chinese naionals, eight Vietnamese and 46 Myanmar citizens from multiple apartments.

The arrests come as Naypyitaw and Beijing trumpet crackdowns on cyber-fraud syndicates in notorious border scam hubs.

Those reportedly detained included a high-profile target of China’s Public Security Ministry — the first arrest of a warranted Chinese scammer in Myanmar in months. Also seized from the condo were over 120 computers and laptops and nearly 200 mobile phones.

Authorities said the gang ran online investment fraud schemes targeting Chinese, Japanese, South Korean and Indian citizens, while separate Telegram-based operations targeted victims in Brazil and Colombia through fake e-commerce platforms.

The raid came shortly after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi pressed Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe to intensify efforts to combat scams and prevent a “resurgence of chaos” in Karen State’s Myawaddy crime hub on the Thai border.

Analysts say the Yangon bust signals a growing shift of Myanmar’s online scam industry from border enclaves to urban centers.

After the 2024 collapse of notorious fraud compounds in northern Shan State’s Laukkai and crackdowns along the Chinese and Thai borders, many scam syndicates dispersed in small, mobile operations through remote eastern and southern Shan, according to regime arrest reports and independent monitors.

However, many that had fled to Myawaddy have since moved deeper into the country under the protection of regime-aligned militias and other armed groups.

In September, 28 foreign and Myanmar nationals were arrested in Mandalay — the country’s second city — over an online gemstone scam involving Chinese, Indonesian and Malaysian suspects. The gang was charged with selling fake jade products via livestream and transferring the profits to accounts in Indonesia and Malaysia.

While the Nov. 12 raid was the first of its kind reported in Yangon, former fraudsters told The Irrawaddy that scam operations have long established a foothold in the commercial capital, targeting overseas victims through operations based in condominiums, housing estates and companies registered as legitimate businesses.

Analysts say enforcement efforts target low-level operators while overlooking the networks and militias behind the multibillion-dollar industry. Among them is the regime-aligned Karen Border Guard Force, whose Western-sanctioned leaders remain untouched even as the regime hails the demolition of scam compounds in Myawaddy.

World.title: ASEAN Seeks ‘Calibrated Engagement’ With Myanmar: Statement
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines—Southeast Asian leaders agreed Sunday on pursuing a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar’s post-coup government, according to a joint statement, as the regional bloc seeks a path towards normalization.

Myanmar is still a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but it has been frozen out of high-level meetings since a military junta seized power in a coup in 2021.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Bangkok has called for a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar in an effort to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC) plan aimed at ending the war between the military and a coalition of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority armed groups.

ASEAN leaders meeting in Manila adopted that language in calling for the pursuit of “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground,” according to the joint statement.

“Subject to sustained and concrete progress in the implementation of the 5PC by Myanmar, ASEAN may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation,” the statement said.

The five-point plan has yielded little in the half-decade since it was agreed to, with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos conceding at a May summit he had not seen “any progress in Myanmar.”

On Sunday, in opening remarks at an ASEAN leaders’ retreat in Manila, he repeated a question he had posed to the group six months earlier: “What more can we do for Myanmar?”

“I hope our session leads to practical and forward-looking discussions on how we can further advance the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, make our efforts more responsive to the realities on the ground, and support a peaceful, inclusive, Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led process,” he said.

The ASEAN bloc’s rotating chair will pass at the end of this year from the Philippines to Singapore, a city-state analysts say opposes normalizing ties with Myanmar.

In 2028, it will be the turn of Thailand, which shares a long border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations.

“We believe it’s crucial to have someone at the table who can really talk on policy issues because engagement requires that they have someone who can really convey to us the position of Myanmar,” Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told AFP in Singapore on November 5.

“This is not about… recognizing… upgrading their position. But I think in reality, what is important is that we need someone at the table who can speak on behalf of Myanmar.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation.
