World.title: Seven-year-old boy forced to empty clogged school toilet without gloves, parents say
World.content:
A seven-year-old boy was forced to empty the contents of a clogged Te Puke school toilet into a bucket without any gloves, his parents say.

The parents have removed the boy and his older brother from the school after a heated confrontation with the school principal over the incident.

Megan* says she could not believe what she was hearing from her children after picking them up from Paengaroa School last Thursday.

"My 10-year-old says: 'Elijah* (her seven-year-old) had to clean out the toilet today with his bare hands'."

She said her eldest son told her a staff member took Elijah from the playground and told him to empty the contents of a toilet he had clogged - including faeces - into a bucket without any gloves.

She was told Elijah was then taken to the office and made to wait with his nose against the wall for hours.

"I was horrified. At first I didn't know if it was real."

Her husband Bryn* went to the school the next morning and asked to see the principal, who agreed to speak with him and Elijah.

RNZ has heard a recording of what the parents said was part of the meeting.

In the recording, a child's voice can be heard as both the principal and Elijah's father raise their voices.

A man - who Bryn said was the principal - said the staff member initially believed the toilet was blocked with toilet paper, but not faeces.

"[The principal] started screaming at my son about how it was his fault and if he hadn't [clogged the toilet] we wouldn't be in this position," Megan said.

The mother said after going back and forth about whether the staff members' actions were appropriate, the principal suggested her husband take their child to another school.

They had since removed both their children from the school.

Megan said the school did not contact her or her husband after the incident.

She said Elijah had been on a waiting list for a formal autism and ADHD evaluation for more than a year.

While her son struggled with concentrating, she described him as "the nicest child".

She wanted an apology from the school and for the principal and the staff member involved to be stood down.

"I want them to publicly admit that they messed up and that it did happen."

Paengaroa School did not respond to specific questions from RNZ about the parents' account of what happened.

But in a statement, it said it was aware of "concerns raised following an incident at the school last week".

"The school is taking the matter very seriously. We are seeking advice to ensure we follow a thorough process to carefully investigate the situation.

"For the privacy of those involved and to protect the integrity of the investigation, the school is not able to provide further details at this stage."

Ministry of Education Bay of Plenty Waiariki director Tui Rolleston confirmed the ministry had received a complaint about the matter and were in contact with the school.

"We understand this has been a difficult situation for the family. The school has met with the parents and is responding to the concerns raised in line with its responsibilities, and we're also working with the school to provide additional support for this student.

"As this concerns a child, we won't be commenting further."

World.title: Racehorse So You Are dies of colic 13 days after running in Melbourne Cup
World.content:
Australian racehorse So You Are has died from a "severe bout of colic", just 13 days after finishing eighth in the Melbourne Cup.

Trainer Bjorn Baker announced today that the five-year-old had been rushed to hospital with colic, which refers to abdominal pain in horses.

"We are devastated to share the news that So You Are has died following a severe bout of colic," the statement said.

"He had been enjoying a well-earned spell when he was found showing signs of colic this morning. He was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment, but sadly could not be saved.

"Beyond his achievements on the track, So You Are was a much-loved horse, and his loss will be deeply felt by everyone who knew and cared for him."

So You Are was trained by Baker at Warwick Farm in Sydney, and had a terrific spring where he won four times, including a trio of Group 3 races at Rosehill, Randwick and Bendigo.

He was owned by Stuart Ramsey, a long-time breeder and racehorse owner, and his wife Trish.

So You Are ran in the Melbourne Cup 13 days ago, finishing eighth in a race won by Point of Law.

So You Are was running second in the home straight with about 600 metres left in the race, leading the chase for long-time leader Royal Supremacy.

World.title: NRL reveals 2027 Magic Round matches, Broncos headline Thursday clash
World.content:
The NRL will bank on the crowd-pulling status of a Brisbane and Penrith clash to quell their Thursday night fears and keep all of Magic Round at Lang Park in 2027.

Head office has today confirmed all nine matches for next year's Lang Park extravaganza, as one of several components of the draw to be released this week.

Penrith and Brisbane will kick off the round on May 13, before a Friday night showdown between the Sydney Roosters and Dolphins the following evening.

2027 Magic Round matches all times in AEST Thursday, May 13 Penrith Panthers vs Brisbane Broncos, 7:50pm Friday, May 14 Wests Tigers vs Canberra Raiders, 6pm

Sydney Roosters vs Dolphins, 8pm Saturday, May 15 Perth Bears vs Parramatta Eels, 3pm

South Sydney Rabbitohs vs North Queensland Cowboys, 5:30pm

Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks vs Melbourne Storm, 7:35pm Sunday, May 16 Gold Coast Titans vs Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles, 2pm

New Zealand Warriors vs St George Illawarra Dragons, 4:05pm

Canterbury Bankstown Bulldogs v Newcastle Knights, 6:15pm

The NRL's expansion to 18 teams had threatened to cause a scheduling headache next year, as will the league's eventual growth to 20 sides as soon as 2029.

For now, though, head office has found a solution, with women's Origin to move to Townsville and be played on the Wednesday night.

The other issue for the NRL will be crowds, given most fans have previously travelled on the Friday.

For the NRL's first Magic Round in 2019, a crowd of only 17,113 attended the Thursday night between Gold Coast and Cronulla.

That prompted the weekend to be reconfigured when it returned after a COVID break in 2021, with all games played on Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

But the NRL will rely on the fact that the Panthers-Broncos clash would go close to selling out Lang Park even outside of Magic Round.

In the weekend's other games, Wests Tigers will play Canberra in the Friday 6pm match-up, before the preliminary final repeat between the Roosters and Dolphins.

Cronulla's clash with Melbourne is the drawcard match on the Saturday night, with Perth to play Parramatta and South Sydney facing North Queensland beforehand.

Gold Coast will play Manly in the first Sunday game, and the Warriors will be the nominal home team against St George Illawarra in the 4pm time slot.

Canterbury and grand finalists Newcastle will close out the round on the Sunday night.

Meanwhile, the move of women's Origin to Townsville comes after the series opener had found a home at Lang Park, pulling in crowds of more than 20,000 for the past three years.

The last match played in Townsville, in 2024, drew a crowd of 22,819.

AAP

World.title: Can non-alcoholic beer really be used as a sports drink for athletes?
World.content:
It seems like a dream come true considering the West's long-standing love affair with beer, but is non-alcoholic beer a genuine contender as a sports drink for rehydration?

The concept first hit the mainstream in 2018 when, during the Pyeongchang Winter Olympics, the German team was drinking a label that had donated 3,500 litres to the athletes' village.

One of the skiers even told the BBC that the alcohol-free wheat beer was "extremely healthy" and, because it was isotonic, added that it was "good for us sports guys".

Since then, a variety of brands have entered the market, with many adding electrolytes — or minerals that have a positive or negative charge when dissolved and help maintain cellular fluid balance — and marketing them as sports beers.

But is there any truth to the concept, or is it simply a marketing gimmick launched off society's enduring taste for a fermented drink created with malt, hops and yeast?

Is it true?

"It's only good because it contains water, which is good for rehydration," said Associate Professor Evangeline Mantzioris, Adelaide University Bachelor of Human Nutrition program leader.

Evangeline Mantzioris says non-alcoholic beer is essentially a soft drink and is hydrating. (ABC News)

She said that while regular beer above 4 per cent alcohol content was dehydrating due to its diuretic properties — which increase urine production to flush extra salt and water from the body — low-alcohol beer did have some hydrating qualities.

"But generally, because of the health perspective, we wouldn't recommend it because alcohol is deemed as a known carcinogen," Dr Mantzioris said.

The rise of non-alcoholic beer overcomes that, however, particularly as modern techniques allow for increasingly well-crafted beverages that are drawing closer to their alcoholic cousins in taste and profile.

"It's essentially a soft drink because it doesn't have alcohol in it, right? So it will be hydrating," Dr Mantzioris said.

"But if this non-alcohol beer product gets athletes, and I'm thinking local footy clubs, to drink more and not get drunk … and it's a good-tasting thing, then it's good from that perspective."

What's in it?

Less clear, however, is the benefits non-alcoholic beer can offer beyond its basic hydrating qualities.

"It's got a little bit of carbohydrate in it," Dr Mantzioris said.

"One brand looks like it's 1.9 grams of carbs per 100 millimetres. That's too low for making any reasonable difference for an athlete to refuel and restock on carbohydrate in their body. Generally, we look at about 6 to 8 per cent.

"It also has selected electrolytes added, and those electrolytes aren't a whole lot different to what you find in normal beer.

"For most Australians, we don't need extra sodium in their diet. We're well above our requirements for sodium."

The secret to making good alcohol-free wine and beer The popularity of low- and no-alcohol beer and wine is booming, with the majority produced in Australia.

She said it also had a "little bit of magnesium in it and a little bit of potassium".

"Are they useful amounts?" Dr Mantzioris said.

"Well, yeah, but it wouldn't make a big difference to most people because they would get most of that stuff through eating food."

Then there were polyphenols, an antioxidant found in beer, particularly those of a darker variety.

"They're found in virtually every plant food, so fruit, vegetables, grains, and they can act as antioxidants in your body, so they can reduce the oxidative stress that's occurred following exercise," Dr Mantzioris said

"Just breathing and living causes oxidation in your body."

This is when reactive molecules, or free radicals, react with vital cellular components and can cause damage to DNA and proteins.

"But we're not going to promote alcohol as a way of getting polyphenols into people," Dr Mantzioris said.

Milk an effective option

The South Australian Sports Institute's sports dietician Olive Warnes said their preferred option for athletes was water supplemented with electrolytes to help replace fluids and essential minerals lost through exercise.

Milk is considered an excellent choice for refuelling as it provides carbohydrates, protein and electrolytes. (Flickr: steves71)

"When selecting protein or carbohydrate recovery drinks, athletes should prioritise products that have been batch tested," she said.

"Milk is another effective recovery option that is often overlooked.

" It naturally provides carbohydrates, protein and electrolytes, making it an excellent choice for refuelling, muscle repair and rehydration following exercise. "

In fact, milk is near the top of the Beverage Rehydration Index (BRI), second only to the oral rehydration solutions people can buy from chemists.

The BRI was established following a study led sport and exercise nutrition professor Ronald J Maughan from Loughborough University, Scotland.

It aimed to identify beverages that promoted longer-term fluid retention, and investigated the effects of 13 different commonly consumed drinks on urine output and fluid balance when ingested in an euhydrated state (a state of balanced hydration).

The National Insitute of Health's Beverage Rehydration Index is often referred to by dieticians. (X: @Jeukendrup)

At the top of the list behind oral rehydration solutions was skimmed milk, followed by whole milk and orange juice — all of which the body retained longer than still water, which was the control fluid in the study.

The body also retained cola and tea marginally longer than still water, and sparkling water and sports drinks marginally less.

Beer and then coffee were significantly lower than water on the BRI.

Rehydration is rehydration

Dr Mantizioris said athletes requiring hydration after exertion generally picked beverages above the BRI's rate of still water.

"Rehydration for an athlete is incredibly important, both from the perspective of performance and being well-hydrated during their training or performance, and also for their health," she said.

Evangeline Mantziroris holds the SANFL Premiership cup. (Supplied: Evangeline Mantzioris)

"So essentially, when you're talking to an athlete, you pick the drink that they are most likely to drink, irrespective of what the beverage hydration index might say.

"If you want to drink a cup of tea and that is what will make you drink lots of water, go for it, or if your thing is cola, go for it, because hydration is just so important for an athlete."

World.title: Fowler headlines big-name Matildas returns for Colombia friendlies
World.content:
Mary Fowler and Kyra Cooney-Cross will return to the Matildas for upcoming friendlies against Colombia in Australia.

Coach Joe Montemurro will also welcome back Alanna Kennedy and Teagan Micah from injury and concussion respectively.

Manchester City gun Fowler withdrew from last month's friendlies against Germany and Haiti for personal reasons.

Latest Matildas squad Alexia Apostolakis, Mackenzie Arnold (GK), Ellie Carpenter, Steph Catley, Kyra Cooney-Cross, Caitlin Foord, Mary Fowler, Daniela Galic, Charli Grant, Winonah Heatley, Kahli Johnson, Alanna Kennedy, Sam Kerr, Chloe Lincoln (GK), Leticia McKenna, Teagan Micah (GK), Alana Murphy, Courtney Nevin, Hayley Raso, Amy Sayer, Remy Siemsen, Kaitlyn Torpey, Tori Tumeth, Emily van Egmond, Clare Wheeler, Tameka Yallop

The 23-year-old returned to Australia and spent time with partner, rugby league star Nathan Cleary, after his horror lower-leg injury.

Cooney-Cross has not played for Australia since March's Asian Cup.

Her mother, Jessica, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive form of bile-duct cancer in January and died in July.

Cooney-Cross took time away from football then returned to playing at Arsenal in August, but was given time to be ready to rejoin the Matildas.

Fowler and Cooney-Cross will both be crucial to Australia's Women's World Cup hopes next year, and Montemurro will relish being able to use them for the first time in months.

Goalkeeper Micah missed the Asian Cup due to her latest concussion setback and has not played since.

Tameka Yallop is back in the Matildas squad for the first time since missing the Asian Cup with a hamstring injury. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Veteran Tameka Yallop has been recalled for the first time since missing the Asian Cup with a hamstring injury.

Forward Kahli Johnson (Calgary Wild FC) has also been recalled.

Striker Holly McNamara is sidelined until about Christmas with a hamstring injury.

The games in Canberra on November 28 and Geelong on December 2 are Australia's last before the Women's World Cup draw on December 11.

Australia is ranked world number 15 and needs good results against Colombia (number 19) to consolidate a ranking inside the top 16 and secure a place in Pot Two of the draw.

AAP

World.title: Walsh 'disappointed' after seeing Aussie fans cheering against Kangaroos
World.content:
Reece Walsh has taken aim at Australia "supporters" who wanted the team to lose the World Cup final, while launching an impassioned defence of the Kangaroos team culture.

The 24-year-old starred in the 32-12 final win over New Zealand at Lang Park on Sunday. In the dressing sheds former skipper Darren Lockyer presented him with the Harry Sunderland Medal, judged by Australia selectors and given to the team's best player of the tournament.

He was also presented with the Kangaroos players' player award for the World Cup by current number six Cameron Munster, who won it during last year's Ashes tour.

Walsh, who takes a keen interest in social media, has been irked by those who downplay Australia's "culture" as compared to other nations at the World Cup.

"I can see the culture and I can feel it," he said.

"I have seen it multiple times on social media, people disrespecting us and saying, 'I hope Australia loses just to make the game better.' No. If you are an Aussie you need to support and be proud of that.

"You would never see … a Tongan fan saying, 'I hope Tonga loses.' Social media is a big thing and I was a little bit disappointed in seeing some people come out in Australia and saying they didn't want to see us win.

"That was why I got so emotional [during the national anthem], seeing my family and knowing how much they care and how much Aussies care.

" I think that is an area we can get a lot better at … getting behind each other. "

Walsh said there were those outside the team's four walls that underplayed how much the players cared about their country and the badge they wore. He highlighted team captain Isaah Yeo as a great example.

"Isaah Yeo has had a torn pec and he has played five weeks of extra football for this badge, for this team, for us boys, for this country. That's culture," Walsh said.

"We love this country. We love winning. Culture is not just about cheering. It is about winning, being connected and turning up for your mate."

Walsh said the Australian team had players of other heritages, including himself and prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, who still united for the Kangaroos.

Kangaroos star Tino Fa'asuamaleaui (centre) represents Australia despite his Samoan heritage. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"Tino is of Samoan heritage and I know he is so proud of that. He sat us down two weeks and … said how much he loves the jersey and wants to go out here and do Australia proud and us proud," Walsh said.

"I am the same. I am a proud Maori too. My mum is from there. I know when I pull on this jersey how much it means to me and how much my family care.

"My old man raised five kids as a single dad. That is what he done for me to be able to represent my old man and our last name and wear [the jersey] with pride."

Walsh did not have his best year at Brisbane but finished with a bang and justified his Kangaroos selection.

"It has been a tough year for myself and there were probably a lot of people that thought and said I shouldn't be here," he said.

"Having the support of the boys and the coaching staff and everyone behind me gave me the strength and confidence to go out there and do my job. The only thing that matters is winning and that is what we did."

AAP

World.title: Renshaw concerned about Khawaja's wellbeing amid sandpaper controversy
World.content:
Australian batter Matt Renshaw has checked in on the wellbeing of Usman Khawaja after Pat Cummins's stinging press conference rebuke of his ball tampering claims.

Cummins labelled some of the claims Khawaja made in his book, Sabr, "utter nonsense" in a 69-minute minute presser on Friday morning, casting some doubt on the pair's friendship moving forward.

Renshaw, who is also friends with Khawaja, reminded everyone of the human side of the ongoing saga after scoring 63 in Australia's 135-run loss to England in the second ODI on Sunday night in Adelaide.

"I have spoken to Usman, just checking in on him," Renshaw said.

"Haven't really spoken too much about what's going on, just sort of checking on him as a human — obviously there's a lot going on.

"I wasn't there in Cape Town when it happened so I have got no idea what was going on, so tough for me to comment on that.

"But yeah, I think everyone as humans, obviously everything is going on, but I think the biggest thing is making sure everyone's OK."

Khawaja has received support from David Warner on multiple occasions, while Chadd Sayers, who played one Test on the 2018 South Africa tour, also backed him on Sunday prior to the one day clash.

Despite the ongoing accounts from Khawaja, Warner and Sayers, Cricket Australia at this stage remains unwilling to re-open its investigation into the scandal.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Worrying signs as Wallabies leave it too late to fire in Scotland defeat
World.content:
It might be unfair to be overly critical about the Wallabies' latest defeat, this time to Scotland at Murrayfield.

Its narrow nature, 15-12, is one aspect.

The conditions too have to be considered.

Scotland beat Wallabies in desperate, dour Murrayfield arm-wrestle The Wallabies fall to a fourth straight defeat as Scotland claims a 15-12 victory in a dour display at Murrayfield.

Dank and grey, the lingering firework smoke above the playing surface was reminiscent of some primordial Celtic realm.

This was an afternoon of such monochrome dreariness that even Scotland couldn't muster much of their usual attacking verve.

It was far removed from the bright lights of Friday night in Paris or Saturday afternoon in Cardiff.

Opposing skippers Rory Darge and Harry Wilson both referred to the game as descending into an arm-wrestle, though at times the contest we witnessed was so bad that calling it as such would almost be cruel to practitioners of that maligned pastime.

But then again, autumnal Scottish afternoons are just not what the proponents of free-flowing, attacking rugby union had in mind as ideal conditions for their craft.

Les Kiss said as much to UK broadcaster ITV, describing the game as "turgid".

"I think [Gregor Townsend] and I both would have preferred some drier weather," he added.

Both teams struggled to hold the ball in cold and wet conditions. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Undoubtedly, the conditions were reflected in the Scottish play as the hosts produced a litany of errors, most of which were a by-product of a series of over-complicated running lines that looked perfect when drawn up in the dryness and warmth of the training rooms, but less so when countered by the freezing rain and fast-pressing Wallabies defence.

That defence is worth pointing out as a positive.

The Wallabies had conceded seven tries in each of their previous three games, letting 138 points be scored against them. Shipping just two against Scotland marked a huge improvement.

But neither side hit the attacking heights both are capable of — a familiar failing of this Wallabies team at present.

Where the Scots' limitations seemed a result of over complication, the Wallabies' attacking limits were self-imposed by the bland simplicity of their game plan.

Things started relatively well despite the tricky conditions.

Scotland barged up to the Wallabies line and spun the ball wide to an unmarked Matt Fagerson to open the scoring.

Matt Fagerson scored the opening try. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol)

The Wallabies went up the other end and hit back immediately, Harry Potter finishing a move started by Carter Gordon's driving surge.

This was what the Wallabies didn't have against England; the fly half taking charge, double-pumping the pass as he approached the line before releasing Jeremy Williams, Len Ikitau and finally Potter to score.

A solid move, well constructed, well finished.

It took the best part of an hour before we saw anything of the like again from the men in gold.

Between times, fans were subject to a dour attacking display whenever the Wallabies had the ball in hand, the visitors relentlessly forced to retreat back up field before either kicking the ball away or flat-out losing it.

One-out runners with no passing, no speed in the back line movement, no width, no use of the thrilling attacking talents at their disposal, no way through the walls of Scottish defenders.

One of the most desperate passages came with about a quarter of an hour remaining.

The Wallabies had forced a lineout just outside the Scotland 22, a rare attacking chance. But through 18 phases of bland hit ups with little to no imagination the Wallabies went backwards a handful of metres, and then lost the ball to a Scotland turnover.

A kind observation would have been that the Wallabies were being patient, taking their time to find an opening in a Scottish defence that had significantly tightened its leash.

A less kind one would be that it was clueless and uninventive, destined to fail.

The Wallabies struggled to make anything happen with the ball in hand. (AP Photo: Scott Heppell)

Neither side had anything like clean ball, a litany of errors plaguing the contest in the loose, with the chaotic breakdown simply adding to the confused display from both teams.

But the Wallabies showed they can attack when they want to, adding to the frustration of what had gone before.

Ben Donaldson came onto the field, shifting Gordon to centre, and immediately made an impact, passing wide and giving the visitors the impetus to attack.

With almost his first phase of play, Donaldson immediately looked to move the ball wide, moving laterally at pace to open the Scotland defence — perhaps running himself into a starters spot in Cardiff next week.

Later, Donaldson spun the ball wide to Williams, whose flick pass out the back of the hand released Jorgensen to scoot down the line and score.

As the clock ticked into the red, the ball was again spun wide, Tate McDermott and Harry Wilson releasing Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, almost a non-entity both this week and last in an attacking sense but finally running with the ball in hand.

Jorgensen and Tom Wright were both involved before the latter was bundled into touch, the gun-shy Wallabies now firing from the hip with alacrity.

Suaalii. Jorgensen. Wright. These names had barely been mentioned all game.

Tom Wright and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii were barely seen in an attacking sense. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol)

By the time they were, it was far too late.

Again, perhaps it's unfair to judge the Wallabies too harshly for a sour outing in which both teams struggled to rouse themselves from their mutual stupor.

So attention should shift to Wales, which now awaits inside the Principality Stadium next Sunday (AEDT).

The roof in Cardiff means "conditions" is not an excuse that can be laid down in case of another attacking no-show.

But Wales's defence may yet be just as stingy as it was against the All Blacks, where the Welsh made a stunning 346 tackles.

For reference, Scotland (154) and the Wallabies (194) combined to make 348 at Murrayfield.

The Wallabies have one more chance to prove they are moving in the right direction.

They would do well to find a way to unleash their attacking weapons before it's too late.

World.title: Scotland beat Wallabies in desperate, dour Murrayfield arm-wrestle
World.content:
The Wallabies have delivered another woeful display on their spring tour, falling to a 15-12 defeat against Scotland at Murrayfield.

The defeat was the Wallabies' fourth in a row and piles the pressure on new coach Les Kiss after another display of limited attacking rugby.

A dour contest never really ignited was always destined to be close, with both teams struggling to get their attacks working on a freezing Edinburgh afternoon.

"I thought there were some really nice attacking moments from us," Les Kiss said post-match.

"Our defence definitely turned up.

"Our physicality overall was right up, which was pleasing.

"A couple of moments, that try in the corner with the maul, probably a couple of discipline moments that gave them easy yards just put us on the back foot.

"Full of fight, that's for sure. But you want to win those ones."

In the sort of dank, drizzly conditions that a Scottish autumn is famous for, the match descended into a gruelling arm-wrestle.

With the pre-match fireworks still hovering above the playing field, Matt Fagerson opened the scoring for the hosts inside the opening 10 minute, finishing off a spell of dominant possession in the corner.

The Wallabies hit back straight away, Harry Potter contorting himself to reach over and finish a rare flowing move sparked by the returning Carter Gordon in midfield.

Harry Potter scored for the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Liam Chester)

That was the end of any real attacking impetus for the Wallabies for almost an hour though as the team fell into the habit of one-out hit ups and box kicks.

As the two sides grappled with close-contact battles, former Wallaby Jack Dempsey burrowed over to score, the last points before a 45-minute scoreless spell that stretched deep into the second half.

The Wallabies felt they had hit back just before half time when Ryan Canham dived over from a rolling maul, but it was bought back by the TMO for obstruction by Jeremy Williams.

"It was a tough one," Wilson said.

"They're really trying to crack down on that at the moment and that was probably a really big moment in the end, because 14-all at half time we might have had them there.

"We've got to be better at icing those big moments."

Former Wallaby Jack Dempsey scored for Scotland in the first half. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Neither side could get going in the second half, the Wallabies defence standing tall despite Billy Pollard sin binning just after the break.

A Russell penalty looked to have sealed the game for the Scots, before Max Jorgensen scored a brilliant try in the final minute, an attacking raid of such class it raised questions as to why there had been no go-forward before then.

The Wallabies even had one chance to win the game late when Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii made a line break and Tom Wright was freed down the right wing.

However, he was bundled into touch and the Scots held on.

The Wallabies next head to Cardiff to take on a Wales team buoyed by beating the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years.

Look back on how all the action unfolded from Murrayfield in our live blog.

Tech.title: Sony’s PlayStation 5 accessories are cheaper ahead of Black Friday
Tech.content:
Several retailers are offering discounts on PlayStation 5 games, including deep price cuts on recent console-exclusive hits like Marvel’s Wolverine , Ghost of Yotei , Saros , and hundreds more. We’ll cover a bunch of those in the coming days, but this post is focused on the great hardware discounts that are happening, including $20 off the stellar DualSense wireless controller and its many color schemes, as well as $30 off the customizable DualSense Edge . The big sale also extends to headsets , console covers , and even Sony’s 27-inch monitor that has a hook to charge your controller.

Sitting out from the discounts, at least for now, are new PlayStation 5 consoles. Tech.title: Trump says it ‘certainly isn’t a bad idea’ for Jensen Huang to return to Nvidia
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, Trump told reporters on Monday that he’s open to seeing Huang return and that he’s not certain that the woman Huang reportedly had an affair with was in fact a spy.

“I think having Jensen go back– a lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea.” Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang return as CEO, adding, “I threw out the name of Tim Cook, but I would say that Jensen’s reinstatement– I think he learned a big lesson, I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.” Trump has suggested Tim Cook step in as Nvidia’s CEO multiple times now.

When asked about reports that Alice Huang, one of the women Jensen Huang allegedly had an affair with, was a Chinese spy, the president repeatedly claimed he wasn’t sure if it were true. “I don’t know that she’s a spy at all, nobody’s proven that,” Trump said.

Trump also denied that Marco Rubio told him Alice Huang was a spy. “Usually what happens with that is that, any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” Trump said. “I don’t know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don’t. I don’t know that, you know, Jensen obviously has two things going. He has a family situation, which is a rough deal, and what he wants to do is sell chips.”

Trump went on to say national security “was not put at risk” by his close relationship with Jensen Huang.
