Tech.title: Mercedes’ New Point-to-Point Driver Assist Helped Me Overcome My Fear of Driving
Tech.content:
“This can go one of two ways,” I think as I slide behind the wheel. “Either this makes city driving a lot less intimidating, or I regret ever giving it a try.”

As someone who rarely drives – and doesn’t even own a car – in San Francisco, I was eager to see whether Mercedes-Benz’s new point-to-point driving assistance system could ease my anxiety as I navigated the city’s notoriously challenging streets. How would it handle the many four-way stops, steep inclines, pedestrians, cyclists and double-parked robotaxis?

After an hour of weaving through these complex environments, I walked away feeling more at ease than when I started. That’s largely because I barely had to lift a finger – or a foot.

I got an early opportunity to try Mercedes-Benz’s new point-to-point driver assistance system, MB.Drive Assist Pro, which will roll out to select California customers in December before expanding to the rest of the US next year. The Level 2 system handles functions like steering, braking and acceleration, but the driver has to be attentive and ready to take over at any moment. However, I hardly ever needed to.

As I made my way through San Francisco’s Financial District, Marina and North Beach in a Mercedes-Benz GLC 400, I repeatedly had to resist the urge to tap the brakes, press the accelerator or grab the steering wheel out of instinct. But within minutes, my apprehension had given way to awe at just how much the system could handle and how little I needed to do. With MB.Drive Assist Pro engaged, I watched as the vehicle obeyed traffic signals, yielded the right of way and even maneuvered around stalled robotaxis. Occasionally, I had to briefly place my hands on the wheel so it would know I was paying attention, but I didn’t find it bothersome at all.

There were moments when I had to take control. At one intersection, a pedestrian was preparing to cross, but the system persisted in making a right turn. (The death glare I got was a sign I needed to take over and tap the brakes.) Further down the road, I grabbed the wheel to steer around a parked truck unloading cargo. Other times, my patience was tested as the car came to a complete stop at every stop sign (rolling stops are my forte, sorry not sorry). To its credit, though, the vehicle subtly asserted itself at four-way stops by inching forward as we waited for our turn.

Bringing partial automation to more drivers

Unlike Level 4 robotaxi services like Waymo and Zoox, Level 2 systems like MB.Drive Assist Pro aren’t fully autonomous, but can take some of the stress out of everyday driving, particularly in dense urban environments.

Tesla’s so-called Full Self-Driving (Supervised) offers similar capabilities, navigating city streets, maneuvering around obstacles, making turns, changing lanes and responding to traffic signals, while still requiring driver supervision. Other systems like GM’s Super Cruise, Ford BlueCruise and BMW Highway Assistant offer hands-free driving on compatible roads, but are primarily designed for use on highways rather than complex city streets.

For someone who doesn’t typically drive, I spent a lot of time behind the wheel of various Mercedes-Benz vehicles for these demos, which included parking and braking features. Mercedes

A feature like MB.Drive Assist Pro could not only bring increasingly advanced driver assistance technology to more car owners but also lay the groundwork for a future in which autonomous driving becomes more common in personally owned vehicles.

“We’ve clearly shown that the autonomous driving sector is an area that we will continue to develop and [be] involved in, and being one of the first companies to offer a system like you guys experienced today shows that we’re committed to be in that space and continue to grow,” Jason Hoff, CEO of Mercedes-Benz North America, said during a reporter roundtable following the demos.

Point-to-point driver assistance tech and availability

MB.Drive Assist Pro uses 27 sensing components, including 10 cameras, five radar sensors and 12 ultrasonic sensors scattered throughout the vehicle. This hardware is currently available on certain 2027 Mercedes vehicles, including CLA Electric, GLE, GLS and S-Class cars. Starting with 2028 models, the company says more of its US passenger vehicles will be equipped to support the new feature.

Nvidia’s Alpamayo Stack powers the vehicle’s autonomous driving capabilities, using AI to interpret complex road scenarios and reason through driving decisions. It works alongside Nvidia’s Halos safety tech, including Halos OS, which provides safety guardrails to help ensure the vehicle follows the rules of the road, like stopping at a red light or waiting for an intersection to clear before crossing.

With Level 2 driving, there’s a mental hurdle that drivers like me will need to overcome and a certain degree of control we’ll have to relinquish to let the system do its thing. For instance, I sometimes found myself getting nervous as the car confidently moved into the oncoming lane to pass a stalled vehicle, even with approaching traffic. I was assured by the Mercedes team that the system can determine whether there’s enough room to safely squeeze through and otherwise wouldn’t attempt the move. Still, it’s not something I’d personally feel comfortable doing if I were in full control.

Dozens of cameras and sensors throughout the vehicle help make Level 2 autonomy possible. Mercedes-Benz

Some of this simply comes down to a learning curve. Over the hour I spent behind the wheel, I found myself feeling less anxious and more trusting of the system. I’d imagine that confidence would only grow with repeated use of MB.Drive Assist Pro, so drivers can feel less apprehensive about the car taking the lead, even if some decisions still occasionally give them pause.

MB.Drive Assist Pro will be available nationwide starting next year, with one-month, one-year and three-year subscription options. It’ll come to eligible Mercedes-Benz models including the 2026 CLA electric sedan, 2027 CLA sedan, 2027 GLC electric SUV, 2027 GLE SUV and coupe, 2027 GLS SUV and 2027 S-Class sedan. The system launched in China alongside the new CLA in late 2025. The upcoming rollout will bring it to the US and Germany as well.

Customers can factory-order MB.Drive Assist Pro, or purchase it digitally through the Mercedes-Benz store; it will be delivered as an over-the-air update. Mercedes hasn’t yet shared pricing.

Hands-free driving on highways

Mercedes is also bringing hands-free highway driving to the US in spring 2027. I had the chance to try out that tech early as well, which proved to be an even bigger test of my trust.

As I drove from Alameda, across the Bay from San Francisco, onto Interstate 880 in a GLS 580, I took a deep breath and prepared to hand over some control to the car. After pressing the Resume button on the steering wheel (or adjusting the cruise control speed), I could activate Hands-Free Highway Assist. The feature comes with a few restrictions: you have to be on a freeway, not in an exit lane and away from construction zones or particularly sharp curves. You also can’t be driving faster than 85 mph.

Hands-Free Highway Assist lets you kick back a bit as the vehicle drives, slowing down and speeding up with traffic. A capability called Proactive Lane Change Assist can automatically switch lanes to overtake a slower vehicle or approach an upcoming exit based on the navigation route.

Hands-Free Highway Assist can make long journeys less tiring by handling tasks like lane changes while following the flow of traffic. Mercedes-Benz

As with MB.Drive Assist Pro, you have to watch the road and be ready to take over at any time while using Hands-Free Highway Assist. Given the high stakes and high speeds, I wasn’t as hands-off with the highway driving feature as I was in the urban environment. Driving on the highway already feels nerve-wracking to me even when I’m in full control, so I couldn’t quite overcome the mental hurdle of letting go, physically and metaphorically, for more than about a minute at a time. I’d activate the feature, panic, then reactivate it. (Clearly, I’m a huge thrill seeker.)

One key hurdle is that it can be difficult to know when Hands-Free Highway Assist has been activated. An icon appears on the dashboard showing a green steering wheel with gray hands and two As on each side when the feature is available. Those hands will disappear when the feature is active, leaving only the green steering wheel and As. The icon turns red when you need to take over. Still, it was a little tricky to tell when the feature had correctly been enabled and when I hadn’t yet met all the requirements. Again, part of this is the learning curve, but it’s a big lesson to learn at 65 mph.

If you see this alert, you’ll know it’s time to take over. Mercedes-Benz

Still, when I was brave enough to activate the feature, it was impressive to witness the vehicle smoothly weaving across lanes on its own and following the flow of traffic, especially when I had the chance to try it again later in the afternoon on the S 580E. It seems like a handy capability that can make long-haul journeys and daily commutes a little less miserable.

Hands-Free Highway Assist will be available in the US in the spring, and pricing has yet to be determined. An early access program will give select California customers the chance to access the feature next month, alongside MB.Drive Assist Pro. Hands-Free Highway Assist will be on vehicles that support MB.OS (Mercedes’ in-house operating system) as part of the MB.Drive Assist offering, which already includes Steering Assist, Lane Change Assist and Proactive Lane Change Assist. The new feature will arrive via an over-the-air update.

After a day of stepping outside my comfort zone in more ways than one, it was fascinating to get a glimpse of where automotive technology is headed – and how it could make everyday drives, even the more stressful ones, feel a little less daunting. But for now, I hopped into an Uber and returned to my usual routine of avoiding the driver’s seat.

Tech.title: Apple Launches New App to Study How People Use AI for Health
Tech.content:
Since 2019, when Apple first launched its Research app, the company has partnered with medical universities and institutions to run a range of health studies on hearing, heart health and movement, women’s health and, most recently, the Apple Health Study, which covers a wide variety of health areas.

On Sunday, Apple launched its latest study, and it comes with its own app: the Apple Health AI Study.

During a press briefing, Apple said the study aims to understand how people interact with conversational health AI tools. To do so, it will examine comprehension, response quality, the drivers of user trust and everyday health actions.

More from CNET

The goal? To inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for both Apple and the industry and to explore how health AI might help people prepare for doctor’s visits. Key questions the study aims to address include: Do users understand the information provided by health AI? Do they trust it? Is it helpful?

This is particularly relevant considering that one in three US adults use AI chatbots for health information.

Study data will not be used to train AI models, but it may inform Apple’s feature development.

Apple’s study partner

To facilitate the study, Apple is partnering with OpenEvidence, an AI platform designed specifically for doctors. It generates answers using medical information from these partners: The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, National Comprehensive Cancer Network, Nature and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.

The Apple Health AI Usage Study combines an Apple-designed research experience with OpenEvidence’s AI technology. Apple

In the dedicated app, study participants can ask the AI their text-based health questions and then see answers with linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations. They can also choose to share their HealthKit data, including sleep, lab results, activity and resting heart rate, for more personalized answers.

HealthKit is Apple’s hub for health and fitness data collected on the iPhone and Apple Watch.

Who’s eligible?

The Apple Health AI Usage Study is open to 200,000 participants. You must be in the US and age 21 or older to participate. An Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later is also required.

Why an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone? According to Apple, the study app requires the processing capabilities of those iPhones, and it uses on-device Apple Foundation Models that are part of Apple Intelligence. These models provide access to any large language model. For example, as part of the study, these models are used to classify question categories.

What’s required?

Each participant is asked to participate for up to 12 months. During this time, they can ask questions about general health, specific symptoms, recovery from a procedure and their own uploaded health data, as examples.

After each response, participants will rate the answer and describe what went well and what could be improved. Apple

In addition to a baseline survey, participants will receive monthly surveys and additional surveys specific to preparing for doctor’s visits.

Participants will also be prompted to check in with the app. For instance, if you have a paired Apple Watch, you will receive notifications to check in, along with suggested topics to explore.

If there is a complete lack of participation, a participant may potentially be removed from the study.

After the doctor’s visit, there will be surveys to see how things went and whether the tools provided to prepare for the visit were helpful. Apple

Study privacy

After downloading the Apple Health AI Study app, participants must complete a mandatory onboarding process that includes informed consent. They will also be asked to share their demographic information, such as race, age and education level, which will be used to explore how these factors may affect their preferences and communication needs. Then, they can start asking the AI questions.

The iPhone first processes questions using tools designed to remove details that could identify participants. They then go to a secure cloud-based study environment managed by a third-party study support contractor called UST Global, where queries are delinked from individual participant IDs and screened using tools designed to further remove any remaining personal details. Lastly, this info is sent to OpenEvidence, where answers are generated using supporting reference materials.

OpenEvidence will delete both question and response data within 24 hours.

A small group of Apple researchers will have access to coded versions of survey responses, separated from personally identifiable information, summaries of conversations and categories of the most common conversation types.

Within the study app, there are also safety guardrails that detect concerning questions and respond by suggesting that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed.

There is no live monitoring, and study staff won’t contact participants if any questions related to self-harm are asked.

It’s also up to the participant whether they share any HealthKit metrics. They will first have to choose to upload their clinical health records to Apple’s Health app, and then separately choose to share those records from the Health app to the new Apple Health AI Study app.

Availability

The Apple Health AI Study app is now available in the App Store. As of now, there is no set publication date for the study.

Tech.title: Make iOS 27 Less Glassy and Siri Less Clingy With These Settings
Tech.content:
The Liquid Glass setting in Display & Brightness lets you trade some of the translucent effect for a more solid look. Patrick Holland/CNET

Liquid Glass, Apple’s translucent design language, is front and center in iOS 27, with menus and controls that let your wallpaper and app content show through. If the see-through look makes text harder to read or simply isn’t your taste, a setting in Display & Brightness can tone it down further for you.

That’s one of five iOS 27 defaults worth revisiting, along with how long Siri keeps your conversations, whether those conversations sync across devices, when subtitles appear on videos and how much Siri learns from individual apps. Each one takes a few taps to change, but it isn’t too difficult to do so. We’ve outlined how to do so in this article.



More from CNET

Make Liquid Glass easier to read

Apple introduced Liquid Glass with iOS 26, giving menus, buttons, notifications and other interface elements a translucent appearance. Not everyone was a fan of the new design, and with iOS 27, you now get more control over exactly how transparent the interface looks.

Go to Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass. Drag the slider to the right to add more tint and opacity, making buttons and text easier to distinguish from whatever is behind them. Moving it left makes the interface more transparent.

If the most opaque setting still isn’t enough, go to Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size and turn on Reduce Transparency. This makes translucent backgrounds more solid across iOS, although it overrides the regular Liquid Glass appearance controls.

More tint makes Liquid Glass easier to read. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

Stop Siri from keeping your conversations forever

The new Siri AI works similarly t ChatGPT or Claude in iOS 27. It now comes complete with a dedicated app where you can revisit previous conversations. Those chats sync through iCloud so you can start a conversation on your iPhone and continue it on another Apple device, such as your Mac.

By default, iOS 27 keeps those conversations forever, but there is a way to automatically get rid of older conversations if you don’t want them piling up.

If you don’t need a permanent archive of everything you ask Siri, go to Settings > Siri > Keep Conversations and choose 30 Days or 1 Year. Selecting either option permanently deletes conversations beyond that timeframe.

Siri keeps your conversations forever unless you choose a shorter limit. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

While you’re there, tap Opens To and select A New Conversation if you want the Siri app to open with a blank chat instead of showing your recent conversations every time.

Siri AI requires an iPhone 15 Pro or 15 Pro Max, iPhone Air or an iPhone 16 or later.

Turn off Write with Siri if you never use it

iOS 27 puts a new Write with Siri button above the keyboard in apps including Messages, Mail and Notes. You can ask Siri AI to draft something from scratch, proofread what you’ve written or rewrite it in a different tone.

The thing is, I’m not a big fan of the AI writing tools, so I don’t use them at all.

If you prefer writing without the extra AI prompt like I do, you can restrict Siri’s writing features by using Screen Time. Go to Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions, turn on the restriction and then tap Siri > Writing Assistance > Don’t Allow.

Screen Time lets you completely disable Siri’s writing tools. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

This disables access to the writing tools across your iPhone, rather than simply hiding the keyboard button, so only do this if you don’t use Apple’s AI writing tools at all. You can return to the same menu and choose Allow if you want them back. Apple documents the restriction under its Apple Intelligence Screen Time controls.

Stop Siri from activating so easily

Introduced back in iOS 17, Siri can now wake up when you simply say “Siri” instead of “Hey Siri.” The one-word command is convenient, but it also makes accidental activations more likely whenever someone says Siri’s name in a conversation or a video they’re watching online.

Siri goes absolutely bonkers whenever I’m in work meetings about Apple features.

To disable the feature, go to Settings > Siri > Talk to Siri. Choose “Hey Siri” instead of “Siri.”

Requiring “Hey Siri” can help prevent accidental activations. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

You’ll still be able to bring up Siri with your voice, but the extra word makes it less likely to wake up when you aren’t talking to it directly.

This isn’t exclusive to iOS 27, but it’s been annoying me more recently, so thought I would throw it in here, especially with Siri AI being the prominent feature on this update.

Stop subtitles from automatically appearing in videos

iOS 27 now automatically shows subtitles on videos in Photos, Safari and other apps that use Apple’s video player. I don’t mind captions when I need them, but they can take up too much of the video and distract me from whatever I’m watching.

They don’t appear randomly though. By default, iOS can turn them on when the video is in another language, when your iPhone is muted or when you skip back.

Whenever subtitles appear in Apple’s video player, you can tap the video to show the playback controls, tap the More Controls button, select Subtitles and choose Off.

You can disable subtitles per video. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

If iOS keeps turning them on because it thinks the video is in another language, go to Settings > Accessibility > Subtitles & Captioning. Under Automatic Subtitles, turn off When Languages Don’t Match.

The same menu also has switches for Show When Muted and Show on Skip Back, so you can disable those behaviors individually without turning off every automatic subtitle feature.

You can also disable each automatic subtitle trigger individually. Nelson Aguilar/CNET

Some apps and websites use their own video players, so you may need to find a separate CC or subtitles button instead.

For more on iOS 27, check out this article on the features it brings to your iPhone and how Siri AI helped one of my colleagues avoid eating diarrhea lettuce.

Tech.title: Xbox Game Pass Subscribers Can Play Football Manager, Warhammer Survivors and More Now
Tech.content:
On Tuesday, Nov. 3, Microsoft announced the games it’s adding to its Xbox Game Pass service in the first half of November. However, Rockstar Games is preparing to release Grand Theft Auto 6 on Nov. 19, so that game will likely take up a lot of your playtime from then on. That still leaves plenty of time to give these upcoming Game Pass titles a shot. I’m particularly excited about Warhammer Survivors. Xbox Game Pass, a CNET Editors’ Choice award winner, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 a month. More from CNET

Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School

Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Class is back in session in this puzzle game. This sequel to the award-winning Escape Academy brings you more puzzles to solve and a series-first open-world format. That makes the campus one big puzzle room filled with secrets, traps and more. If you get stuck, you can always chill with your friends and enjoy student life away from the classroom. Warhammer Survivors

Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Poncle, the creator of the indie hit Vampire Survivors, teamed up with Auroch Digital to let you bring your favorite Warhammer primarchs and champions into bullet-heaven action. Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Get ready for the most immersive matchday experience yet in the latest installment of the long-running Football Manager series. You’ll shape your club and define your team’s style, and you can get lost in the wider football universe thanks to smart news and events that mirror the drama of the football calendar.

In addition to the titles above, Xbox is also adding these games to Game Pass soon:

Tech.title: No, the World Won’t Shut Down on Nov. 17. What the Blackout Rumors Get Wrong
Tech.content:
As global conspiracy theories go, this is a juicy one.

On Tuesday, Nov. 17, at around 2:20 p.m. ET, the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Federal Communications Commission are planning a test of the Emergency Alert System. That’s when all hell is supposed to break loose. At least, that’s what you might believe if you only rely on social media.

Coming just days after an abrupt and disruptive government-ordered shutdown of air travel in the US and technical issues that caused an unwelcome outage of widely used Microsoft workplace software, the test will be happening in an atmosphere of heightened anxiety.

More from CNET

Videos across Facebook, Instagram and TikTok have floated the theory that this emergency test signals a catastrophe is coming, potentially stemming from a cyberattack or a digital disruption that could knock out electricity, internet and other services. Many have started scrambling to buy emergency supplies, pointing to the need for a 90-day stockpile of food, water, cash and essential medicines in case hackers wipe out bank accounts and shut down the web.

Similar rumors have spread globally, as the governments of France, the UK and Canada have put renewed attention on the importance of households being able to survive a potential weather-related crisis or technological disaster.

How extreme have the conspiracy theories gotten? Some have cited a 2023 Simpsons episode as proof, which referenced a massive Nov. 17 blackout in Lisa’s future, even though it didn’t mention a year.

For Gen Xers and Boomers, this panic could feel familiar. Leading up to the year 2000, there were fears that a potential computer-related disaster, known as Y2K, would cause widespread chaos and disruption, based on the belief that older digital systems couldn’t handle the calendar change. The new year ended with only minor glitches, thanks to a significant global effort to update computer systems to avoid the bug.

Before we delve into the suspicions, let’s start with a bit of debunking: CNET spoke with multiple experts in disaster preparedness and cyberattacks, who all cautioned against letting our guard down. But remember that no federal agency or institution has mentioned a blackout. Unless hackers decide to take advantage of the hysteria already generated, there’s no reason to think Nov. 17 is any riskier than any other date.

Richard Mariano, a protective intelligence expert at Kronus Intelligence, who spent nearly three decades with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, said that people share all sorts of things that get picked up and go viral. “Then it creates panic where panic is not necessary,” he said.

Mariano said too many people are spreading fear rather than seeking the truth. “On every one of these social media posts that is suspect or has some form of conspiratorial edge to them: source it, source it, source it.”

What is happening on Nov. 17?

Next week’s nationwide Emergency Alert System, or EAS, is similar to the public tests Americans have experienced since 1963, when the Emergency Broadcast System replaced an older radio-based warning system called CONELRAD. In 1997, the Emergency Broadcast System was replaced by the EAS, part of FEMA’s Integrated Public Alert and Warning System, which broadcasts emergency alerts to any wireless device in the country, including phones, radios and televisions. The system was designed for the president to communicate with US households within 10 minutes of a national emergency.

The Nov. 17 test will consist of a nationwide EAS message issued by FEMA, noting that no public action is required. The test will include standard alert tones to support accessibility for those who are deaf or hard of hearing and should last about a minute. This time around, wireless emergency alerts will not be triggered on mobile phones, so don’t expect a notification on your cellphone. After the alert, programming should resume as normal on TV, radio and other broadcast channels.

Many equate the emergency system with threats of nuclear war, but it could also be used to alert people to a major weather event, a national cyberattack or even AMBER alerts at the local level (without a presidential message). So it’s natural there might be some anxiety.

“With this event simulating an activation of an emergency notification system, it would be a logical next step to worry about what happens if something bad happens during that test,” said Robby Winchester, chief global professional services officer at SpecterOps, a Virginia-based security company,

But, all in all, these system tests are routine. Local stations conduct a weekly test, and federal law requires a nationwide EAS test every three years. In addition to helping people get used to responding to alerts, the tests also allow the government to identify potential technical or operational issues it needs to fix before an actual emergency alert.



FEMA has a backup date of Dec. 3 in case it can’t perform it on Nov. 17 — which could happen if the agency is dealing with a real emergency or if there are technical issues. Representatives from the FCC and FEMA did not respond to a request for comment.

Why are blackout rumors spreading?

Another factor that helped spark conspiracy theories was a Pentagon order requiring military bases to stock enough supplies for 90 days without outside support. Dubbed “Fortress America,” the initiative memo (PDF) was released in late September but got more attention as the November date approached.

The timing of that memo coincided with the UK launching a campaign on Oct. 22 called Be Ready, urging citizens to keep enough supplies (PDF) such as water, food, medical kits and pet products to last at least three days. Other countries, including Japan, Sweden and about a dozen more, are also urging citizens to prepare for emergencies.

Still, the blackout rumor isn’t solely driven by government communications. Heightened global instability over the past few months has also played a major role. Just in the last month, the Federal Aviation Administration called a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights; a major Microsoft Outlook outage kept millions of people from working; PHP vulnerabilities exposed websites to hacking; and cyberattacks have targeted supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe.

On the financial side, Nvidia’s CEO scandal led to a stock plunge and fears of an AI bust, while Paraguay just experienced a major digital bank collapse that froze millions of accounts. The ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine have sparked national security concerns, and floods in Nepal and fires in Indonesia demonstrate the increased dangers of climate change.

Though there’s never been a nationwide power outage in the US (several regional outages have been triggered by overloaded lines and software bugs), The New York Times reports that there’s still no comprehensive plan for what to do if the country goes completely dark.

All the online chatter surrounding Nov. 17 has raised concerns that warnings of a potential cyberattack might inadvertently trigger one.

Winchester said that even though there’s no specific information indicating an imminent crisis, “it is common for attackers to use current events of all types to help with achieving successful attacks.” The upside? If people are being spurred by government notices and their anxiety over global instability to prepare emergency supplies, it could actually help in the event of a real threat or disaster.

How to prepare for a disruption (on any date)

Regardless of whether you buy into the Nov. 17 conspiracy theories, it doesn’t hurt to have some supplies at the ready, which could be useful in the event of a digital disruption or weather event, even if it doesn’t involve nuclear weapons or hackers.

“We live in a world where there are many threats to our communities, our families and ourselves,” said Philip Farina, chief advisor for Risky Business and a federal law enforcement veteran. “Understanding the basics of self-reliance is important. Even preparing for a residential fire, which is very common, can help to save lives and protect us better.”

You don’t need to buy enough for 90 days off the grid (and most of us can’t afford that), but it’s recommended that families have at least three days’ worth of food and supplies. Some of the basics listed on Ready.gov’s Build a Kit page include:

A gallon of water per person per day

Several days’ worth of nonperishable food

A battery-powered or hand-crank radio to keep up with alerts

A flashlight

A first-aid kit

Batteries

A cellphone with a backup battery

Optional: Pet supplies, sleeping bags, cash, a fire extinguisher and books or games for children

While warnings from governments can spark panic and distrust, they can be beneficial at a time when we’re so reliant on the internet and cell service, which can be easily disrupted. Mariano said it’s worth being prepared in the “old-fashioned ways.”

Tech.title: Before Grand Theft Auto 6, CNET Staff Relive Their Favorite GTA Moments
Tech.content:
Rockstar Games is set to release Grand Theft Auto 6 on Thursday, Nov. 19, with both PlayStation and Xbox saying it’s the most preordered game in the history of either platform’s digital storefront. Given the 13 years of buildup and hype surrounding the game, that’s perhaps not surprising.

Though the series has evolved over time, Grand Theft Auto has been a pop culture behemoth since its inception in 1997, thanks to its biting satire, complex storylines and cinematic gameplay.

CJ and Big Smoke’s train chase

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is still my favorite GTA game. Rockstar Games

I have so many memories of playing Grand Theft Auto games at an age some might call “too young.” I’d go over a friend’s house and we’d boot up Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas on his PlayStation 2 and do whatever we wanted. It wasn’t until later that I found out there were missions to accomplish. And the funniest part for me was failing the mission Wrong Side of the Tracks in San Andreas. The character Big Smoke would utter the iconic line, “All we had to do was follow the damn train, CJ!” That line is funny, goofy and a good reminder that beneath the guns and violence, these are inherently silly, unserious games.

– Zachary McAuliffe, senior writer

Cockney coppers in London

Yes, this is a real Grand Theft Auto entry, a semisequel to the original Grand Theft Auto, released in 1999. Rockstar

I still quote the policemen from GTA London 1969 who yell, “Stop right there! Oi!” My friends and I in college would play it hotseat-style on my ancient laptop, and the cockney coppers became a meme (or “banter” as we called it back then, onions hanging from our belts as was the fashion).

– Nick Hide, managing copy editor

Video game dance moves

Ready to boogie the night away. Rockstar Games

I’ll say walking out of Blockbuster with a copy of GTA: Vice City as a teen whose most hard-core games before that were maybe Twisted Metal and Shivers 2 made me feel like a rock star. Tearing across the city, blowing red lights and running over onlookers was an absolute thrill, especially since my friends and I didn’t even have our learner’s permits yet.

The moment that sticks with me the most, however, was the infamous private dance scene in the Pole Position mission. I was playing over a long weekend at my best friend’s house, taking turns at the wheel, when we finally got to the scandalous part we’d read about on the internet. But instead of titillated, she and I were reduced to fits of giggles as the pixelated private dancer blockily gyrated on screen. And – sorry to our parents – after regaining composure, we immediately got to copying the unsultry choreo and teaching it to our friends. These moves would be busted out at the most opportune moments, even when we got old enough to go to real clubs. Sadly, it’s never earned us as much as a free drink.

– Faith Chihil, social producer

Postgraduation stress relief

Nothing says blowing off steam like blowing up a few cars. Rockstar

When GTA 5 came out in 2013, I had just graduated from college, moved back home with my parents and had no idea what to do with my life. So I waited several hours in line at my local GameStop, along with hundreds of other people, to be the first to get the game. I rushed back home and played for an irresponsible amount of time. There was something comforting about having an entire world to explore when I felt stuck in my own. Mostly, though, I made life worse for the people of Los Santos. My degree wasn’t opening many doors, but carjacking was.

– Nelson Aguilar, writer



Grand Theft Auto 5’s huge map

GTA 5 featured a huge map, but GTA 6 promises an even larger one. Rockstar Games

Forget the explosion-packed heists or the bullet-riddled car chases around city streets; my favorite GTA moment is when I discovered just how vast the GTA 5 map was and how much of it I could explore on foot. Or by helicopter.

GTA 5’s map was considered massive when it launched, and while I thoroughly enjoyed playing through the game’s actual storylines, I spent just as much time (if not more) simply seeing what’s out there beyond the expected play zones.

The GTA 6 map is apparently at least twice the size of that of GTA 5, and I’m super hyped to settle into hour after hour of serene exploration of a whole new landscape.

– Andrew Lanxon, editor at large

For more on GTA 6, here’s what we know about the game and how to prep your console for the massive file size.

Tech.title: Meet the Custom-Built Machine That Has Folded the iPhone Duo Nearly 500,000 Times
Tech.content:
We’re now nearly halfway through November, and CNET’s lab continues to work overtime testing Apple’s first folding phone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. We purchased this model of the Duo more than three weeks ago, and since then, its only job has been to bend and flatten.

How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? On Friday, Nov. 13, we passed 450,000 folds, and there was also an interesting change in the phone’s behavior.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. My team and I designed and built a proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

My team of engineers and testing experts has been watching the iPhone Duo open and close over and over for the past three weeks to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

The Samsung Galaxy Note 8 above, in the same machine, lasted more than 260,000 folds before we swapped it out for the Duo. Matthew Murray/CNET

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.
